arabic-numerals-and-the-spread-of-zero.context_blurb:
The ten digits used everywhere today, 0 through 9, travelled thousands of miles to reach Europe. Muslim scholars took them up as the caliphate spread east, refined them in Baghdad, and passed them west through Spain and Sicily, until an Italian merchant's son, Fibonacci, urged them on European bankers as far quicker than Roman numerals.

English calls them Arabic numerals, but the Arabs only carried the digits; they had learned them from India, where the symbols were first invented, so historians prefer the honest name Hindu-Arabic numerals. The chain runs from India, through the Arab world, to Europe, and the strange, powerful idea of zero travelled with it, making place value and long division possible.

Around 825 a Baghdad mathematician named al-Khwarizmi wrote a book explaining the Indian system of counting, and when it was translated into Latin his name became Algoritmi, which in time gave English the word algorithm, a step-by-step method for solving a problem.

archimedes-eureka-and-the-siege-of-syrac.context_blurb:
Archimedes of Syracuse, a Greek city on the island of Sicily, was the greatest mathematician of the ancient world and an inventor whose feats turned into legend within a few generations. He lived in the third century BC as a friend of the city's King Hiero, and he died when Rome captured Syracuse in 212 BC.

King Hiero suspected that a goldsmith had slipped cheap silver into a gold crown, and he wanted proof without melting it down. Archimedes saw that silver is bulkier than gold for the same weight, so he compared how much water the crown pushed out of a full tub with how much an equal weight of pure gold displaced; a cheat would spill more. The idea struck him as he lowered himself into a bath and watched the water rise, and the story says he sprang from the water and dashed through the city crying Eureka, Greek for I have found it. The tale comes from the Roman writer Vitruvius, two centuries later. A water-lifting machine still bears his name: the Archimedes screw, a spiral turning inside a tube that carries water uphill as you crank it, used to drain ships and to water fields, though the device may be older than he was.

He understood how a lever turns a small push into a huge lift, and he boasted that, given somewhere to stand, he could shift the Earth itself. To prove it to King Hiero, Archimedes sat on the shore working a system of compound pulleys and, with one gentle pull, set a fully loaded three-masted merchant ship gliding through the water as if it moved by itself. Hiero declared that Archimedes should be believed in everything he said.

In 214 BC, during Rome's war with Carthage, the general Marcellus attacked Syracuse by land and sea, and Archimedes turned the city walls into a weapon. His most feared machine, which the Romans called the Claw, swung an iron hook on a crane over the wall, seized a warship by the prow, lifted it clear of the water and then let it drop, capsizing it or smashing it on the rocks. The Romans grew so frightened, Plutarch says, that the mere sight of a rope or a stick of wood above the wall sent them running, crying that Archimedes was training another engine on them. A later legend, first told centuries after his death, claims he burned the Roman fleet by aiming mirrors to concentrate sunlight into a beam of fire, but no historian of his own era mentions any mirror, and serious scholars doubt it.

When Syracuse fell in 212 BC, a Roman soldier found the old man, about 75, so absorbed in a geometric figure he had traced in the sand that he refused to come along until it was done, and the angry soldier killed him. His most famous last words, telling the soldier not to disturb his circles, are a later paraphrase; the oldest surviving version has him beg the man not to disturb his drawing.

Archimedes prized pure mathematics above all his machines. To pin down pi, the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, he trapped the circle between two polygons of 96 sides, one drawn inside it and one outside, and proved that pi lies between 223/71 and 22/7, the best value in the world for nearly 400 years. The result he loved most showed that a sphere fits a cylinder in an exact ratio, two-thirds of its volume and two-thirds of its surface, and he asked for a sphere set within a cylinder to be carved on his tomb. About 137 years after his death, Cicero, serving in Sicily, went looking for the grave, and the people of Syracuse told him there was no such tomb; he found it anyway, choked in brambles near an old city gate, and knew it by that carving.

archimedes-of-syracuse.context_blurb:
Archimedes lived in Syracuse, a rich Greek city on Sicily, in the third century BC. A friend and relative of its kings, he was the greatest mathematical mind of the ancient world and a builder of astonishing machines, and the stories about him blurred into legend within a few generations.

Asked by King Hieron to find out, without melting it, whether a golden crown had been cut with silver, he saw the answer while climbing into a bath and watching the water rise, and the legend says he jumped out and sprinted naked through the streets crying Eureka, meaning that he had found it. The water he displaced measured the crown's exact volume, so he could compare it with pure gold. He is credited with the Archimedes screw, a spiral sealed in a tube that, as you crank it, scoops up pocket after pocket of water and lifts it uphill against gravity; the same design still drains the low-lying Nile delta.

Sure of the lever's power, he boasted that with a long enough lever and somewhere to stand he could move the Earth itself; Plutarch's version is bolder still: given another world to stand on, he could move this one. When the Roman fleet besieged Syracuse in 214 BC, his giant crane, the Claw of Archimedes, swung its iron hook over the harbour wall, seized a warship by the bow, hauled it into the air and then let go, capsizing it or dashing it on the rocks. The Roman general Marcellus joked bitterly that Archimedes used his ships like cups to ladle water from the sea.

Plutarch says the Romans lost their nerve completely: at the sight of a mere rope or stick of wood above the wall they would cry There it is! and turn and flee, sure that Archimedes was about to aim some new engine at them. Yet Plutarch also says that Archimedes thought engineering, like every craft that serves daily needs, beneath a true thinker, so he left no written instructions for any of his machines, and when the engines were gone, their secrets went with him.

When the city fell in 212 BC, legend says a soldier came upon the old man bent over a figure traced in the sand, and Archimedes told him not to disturb his circles, so the soldier ran him through. Plutarch's account has no such line, only Archimedes refusing to leave until his proof was finished, so the famous words are a later polish. Marcellus had ordered his men to take Archimedes alive, and afterwards he turned away from the killer as from a polluted man, then sought out Archimedes' relatives and honoured them. Some 137 years later Cicero, then a Roman official in Sicily, found the forgotten grave under brambles and thorns, though the locals swore it was gone, and knew it at once by the carving on a small column: a sphere inside a cylinder, the shape Archimedes had asked for.

In The Sand Reckoner he set out to count the grains of sand needed to fill the whole universe, and since Greek number words stopped at the myriad, ten thousand, he first had to invent a fresh way of naming numbers far beyond anything the Greeks had words for, reaching about 8 followed by 63 zeros.

Before him, people found pi by measuring round things and estimating; Archimedes squeezed the circle between polygons of 96 sides inside and outside it and proved that pi lies between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7, the first time its value was nailed down by proof rather than by measuring tape. One of his lost books, The Method, survived only because around 1229 a monk scraped its parchment clean and wrote a prayer book over it; the Dane J. L. Heiberg, working with a magnifying glass in 1906, read the faint text underneath and found Archimedes using ideas close to calculus, some 1,900 years before Newton and Leibniz.

aristotle-as-natural-philosopher.context_blurb:
Aristotle, the Greek philosopher of the fourth century BC who studied under Plato and tutored Alexander the Great, was also a tireless watcher of living things. On the island of Lesbos he dissected animals and questioned the people who handled them, and for nearly two thousand years Europe and the Islamic world called him simply the Philosopher.

He cross-checked his dissections against the first-hand knowledge of fishermen, sponge divers and beekeepers. He saw that whales and dolphins belong apart from fish, since they come up to breathe air and give birth to live calves. He described the mouth of the sea urchin, with five teeth meeting in the middle, as like a horn lantern with its panes left out, and zoologists still call it Aristotle's lantern. He urged his students to study even the lowliest creatures without disgust, promising that every animal would reveal something of nature and something of beauty.

Some of his observations were wrong. He called the ruler of a bee colony the king bee, assuming as his age did that leaders were male, but Luis Méndez de Torres of Spain showed in 1586 that the ruler was really a queen, a female who lays the eggs. Others were brilliant. Long before anyone sailed around the world, he argued the Earth is a ball, because during a lunar eclipse the shadow it throws on the Moon is always round, and only a sphere casts a round shadow from every angle. He added that ships' hulls vanish over the horizon before their masts. He wrote that the male octopus has a special mating arm that can snap off inside the female, and when Georges Cuvier found such a loose arm in 1829, he was so puzzled that he took it for a parasitic worm and gave it a worm's name, Hectocotyle. The arm is real, and it is still called the hectocotylus.

Eels stumped him, because no one had ever seen an eel egg or a baby eel, so he decided they had no parents and arose on their own from the mud, the guts of the earth. In fact eels breed far out in the Sargasso Sea, where no ancient Greek could watch them spawn. In one of the first experiments in embryology, he opened hens' eggs day after day and watched the chick form, noting that the heart appears first of all and is the first organ to beat. He ranked all of nature in one fixed order, from lifeless matter through plants and animals up to human beings, a ladder he called the scala naturae and that later ages named the Great Chain of Being.

That same heart, he concluded, was the seat of thought and feeling, while the pale, bloodless brain had the humble job of cooling the overheated heart, like a radiator. Medical students learned a heart-centred body until the 1500s. He pictured the heavens as crystal shells, one within another, around a motionless Earth, with the Moon, Sun and each planet riding its own, and all the stars together fixed on the single outermost sphere. Yet his habit of looking first and arguing from evidence outlived his errors. Early in 1882, weeks before his death, Charles Darwin read a new translation of Aristotle's Parts of Animals and wrote that Linnaeus and Cuvier, the two men he had always worshipped as scientists, were mere schoolboys beside old Aristotle.

aristotle-the-lyceum-and-tutoring-alexan.context_blurb:
Aristotle was born in Stagira in northern Greece in the fourth century BC and studied under Plato in Athens for about twenty years. After Plato died he became tutor to a Macedonian prince, then came back to Athens and founded his own school. He wrote on nearly everything the ancient world counted as knowledge, from logic to living things.

In 343 BC King Philip of Macedon hired him to teach his thirteen-year-old heir at a royal estate called Mieza, and for three years Aristotle schooled the boy in Homer, science and the art of speaking; the boy was Alexander the Great. Plutarch, writing almost 400 years later, said that visitors to Mieza could still see Aristotle's stone seats and the shady walks where he had taught. Alexander never forgot his lessons: after defeating the Persian king Darius in 331 BC he kept Homer's Iliad, in a text Aristotle had corrected for him, inside a jewelled casket taken from Darius's tent, and slept with it under his pillow beside his dagger. The story comes from Plutarch.

Around 335 BC Aristotle opened his own school in Athens, the Lyceum, in Apollo's sacred grove, and because he walked about as he taught instead of sitting down, his followers were called the Peripatetics, the walkers. Unlike Plato's Academy, which stood on private, walled grounds, the Lyceum met on public land and taught anyone for free, because Aristotle was a foreigner, not a citizen of Athens, and by law could not own property there.

At the Lyceum he gathered manuscripts, maps and specimens for students to examine, a collection scholars see as the ancestor of both the museum and the research library. For some two years he cut open marine animals beside a lagoon on Lesbos, and among his oddest discoveries was that the dogfish, a little shark, nourishes the pup inside her through a cord and a placenta, much as a mammal does; the anatomist Johannes Müller confirmed it in 1842. He also reported that a male river catfish stands guard over its eggs for some six or seven weeks, chasing off intruders and murmuring, and after centuries of doubt Louis Agassiz, a Swiss naturalist, confirmed it in the 1850s and named the fish Silurus aristotelis, Aristotle's catfish.

Another claim was dismissed as a fisherman's tale for some two thousand years: that one arm of the male octopus breaks off inside the female during mating; nineteenth-century zoologists found that he was right, and the arm is now called the hectocotylus. Aristotle also invented formal logic, showing that some conclusions follow from the shape of an argument alone: if all A are B and all B are C, then all A are C, whatever A, B and C may be. He called this the syllogism. In the Politics he described man as a political animal, built by nature for the life of the city, so that anyone able to live wholly outside a community must be below humanity, a beast, or above it, a god.

After Alexander died in 323 BC, the Athenians charged Aristotle with impiety, the charge on which Socrates had been put to death, and he fled to Chalcis, saying he would not let Athens sin twice against philosophy. He died there the next year.

armenian-genocide.context_blurb:
During the First World War the rulers of the Ottoman Empire, the Young Turk government, set out to destroy the Armenians, an ancient Christian people who had lived under Ottoman rule for centuries. Perhaps a million and a half Armenians were murdered or driven to their deaths. The man who directed the killing was the Interior Minister, Talaat Pasha. Turkey still officially denies that it was deliberate.

It began on the night of 24 April 1915 in Constantinople, when Talaat ordered mass arrests aimed first not at soldiers or rebels but at the community's educated leaders: its doctors, lawyers, teachers and poets. Armenians call that night Red Sunday and mark 24 April every year. Among those seized was Komitas, the priest-composer who had preserved Armenia's folk music by noting down thousands of village songs; friends, among them the American ambassador, won his release, but he had seen the slaughter, and he broke down and spent his last twenty years silent in asylums.

In May 1915 the government dressed the killing in law: its decree, the Tehcir Law, presented the deportations as a temporary resettlement, carried out for the people's own safety. The desert told the truth. Whole villages were driven on death marches toward Syria, dying of thirst, hunger and massacre on the way. The marches ended near Deir ez-Zor, a town on the Euphrates, and Jesse B. Jackson, the United States consul at Aleppo, counted some 150,000 starving Armenians scattered around it.

Henry Morgenthau, the American ambassador in Constantinople, watched the deportations himself and cabled Washington in July 1915 that a campaign of race extermination was in progress. When he begged Talaat again and again to stop, Talaat brushed him off: the question was settled, he said, for there were no more Armenians.

Americans answered with one of the first great relief campaigns in history. American schoolchildren sent their pennies for the starving Armenians, and Near East Relief, whose rallying cry was They Shall Not Perish, rescued more than a million people and brought up 132,000 orphans. Aurora Mardiganian, a teenage survivor who had been marched more than 1,400 miles and sold in a slave market before escaping to America, did what few survivors could bear to do: in 1919 she starred in a Hollywood film of her own story, playing herself.

The men who ordered the killings were never put on trial, so survivors set out to punish them. In 1921, on a Berlin street, Soghomon Tehlirian, a young survivor who had seen dozens of his relatives die, shot the exiled Talaat dead, and at his trial he told the court that he had killed a man but was not a murderer. His defence put the genocide itself in the dock, and after hearing the evidence of the massacres, the German jury acquitted him in barely an hour.

A Polish-Jewish law student, Raphael Lemkin, was haunted that no law on earth could punish what had been done to the Armenians, and in 1944 he coined a name for the crime of wiping out an entire people on purpose: genocide, from the Greek genos, a people, and the Latin -cide, killing. The world's forgetting mattered: in August 1939, days before he invaded Poland, Hitler, reports say, waved away his generals' worries by asking who, after all, now spoke of the destruction of the Armenians. The exact wording comes from a disputed transcript, but the lesson stands: when the world forgets one genocide, it invites another.

armistice-of-november-11-1918.context_blurb:
At 11 o'clock on the morning of 11 November 1918, the guns of the First World War fell silent on the Western Front. Before dawn that day German delegates had signed the armistice in a railway carriage hidden in the Compiègne forest north of Paris, where Marshal Ferdinand Foch laid down the Allied terms. Germany's armies were crumbling, and its Kaiser had fled.

The hour was built from one number repeated three times: eleven o'clock on the eleventh day of the eleventh month. It became Armistice Day, now Veterans Day in the United States and Remembrance Day across the Commonwealth.

Commanders knew the ceasefire was hours away, yet attacks went on, and the American Private Henry Gunther rushed a German machine-gun post even as its gunners stood up waving at him to stop; they fired, and he was shot at 10:59 a.m., sixty seconds before the ceasefire. He is counted as the last soldier of any nation killed in the war, one of about 2,738 men who died on its final day.

The carriage itself had a bitter sequel: in June 1940 Adolf Hitler had it hauled back to the same clearing so that he could force a beaten France to surrender inside it, and he even sat in Foch's old chair. The SS later destroyed the carriage in 1945.

art-and-disillusionment-after-the-war.context_blurb:
The slaughter of 1914 to 1918 shattered the old faith that reason and technology would keep making the world better, and the artists who came after the war broke the inherited rules on purpose. The Dada movement mocked the very idea of fine art, and the Surrealists who followed mined dreams for images both tender and nightmarish.

In 1917 Marcel Duchamp bought an ordinary porcelain urinal, turned it on its back, wrote the false signature R. Mutt on it, gave it the title Fountain, and entered it in a New York exhibition as sculpture. The show had promised to hang any work whose artist paid the fee, yet it rejected Fountain an hour before opening, and Duchamp, secretly on the board, resigned in protest. It became the most famous piece of Dada anti-art.

Salvador Dalí said the limp, melting pocket-watches of The Persistence of Memory, painted in 1931, came to him after he watched a runny Camembert cheese soften on his plate at dinner. He built such dream-images with what he called his paranoiac-critical method, coaxing a trance-like state so that his hand would paint the logic of dreams.

articles-of-confederation-their-failures.context_blurb:
After declaring independence, the thirteen states needed a government while the war went on. The Articles of Confederation, ratified in 1781, gave them one: a weak Congress with no power to tax, no power over trade between the states, no national courts and no president. The states kept nearly all real power, and once the war ended, the weakness showed.

Congress could only beg the states for money through requisitions, and when it made its final appeal before the Constitution replaced the Articles, for $3.8 million, the states paid in a grand total of $663. They treated such demands, as one phrase of the day put it, as mere recommendations. A government that can ask but cannot collect cannot pay its soldiers or its debts, which is why the Constitution gave Congress the power to tax.

Meanwhile states slapped tariffs on one another's goods as if they were foreign countries, and Benjamin Franklin compared New Jersey, squeezed between the ports of New York and Philadelphia, to a barrel with a tap at each end. New Jersey struck back by taxing a New York-owned lighthouse on Sandy Hook. In 1787 a convention in Philadelphia met to amend the Articles and wrote the Constitution instead.

aryan-migrations-the-vedas.context_blurb:
Around 1500 BC, by the leading scholarly model, herders speaking an Indo-European language moved from the Central Asian steppes through the mountain passes into north-western India, mixing with the peoples already there. The word Aryan, which later took on an ugly political history, is used here only in its old Indian sense. In India these people composed the Vedas, the hymns from which Hinduism grew.

The oldest, the Rigveda, holds more than a thousand hymns in Sanskrit, and its very first word is Agni, god of the sacred fire, who is praised in the opening hymn and in some 200 others.

One whole book, or mandala, of the Rigveda, all 114 hymns of the ninth, belongs to Soma, the god of a holy plant whose juice priests pressed and filtered for the sacrifice. Soma ranks with Agni and Indra as the Rigveda's three chief gods. Its verses were passed down by memory and voice, with nothing written, for almost all of their history; the Gayatri mantra, addressed to Savitr, god of the sun, is still chanted daily by Hindus some thirty centuries later.

Reciters guarded against error by chanting the verses in braided patterns, even backwards, and the check works because reversing the order of Sanskrit words does not change their meaning. The hardest pattern, the ghana-patha or bell, weaves the words back and forth like a ringing bell. In 2008 UNESCO placed Vedic chant among the treasures of humanity's living heritage, calling it a perfect canon, unchanged in word order and even in sound, and perhaps the oldest unbroken oral tradition in existence.

The Nasadiya Sukta, the Rigveda's great hymn about creation, wonders how the universe began and refuses a confident answer, ending with the thought that even the god watching from the highest heaven may not know; Carl Sagan praised it as proof of ancient India's tradition of skeptical questioning. Around 1380 BC, in northern Syria, the Hittites and the kingdom of Mitanni sealed a treaty with oaths sworn by Indra, Mitra, Varuna and the twin Nasatyas, the very gods praised in the Rigveda, turning up a long way west of India.

Kikkuli, a horse-trainer of Mitanni, wrote a training manual whose lap counts use words such as aika for one and panza for five, close copies of Sanskrit eka and pancha, hard evidence that the Mitanni elite spoke an Indo-Aryan tongue. The earliest chariots with spoked wheels yet discovered lie in graves of the Sintashta culture in the southern Urals, from about 1950 BC, alongside the earliest known bits and bridles, and scholars see these steppe people as forebears of the Indo-Aryans who composed the Vedas. That reconstruction, built from language, archaeology and genetics, is still debated.

assassination-of-archduke-franz-ferdinan.context_blurb:
On 28 June 1914 Franz Ferdinand, the archduke who stood next in line for the Austro-Hungarian crown, rode with his wife Sophie in an open car through Sarajevo, the capital of Bosnia. Along the route waited a band of young Bosnian Serb conspirators who wanted to tear Bosnia away from Austrian rule. Before noon the Archduke was dead, and within weeks Europe was at war.

Nedeljko Čabrinović struck first, hurling a hand grenade from the riverside crowd, but it skipped off the car's folded-back roof, rolled into the street and exploded under the next car in line, wounding about twenty people and leaving the Archduke unhurt. Čabrinović swallowed cyanide and leapt into the Miljacka River, but the poison was old and only made him vomit, and in that dry summer the river was barely ankle-deep, so he was hauled out and arrested.

Shaken, Franz Ferdinand decided to visit the wounded in hospital, and the governor, Potiorek, picked a safer route by the river. But nobody told the drivers the route had changed, so they turned the old way, onto Franz Joseph Street. When the governor shouted at the driver, Leopold Lojka, that he was on the wrong road, Lojka braked and tried to back up, and the engine stalled. That wrong turn left the car stopped dead in front of Schiller's delicatessen, exactly where Gavrilo Princip, a nineteen-year-old conspirator, happened to be standing. Princip fired twice from about a metre and a half away. A bullet tore into the Archduke's neck, and as he bled to death he thought of his wife, also hit, begging Sophie not to die but to live for their children. Both were dead by about half past eleven.

A popular story says Princip had just stopped for a sandwich when the car appeared, but nothing in the court records supports it; the tale was born in a Brazilian novel of 2001 and spread through a documentary two years later. The shots came around 10:55 a.m., too early for lunch. A month later Austria-Hungary went to war with Serbia, and the web of alliance promises dragged in the great powers within a week: Russia, Germany, France, Belgium and Britain were all at war.

The plot ran deeper than a few angry students. The conspirators chose the date on purpose: 28 June was Vidovdan, St Vitus Day, the anniversary of the Battle of Kosovo in 1389, where Prince Lazar fell fighting the Ottomans, the holiest day in the Serbian year. Their pistols, bombs and training came from a Serbian secret society, the Black Hand, led by Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević, known as Apis, the head of Serbia's military intelligence. At his trial Princip called himself a Yugoslav nationalist who wanted the South Slavs united and free of Austria, and when the court asked how he meant to achieve it, he answered: by means of terror. Austrian law did not allow anyone under twenty to be hanged, and Princip had been born 27 days too late, so he received the longest prison sentence the law allowed, twenty years. He died of tuberculosis in prison in 1918.

athens-vs-sparta-two-rival-city-states-t.context_blurb:
In the fifth century BC the two strongest Greek city-states were Athens and Sparta. Each was a polis, an independent city with its own laws, army and way of life. Athens was a seafaring democracy, rich from trade and bursting with philosophy, drama and art; Sparta was an inland warrior state ruled by two kings and a council of elders. Their rivalry ended in a war that lasted a generation.

An Athenian boy stayed at home to study music, poetry and argument, but a Spartan boy was taken from his parents at seven to live in army barracks and enter the agoge, the city's brutal military schooling. Sparta despised trade and greed, so, the story goes, it used heavy bars of iron for money, so bulky that a small fortune filled a room and needed oxen to move it. A later law forbidding Spartans to own gold and silver coins is better attested than that legend. Spartans prized few words, which is why a short reply is still called laconic, after their region, Laconia; when Philip of Macedon warned that if he invaded Laconia he would burn their city to the ground, they sent back one word: If.

In a single lifetime Athens produced great philosophers, playwrights and the earliest true historians, and it staged the world's first plays at a yearly festival in honour of Dionysus, the god of wine. Its democracy was direct: the citizens' Assembly gathered on the Pnyx hill some forty times or more each year, and any male citizen, even an ordinary farmer, could climb the speaker's platform and argue before the whole Assembly himself. Women, slaves and foreigners, most of the people, had no vote. Athenians could also vote to send any man away for a decade, with no crime charged, by scratching names on broken pots, and once an illiterate citizen asked a stranger to scratch the name Aristides for him, never guessing he was speaking to Aristides; asked why, the man said he was simply tired of hearing Aristides called the Just. Aristides wrote his own name and was banished, and those pottery shards gave us the word ostracism. Over the city's war dead Pericles, Athens' greatest statesman, gave its most famous speech, boasting that Athens threw its city open to all the world and never drove foreigners out, while Sparta was known for expelling them.

Sparta had surprises of its own. Its girls ran races and wrestled, and its women had more freedom than any others in Greece. Gorgo, wife of King Leonidas, was once asked by an Athenian woman how Spartan wives came to rule their men, and she replied that Spartan women were the only ones who gave birth to real men. Spartan mothers sent their sons to war with a famous five-word charge, telling each one to return with his shield or upon it: home in victory carrying it, or home dead on top of it, since a man who fled threw his heavy shield away.

Athens trusted ordinary people with its courts, filling juries of 500 or even 2,500 citizens, and it chose them with the kleroterion, a slotted stone that took bronze name-tickets and let coloured balls fall down a tube, picking each day's jurors purely at random so that no bribe could choose a friendly jury. Every Spartan citizen could train for war full-time because conquered serfs, the helots, worked the land, and since they far outnumbered their masters, the Spartan magistrates declared war on them every year, so that any Spartan could kill a helot without guilt.

In the end the rivals fought a 27-year war, from 431 to 404 BC, and land-power Sparta could not beat sea-power Athens until it took Persian gold, from the very empire the Greeks had once united to defeat, built a fleet and beat Athens at sea. Its admiral Lysander destroyed 168 Athenian ships at Aegospotami in 405 BC and starved Athens into surrender.

augustus-and-the-founding-of-the-empire.context_blurb:
Augustus was born Gaius Octavius in 63 BC, the great-nephew of Julius Caesar. He was a teenager when Caesar was murdered, and in the fifteen years that followed he outplayed every rival and turned the dying Roman Republic into the Roman Empire. He ruled for more than forty years and died in his bed, which few emperors after him managed.

When Caesar was stabbed to death on the Ides of March, 44 BC, his will named young Octavius his adopted son and chief heir, and the boy at once claimed the inheritance that mattered most: Caesar's name. Overnight a teenager became Caesar, and the name later became a title for emperors. Before the Battle of Philippi in 42 BC, where Brutus and Cassius, Caesar's killers, waited, he vowed a temple to Mars if he was granted vengeance, and after victory he crowned his new Forum in Rome with the Temple of Mars the Avenger, Mars Ultor.

At Actium in 31 BC his fleet had Mark Antony's cornered, and when Cleopatra's Egyptian ships broke away toward the open sea, Antony left his whole navy behind to follow her and threw away both the fight and his hopes of ruling Rome. In 8 BC the Senate gave the old month Sextilis his name, because in that month he had first held the consulship, taken Egypt and finished the civil wars; we call it August.

On 16 January 27 BC the Senate gave him a title no Roman had carried before: Augustus, a word of religious awe meaning the revered one. He never called himself king, rex, the word Romans had hated since they drove out their kings; he chose princeps, first citizen, while quietly holding all the armies. His system is called the Principate. His favourite motto was festina lente, make haste slowly, and he explained that a job done well is a job done fast enough.

He rebuilt the capital so thoroughly that he could boast, as Suetonius records, that he had found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble. In the Forum stood the shrine of Janus, two-faced god of doorways, whose double doors, the Gates of Janus, stood open while Rome fought anywhere and closed only in total peace; in seven hundred years they had been shut twice, and Augustus shut them three times. Those closed doors stood for the Pax Romana.

The cruellest blow fell in AD 9, when Varus and three legions were ambushed and destroyed in Germany's Teutoburg Forest, and Suetonius says the old emperor beat his head against a door for months, crying out to Varus to give him back his legions.

In old age he wrote his own record of his deeds, the Res Gestae, set up in bronze at his tomb, and in it the only title he gives himself is first citizen; the words king and emperor never appear. The best surviving copy is carved into a temple in Ankara, in Turkey. In one honest sentence he admits the secret of his rule: he held no more legal power than his fellow officials, but in authority, auctoritas, the weight of personal influence, he surpassed them all.

On his deathbed in AD 14, aged seventy-five, he called for a mirror, had his hair combed, and asked his friends whether he had played his part well in the comedy of life, then quoted an actor's request for applause. His last words were to his wife, Livia. Power passed to his stepson Tiberius, and with that handover the Republic lost its elected leaders for good: rule now passed within a family, exactly what the Republic had spent centuries guarding against. The Senate declared the dead Augustus a god.

auschwitz-and-the-death-camps.context_blurb:
Auschwitz was the largest of the death camps Nazi Germany built to murder the Jews of Europe. The SS ran it from 1940 to January 1945 beside the small town of Oświęcim, and trains brought victims to it from across occupied Europe. Today it is a memorial and museum, and the anniversary of its liberation is the world's day of Holocaust remembrance.

The camp was not in Germany at all: Germany invaded Poland in September 1939, and the SS built the camp about 40 miles west of Kraków, in occupied Poland. Over its main gate the SS made prisoner metalworkers forge the lying slogan Arbeit macht frei, work sets you free, and the prisoners quietly set the B of ARBEIT in upside down, a protest the guards never caught that can still be seen today. Auschwitz was the only Nazi camp that tattooed a number on the left forearm of each prisoner it spared for forced labour, a mark survivors carried for life. The poison in its gas chambers, Zyklon B, was no secret weapon but an ordinary pesticide for killing insects and rats, pellets of hydrogen cyanide that farmers and shopkeepers had bought before the war.

The complex had three parts, the original main camp, Monowitz, a slave-labour camp serving a synthetic-rubber factory, and Birkenau, the killing centre with its gas chambers and crematoria, and there the SS murdered over a million people, most of them Jews, in less than five years. The Auschwitz museum counts about 1.1 million dead, and about one million of them were Jews, the people Hitler's regime had condemned to total extermination, its so-called Final Solution. Between late April and early July 1944, with the war nearly lost, Adolf Eichmann rushed the Jews of Hungary to Auschwitz, about 426,000 men, women and children deported within ten weeks, the majority murdered on the day they arrived.

The SS kept the condemned quiet with a soothing lie, telling them they were going to take a shower; then the doors were sealed and the Zyklon B was dropped in. On the arrival ramp the SS doctor Josef Mengele sorted new arrivals with a wave of the hand, right to work and left to the gas, and the prisoners called him the Angel of Death. He chose twins for cruel experiments. Rudolf Vrba and Alfred Wetzler, two young Slovak Jews, escaped that April and lay hidden for three days in a hollow pile of timber, having spread gasoline-soaked tobacco around it to throw the tracking dogs off their scent. Once free, they wrote the first detailed eyewitness report of the gas chambers to warn the world.

On 27 January 1945 soldiers of the Soviet Red Army reached the camp and found about 7,000 prisoners still alive, most too sick and starved to stand, because the SS had driven away nearly everyone who could walk. In the warehouses the SS left behind they found thousands of suitcases, some 2,100 of them still painted with their owners' names, packed by people who had believed they were starting a new life. They also found seven tonnes of human hair and some 110,000 shoes.

On 7 October 1944 the Sonderkommando, Jewish prisoners made to work the Birkenau crematoria, rebelled with gunpowder that women prisoners had carried out of a munitions factory in tiny amounts, and before the SS crushed them they destroyed Crematorium IV with explosives. In January 1945 the SS publicly hanged four young women, among them Roza Robota, for supplying the powder. At Nuremberg the camp's commandant, Rudolf Höss, was asked how the guards knew when the people in a gas chamber were dead, and he answered flatly that they knew because the screaming stopped. Höss, who had lived as Franz Lang after the war until the Nazi-hunter Hanns Alexander found him, was condemned by a Polish court in 1947 and hanged at Auschwitz itself, on a small gallows beside the crematorium of the camp he had run.

avicenna-ibn-sina-and-islamic-medicine.context_blurb:
Ibn Sina, known in Latin as Avicenna, was a Persian born around 980 who became perhaps the most important doctor of the Middle Ages, and a philosopher who tried to join Aristotle's thought with Islam. His influence ran through Islamic and Christian scholars alike, from al-Ghazali and Averroes to Thomas Aquinas.

He claimed to have mastered every science by the age of eighteen, but Aristotle's Metaphysics beat him: he read it forty times without understanding it, until a bookseller talked him into buying a cheap little commentary by al-Farabi, for three dirhams, and suddenly the whole thing made sense. He was so happy that he gave thanks to God and handed out alms to the poor.

His Canon of Medicine, five books and over a million words long, was translated into Latin in the twelfth century and was still a set text at Padua and Bologna in the 1600s, and doctors trusted it so completely that they called it the Medical Bible. A book written in the Islamic world trained Europe's doctors for centuries.

aztec-mass-human-sacrifice-templo-mayor-.context_blurb:
In 1487 the Aztec ruler Ahuitzotl held the dedication of the enlarged Great Temple, the Templo Mayor, at the heart of his island capital, Tenochtitlan, where Mexico City stands today. Over four days of ceremony, priests sacrificed captives in vast numbers. Some modern historians long dismissed the Spanish accounts of such killing as propaganda; archaeology has since shown the practice was real.

Ahuitzotl, the greatest conqueror among the Aztec rulers, took his name from a water monster of legend, and his name-glyph showed the beast with a human hand at the end of its tail, a creature said to lurk in lakes and grab whatever came to the water's edge. The temple re-created a myth: when the war god Huitzilopochtli sprang fully armed from his mother's womb, he killed his sister, the goddess Coyolxauhqui, cut her body to pieces and flung her head into the sky, where it became the moon. In 1978 workmen behind Mexico City's cathedral hit upon a huge carved stone showing her broken body, and the find launched the excavation of the buried temple.

The Templo Mayor rose about 180 feet above the market, and on its summit stood twin shrines: a blood-red one for Huitzilopochtli, god of war and the sun, and a rain-blue one for Tlaloc, god of rain. Four priests held each victim down over a stone block; a fifth slashed open the chest beneath the ribs with a flint or obsidian blade, tore out the still-beating heart and lifted it up to the sun. At the spring festival of Xipe Totec a captive was tethered by a single ankle to a circular stone and made to fight fully armed Eagle and Jaguar warriors, and he was handed a wooden club fitted only with feathers, while theirs were edged with razor-sharp obsidian. Mexican archaeologists working beside the temple uncovered the Huey Tzompantli, built in Ahuitzotl's era, a rack some 112 feet long and a tower of hundreds of real skulls cemented in lime, proof that the great skull racks the Spaniards described were no invention.

The temple stood for Coatepec, the Snake Mountain of the myth, so every body thrown down its steps landed on the great Coyolxauhqui stone at the base and acted out the moon goddess being hurled down the mountain by her brother. When scientists sorted the skulls of the Huey Tzompantli by size and tooth growth, they expected captured warriors, but they also found the skulls of women, and of three or more young children, which the anthropologist Rodrigo Bolaños called a first. The Aztecs believed the sun fought an endless war against darkness and that human blood, the payment of debts, kept it moving; Diego Durán, a Spanish friar, put the dedication's victims at 80,400, about fourteen deaths a minute for four days and nights, which most historians reject as impossible, estimating the real toll at about 20,000. Each spring the priests of Xipe Totec, Our Lord the Flayed One, patron of spring and of goldsmiths, skinned sacrificed captives whole and wore the skins for twenty days; the dried skin was called a golden garment, and shedding it was likened to a maize seed losing its husk.

The Spanish conquest raised hard questions of its own. In a Salamanca lecture of 1539, Francisco de Vitoria taught that rights rest on human nature and reason rather than on Christian faith, so the native peoples had truly owned their lands and lawfully governed themselves before Spain arrived. At the great debate in Valladolid in 1550, Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda argued that the Indians were natural slaves, but Bartolomé de las Casas, a Dominican friar, answered that they were rational and free, to be won over by argument and never by force.

aztec-religion-and-human-sacrifice.context_blurb:
The Aztecs ruled central Mexico from their island capital, Tenochtitlan, in the 1400s and early 1500s, and their religion included one of the most intense systems of human sacrifice ever recorded. They believed the sun and the war god needed human blood and hearts to keep the universe running. The Spanish who arrived in 1519 were horrified, and modern digs have confirmed their accounts.

On top of the great pyramid, the Templo Mayor, stood two shrines: Tlaloc's, decked in blue and white for water and life, and the war god Huitzilopochtli's, painted red, the colour of blood. The pyramid was built as Coatepec, Snake Mountain, the sacred hill where the war god was born, so carved serpent heads lined its great stairway from bottom to top. The priest's sacrificial knife, the tecpatl, was chipped from obsidian, a black volcanic glass that takes an edge sharper than a modern scalpel.

In the Aztec creation story a humble god covered in sores, Nanahuatzin, leapt into a sacred fire at Teotihuacan to become the Fifth Sun, but the new sun hung motionless until the other gods fed it their own blood. Human sacrifice, the Aztecs believed, repaid that divine debt and kept the sun moving. In the standard rite priests held the victim over a stone block while one cut out the beating heart, which the Aztecs called the precious eagle-cactus fruit and laid in a carved stone bowl, the eagle vessel. In times of drought priests offered small children to Tlaloc and made sure they wept on the way to the altar, because their tears were believed to call down the rain. Excavators at the temple found the remains of at least 42 children sacrificed during the drought of 1452 to 1454.

Afterwards the body was rolled down the steep steps and landed on the great Coyolxauhqui stone, a disc showing the moon goddess cut to pieces, because each falling body repeated the myth in which the war god hurled his sister down Snake Mountain. Electrical workers found that 8.5-ton stone in 1978. At the spring festival Tlacaxipehualiztli, priests of Xipe Totec, Our Lord the Flayed One, went about dressed in the skins of captives who had been sacrificed and flayed, wearing them for twenty days and then shedding them as a maize seed sheds its husk, standing for new growth in spring. The same festival held the so-called gladiatorial sacrifice, in which a prisoner tethered to a circular stone fought elite Jaguar and Eagle warriors armed with obsidian-edged weapons, while he was given a club whose obsidian blades had been swapped for feathers. Few survived.

When famine struck in the 1450s, Tlacaelel, the priest who shaped Aztec policy, expanded the Flower Wars against neighbours such as Tlaxcala, wars meant not to kill the enemy or seize land but to capture enemy warriors alive for sacrifice. Tlaxcala was left unconquered on purpose, a standing source of captives. For the festival of Toxcatl a flawless young captive spent a whole year as Tezcatlipoca's earthly double, the god made flesh, dressed in gold and turquoise and honoured so deeply that people kissed the ground before him, and at the year's end he climbed the temple steps, breaking a clay flute on each, and the priests cut out his heart. Once every 52 years, at the New Fire Ceremony, all fires were doused and people feared the sun would never rise again; at the decisive midnight priests on the Hill of the Star kindled the new flame in a sacrificed man's opened chest, and runners spread it to every hearth.

Bernal Díaz del Castillo, one of the Spanish conquerors, heard the temple's great snakeskin drum boom for miles and watched 62 of his captured comrades dragged up the steps to the altar, and he wrote that every day he dreaded being dragged up those same steps himself.

babylon-and-the-hanging-gardens.context_blurb:
Some twenty-six centuries ago Babylon, on the Euphrates, was the mightiest city on earth. Its king, Nebuchadnezzar II, rebuilt it with mighty walls, glittering gates and a towering temple, and later Greek writers listed its Hanging Gardens among the ancient world's Seven Wonders. Whether those gardens ever stood there is another matter.

Nebuchadnezzar's northern entrance, the Ishtar Gate, was faced with deep-blue glazed brick, and across it marched golden beasts, each sacred to a god: the lion of Ishtar, the bull of the storm god Adad, and the scaly dragon-snake of Marduk, Babylon's chief god. The Processional Way leading up to it was lined on both sides with more than 120 striding lions in bright glazed brick, the beast of Ishtar, watching as priests carried the gods' statues past at New Year. You can still walk through the gate today, rebuilt in Berlin's Pergamon Museum: the German archaeologist Robert Koldewey sent the fragments to Germany in nearly 800 crates, and over decades they were cleaned and pieced together again.

The story goes that the king raised the Hanging Gardens for Queen Amytis, who pined on the flat plain for the green, forested mountains of her homeland, though no Babylonian text mentions any such queen. The Greek historian Diodorus, writing centuries later and never having seen them, described the gardens as a man-made green mountain about 20 metres high, its planted terraces rising one behind another like the seats of a theatre. Above the city rose Etemenanki, a ziggurat of baked brick and tar in seven stepped terraces with a shrine on top, perhaps 91 metres high, which Nebuchadnezzar boasted would touch the sky; the Hebrew Bible remembers it as the Tower of Babel.

In 587 BC Nebuchadnezzar's army broke into Jerusalem, burned the city's holiest building, the Temple of Solomon, carried off its gold and silver vessels, and led thousands of Jerusalem's people away as captives to Babylon. Half a century later the Persian king Cyrus let the exiles go home.

Babylon's own end came in 539 BC. The Bible says that on its last night King Belshazzar held a wild feast, drinking from the golden cups taken from the Temple in Jerusalem, when a hand appeared out of nowhere and wrote on the wall, which is why we still speak of the writing on the wall. That same night Cyrus the Great of Persia captured the city with hardly a battle: he diverted the Euphrates into an old channel until the riverbed ran low, and his soldiers waded in beneath the mighty walls.

For all the vivid accounts by the priest Berossus, by Diodorus and by Strabo, archaeologists digging at Babylon for decades found nothing at all of the gardens, not a single trace; of all the Seven Wonders, they alone have never been found. Strabo claimed that concealed water-screws lifted river water up to the highest terraces, working against gravity to keep the trees green. Stephanie Dalley, a British scholar, believes the gardens were real but stood in another city: Nineveh, where the Assyrian king Sennacherib, a century earlier, boasted of a vast park of trees beside his palace, and where carvings show trees on tiered, arched terraces. Her case is still debated.

bach-baroque-counterpoint.context_blurb:
Johann Sebastian Bach (1685 to 1750) was a German organist and composer who spent his last decades as music director of St Thomas's church and school in Leipzig. In his lifetime many thought him old-fashioned; today his music stands near the heart of the Western tradition. Above all he was the master of counterpoint, several independent melodies woven together at once.

His favourite form was the fugue, in which a single voice announces a brief theme, then the next voice enters with the same theme while the first carries on, and so on; its name comes from the Latin fuga, to flee or to chase, because the voices seem to pursue one another. Bach had twenty children by two wives, first his cousin Maria Barbara and then the singer Anna Magdalena; only about ten grew up, and four of his sons became famous composers in their own right, among them Carl Philipp Emanuel and Johann Christian.

In his own fair copy of the St Matthew Passion, which sets the Gospel account of the arrest and crucifixion of Jesus, Bach inked the words of Jesus and the Gospel text in deep red, so that they stand out on the page. After his death the Passion went unperformed for some eighty years, until in 1829 the twenty-year-old Felix Mendelssohn conducted it in Berlin and relaunched Bach's fame.

The Passion is written for two complete orchestras and two full choirs, set in the church's two organ lofts so that the forces can answer each other across the nave. Keyboards of his day were tuned so that many keys sounded sour, so Bach wrote The Well-Tempered Clavier, a prelude and a fugue in every one of the 24 keys, major and minor, to prove a new tuning made every key playable. A famous legend says he wrote the gentle Goldberg Variations so the young harpsichordist Johann Goldberg could play Count Keyserlingk to sleep, and that the grateful count rewarded Bach with a golden goblet filled with 100 gold coins; scholars think the tale is mostly myth.

In 1747 the ageing Bach visited King Frederick the Great at Potsdam, a flute-playing king who owned the newest keyboards, and when Frederick handed him a long, twisting theme of his own and dared him to make a fugue on it, Bach improvised one on the spot. He went home and built a whole work, The Musical Offering, on the king's theme. One piece in it is a musical palindrome: one player plays a line forward while a second plays the same line backward, and because crabs walk backwards it is called the Crab Canon. Because in old German notation B means B-flat and H means B-natural, the notes B-flat, A, C and B-natural spell B-A-C-H, and Bach hid that signature as a theme in the vast closing fugue, left unfinished, of The Art of Fugue.

That fugue breaks off mid-phrase just after the B-A-C-H theme enters, and on the page Bach's son Carl Philipp Emanuel wrote that at this point, where the name BACH appears, the composer died. Modern scholars doubt he literally died mid-note, but the broken-off page is real. Another tale, reported by the critic A. B. Marx, claims the Passion's score was nearly lost because a Berlin shop wrapped its cheese in pages torn from it, until Carl Friedrich Zelter rescued a copy; scholars think the cheese-shop story is at least exaggerated.

bartolom-de-las-casas.context_blurb:
Bartolomé de las Casas first crossed to the Caribbean around 1502 as a young Spanish colonist, and the crown gave him an encomienda, an estate whose Indians were forced to labour for him. For years he saw the native workers flogged, starved and driven until they died. Around 1514 his conscience broke.

He gave his Indians back to the governor and became the fiercest enemy of the system he had profited from, spending the rest of his life denouncing it in books and before kings. He made mistakes too: early on he proposed shifting the burden onto imported African slaves, a proposal he later renounced and bitterly regretted.

In 1550 Emperor Charles V halted Spain's conquests and summoned theologians to Valladolid, and when Sepúlveda argued that the Indians were barbarians, fit by Aristotle's rule only to be ruled, Las Casas answered that they were fully rational human beings, able to govern themselves, so no people are slaves by nature. The judges named no winner, but it was the first formal debate in history over the rights of a conquered people, and a root of the natural-rights tradition.

bartolomeu-dias-rounds-cape-of-good-hope.context_blurb:
For decades Portuguese captains had crept down the coast of Africa, hoping to find a sea route to India's spices that would bypass the Muslim merchants who controlled the overland trade. In 1488 Bartolomeu Dias, with three small ships, became the first European known to round Africa's southern tip, after storms drove him far out of sight of land.

Dias called the cape after the gales that had almost sunk him, Cabo das Tormentas, the Cape of Storms, but King John II of Portugal, thinking of the road to India it opened, renamed it the Cape of Good Hope.

Dias longed to press on to India, but his crew, months at sea and short of food and drink, refused to go further; a council allowed him just three more days, and then he had to turn back. He reached Lisbon in December 1488, after sixteen months away, and it was Vasco da Gama who later finished the route. Years afterwards Dias was lost at sea near the very cape he had found.

bastiat-and-the-seen-versus-unseen-the-b.context_blurb:
Frédéric Bastiat was a French economist, journalist and member of the National Assembly who died of tuberculosis in 1850, aged forty-nine. In his last years he wrote short, witty pamphlets, full of parables a child can follow, attacking tariffs, make-work schemes and the idea that destruction or waste can make a country richer.

In his mock Petition of the Candlemakers, the makers of candles and lamps beg the government to save them from a foreign rival who floods France with light at an impossibly low price, and that unbeatable rival is the sun; they demand a law shutting every window and skylight. The joke exposes the logic of tariffs that punish cheap competition.

In What Is Seen and What Is Not Seen, a careless boy breaks a shop window and onlookers say it is good for trade, since the glass-mender gets six francs of work, but Bastiat points to what nobody sees: the shopkeeper can no longer spend those six francs on new shoes or another book for his library. The money only moves; it is not created. The town is no richer, and destruction never makes a society wealthier.

bataan-death-march.context_blurb:
Days after the attack on Pearl Harbor at the end of 1941, Japanese troops invaded the American-held Philippines. The American and Filipino defenders fell back onto the jungle-covered Bataan Peninsula of Luzon, with no ships to resupply them, living on a quarter of their normal rice ration. What followed their surrender became one of the worst atrocities of the Pacific war.

Japan's planners had allowed 50 days to take Bataan, but the defenders held out for 99 days before Major General Edward King surrendered on 9 April 1942. Some historians link the cruelty that followed partly to Japanese commanders' fury at the long fight and to their having no plan for so many prisoners. Japanese guards marched some 76,000 prisoners about 65 miles north, beating, bayoneting or shooting those who fell behind, and between seven and ten thousand died on the march.

Their commander, Lieutenant General Masaharu Homma of the Japanese 14th Army, faced 43 charges after the war and was held responsible for what his men did, and he was executed by firing squad on 3 April 1946.

battle-of-britain.context_blurb:
In June 1940 France fell, and Britain stood alone against Nazi Germany in Western Europe. Before Hitler could send an army across the English Channel, his air force, the Luftwaffe, had to destroy the Royal Air Force, and from July to October 1940 it tried. That fight was the Battle of Britain.

No armies clashed on land and no fleets met at sea: for the first time in history, a major battle was decided entirely in the air. The sleek Supermarine Spitfire won the glory, but the plainer, tougher Hawker Hurricane shot down about 60 percent of the enemy aircraft destroyed, more than all other British defences together, tearing into the bomber formations while Spitfires took on the German fighters above. Britain's hidden advantage was radar: Chain Home, a line of towers along the coasts facing the enemy, could pick up raiders as far as 200 miles off, before they had even left French skies. Outnumbered day after day, the RAF's fighter pilots won a name from Winston Churchill that has clung to them ever since: the Few.

On 20 August 1940 Churchill told the House of Commons that never in the long history of war had so many owed so much to so few. Days earlier, watching every squadron go up at once from an operations room, he had told General Ismay that he had never been so moved. The Junkers Ju 87 Stuka, the screaming dive-bomber that had terrified Poland and France, proved slow and helpless against Spitfires and Hurricanes; it lost over a fifth of its force in ten August days, and the Luftwaffe withdrew it from the battle. Nearly one pilot in five was not British, and No. 303 Squadron, flown by pilots from Poland who had escaped when Germany overran their country, joined two months late yet finished as the top-scoring squadron in Fighter Command.

Behind the pilots stood the Dowding system, the world's first integrated air-defence network, tying together radar, observers on the ground, telephones, map rooms and radio, so fighters took off only against real, detected raids and never wasted fuel, pilots or planes patrolling empty sky. At its headquarters, Bentley Priory, the battle was followed on a giant map table where women of the WAAF, the Women's Auxiliary Air Force, pushed coloured counters with long rods to show each German formation, while controllers watched from a gallery above. By early September the Luftwaffe believed Fighter Command was nearly finished, but after British bombers raided Berlin, Hermann Göring switched from hitting the RAF's airfields to bombing London, beginning the Blitz on 7 September, and that blunder gave the exhausted RAF time to recover.

Before the war, commanders expected fighters to catch between a third and a half of incoming raids, but the system guided them onto about nine raids in ten, which in effect roughly tripled Fighter Command's strength. Yet in November 1940 the man who built it, Air Chief Marshal Hugh Dowding, was sacked from Fighter Command, partly over the Big Wing feud: Douglas Bader, the ace who flew with artificial legs, and Trafford Leigh-Mallory wanted huge massed wings, while Dowding and Keith Park had won with quick squadron-by-squadron scrambles. By May 1941 the German air offensive had stopped, the first major setback of the war for Nazi Germany.

battle-of-gaugamela-331-bc-alexander-bea.context_blurb:
In 331 BC, on the open plain of northern Mesopotamia, in today's Iraq, the Macedonian king Alexander the Great fought the decisive battle of his war against the Persian Empire. King Darius III brought a far larger army, with cavalry from across Central Asia, scythed chariots and even elephants. Alexander had a smaller, superbly drilled army and a gift for finding the weak point in an enemy line.

Darius had his men level the plain smooth so that his cavalry and some 200 scythed chariots could charge freely, but the flat ground made ideal footing for Alexander's tightly packed phalanx of spearmen. Alexander's light troops shot the chariot drivers and grabbed the reins, and the phalanx simply opened lanes to let the rest rumble through.

When a gap opened in the Persian line, Alexander packed his Companion cavalry into a giant wedge, rode at its very tip, and drove straight at Darius. Darius turned and fled in his chariot, and when his soldiers saw their king run, the Persian army collapsed. Alexander soon entered Babylon, Susa and Persepolis as master of the Persian Empire.

battle-of-hastings-the-norman-conquest-1.context_blurb:
In 1066 England had three would-be kings. Harold Godwinson was crowned in January; Harald Hardrada, the giant Viking king of Norway, invaded from the north; and William, Duke of Normandy, crossed the Channel from France. By Christmas William wore the crown, and his French-speaking lords spent a generation remaking England, down to the very words its people speak.

The whole story is told on the Bayeux Tapestry, nearly 70 metres long, which is not really a tapestry, since a tapestry is woven on a loom: it is a long strip of linen embroidered with coloured wool, like a medieval comic strip. After his victory William built Battle Abbey on the battlefield itself, and tradition says he set its high altar on the very spot where Harold fell. The fighting took place some seven miles inland from Hastings, near the town still called Battle.

On 25 September 1066 Harold crushed the Norse invaders at Stamford Bridge in the north, where Hardrada and Harold's own traitor brother Tostig both died; the Norsemen had come in about 300 ships, and the survivors needed only 24 to sail home. Three days later William landed on the south coast, and Harold's exhausted army had to force-march some 200 miles south to meet him. On 14 October the two armies met on a hill, and the English fought entirely on foot, Harold's housecarls locked shoulder to shoulder behind a wall of shields with two-handed battle-axes, against William's mounted knights and archers.

Omens and legends cling to that year. That spring a fiery star had blazed across the English sky, an omen of doom for Harold, and the Tapestry shows it above frightened onlookers marvelling at the star: it is the first known picture of Halley's Comet, which returns about every 76 years. Before Stamford Bridge, legend says, Hardrada demanded land of the English king, and a messenger offered him six feet of English ground, or a little more since he was so tall, meaning a grave. At Hastings, the story goes, a Norman minstrel named Taillefer rode out ahead of the army singing and juggling his sword in the air, then charged the English line alone and was the first man to die. In mid-battle a rumour spread that William was dead and his men began to run, so he tore off his helmet and rode along his lines to show his bare face, shouting that he lived. The English line held all day, until, the chronicler William of Poitiers says, the Normans used one trick twice: they pretended to flee, then wheeled round and cut down the English who chased them downhill. Some historians suspect the tale was polished to hide a real Norman rout.

William's whole claim rested on a broken oath: the Norman story was that Harold had earlier sworn to back William with his hands on holy relics kept in a chest, which made his taking of the crown a sacred crime and won William the Pope's banner. Everyone pictures Harold shot through the eye by an arrow, but the earliest account, the Carmen de Hastingae Proelio, written within months, has no arrow at all: four knights set upon him, one running him through with a lance and another beheading him. The famous arrow on the Tapestry may itself be a later repair. When the north of England rebelled in 1069 and 1070, William burned and starved whole villages, and in 1086 the Domesday Book, William's great survey of his kingdom, still labelled estate after estate there with one word: waste. By then Normans held some nine-tenths of England's land.

battle-of-iwo-jima.context_blurb:
In February 1945 United States Marines stormed Iwo Jima, a speck of volcanic rock in the Pacific about halfway between American bomber bases and Tokyo. About twenty thousand Japanese soldiers under General Tadamichi Kuribayashi waited for them underground. The five-week fight cost nearly 7,000 American lives, and most of the defenders died fighting.

Its Japanese name, Iōtō, means Sulfur Island, and the air really did stink of sulfur. It mattered because its airfields lay on the bomber route to Japan. The beaches were soft black volcanic ash, piled as deep as fifteen feet, so boots and vehicles sank, men slid backward with every step, and no one could dig a proper foxhole. American planners expected a five-day fight, but Kuribayashi had honeycombed the rock with 11 miles of tunnels, and the battle lasted 36 days.

On 23 February the Associated Press photographer Joe Rosenthal was atop Mount Suribachi as six Marines heaved a large flag aloft on a piece of pipe, and with only a split second he swung up his bulky camera and pressed the shutter blind, never looking through the viewfinder. That single frame, which he nearly missed, won the Pulitzer Prize. It was the second flag raised there that day: the first had been a small one that an officer wanted as a keepsake, so the battalion commander, Chandler Johnson, sent for a new flag and told them to bring a bigger one that Marines all over the island could see.

The island's value showed quickly: on 4 March, with fighting still raging, a damaged B-29 bomber named Dinah Might, a pun on dynamite, landed safely on its runway, the first of some 2,400 crippled bombers that would land there, saving an estimated 27,000 airmen. Admiral Chester Nimitz, reading the casualty lists, said that among the men who served on Iwo Jima, uncommon valour was a common virtue, words now carved on the Marine Corps War Memorial.

When two grenades landed in a trench among his comrades, Jack Lucas, a private first class of just seventeen, threw himself on top of both, pressing one deep into the soft ash; one failed to explode, the other blew up beneath him, and he survived to become the youngest Marine ever awarded the Medal of Honor. He had joined at fourteen by forging his mother's signature. Gunnery Sergeant John Basilone, already a national hero with the Medal of Honor from Guadalcanal, insisted on returning to combat, and on the first day at Iwo Jima, as he led his machine-gunners forward toward the airfield, a mortar shell burst beside him and killed him. Over the opening two days of the landings, six Navajo Code Talkers passed more than 800 messages with no mistakes at all, using a code built on their own language that the Japanese never cracked, and Major Howard Connor declared that without the Navajos the island would never have been taken.

Kuribayashi had banned wasteful banzai charges, and his written Courageous Battle Vows, found later in captured pillboxes, ended by ordering every man to take ten enemy lives before giving his own. That is why the tiny island cost so much. Yet he knew his enemy: as a young officer posted to America he had spent time at the University of Michigan and Harvard, and having seen American factories up close he warned his family that of all nations on earth, America was the one Japan should least want to fight. Most likely he died leading a final attack early on 26 March 1945, and the Americans never identified his body, because he had stripped off every badge of his rank before the charge.

battle-of-kursk.context_blurb:
In July 1943 Hitler launched his last great offensive in the East, Operation Citadel, against a huge bulge in the Soviet lines around the city of Kursk in western Russia. German Panther and Tiger tanks were to cut the bulge off from north and south. Instead the battle, the largest tank battle in history, ended Germany's hopes on the Eastern Front for good.

The Red Army was ready because Moscow knew the plan almost as soon as Hitler approved it, through the Lucy ring, Rudolf Roessler's spies in Switzerland, and through Britain's Ultra codebreakers reading German radio messages, so the Soviets spent weeks laying minefields and gun lines exactly where the pincers would strike.

At Prokhorovka on 12 July, General Pavel Rotmistrov's tanks were badly mauled, yet he assured Stalin that his men had knocked out 400 German tanks, 70 of them Tigers, by heroic ramming; when the historian Ben Wheatley studied Luftwaffe aerial photographs of the field, they showed German losses that day of about five tanks, against 250 or more Soviet ones. Many of Rotmistrov's tanks had charged into an anti-tank ditch dug by their own side. Hitler called off the offensive within days, and from then on the initiative belonged to the Red Army.

battle-of-marathon-490-bc-and-the-runner.context_blurb:
In 490 BC a Persian army sent by King Darius I came ashore at Marathon, about 26 miles from Athens, to punish the city for helping Greek rebels against Persia. Outnumbered, the Athenians had to face the world's greatest empire almost alone. Their victory became a founding memory of the West, and it gave a famous race its name.

Athens dispatched Pheidippides, a soldier and trained courier, to run over the mountains to Sparta, Greece's mightiest warrior city, and ask for help, and Herodotus says he covered about 150 miles in two days. On that run, Pheidippides said, the god Pan hailed him by name in the hills of Arcadia and complained that Athens neglected him; after the war the Athenians built Pan a shrine below the Acropolis. The Spartans agreed to help but would not march yet, because their religious law forbade them to set out before the moon grew full, and they arrived only after the battle.

Short of men to fill a front as wide as the Persian one at normal depth, the general Miltiades weakened his centre to just four ranks and packed his wings, and as the centre gave way on purpose, the strong wings swung in and surrounded the Persians. Before that, in the first charge at a run recorded for any Greek army, the Athenians raced across nearly a mile of plain, and the Persians, seeing men with no horsemen or archers rush an empire, thought they had gone mad. The 192 Athenians who fell were cremated and buried where they died, under a great earthen mound, the Soros, which still stands on the plain. When the defeated Persians ran for their boats, Cynaegirus, brother of the playwright Aeschylus, grabbed a ship's stern with his bare hands and tried to hold it back, and a Persian cut off his hand with an axe.

Winning did not end the danger: the Persian fleet rowed around Cape Sounion to seize the undefended city, so the weary hoplites force-marched about 25 miles back to Athens and lined the shore, and the Persians gave up and sailed home. That march of a whole army is the real marathon. The legend of a messenger who announced the victory and then fell dead is not in Herodotus at all; it first appears in Lucian, a satirist writing some 600 years later, whose runner cries that they have won and dies.

Robert Browning's 1879 poem Pheidippides retold that legend, and it moved the Frenchman Michel Bréal to propose a new Olympic race, the marathon, for the first modern Games. At those Games in Athens in 1896 the race was won by Spyridon Louis, a 23-year-old who earned his living as a water-carrier, hauling his father's mineral water into a city with no central water supply. The distance grew odd later: at the 1908 London Games the course was stretched to start at Windsor Castle and finish in front of the royal box, making it 26 miles 385 yards, now the standard.

battle-of-midway.context_blurb:
In June 1942, half a year after the attack on Pearl Harbor, Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto sent the Japanese navy against Midway, a tiny American atoll in the central Pacific, hoping to lure out and destroy the American carriers. Admiral Chester Nimitz was waiting for him. In a single day, 4 June, the balance of the Pacific war changed.

Navy codebreakers in Hawaii, led by Commander Joseph Rochefort, could read Japanese plans to strike a target called only AF but could not prove it was Midway, so Captain Wilfred Holmes had the island broadcast, uncoded, that its water-purifying plant had failed, and within a day the Japanese reported that AF was short of fresh water. AF was Midway, and the ambush was set. Nimitz wanted every carrier he had, so the USS Yorktown, badly damaged a month earlier at the Coral Sea, was patched up at Pearl Harbor in about 72 hours instead of months, and when she sailed for Midway, yard workers were still on board, finishing the job at sea. On the day, Torpedo Squadron 8 attacked in slow, outdated Devastators with no fighter cover, and Zeros shot down all fifteen planes; the only survivor, Ensign George Gay, hid in the ocean under a floating seat cushion from his plane and watched the carriers burn. By evening American dive-bombers had sunk all four Japanese fleet carriers, the Akagi, Kaga, Soryu and Hiryu, the same ships that had struck Pearl Harbor, and that single day turned the tide of the Pacific War.

Wade McClusky, leading the Enterprise dive-bomber group, reached the expected spot and found nothing but sea, yet low on fuel he kept searching, caught sight of a single destroyer, the Arashi, speeding north by herself, and guessed she was rushing to catch up with the carriers. He followed her straight to them. From about 10:22 the Dauntless dive-bombers fell out of the sky almost unopposed and within some five minutes wrecked the Akagi, Kaga and Soryu, because their flight decks were packed with planes being armed and refuelled, among bombs and fuel hoses, and a few hits set off chain explosions. Lieutenant Dick Best put his bomb into the Akagi that morning, and that afternoon his bomb helped finish the Hiryu, the last Japanese carrier still fighting, so he alone of all the war's pilots helped send two enemy carriers to the bottom in a single day. As the burning Hiryu sank, Rear Admiral Tamon Yamaguchi, among Japan's best carrier admirals, was offered a way off and instead stayed aboard to die with the ship beside her captain, Tomeo Kaku.

The deeper reasons for the victory took years to piece together. Yamamoto's armada was the biggest Japan ever assembled, with the giant battleship Yamato, but he scattered it in separate forces hundreds of miles apart, unable to support one another, so only Nagumo's four carriers ever fought and the Yamato saw no action. The carrier commander, Vice Admiral Chuichi Nagumo, had his reserve planes switched from bombs to torpedoes when American ships were sighted, and then, instead of launching a hasty attack, he delayed to land his returning Midway strike first, leaving his decks jammed with fuelled, armed aircraft at the worst possible moment. The slaughtered torpedo squadrons, though they hit nothing, had drawn the Zeros down to skim the waves, leaving the high sky open for the dive-bombers. Even the Arashi's dash had an American cause: she had lingered to depth-charge the American submarine Nautilus, and her race to catch up laid the trail McClusky followed.

battle-of-new-orleans-andrew-jackson.context_blurb:
In January 1815 a veteran British army, fresh from the wars against Napoleon, came to seize New Orleans, the port that controlled the lower Mississippi. General Andrew Jackson met it with a mixed army of U.S. regulars, Tennessee and Kentucky riflemen, Louisiana militia, free men of colour, Choctaw warriors and a band of pirates, all dug in behind earthworks across the road.

The British had tried to buy the pirate Jean Lafitte, whose smugglers hid in the swamps below the city, with $30,000 and a Royal Navy captaincy, but Lafitte handed their letters to the Americans and joined Jackson in exchange for a pardon. Jackson had once called Lafitte's men hellish banditti, but about 50 of them worked his cannons.

On 8 January Jackson's men shattered the British assault within some thirty minutes, the finest American victory on land in the whole war, yet no one on the field knew that the peace treaty ending the war had already been signed at Ghent, in Belgium, on Christmas Eve, two weeks before. News could cross the Atlantic no faster than a sailing ship. The victory still made Jackson, Old Hickory, a national hero on the road to the presidency.

battle-of-okinawa.context_blurb:
From April to June 1945 American soldiers and Marines fought for Okinawa, an island about 400 miles south of Japan's home islands, in the largest amphibious assault of the Pacific war. More than 100,000 Japanese defenders fought from caves and hills, kamikaze planes struck the American fleet offshore, and Okinawan civilians died in terrible numbers.

In April Japan sent the Yamato, the largest battleship ever built, toward the island on a one-way mission: to run herself aground on the beach and fight as a fixed fortress until she was destroyed. She never arrived. On 7 April American carrier planes struck her with bombs and torpedoes, and she rolled over and exploded, taking some 2,498 of her crew with her.

Over 12,000 Americans died in the 82 days of fighting, along with about a hundred thousand Japanese troops and tens of thousands of Okinawan civilians, perhaps as many as 150,000, and American planners used that toll to estimate what invading mainland Japan would cost, a reckoning that weighed on the decision to use the atomic bomb.
