battle-of-plataea-479-bc-persia-driven-o.context_blurb:
In 479 BC, a year after the Greek fleet beat the Persian navy at Salamis, the land armies of the Greek cities, led by Sparta under the regent Pausanias, met the Persian army that Xerxes had left behind under his general Mardonius. On a dusty plain in central Greece the Spartan heavy infantry crushed the Persians, Mardonius was killed, and Persia's attempt to conquer Greece was over.

Before the battle, when Pausanias ordered a pull-back, the Spartan officer Amompharetus refused to retreat from the enemy, lifted a large stone and set it at his commander's feet, saying that with this pebble he voted not to run from the strangers. Spartans voted with pebbles, so the boulder was a defiant joke and a vote at once.

After the victory Pausanias had Mardonius's cooks lay out the lavish Persian feast they had been preparing, set a plain Spartan supper beside it, and laughed that a man who ate this well must have been a fool to come and rob the Greeks of their poverty.

battle-of-salamis-480-bc-themistocles-na.context_blurb:
In 480 BC the Persian king Xerxes invaded Greece with an army far larger than any Greek city could face. The Athenians abandoned their city to him, and their commander, the clever, scheming Themistocles, staked everything on the fleet. The sea battle at Salamis, in a narrow strait west of Athens, became one of history's great upsets of the small over the large.

Xerxes had perhaps 600 to 800 warships against some 370 Greek triremes, so the Greeks lured his huge fleet into the cramped strait of Salamis, where its numbers counted for nothing and the nimble Greek ships could ram the crowded Persians one by one. Xerxes did not fight at sea: he watched from a throne on the hillside of Mount Aegaleus above the water, with scribes beside him to record the names of his bravest captains for reward, expecting to witness a victory.

The night before, Themistocles had sent Sicinnus, the Persian tutor of his own sons, to Xerxes with a lie: the Greeks were quarrelling and about to flee, so Xerxes should block the strait at once, and Xerxes sealed the narrows, trapping his own fleet inside. Themistocles had prepared Athens for this: when the Delphic oracle said only a wooden wall would save the city, and some read it as a ring of thorn bushes on the Acropolis, he argued that the wooden wall was their fleet of ships, and won the city over. He noted the oracle called the island divine Salamis, so the deaths it foretold would be the enemy's.

Queen Artemisia of Caria, the one woman captain in the Persian navy, escaped a pursuing Athenian by turning and sinking a friendly ship, and Xerxes, mistaking the wreck for a Greek one, exclaimed that his men had become women and his women men. Her bravest-looking act had been sinking one of his own.

battle-of-stalingrad.context_blurb:
From the summer of 1942 to February 1943 the German Sixth Army and the Red Army fought for Stalingrad, an industrial city on the lower Volga. It was the deadliest single battle of the Second World War and the turning point of the war in the East. From Stalingrad onward, the Germans were driven back toward Berlin.

The city had been called Tsaritsyn until 1925, when it was renamed for the Soviet Union's rising leader, Joseph Stalin, so taking or holding it became a point of personal honour for both Stalin and Hitler. As the Germans drove toward the Volga, Stalin issued Order No. 227 on 28 July 1942 to stop the Red Army falling back, and it is remembered for its battle cry: Not one step back! The order posted armed blocking detachments behind the Soviet lines with orders to shoot on the spot any Red Army man who retreated without orders, and in three months they executed about 1,000 men and sent 24,000 to penal battalions. Soviet soldiers fought heroically, and a murderous regime drove them on; both are true.

In the ruined city the fighting shrank to single rooms, cellars and stairwells that changed hands again and again, and the Germans called it Rattenkrieg, the War of the Rats. About thirty Soviet soldiers took a four-storey block of flats, ringed it with wire and mines and held it for some two months; it is still called Pavlov's House, after the sergeant, Yakov Pavlov, who led the defence. At the city's southern edge, about 50 Soviet defenders held a massive steel-and-concrete grain elevator against three German divisions, fighting floor by floor. Vasily Zaitsev, the Red Army's star sniper, had some 225 kills to his name within five weeks, a skill he had learned as a boy hunting deer and wolves in the Ural Mountains. His fame grew into a legend of a duel with a German marksman sent to hunt him, later the subject of several films, but the historian Antony Beevor, checking the Russian Defence Ministry archives, concluded that the duel never happened and was a Soviet propaganda invention.

Operation Uranus, the Soviet counterstroke of 19 November, did not strike the Germans head-on: its pincers smashed through the weaker Romanian armies guarding the flanks and met near Kalach, trapping about 290,000 Axis troops in the city. Hermann Göring promised Hitler that the Luftwaffe would supply the trapped army by air with 300 tons a day, but over 71 days the airlift averaged only about 120 tons, and it cost more than 266 transport planes.

On 30 January 1943 Hitler made the trapped commander, Friedrich Paulus, a field marshal, a rank no German had ever surrendered in, as a hint that Paulus should shoot himself, but Paulus surrendered the next morning, telling his aide he was not going to do them such a favour. Of some 91,000 Germans taken prisoner, only about 5,000 to 6,000 ever came home. In captivity Paulus turned against the Nazis, testified for the prosecution at Nuremberg, and refused to call Hitler by his title, dismissing him as the Bohemian corporal.

battle-of-the-atlantic-and-u-boats.context_blurb:
The Battle of the Atlantic was the longest campaign of the Second World War, lasting from its first day, 3 September 1939, to Germany's surrender in May 1945. German submarines, the U-boats, hunted the merchant ships that carried food, fuel, weapons and soldiers from America to Britain, and for three years they sank ships faster than Allied yards could build them.

Winston Churchill later confessed in his memoirs that nothing in the whole war truly frightened him except the U-boat peril, the danger that submarines would cut the Atlantic lifeline and starve Britain into surrender. To survive, merchant ships sailed not alone but in a convoy, dozens of them packed in columns and ringed by warships, since escorts could protect only ships that kept together. The Germans answered with wolfpacks, many U-boats swarming one convoy at night.

The U-boats struck early: in October 1939 Günther Prien crept U-47 past sunken blockships into Scapa Flow, the British fleet's chief anchorage, and within thirteen minutes sank the battleship HMS Royal Oak. Their richest hunting ground was the Black Pit, the mid-Atlantic gap about 500 miles across, beyond the reach of land-based planes, where no aircraft could watch over the convoys. It closed only in May 1943, when very-long-range bombers and escort carriers could at last cover the whole crossing.

Codebreaking helped turn the battle: in May 1941 British escorts forced U-110 to the surface, a boarding party under Sub-lieutenant David Balme climbed down into the dark hull, and they carried out an Enigma machine, unharmed, with its codebooks, helping Bletchley Park read U-boat signals and steer convoys away from waiting wolfpacks.

battle-of-the-bulge.context_blurb:
On 16 December 1944 Hitler launched his last great offensive in the West, striking without warning through the snowbound, thinly held Ardennes forest of Belgium. For six bitter weeks the Americans fought back in the largest battle the U.S. Army has ever fought, and the offensive used up Germany's last reserves.

The German breakthrough pushed a deep dent into the Allied front, and because of that swelling shape on the war maps, American soldiers called the fight the Battle of the Bulge. At Bastogne, where American paratroopers of the 101st Airborne were surrounded, the Germans sent a written demand for an honourable surrender, and Brigadier General Anthony McAuliffe typed a one-word reply: NUTS! When the German envoy was puzzled, an American colonel explained that it meant go to hell.

Hitler, who codenamed the attack Watch on the Rhine, aimed to smash through Belgium and seize the port of Antwerp, which would have choked Allied supplies and split the British and American armies apart. English-speaking German commandos in American uniforms drove captured jeeps behind the lines, so at checkpoints GIs quizzed each other on American pop culture, such as the name of Mickey Mouse's girlfriend, trivia any homegrown American knew and a disguised German might miss. Otto Skorzeny led the commandos.

On 17 December SS soldiers led by Joachim Peiper machine-gunned about 84 unarmed American prisoners in a field at a crossroads called Baugnez, outside Malmedy, the largest massacre of American soldiers in Europe, and more than 50 survived only by falling down and playing dead, then running once the SS moved on. With fog grounding the supply planes, General George Patton had his chaplain, James O'Neill, compose a prayer for good weather, and copies went out on cards to his men; the weather broke on 23 December, supply drops and fighter-bombers returned, and Patton pinned a Bronze Star on the chaplain.

On 19 December Patton astonished a conference of generals by vowing to attack within two days, and he did what generals call impossible: he wheeled the entire Third Army, a quarter of a million men with their tanks, 90 degrees from facing east to driving north in the dead of winter. His tanks broke through to Bastogne on 26 December, and by late January the German attack had been beaten back.

battle-of-the-coral-sea.context_blurb:
In May 1942 Japan sent an invasion force toward Port Moresby, on the southern coast of New Guinea, to threaten Australia. American codebreakers saw it coming, and American and Australian ships moved to meet it in the Coral Sea. The Americans lost the carrier Lexington, but the Japanese turned back, and two of their big carriers were too damaged or depleted to fight at Midway a month later.

It was the first naval battle in history in which the opposing fleets never saw or fired directly on each other: carrier aircraft did all the fighting, striking ships far over the horizon, and from then on the aircraft carrier, not the big-gun battleship, ruled the sea. The age of fleets slugging it out with cannon at close range was over.

On 7 May Lieutenant Commander Robert Dixon led the Lexington's dive-bombers onto the Japanese carrier Shoho, the first enemy carrier the United States sank in the war, and he radioed back: Scratch one flat top!

battle-of-the-somme.context_blurb:
The Battle of the Somme, fought across the chalk country of northern France from July to November 1916, was the bloodiest campaign in British history. Sir Douglas Haig launched it with the French to relieve their army at Verdun. When it died out in the autumn mud, the front had moved only a few miles, at a cost of about a million casualties on both sides.

Many of the dead belonged to Pals battalions, raised on a simple promise: men who lived, worked or grew up together could enlist together and fight shoulder to shoulder, so a single bad morning could wipe out a whole community's young men. On 1 July the Accrington Pals attacked the village of Serre with about 720 men and lost 585 in roughly half an hour, and the British Army suffered about 57,470 killed and wounded, its worst day ever.

Two minutes before the attack, British tunnellers fired the Lochnagar mine, 60,000 pounds of explosive beneath the German position at La Boisselle, and the blast was said to be the loudest man-made sound in history up to that time. It left a vast crater, still the largest ever made by war, which survives today as a memorial.

battle-of-tours-charles-martel-732.context_blurb:
In the early 700s the armies of the young Islamic empire swept across North Africa, crushed the Visigothic kingdom of Spain within a few years, and pushed north over the Pyrenees into Gaul, the land of the Franks. In 732 Charles, the leader of the Franks, not a king but the mayor of the palace who held the real power, met them in battle near Tours.

Chroniclers were so struck by the way he crushed that advance that they nicknamed him Martel, from the Latin Martellus, the Hammer, and the name stuck. His grandson was Charlemagne, crowned emperor in 800.

The Frankish infantry stood like a wall through the day while al-Ghafiqi's horsemen charged again and again, until a rumour swept the Muslim camp that the Franks were looting their baggage and plunder, and so many men rushed back to protect it that the line collapsed. Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi was killed trying to rally his men, and Arab sources call the battle the Pavement of the Martyrs. Historians still debate how decisive it was, but later Europe remembered it as the stand that kept Gaul from going the way of Spain.

battle-of-verdun.context_blurb:
From February to December 1916, along the Meuse River in eastern France, German and French armies fought the Battle of Verdun, the longest battle of the First World War. The ring of old forts around Verdun meant so much to France that its army would defend them at any cost, and nearly 700,000 men were killed, wounded or missing.

Fort Douaumont, France's mightiest stronghold at Verdun, fell on 25 February, only the fifth day, without the Germans firing a single shot: a small raiding party slipped in through an unguarded passage and captured its surprised garrison of about 57 older reservists. General Philippe Pétain ordered the line held, and the French defenders took up the vow that became the soul of the battle: They shall not pass!

With the railways into Verdun cut, France supplied the whole battle along one narrow road from Bar-le-Duc, the Sacred Way, and at its June peak one lorry went by every fourteen seconds, day and night. That month the defenders of Fort Vaux, under Major Sylvain Raynal, battled room by room through its tunnels, parched and choking on gas, cut off from every telephone, and Raynal sent out his final message by his last carrier pigeon, Le Vaillant, which delivered it though mortally gassed. The pigeon was later awarded the Legion of Honour, and Raynal, who surrendered on 7 June, was honoured even by his captors.

Erich von Falkenhayn, Germany's army chief, had picked Verdun for exactly that reason: he did not really want the town, he wanted the killing, and he summed up his aim as to bleed France white. About 300,000 men died there.

beethoven-the-deaf-composer-and-the-nint.context_blurb:
Ludwig van Beethoven (1770 to 1827) was a German composer who moved to Vienna as a young man and changed Western music for good, carrying it from the classical world of Haydn and Mozart into the Romantic age. In his late twenties he began to lose his hearing, and for his last ten years he was almost completely deaf. He kept composing, and wrote some of his greatest music without hearing it.

His Fifth Symphony, finished in 1808, opens with four notes that may be the best-known phrase in all music: short, short, short, long, da-da-da-DUM. At the premiere of his Ninth Symphony in 1824 he was so deaf that he went on conducting after the last chord, unaware that the hall behind him had risen to cheer, until the young singer Caroline Unger turned him around to face the crowd so he could see the applause he could not hear.

Until then a symphony belonged to the orchestra alone, but in the last movement of the Ninth Beethoven added a full singing chorus, setting Friedrich Schiller's poem Ode to Joy, the first major symphony ever to do so. The melody of that Ode to Joy is now the official anthem of the European Union.

That night, 7 May 1824, Beethoven flung his arms about and called out the tempos, but Michael Umlauf, the actual conductor, had warned the musicians to watch only him, and by the end Beethoven had fallen several bars behind the music. The Fifth's short-short-short-long rhythm matches the Morse code for the letter V, dot-dot-dot-dash, so in the Second World War the BBC broadcast those four notes as the signal of the V for Victory campaign. Going deaf in his forties, he found a way to feel his piano: he set a wooden stick on the piano's soundboard and bit down on its other end, clenching it between his teeth so the vibrations carried through his jawbone.

In 1802, at Heiligenstadt outside Vienna, the 31-year-old wrote a despairing letter to his brothers, never sent and found only after his death, admitting he had nearly taken his own life and that only his art had held him back, because he could not leave the world before producing all the music he felt called to write. Almost everyone has heard that Beethoven called the Fifth's opening fate knocking at the door, but the line comes from his secretary Anton Schindler, who is now known to have forged entries in Beethoven's notebooks, so historians doubt it.

On his deathbed in March 1827 he was told that his London publisher's present of fine wine had come, and his last words, those at his bedside said, were: Pity, pity, too late! A romantic legend gives him a Latin farewell telling his friends to applaud because the comedy was finished, but Anselm Hüttenbrenner, a friend at his bedside, rejected that story in 1860, because he had not been in the room for the religious rite the remark was said to follow. Beethoven wanted doctors to study his illnesses once he was gone, and in 2023 geneticists read his DNA from verified locks of hair and found a genetic tendency toward liver disease and a hepatitis B infection, which together with his heavy drinking probably wrecked his liver and killed him.

bell-edison-and-the-late-century-inventi.context_blurb:
In the last quarter of the 1800s, a few American inventors turned invention itself into an industry. Alexander Graham Bell, a Scottish-born teacher of the deaf working in Boston, carried a person's voice along a wire. Thomas Edison, a mostly self-taught Midwesterner, built a research laboratory in New Jersey that poured out patents, and then fought a bitter, dirty war over how electricity should reach American homes.

One night in March 1876 Bell was testing his new telephone in Boston when acid splashed onto his clothes. He called out through the instrument, telling Mr. Watson to come here because he wanted to see him, and his assistant Thomas Watson, listening in another room, heard every word: the first full sentence ever spoken by telephone. A year later it was Edison's turn to astonish the world. In 1877 his mechanic John Kruesi built, in about thirty hours, a phonograph that stored sound on tinfoil, and to test it Edison recited the nursery rhyme about Mary and her little lamb, which the machine then spoke back to him. Edison ran his laboratory like a factory. He vowed to turn out a minor invention roughly every week and a half and a major one twice a year, and the newspapers, dazzled by his lab in Menlo Park, New Jersey, nicknamed him the Wizard of Menlo Park. In the end his name went on 1,093 American patents, still among the most for any one person.

His most famous hunt was for a practical electric light. A bulb needs a filament, the thin thread that glows inside it, and Edison's team tried more than 1,600 materials before a cotton thread, charred into carbon, glowed for about thirteen and a half hours on 21 October 1879. Charring the cotton made it resist the current, so it glowed instead of burning up. Half a day of light was no use in a home, so the search went on. The winner was carbonized bamboo: charred bamboo fibres made a tough filament that lasted beyond 1,200 hours and lit American houses for years. Edison did not invent the glowing bulb from nothing, but he built the first long-lasting one, plus the wires and generators to light a whole city. He had no faith in sudden flashes of genius: invention, he said, and confirmed in a letter of 1927, was one percent inspiration and the other ninety-nine percent perspiration.

Then came the War of the Currents. Edison backed direct current, or DC, which was safe but lost strength over any long distance. The industrialist George Westinghouse and the inventor Nikola Tesla championed alternating current, or AC, which flips direction many times a second, so transformers could step it up to high voltage for long trips over thin wires and step it down again for safe use at home. AC won; it is the current in every wall socket today. To make the public dread it, Edison's camp invented a creepy verb for killing someone with electricity: to be Westinghoused, named after the businessman who backed the rival current. Westinghouse struck back at Chicago's World's Fair of 1893, whose lighting contract he had won by underbidding Edison's people, and when over a hundred thousand bulbs blazed there on AC at once, the glowing fairgrounds became known as the White City. The display proved AC safe.

The fight had already turned ugly. On 30 July 1888 at Columbia College, Edison's man Harold Brown shocked a dog in front of electricians and reporters: the animal lived through 1,000 volts of direct current, then died when Brown switched to alternating current at just 330 volts. The rigged show was meant to brand AC a killer even at low voltage. In August 1890 the first electric chair, running on AC, was used on a condemned man named William Kemmler, and the job was botched so badly that he was still breathing after the first jolt. Westinghouse, who had fought to keep his current out of executions, said bitterly that an ax would have done a better job. The current war was effectively over by the mid-1890s, when AC from Niagara Falls carried power 26 miles to Buffalo. A popular story says Edison electrocuted Topsy, a circus elephant, to scare people away from AC, but historians reject it: Topsy was killed at Coney Island in 1903, after Edison had left his electric company and nearly a decade after the war was over, and Edison's film company only recorded her death.

benedict-arnold-s-treason.context_blurb:
Few generals in George Washington's Continental Army were bolder than Benedict Arnold during the American Revolution. He fought in the invasion of Canada and was badly wounded in the leg leading a charge at Saratoga. Yet by 1780 he had begun the plot that turned his name into the American word for traitor.

Arnold felt cheated by slow promotion and snubs from Congress, and he was deep in debt. Placed in command at West Point, the fort that controlled the Hudson River, he secretly agreed to surrender it to the British in return for 20,000 pounds and the rank of general in their army. Losing that fort would have handed the British the great river.

The plot fell apart by chance. Near Tarrytown, New York, three militiamen, John Paulding, Isaac Van Wart and David Williams, stopped the British courier, Major John Andre, and when they searched him, the West Point plans turned up folded inside his boot. Andre offered them a bribe to let him go, and they refused. He asked to die a soldier's death before a firing squad, but on 2 October 1780, aged 29, he was hanged at Tappan. Arnold escaped to the British, collected only about 6,000 of his promised pounds, and died in London in 1801, trusted by no one.

benedictine-monasticism-monastery-life.context_blurb:
In the early 500s, as the old Roman world broke apart, an Italian named Benedict of Nursia wrote a short rulebook for men who wanted to live together in prayer. His Rule ran Benedictine monasteries across Europe for a thousand years, and those houses of monks copied its books, farmed its land and fed its travellers.

Around the year 500, young Benedict left the city behind to look for God in the wild, living three years as a hermit in a cliffside cave at Subiaco. Pope Gregory the Great, who wrote the only real life of Benedict, tells how a monk called Romanus kept the young hermit alive by secretly letting bread down to him on a rope from the monastery above. About 529 Benedict climbed to a mountaintop in the south of Italy, pulled down an old pagan temple to Apollo that stood on the summit, and on its site raised Monte Cassino, the cradle of the Benedictine order.

The Rule he wrote there runs to 73 chapters, and it opens with a single quiet command, Listen: the monk is told to bend the ear of his heart to his master's teaching. Its whole spirit fits into a two-word Latin motto, ora et labora, which means pray and work, and Benedict split the day into roughly three parts, about eight hours of prayer, eight of work and eight of sleep, so that no monk lived by prayer alone or by labour alone. His reason for filling the day was blunt: idleness, he wrote, was the soul's enemy, so every waking hour belonged to work or holy reading. Chapter 53 orders that every traveller at the gate, rich or poor, be received as Christ himself, because Christ promised to say that he was a stranger and they welcomed him. The Rule was humane rather than harsh. Benedict admitted he had read that wine is not proper for monks, yet he granted every monk a daily hemina of wine, roughly a quarter-litre or half a pint, and the abbot could grant more on hot days or after heavy labour. Chapter 7 lays out twelve steps of humility, each harder than the last; the ninth tells a monk to keep silent until someone speaks to him, and the tenth tells him not to be quick to laugh.

For close to ten centuries monks served as the librarians of Europe, and in the scriptorium they copied out not only the Bible and the Church Fathers but the pagan classics of ancient Greece and Rome, writings the Church could easily have let die. Almost every book that survived to the age of printing passed through their hands, and the work was punishing: it strained the eyes and bent the back, as one monk complained. In the eleventh century a weary English scribe scribbled a tiny prayer in his own Old English tongue into a margin, God helpe minum handum, meaning God help my hands. Around 800, Irish monks painted the Book of Kells, a great copy of the Gospels so crowded with tiny woven patterns and beasts that Gerald of Wales, seeing such a book in the 1180s, called it the work not of men but of angels. Monks guarded their precious books with curses. One, written about 1172 into a Bible in Germany, wished that a book thief might die, be roasted in a frying pan, be seized by fever and the falling sickness, and be broken on the wheel and hanged. Women painted books too. In 2019 scientists spotted more than a hundred flecks of ultramarine, a blue ground from Afghan lapis lazuli and dearer than gold, in the crusted tartar of a German nun buried around 1100: she had licked her brush to a fine point again and again while painting manuscripts.

Legends grew around the monks as well. Dom Pierre Perignon, a real Benedictine who tended the wines of Champagne at Hautvillers Abbey in the 1600s, never cried out that he was drinking the stars; that line was invented for a 19th-century advertisement long after his death, and he did not invent sparkling champagne either.

benjamin-franklin-inventor-diplomat-foun.context_blurb:
Benjamin Franklin was born in Boston in 1706, the son of a candlemaker, and ran away as a teenager to seek his fortune in Philadelphia. He became a rich printer, a world-famous scientist, an inventor and a diplomat, and he signed the founding documents of the United States. He was also the founder most willing to laugh at himself.

He arrived in Philadelphia in 1723 broke and starving, bought three great rolls at a bakery, and marched up the street with one roll under each arm while eating the third. A girl named Deborah Read watched from her father's doorway and thought he looked absurd. Later she married him.

Franklin made his money in print. From 1732 he wrote a best-selling almanac under the name of a folksy invented author, Richard Saunders, called Poor Richard, so the book became Poor Richard's Almanack. Many of its sayings are still everyday English. In 1754 he published America's first political cartoon, a snake chopped into eight pieces, each standing for a colony, above the words Join, or Die. An old belief held that a cut snake could live again if its pieces were joined before sunset, so the divided colonies would die unless they united. Franklin also loved inventing. Tired of switching between reading glasses and distance glasses, he had both lenses cut in half and set in one frame, distance above and reading below, and his double spectacles are what we call bifocals. In 1761 he built a musical instrument of 37 glass bowls, nested one inside another and turned by a foot pedal, played with wet fingertips on the turning rims, and he called it the armonica, from the Italian word for harmony. Mozart and Beethoven wrote music for it.

His fame rested on electricity. In June 1752, to test his hunch that lightning was a giant electric spark, Franklin and William, his grown son, sent a silk kite up into a thunderstorm, a metal key hanging from the bottom of its wet string. When Franklin moved his knuckle near the key, a spark jumped across to it, proof that the storm's lightning was electricity. He turned the discovery into a life-saver. His lightning rod, a pointed metal rod on the roof joined to a wire, catches a strike and carries the electricity safely down into the ground, so the building never catches fire. Some of the first went up on Independence Hall. Later, as America's envoy in Paris, Franklin became a star. Instead of the powdered wig a French gentleman put on, he went about in a plain fur cap, and the French loved it so much that fashionable women piled up their hair in a tall style named after him.

Franklin never patented his inventions, explaining in his Autobiography that since we all benefit from the inventions of others, we should be glad to serve others freely with our own. As a diplomat he won his greatest prize on 6 February 1778, when he talked France into an alliance with the young United States. France sent money, weapons and above all a powerful navy, and the French fleet tipped the war toward an American victory.

At the Constitutional Convention in 1787 the old man sat through months of uncertain debate facing the half-sun carved into the chair where George Washington presided. As the delegates signed, Franklin said he had often wondered whether that sun was rising or setting, and that at last he was happy to know it was rising and not going down. In his last years he turned openly against slavery, which he had once tolerated, and led the Pennsylvania Abolition Society. His final public act, a few weeks before his death in April 1790, was to sign the society's petition urging the first Congress to end slavery and the slave trade and so remove a deep inconsistency from the American character.

benjamin-franklin-science-and-the-enligh.context_blurb:
Benjamin Franklin, born in Boston in 1706, was a printer, writer, scientist, inventor and Founding Father. His experiments with electricity made him famous across Europe, and his practical gadgets solved ordinary problems. He belongs to the Enlightenment, the age that trusted reason and experiment to improve human life, and he tested ideas with his own hands.

Arriving in Philadelphia in October 1723, broke and hungry at seventeen, he bought three big rolls and marched up Market Street with one tucked under each arm, eating the third. A girl who would one day be his wife saw him and thought he looked ridiculous. He had been inventing for years by then. At about eleven, keen to swim faster, he shaped two oval boards about ten inches long, cut a thumb hole in each, and wore them as paddles on his hands. They let him push more water, though they tired his wrists.

His inventions came from his own needs. Fed up with changing glasses whenever he looked from a book to the far side of a room, he ordered both lenses split and fitted together in one frame, the far-seeing half above and the reading half below: bifocals, which still work that way. His most famous work was with electricity. In 1752 he sent a silk kite up into a storm, a metal key fixed to its wet string, while he held a dry silk ribbon under shelter; as he brought his knuckle near, a spark leapt from the key. The loose threads of the twine also stood on end, pushing each other apart, so the storm had charged the key: lightning was electricity. He used the discovery to invent the lightning rod, sharp iron points on a roof that draw the charge from a storm and carry it down a wire into the ground. Tall buildings still wear them.

Paintings love to show a forked bolt striking his kite, but that never happened; the kite only soaked up charge from the cloud. A real bolt would almost certainly have killed him, and in 1753 Georg Wilhelm Richmann was killed trying a similar experiment. Franklin was a writer before he was a scientist. At sixteen, barred from writing for his brother James's paper, the New-England Courant, he invented a sharp-tongued, middle-aged widow named Silence Dogood and slid her letters, in disguised handwriting, under the shop door at night. James printed fourteen before discovering the author and flying into a rage. Of all his inventions, Franklin said the glass armonica, a row of spinning glass bowls played with wet fingertips, gave him the greatest personal satisfaction. In 1754, as war with the French broke out on the frontier, he printed a snake cut into eight pieces, each marked with a colony's initials, under the caption JOIN, or DIE. Folk belief said a cut snake could live again if joined before sunset; a divided America would die, a united one would live.

When his iron fireplace, the Franklin stove, heated rooms better than an open hearth, the governor of Pennsylvania offered a patent, but Franklin refused it so that anyone could copy the design for free. He believed that since we enjoy the inventions of others, we should serve others with ours. He also coined the plain English words battery, charge, conductor, positive and negative to describe what he was finding, and the Royal Society gave him its Copley Medal in 1753. Other electrical words came later, each named after a different scientist. As colonial postmaster, he wondered why British mail ships crossed the Atlantic two weeks slower than American ones, and his whaling cousin Timothy Folger explained that the British sailed against a strong, warm current, which Franklin charted in 1769 and named the Gulf Stream. He later measured it with a thermometer and found it warmer than the sea on either side.

The French statesman Turgot praised him in a Latin line that sculptors later cut into busts of Franklin. It said that Franklin had snatched the thunderbolt from heaven and, later, the scepter from tyrants, for taming lightning and helping to topple a king. His conscience grew too. As a young printer Franklin had owned enslaved people and run ads for slave sales, but in 1787 the Pennsylvania abolition society chose him as its president. His last public act before he died in 1790 was signing the society's petition calling on the first Congress to abolish slavery.

berlin-blockade-airlift.context_blurb:
After the Second World War the victors carved defeated Germany into four zones, run by the Americans, the British, the French and the Soviets, and they divided Berlin, the old capital, the same way, although the whole city lay far inside the Soviet zone. In 1948 the Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin set out to squeeze the Western Allies out of their half of Berlin. For almost a year their pilots answered him from the sky.

On 24 June 1948, without firing a shot, Stalin's forces sealed every road, railway and canal leading into West Berlin, trapping two million people. The city had food for about 36 days and coal for roughly six weeks. The Allies would neither fight their way in by land nor leave the Berliners to Stalin. Instead they chose something never tried on such a scale: they would supply the whole city, every meal and every lump of coal, by air. The British called their part Operation Plainfare, while the Americans named theirs Operation Vittles, after a folksy old soldiers' word for grub.

One American pilot, Lieutenant Gail Halvorsen, wandered over to the airfield fence where hungry German children were watching the planes. He had only two sticks of gum to give the whole crowd. To his amazement the children did not fight over it; they broke the gum into tiny pieces to share, and all they really wanted was to hear about his plane. Moved, he promised to drop sweets for them the next day. So that they could tell his plane from the hundreds roaring in, he said he would give his wings a wiggle as he came in to land, and the children nicknamed him Uncle Wiggly Wings. To keep the chocolate and gum from smashing, he and his crew tied it to little parachutes that they had sewn out of handkerchiefs and pushed them out of the flare chute as they came in. The candy drops became Operation Little Vittles.

The pace was astonishing. At the airlift's height a fully loaded plane touched down about every 45 seconds, day and night, and in the busiest weeks of spring 1949 the gap shrank to about 30 seconds. Not every child could reach the crowds. A girl named Mercedes Simon, who lived near Tempelhof airport, wrote to Halvorsen asking him to drop her candy where he saw her family's white chickens in the yard. He never spotted them, so he posted her sweets instead, and in 1972 she invited him to dinner.

Keeping a city alive took more than food. Of the 4,500 tons the city needed each day, about 3,475 tons was coal, to heat homes and run the power plants, against roughly 1,500 tons of food. On 13 August 1948, Black Friday, a cloudburst over Tempelhof caused a crash, a burst tyre and a plane off the runway while dozens more circled blind. General William Tunner, who had just taken command, then ran the airlift like an assembly line: every pilot got just one shot at landing, with no second attempt, and a pilot who missed flew home with his load rather than circling. Some obstacles were simply removed. When two Soviet-run radio towers stood in the flight path of the new Tegel airport, the French general Jean Ganeval had them blown up, and legend says that when a furious Soviet officer asked how he could do such a thing, Ganeval answered, With dynamite! On 15 and 16 April 1949, in the Easter Parade, the airlift landed almost 13,000 tons of cargo in a single day without a single crash, and after that Stalin could no longer believe his blockade would ever starve West Berlin into surrender. He lifted it on 12 May 1949.

berlin-wall-tear-down-this-wall.context_blurb:
In August 1961 East German soldiers strung barbed wire across Berlin to stop East Germans escaping to the West. It soon became a concrete wall with watchtowers, guard dogs, a cleared death strip and orders to shoot anyone who tried to climb over, and East Germans died attempting it. For 28 years the Berlin Wall stood as the symbol of a Europe split by the Cold War.

On 12 June 1987, with the Brandenburg Gate at his back and bulletproof glass in front of him, President Ronald Reagan spoke to a West Berlin crowd about a hundred yards from the Wall. He spoke straight to the Soviet leader. If Mikhail Gorbachev truly sought peace, Reagan declared, he should open this gate, and then came the ringing challenge: Mr. Gorbachev should tear down this wall.

Reagan's own officials had fought that line. The State Department and the National Security Council sent seven drafts with the challenge cut out, warning that it would embarrass Gorbachev, and Howard Baker, his chief of staff, thought it unpresidential. Reagan overruled every one of them and kept the line, telling his speechwriters simply that he thought they would leave it in. The Wall itself fell on 9 November 1989, two and a half years later.

bernini-baroque-sculpture.context_blurb:
Gian Lorenzo Bernini (1598 to 1680) was the sculptor and architect who shaped Baroque Rome. Trained by his sculptor father, he was carving for popes and cardinals in his early twenties, and he could make hard marble look like soft skin, damp hair, rippling cloth or living leaves. His fountains, churches and statues still fill the city.

His early masterpiece, Apollo and Daphne, carved out of one marble block between 1622 and 1625, shows the nymph Daphne at the instant she turns into a laurel tree as she flees from Apollo. Paper-thin laurel leaves and twigs burst out of her marble fingertips, carved so delicately that they seem to be growing as you watch. He paused partway through to carve his famous David.

Bernini was also a master of stage effects. For the little Cornaro Chapel in Rome he carved the Ecstasy of Saint Teresa between 1647 and 1652: the Spanish mystic Teresa of Avila sinks back on a cloud as a smiling angel holds a golden arrow, just as Teresa described the vision in her own writings. Above the statue he hid a real window, so that daylight pours down onto gilded bronze rays behind the figures and the white marble seems lit from heaven itself.

bessemer-process-and-the-age-of-steel.context_blurb:
Henry Bessemer was an English inventor who, in the 1850s, found a way to make strong steel quickly, cheaply and in huge amounts. Before him, steel was a costly specialty metal for blades and fine tools, and most building was done in brittle cast iron or softer wrought iron. His process turned steel into the metal of rails, bridges, ships and skyscrapers.

Bessemer's idea was to blast cold air up through a vessel of molten iron. His workers were sure cold air would freeze the metal into a useless lump. Instead the iron got hotter still, and flames roared out of the vessel, which Bessemer called a veritable volcano. The air was burning out the carbon and silicon mixed into the molten iron, and those elements caught fire and became the fuel, so the blast heated the metal instead of cooling it.

Cheap steel soon proved its worth on the railways, where soft iron rails could wear out in under six months on busy stretches. In 1862 one Bessemer steel rail was laid in an English line beside ordinary iron rails, carrying the same trains. By the time that single steel rail finally needed replacing, the iron rails next to it had been replaced eighteen times over. Steel rails carried heavier engines and longer trains for decades, and they rapidly took over the railways.

betsy-ross-the-first-flag-legend.context_blurb:
Betsy Ross was a real flag-maker in Philadelphia during the American Revolution who sewed flags for the Pennsylvania navy. A beloved story says she also made the very first Stars and Stripes. Her grandson first told it in public almost a century later, and no record from 1776 confirms it, so historians treat it as a legend.

In the story, a small committee came to the young widow's sewing shop in June 1776, and among the visitors was General George Washington himself, along with the financier Robert Morris and Colonel George Ross, the uncle of Betsy's late husband. The tale even says she knew Washington already, because their pews at Christ Church stood side by side.

When the men showed her a design with six-pointed stars, the legend goes, Betsy folded a scrap of paper, made one snip with her scissors, and opened it to reveal a perfect five-pointed star. The committee is said to have chosen her star for the new flag. It is the most loved detail of the tale, though no one at the time wrote it down.

bill-of-rights-first-ten-amendments.context_blurb:
In 1791 the new American republic added ten amendments to its new Constitution, known together as the Bill of Rights. They list freedoms that the federal government may not take away, from free speech to a fair trial, and Americans still quote them every day. Winning them took a hard political fight, and their story runs through ordinary people who used them.

The First Amendment, which opens by declaring that Congress shall make no law, protects five freedoms in a single sentence: freedom of religion, of speech and of the press, plus the right to peaceful assembly and to petition the government. The Fourth bans unreasonable searches and seizures, so an official who wants to go through your home and papers normally needs a judge's warrant, granted only for good cause. The Fifth says no one can be made to testify against himself, which is why a witness who stays silent rather than convict himself is said to be pleading the Fifth. The Eighth, the shortest of all, bans excessive bail, excessive fines and cruel and unusual punishments in one sentence.

George Mason of Virginia, author of his own state's Declaration of Rights, refused to sign the Constitution in 1787 because it had no bill of rights, saying he would sooner chop off his right hand than sign it in its present form. Ordinary Americans later made those rights real. Clarence Earl Gideon, too poor to hire a lawyer, wrote to the Supreme Court from prison in pencil, and in 1963 the justices ruled unanimously that the state must pay for a lawyer for any defendant who cannot afford one. In December 1965 three Des Moines students, Christopher Eckhardt and the Tinker children, Mary Beth and John, wore black armbands to school to protest the Vietnam War. When they were suspended, they sued, and in 1969 the Supreme Court backed them 7 to 2, ruling that students do not lose their free speech at the schoolhouse gate. Even the paper itself has adventures. Washington ordered fourteen handwritten originals, and when North Carolina's, which a Union soldier carried off in 1865 and sold for five dollars, turned up 138 years later with a dealer asking five million, FBI agents posed as buyers and seized it in a sting.

The deeper story is political. The Anti-Federalists, who feared the new government would crush individual liberty, demanded a bill of rights in return for their support, and the Massachusetts Compromise, worked out by John Hancock and Samuel Adams, showed the way: ratify now, amend at once. Oddly, James Madison, who wrote the amendments and drove them through Congress, had first dismissed written rights as mere parchment barriers, which angry majorities in every state had trampled. He changed his mind to win ratification, and he had promised amendments to beat James Monroe for a seat in the House. Franklin Roosevelt set the first Bill of Rights Day for 15 December 1941, the 150th anniversary, but it fell just eight days after the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor pulled America into the Second World War, and it passed almost unnoticed. In 1982 a Texas university student, Gregory Watson, got a C for a paper on a forgotten amendment of Madison's that would bar Congress from giving itself a pay rise until after the next election. Furious, he poured his own cash into a letter campaign aimed at state legislatures, and in 1992 the states ratified it as the 27th Amendment, about 203 years late. In 2017 the university changed his grade to an A.

Almost every clause is a command to the federal government to keep out, beginning with Congress shall make no law: these are negative rights, a list of what the government may not do, not gifts it hands out. Madison feared that listing some rights would suggest the government held every power not written down. So the Ninth says rights left off the list still belong to the people, and the Tenth reserves every power the Constitution does not hand to the federal government to the states or to the people.

birth-of-athenian-democracy-cleisthenes-.context_blurb:
Around 500 BC the people of Athens, a Greek city-state, began running their city themselves, voting on its laws in person. The experiment grew in stages, through reformers such as Solon and Cleisthenes, and it was narrower than ours. Still, the idea that ordinary citizens could govern was first seriously tried here, and the word for it is Greek.

The Athenians called it democracy, from demos, the people, and kratos, power: literally, people-power. Citizens met on the Pnyx, a hill west of the Acropolis, and voted by a show of hands. They could also vote a man who had grown too powerful into exile for ten years, each voter scratching a name on an ostrakon, a shard of broken pottery used as free scrap, which is why such a vote is called ostracism. Plutarch tells how an illiterate voter handed Aristides, nicknamed the Just, a sherd and, not knowing him, asked him to write Aristides on it because he was tired of hearing the man called the Just; Aristides calmly scratched his own name on it and gave it back. Long before, Athens had lived under the code of Draco, who made death the penalty even for stealing a cabbage, and the orator Demades later quipped that Draco wrote his laws in blood, not ink.

Around 594 BC, poor Athenian farmers who could not repay their debts were being sold as slaves, and the city turned to the poet and lawgiver Solon. He scrapped all of Draco's laws except the one on murder. He set free the citizens who had been enslaved for debt and outlawed loans secured on a borrower's own body, and Athenians remembered the rescue as the seisachtheia, the shaking-off of burdens. He also pulled up the horoi, the stones that marked a field as mortgaged, and in one of his poems he boasted that he had freed the black earth, which had been in bondage. Then he made the citizens swear to keep his laws for ten years and sailed away on a long journey abroad, so no one could pester him into softening them.

Around 508 BC Cleisthenes went after the power of the noble families by sorting citizens not by ancestry but by where each man lived, building ten new tribes that each mixed men of the city, the coast and the inland, so that no single clan or district could deliver a bloc of votes. Daily business went to a Council of 500, fifty men from each tribe picked by lot rather than elected, so an ordinary farmer could find himself governing beside a noble. Cleisthenes called his system isonomia, equality before the law. When his rival Isagoras invited King Cleomenes of Sparta to drive out seven hundred families and break up the council, ordinary Athenians rose, trapped the two men on the Acropolis, and after two days forced them to surrender and leave.

Ostracism could be rigged. Archaeologists digging a well beside the Acropolis found 190 sherds all bearing the name Themistocles, but the handwriting shows that only about 14 hands wrote them, ballots mass-produced in advance. And the voters were few. Women, slaves and resident foreigners were shut out, and only free grown men of citizen birth could vote: about 30,000 to 40,000 men out of a few hundred thousand people in Attica.

birth-of-jazz-louis-armstrong-and-new-or.context_blurb:
Jazz was born in New Orleans in the early 1900s, from blues, spirituals, ragtime, marching bands and Caribbean rhythms. Its greatest early star was the trumpeter Louis Armstrong, born there around 1901, who turned jazz into an art of brilliant solo improvisation. As a boy he was mocked for his huge mouth with names like Gatemouth.

When Louis was about seven, the Karnofskys, a family of Jewish immigrants, gave him work hauling coal and junk and shared their dinner table with him. Morris Karnofsky lent him two dollars toward a five-dollar cornet from a pawnshop. Armstrong never forgot them: he said the family taught him to sing from the heart, and he wore a Star of David until the day he died. On New Year's Eve 1912 the eleven-year-old fired his stepfather's pistol in the street and was sent to the city's Colored Waif's Home, where the bandmaster, Peter Davis, taught him to play the cornet.

In 1926, recording Heebie Jeebies in Chicago, he dropped his lyric sheet, the story goes, and kept going with made-up wordless syllables, which made scat singing a sensation, although scat already existed in New Orleans. In 1928 he recorded West End Blues, which begins with a dazzling trumpet passage played alone, and the jazz historian Doug Ramsey wrote that Mozart, Bartok or Stravinsky would have been grateful to compose it.

In England, Percy Brooks, editor of the magazine Melody Maker, greeted him by squashing the old nickname Satchelmouth into a new one, Satchmo, and Armstrong kept it for life.

boltzmann-entropy-and-the-equation-on-th.context_blurb:
Ludwig Boltzmann was an Austrian physicist of the late 1800s who explained heat by imagining gases as swarms of tiny atoms moving at random. Many leading scientists of his day thought atoms were a useful fiction at best. Boltzmann spent his life fighting for them, and his idea became the backbone of modern physics.

Why does a smashed egg never put itself back together, and why does heat always flow from hot to cold? Boltzmann's answer was not a law forbidding the reverse but simple counting. A broken, jumbled egg can be arranged in vastly more ways than a whole one, so the tidy outcome is so outnumbered that it essentially never happens by chance. That is also why time seems to run one way.

Above his grave in Vienna, on a marble wall unveiled in 1933, is carved his definition of entropy, S equals k log W, where S is entropy, k is the Boltzmann constant and W counts the hidden arrangements that look the same from outside. Yet Boltzmann never wrote it in that tidy form: Max Planck compressed his ideas into the short equation around 1900, while studying the light given off by hot objects.

Critics such as Ernst Mach called atoms a convenient fiction, and in 1906 Boltzmann, worn down and sure he had lost, took his own life. Just two years later, in 1908, Jean Perrin's measurements of Brownian motion, the jittering of tiny specks in water, proved that atoms are real.

borobudur-srivijaya-maritime-se-asia.context_blurb:
Around 800 AD, on the island of Java in today's Indonesia, the Sailendra dynasty built Borobudur, the biggest Buddhist temple on earth, from some two million blocks of volcanic stone fitted without mortar. It rose in a busy maritime world tied together by Srivijaya, a kingdom centred on Sumatra that controlled the sea trade between India and China.

Borobudur is a mountain of nine stacked platforms laid out as a giant mandala. Climbing it is a pilgrimage through the stages of the Buddhist path, from the realm of desire at the hidden base, past the realm of form on the square terraces, up to the formless realm at the top: a journey from worldly desire toward Nirvana. The walls carry 2,672 carved panels of Buddhist stories.

At the summit the carving gives way to calm. On the three round upper terraces stand 72 bell-shaped stupas pierced with diamond-shaped openings, and peering through the stone lattice of each, a visitor finds a seated stone Buddha hidden inside. The temple once held 504 Buddha statues in all.

boston-massacre-1770.context_blurb:
On the snowy night of 5 March 1770, a crowd of Boston men surrounded the British soldiers guarding the Custom House, jeering and hurling snowballs, chunks of ice and oyster shells. In the confusion the soldiers fired, and five colonists died. Paul Revere's engraving of redcoats calmly gunning down orderly citizens turned the night into famous propaganda.

The first to fall, on King Street, was Crispus Attucks, a tall sailor and ropemaker whose ancestors were African and Wampanoag and who had run away from slavery some twenty years earlier, and he is honoured as the first man to give his life for the American Revolution. A newspaper advertisement of 1750 had once offered a reward for his capture.

Boston wanted the soldiers hanged, and no lawyer would touch the case. Then John Adams, a fierce patriot and a future president, agreed to defend the redcoats, because he believed every accused person deserved a defence even in a town that hated him, and telling the jury that facts are stubborn things, he won acquittals for Captain Thomas Preston and six of his eight men. The two convicted of manslaughter escaped the gallows and had their thumbs branded instead.

boston-tea-party-1773.context_blurb:
In 1773 Parliament passed the Tea Act, which let the struggling British East India Company sell tea straight to the American colonies. On the night of 16 December, members of Boston's Sons of Liberty boarded three Company ships at Griffin's Wharf and tipped the whole cargo, hundreds of chests, into the harbour.

The raiders went disguised as Mohawk warriors, blackening their faces with soot and lampblack and wrapping themselves in blankets, which hid who they were and also declared that they saw themselves as Americans of this land, not British subjects. The protest had strict rules. When the raiders caught one of their own stuffing tea into his coat, they made him run a gauntlet along the wharf while every person kicked him as he passed, because the point was to destroy the tea, not to profit from it.

Most people assume the tea was dumped because it cost too much. In fact the Tea Act had lowered the price of the Company's tea by cutting its duty, so that it would undersell the Dutch tea smuggled into the colonies. Patriots saw the cheap tea as a trap to make colonists accept Parliament's right to tax them without their consent. The fight was over the principle of the tax, not its cost, and Britain's harsh reply, the Intolerable Acts, pushed the colonies toward open rebellion.

botticelli-birth-of-venus-and-primavera.context_blurb:
Sandro Botticelli (about 1445 to 1510) was a painter of Renaissance Florence who worked for the powerful Medici family. His graceful flowing lines, floating hair and slightly wistful faces make his work instantly recognisable. His two most famous pictures bring Roman myths to life, and both now hang in the Uffizi Gallery in Florence.

In the Birth of Venus, from around 1485, the Roman goddess of love comes ashore already grown, her red-gold hair streaming in the wind, standing on a giant scallop shell that carries her across the waves. Botticelli painted the shell as pure and perfect as a pearl.

Primavera, Italian for Spring, painted around 1482, is a dreamlike garden full of gods. At its right edge Zephyrus, the blue god of the west wind, catches the fleeing nymph Chloris, and as he does, real flowers spill from her lips while she turns into Flora, goddess of flowers. The golden oranges on the trees behind the figures carry a hidden signature: they echo the gold balls, the palle, on the coat of arms of the Medici family, who paid for the painting.

brunelleschi-s-dome-of-florence.context_blurb:
By 1418 Florence's cathedral, Santa Maria del Fiore, had been rising for over a century, yet a vast eight-sided hole still gaped above its crossing, nearly fifty metres wide. Filippo Brunelleschi solved the puzzle, building the dome from 1420 to 1436. It still crowns the city, and it helped announce the Renaissance to Europe.

The ancient Romans had roofed giant spaces such as the Pantheon, but after Rome fell the secret of how they built such domes was lost for a thousand years, so no one in Florence knew how to close the gap. Before designing anything, Brunelleschi travelled to Rome with the sculptor Donatello, his friend, clambered over the ancient ruins for years, and measured the Pantheon again and again to learn how its dome stayed up.

His dome is really two domes, a shell within a shell, and the 463 steps that visitors climb today wind up through the curved gap between them. A lantern and a gilded copper ball crown the top. That ball, eight feet across, was made in Andrea del Verrocchio's workshop and hoisted up on 27 May 1471, and one of the teenage apprentices helping was Leonardo da Vinci. It stayed put for 130 years until 27 January 1601, when a lightning bolt struck it and knocked it clean off into the square below, where a marble disc still marks the spot. It was rebuilt the next year.

The building's great secret was herringbone brickwork, which Italians call fish-spine: bricks set at angles so that each new ring gripped the one below, so the dome carried its own weight while it climbed, with no wooden centring beneath. To lift millions of bricks hundreds of feet, he invented an ox-driven hoist with a reversing gear, so the load could go up or come down without anyone turning the oxen around. Decades later the young Leonardo sketched these machines. Legend says rival masters demanded to see his plan first, so he challenged them to balance an egg on its end on a marble table, and when none could, he cracked its base flat so it stood. When they scoffed that they could have done that, he said they could build his dome too, once they had seen his design. He also fitted parapets to the hanging work platforms and, to the men's grumbling, watered down the workers' wine, so they would stay steady and clear-headed so far above the ground.

Brunelleschi was not even trained as an architect but as a goldsmith and clockmaker, and in 1401 he had lost the contest for Florence's bronze Baptistery doors to his lifelong rival, Lorenzo Ghiberti. When the city made him share command with Ghiberti, who took credit without understanding the engineering, Brunelleschi, the story goes, pretended to be ill and stayed home until the work ground to a halt, then recovered and took sole charge.

Finished in 1436, it remains, nearly six centuries later, the largest brick-and-stone dome ever built: more than four million bricks and some 37,000 tons, raised without any centring at all. No later engineer, with steel or concrete, has topped it in masonry.

brunelleschi-the-florence-dome.context_blurb:
Filippo Brunelleschi was a goldsmith from Florence who became the great engineer of the early Renaissance. For decades the city's cathedral had stood open to the sky, because no one knew how to raise a dome that huge without it collapsing halfway up. In 1418 Florence held a contest for the design, and Brunelleschi entered it with a plan no rival could match.

Brunelleschi loved to make his point with a show. According to a legend told by Giorgio Vasari, he challenged the doubting judges to stand a raw egg upright on a flat piece of marble, and after each one failed, he struck one end down on the marble so the shell cracked flat and the egg stood. When they complained they could have done the same, he laughed that they could also have raised the dome, had they seen his design.

His boldest move was to raise the dome with no wooden scaffolding rising from the ground beneath it, the support that everyone believed a dome so wide must have while it was being built. His herringbone brickwork let each ring hold itself up. More than six hundred years later it is still the largest masonry dome ever built, and Brunelleschi lies buried beneath it.

buddhism-four-noble-truths-eightfold-pat.context_blurb:
Buddhism began in northern India in the 400s BC with Siddhartha Gautama, a prince who gave up his comfortable life to search for an end to suffering. His followers call him the Buddha, the awakened one. He taught Four Noble Truths: life involves suffering, suffering has a cause, it can end, and an Eightfold Path leads to its end.

The goal, nirvana (nibbana in Pali), is not a heavenly place: the word literally means blown out, like a flame that has been extinguished, the fires of greed, hatred and delusion snuffed out, a peace that can arrive even in this life once craving ends. The path toward it needs balance. When the monk Sona, once a musician, drove himself so hard in meditation that he wanted to quit, the Buddha reminded him that a lute string wound too tight will not play and one too slack will not play either, so effort must be tuned neither too tight nor too slack.

His very first sermon warned against two extremes, a life spent chasing pleasure and a life of tormenting the body, and he spoke from experience: he had lived as a pampered prince and then nearly starved himself as a wandering ascetic before finding the Middle Way between them. He also taught that much of our misery is extra. In the Sallatha Sutta he compared pain to being struck by an arrow; an untrained man who is hurt piles grief, resentment and brooding on top, like shooting a second arrow into ourselves, while a trained disciple feels only the first.

The Second Noble Truth names the cause of suffering tanha, a Pali word that literally means thirst: the thirst for pleasure, the thirst to go on existing, and even the thirst to stop existing. Suffering, in this teaching, is not random; it comes from a grasping that always wants more, or wants out.

bunker-hill-siege-of-boston.context_blurb:
After the first shots of the American Revolution at Lexington and Concord in April 1775, thousands of New England militiamen penned the British army inside Boston. On 17 June 1775 the British attacked the Americans who had dug in overnight on the Charlestown peninsula across the river. The fight is called Bunker Hill, though most of it raged on nearby Breed's Hill.

Short of gunpowder, the Americans were told, so the legend goes, to hold their fire until they could see the whites of the redcoats' eyes, so that no shot was wasted. The order is credited to Colonel William Prescott or General Israel Putnam, though most historians doubt either man said it.

The Americans threw back the first two charges, and the British took the hill only on the third, when the defenders ran out of powder, but it cost them over 1,000 men killed or wounded, about 1,054 against some 450 Americans, and that bloody price showed Britain the colonists would stand and fight. The siege went on until March 1776, when George Washington's cannon, dragged from Fort Ticonderoga, forced the British to leave Boston.

byzantine-empire-justinian.context_blurb:
After Rome's western half collapsed in 476, its eastern half carried on for almost a thousand years from its capital, Constantinople. In the 500s its most ambitious ruler, Justinian, nearly lost his throne to a riot, raised one of the world's greatest churches and gathered all of Roman law into one code.

Historians later named this empire Byzantine, but its own people never used that word: they called themselves Romaioi, Romans, because to them Rome had never fallen, only moved its capital. Justinian was born a peasant in a village called Tauresium. Justin I, the uncle who adopted Justinian and lifted him to power, had begun life keeping pigs before he rose to palace guardsman and finally to emperor. Justinian's wife, Theodora, came from even lower down: she was an actress, the daughter of a man who kept the performing bears of the Green faction at the Hippodrome. A law banned men of senator's rank from marrying actresses, so Justin repealed it.

Chariot racing ruled the city, and its fan clubs, the Blues and the Greens, were rival street gangs. In January 532 two condemned rioters, a Blue and a Green, were being hanged when the scaffold broke and both men survived, and the two gangs, for once united, turned their fury on Justinian. Their war-cry was the Hippodrome's racing cheer, Nika, Greek for Win, and the five-day Nika riot burned half of Constantinople. The rioters even crowned a rival emperor, and Justinian had a ship made ready for escape. According to the historian Procopius, Theodora refused to run, saying that the royal purple, the emperors' colour, made a fine shroud to be buried in. Justinian stayed. He sent the eunuch Narses alone into the packed Hippodrome with a sack of gold, and Narses bribed the leaders of the Blues to walk out on the Greens. Then the generals Belisarius and Mundus sealed the exits, and Procopius reports some 30,000 killed in a single day.

The riot had burned the old church of Holy Wisdom, and within weeks Justinian began a new Hagia Sophia. He chose two mathematicians to design its dome, the geometer Anthemius, from Tralles, and Isidore, from Miletus, and over 10,000 workers completed the church in five years and ten months. A later legend says that when Justinian first walked in, in 537, he gazed up and cried out that he had outdone Solomon, the king who built the great Temple in Jerusalem. Procopius, who saw it new, wrote that the dome seemed not to rest on anything solid but to hang from heaven on a golden chain.

Justinian's minister Tribonian boiled a thousand years of tangled Roman law down into one orderly code, finished around 534 and known as the Corpus Juris Civilis, the Body of Civil Law, which still lies beneath many of Europe's legal systems. Yet Procopius, who praised Justinian's wars and buildings in public, secretly wrote a poisonous attack on the emperor and Theodora, published only after his death, and that book is known as the Secret History.

byzantine-mosaics-and-icons.context_blurb:
Byzantine churches glow with mosaics: pictures made of thousands of tiny cubes of glass or stone, called tesserae. Their subjects were sacred, Christ, the Virgin and the saints, and they taught as well as decorated, since few worshippers could read. In the 700s and 800s a bitter fight raged over whether holy images were idols at all, and many were smashed.

The gold walls hold a secret. Each gold tile was a sandwich: true gold leaf sealed inside two thin skins of glass. As he set them, the mosaic-maker angled each tile slightly differently, so that each one catches the candle flame at a different moment, and as a worshipper walks past, the gold seems to shimmer and ripple as though the wall were alive and moving. The gold background was meant as a window into eternity.

The oldest icon of Christ to survive anywhere is kept in the desert monastery of Saint Catherine on Mount Sinai, painted in the 500s in encaustic, colours mixed into hot wax. Cover one side of the face, then the other, and you meet two different men. The painter made one half a stern judge who sees all and the other half a calm and merciful saviour who blesses. The icon survived only because remote Sinai lay far beyond the reach of the emperors who were destroying images.

byzantium-as-the-bridge-that-preserved-g.context_blurb:
Byzantium, the eastern Roman Empire, spoke Greek and kept copying the Greek classics for a thousand years after the western empire fell. Long before printing, a book survived only while someone kept copying it by hand. When Byzantine scholars travelled west, many fleeing the Turks, the books and ideas they carried helped light the Italian Renaissance.

The losses were huge. Sophocles, the great Athenian playwright, wrote about 120 plays and won more first prizes than any rival, yet only 7 of them survive today. His fellow tragedians Aeschylus and Euripides lost most of their work too, because once the last copy of a play crumbled, it was gone for good.

Even scraps survived by luck. In 1229 the scribe Johannes Myronas scraped and washed the pages of a tenth-century copy of Archimedes to write a prayer book over them, and after 1999 special imaging revealed what lay beneath: his own lost mathematics, including the only surviving copy of his Method of Mechanical Theorems. This reused book is called the Archimedes Palimpsest.

In 1438 the aged Byzantine scholar Gemistos Plethon lectured in Florence on Plato, and Cosimo de' Medici was so moved that he founded a new Platonic Academy and lent his Greek manuscripts to the young Marsilio Ficino to translate. The Florentines called Plethon the second Plato, and the Renaissance love of Plato was a parting gift from a dying empire.

cahokia-and-mississippian-culture.context_blurb:
Around 1100, centuries before any European reached America, Native Americans of the Mississippian culture built Cahokia, the biggest city north of Mexico before Columbus, across the Mississippi from modern St. Louis. Around a great central plaza rose about 120 earthen mounds. By 1350 the city stood empty, and its builders left no writing behind.

Its centrepiece, the flat-topped earthen pyramid now called Monks Mound, about 100 feet high with a footprint broader than the Great Pyramid of Giza, is the largest earthen mound anywhere in the Americas, North or South. The builders had no wheels, no draft animals and no metal tools, so they dug earth from pits and carried it by hand, one woven basketload at a time on their backs, some 55 million cubic feet of it over the decades. Crowds gathered for the city's favourite sport. In chunkey, one player sent a polished stone disc rolling down a smooth court and the others threw spears to land nearest where it would stop, and Cahokia spread the game across the South and the Plains. Some fans bet so heavily that they lost everything. In Mound 72, the archaeologist Melvin Fowler found a powerful man laid on more than 10,000 shell beads arranged in the shape of a falcon, a bird of prey, its wings spread beneath his arms; he is called the Birdman.

Around 1100 somewhere between fifteen and twenty thousand people lived in Cahokia, probably more people than London or Paris held at the same time, and no city in today's United States grew larger until Philadelphia in the 1780s. Its names came later. The great mound is named after a community of Trappist monks who lived nearby in the early 1800s and gardened on its first terrace, long after the builders were gone. In the 1960s the archaeologist Warren Wittry found rings of holes where tall posts had stood, worked out that they tracked the rising and setting sun, and nicknamed the place Woodhenge, after England's Stonehenge. The main ring, about 410 feet across, held 48 red cedar posts.

At the spring and autumn equinoxes, a watcher at the centre of Woodhenge saw the sun come up as if it were climbing out of the front of Monks Mound, half a mile away, and the builders kept that line even as they raised the mound higher. One grave held about 700 fine arrowheads made of stone from four distant regions, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Wisconsin and southern Illinois, which scholars read as proof of trade networks that stretched across half a continent into Cahokia. We do not know what the builders called their city, because the name Cahokia belongs to the Cahokia, an Illini people who lived in the area centuries after the city emptied and were no relation to its founders.

Cahokia's rulers held the power of life and death. Mound 72 held about 272 people buried over roughly a century, and most of them were sacrificial victims. In one pit lay 53 young women, aged about 15 to 30, set out in two neat layers, and their bones showed that they were strangled as sacrifices and then laid in their rows. Why the city emptied is still a mystery. A popular theory said its people cut down so many trees that the bare hillsides sent floods of mud over their fields. In 2021, though, the archaeologist Caitlin Rankin studied the soil layers of the ancient creek beds beside the city and found no evidence that cutting trees had caused any flooding, which leaves the collapse unsolved.

caravaggio-and-the-baroque-tenebrism.context_blurb:
Michelangelo Merisi (1571 to 1610), called Caravaggio after his family's hometown, changed European painting in about ten years of work in Rome. He painted Bible scenes with real Roman faces and dirty feet, lit with stunning drama. He was also violent: in 1606 he killed a man in a sword fight and fled Rome under sentence of death.

His signature technique is called tenebrism, from the Italian tenebroso, meaning dark or gloomy: an extreme kind of light-and-shade in which everything except the lit figures drowns in black, as if a single spotlight fell on a dark stage. Painters across Europe, from Rubens to Rembrandt, learned from it.

While on the run, Caravaggio painted David and Goliath, the boy hero gripping the giant's severed head, and sent the canvas to the papal court in Rome in hope of a pardon. The dead giant's face is his own: Caravaggio painted himself as the defeated villain, begging for mercy. The sword bears letters read as a Latin motto, humility kills pride. He died at 38, in 1610, still far from home.

caravel-compass-astrolabe.context_blurb:
The great ocean voyages of the late 1400s depended on three practical tools that Portuguese and Spanish sailors perfected: the caravel, a light ship that could sail toward the wind; the magnetic compass, first made in China; and the mariner's astrolabe, which measured how high the sun or a star stood. Together they let captains go far beyond sight of land and still come home.

Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492 with two quick caravels, the Nina and the Pinta, while his flagship, the Santa Maria, was a bigger, slower carrack and no caravel at all. The compass came from China. A Song-dynasty army manual of the 1040s describes a magnetised iron fish floated in a bowl of water to find direction at night, and the Chinese called it south-pointing, not north-pointing.

The caravel's great trick was its sail. A square sail works only with the wind behind it, so a ship that ran far along the African coast could get stuck, unable to return. A caravel carried a triangular lateen sail, which let it point within about 55 to 60 degrees of the wind and zig-zag home against it. To find his position, a sailor used his astrolabe. At night he measured the angle of Polaris, the North Star, above the horizon, because it sits almost directly over the North Pole, so the angle it makes above the horizon matches his latitude; by day he used the noon sun.

The mariner's astrolabe was cut with open spokes so the wind passed through it, and it was made thick and heavy on purpose, because a heavy disc hung steadier on a pitching, rolling deck and gave a truer reading. In high seas it still swung enough to throw a ship off course. In 2014 divers found a bronze disc in the wreck of the Esmeralda, lost off Oman in 1503, and although it looked blank, a laser scan revealed worn markings for every five degrees, proof that it was the oldest mariner's astrolabe known. It also bore the arms of King Manuel I of Portugal.

castiglione-the-courtier.context_blurb:
Baldassare Castiglione was an Italian diplomat and courtier at the brilliant little court of Urbino in the early 1500s. In 1528 he published The Book of the Courtier, a set of imagined evenings of conversation about how the perfect gentleman should fight, speak, dress and behave. For two centuries it was Europe's handbook of manners.

Castiglione coined a new word for the gentleman's master skill, sprezzatura: a certain careless ease that hides all the effort and practice behind what one does, so that even hard things look effortless. In the book, Count Ludovico da Canossa calls this the one universal rule. The courtier must avoid any show of strain, because once people glimpse the effort, the grace is destroyed: true art, Canossa says, is the kind that does not seem to be art at all.

Castiglione's close friend Raphael painted his portrait around 1514, and it now hangs in the Louvre. When it came up for auction in Amsterdam in 1639, Rembrandt sketched it, and for decades afterwards its pose turned up again in Rembrandt's self-portraits. Rubens painted a copy too.
