castles-siege-warfare.context_blurb:
A medieval castle was a weapon as much as a home. Over the centuries, European lords built everything from quick forts of earth and timber to huge rings of stone, and attackers answered with rams, siege towers, giant stone-throwers, tunnels, trickery and hunger. Each new attack forced a new defence, and both sides grew cleverer.

Besieging Stirling Castle in Scotland in 1304, England's King Edward I had the largest siege engine anyone had yet made raised against it: a huge trebuchet named Warwolf, which took five master carpenters and some fifty workmen about three months to build. The garrison of about thirty men tried to surrender before it was even finished, but Edward refused, because he was determined to try out his great engine on them first, and he accepted their surrender only afterwards, on 24 July. Defenders had their own traps. The strongest gatehouses had two portcullises, heavy oak-and-iron grilles that dropped on chains, and defenders slammed down the inner one first, then the outer, sealing the attackers inside the killing space between the two.

After 1066, William the Conqueror's Normans had to hold down a conquered country fast, so they built the motte-and-bailey: a great earth mound, the motte, crowned with a wooden tower, above a yard, the bailey, fenced with timber and circled by a ditch, and a small one could rise in weeks. Some 500 to 600 went up across England. Attackers learned to bring down stone. In 1215 King John's miners dug beneath one corner of the keep at Rochester Castle, and to burn away the wooden props he ordered forty of the fattest pigs sent from London; their blazing fat brought a whole corner tower crashing down. Murder holes above the gate passage were real, but the boiling oil of the movies is mostly make-believe, because oil was far too scarce and costly to pour away, so defenders dropped stones or poured boiling water, hot sand or quicklime instead.

Earlier engines stored their force in twisted rope or bent timber, but the trebuchet drew all its power from a heavy falling weight: a counterweight box on the short arm dropped, and the long arm whipped round to fling a stone of up to 350 pounds hard enough to smash a wall. Square towers had a fatal flaw, since miners could dig under a corner, prop it with timber and burn the props until it fell, so in the 1100s and 1200s builders switched to round towers, which have no corner to undermine. A concentric castle rings one full circuit of walls with a second, lower one, and because the inner wall stands taller, archers on both walls can shoot at once, the inner ones firing over the outer ones' heads at anyone caught between. Edward I's Beaumaris Castle in Wales is the finest example, though it was never finished. To hit attackers huddled at the foot of a wall, builders added machicolations, stone galleries that stick out from the top of the wall with openings underneath, so rocks dropped through land right on the men below. They replaced wooden galleries, because stone will not burn.

The Byzantines guarded the recipe for Greek Fire, a liquid flame that clung to ships and men and burned even on water, so jealously that it was never written down plainly, and the secret died with their empire and is unknown today. Emperor Romanos II ranked it with the imperial regalia and the royal princesses as things no foreigner must have. Krak des Chevaliers in Syria, held by the Knights Hospitaller, was almost never taken by force, and in the traditional story the Mamluk sultan Baibars, after a month's siege in 1271, finally got the knights out with a forged letter, supposedly from their own Grand Master, ordering them to surrender.

castro-s-cuba-la-caba-a-the-exiles.context_blurb:
In January 1959 Fidel Castro's revolution overthrew the Cuban dictator Fulgencio Batista, and Castro went on to build a communist dictatorship that has ruled the island for more than sixty years. Revolutionary courts sent prisoners to firing squads, and more than a million Cubans, about one in ten, have fled, many on rafts and small boats across the Florida Straits.

The old Spanish fortress of La Cabana in Havana became a prison and execution ground, and in January 1959 Castro's comrade Che Guevara took charge of its tribunals. The condemned were shot in the fortress's floodlit moat. One of them was Jesus Sosa Blanco, a Batista officer charged with 108 killings, and by one account, as the riflemen raised their guns, he shouted the squad's own commands himself, Attention, Aim, Fire, ordering his own death.

The flight from Cuba never stopped. On 13 July 1994, Cubans escaping on a hijacked tugboat, the 13 de Marzo, were caught seven miles out by Cuban government boats, which rammed the tug and turned high-pressure water hoses on the people crowded on deck until it sank, and 41 of the 72 aboard drowned, 10 of them children. It became the defining tragedy of that summer's rafter crisis, when tens of thousands fled on rafts of inner tubes and planks.

casualties-and-scale-of-wwii.context_blurb:
The Second World War, fought from 1939 to 1945 and from 1937 in China, killed more people than any other war in history. Between 70 and 85 million people lost their lives, about one in thirty of everyone then alive. The Soviet Union lost around 27 million, and Nazi Germany murdered some six million Jews in the Holocaust.

Most of the dead never carried a rifle: about 50 to 55 million civilians died, against roughly 21 to 25 million soldiers, so for every soldier killed about two ordinary people died, from bombing, famine, disease and massacre.

Some soldiers died at the hands of their own side. In the summer of 1942, with the Germans driving deep into Russia, Joseph Stalin issued Order No. 227 on 28 July, remembered by its slogan, Not one step back!, and it set blocking units behind the front whose job was to gun down troops who fell back. Archives suggest that as many as 158,000 Soviet soldiers were executed by their own side during the war, about 15,000 of them in a few weeks at Stalingrad. A real share of the Soviet losses traces to Stalin himself.

causes-of-the-civil-war-and-the-cornerst.context_blurb:
In the winter of 1860 to 1861, after Abraham Lincoln won the presidency, Southern states began leaving the Union, eleven in all, to form the Confederate States of America. Why did they go? Their own leaders wrote the answer down at the time, in declarations of causes, in a new constitution, and in a famous speech by the Confederacy's vice president, Alexander Stephens.

Speaking at Savannah in March 1861, Stephens said the new government's cornerstone rested on what he called a great truth: that Black people were not equal to white people, and that slavery was their natural and normal condition. It is remembered as the Cornerstone Speech, and its claim was false.

South Carolina, the first state to leave, in December 1860, complained that the North had just elected a president whose views were hostile to slavery: Abraham Lincoln, who had not yet even taken office. Mississippi's Declaration of the Immediate Causes, in January 1861, opened by tying the state's whole position to slavery, which it called the world's greatest material interest. The men who decided were hardly neutral: 84 of its 100 delegates owned slaves, and the vote to leave passed 84 to 15. Enslaved people made up more than half of Mississippi's population.

In Savannah, Stephens did not hide what had split the nation: the Confederate constitution, he said, had settled forever the question of slavery, which Southerners politely called their peculiar institution, and slavery was the immediate cause of the break and of the present revolution. He even boasted that the Confederacy was the first government ever built on the supposed truth that Black people were inferior, as if it were an achievement.

The other documents said the same. Mississippi's paper dressed slavery up as nature, claiming that its crops needed a near-tropical climate and that only the Black race could bear the tropical sun. Texas, which left in February 1861, declared that American governments had been founded by and for the white race alone, and praised African slavery as a beneficent and patriarchal system. The Confederate Constitution of March 1861 went further: it barred the Confederate Congress from ever passing any law that denied or impaired the right to own slaves, so the Confederacy could never enact a law abolishing slavery.

Stephens openly broke with the founders: he admitted that they had believed slavery wrong in principle and had assumed the races were equal, and he declared their ideas fundamentally wrong, built on an error. So sure was he that he compared his racial claim to discoveries the world had first rejected and later accepted: the ideas of Galileo, of Adam Smith, and of William Harvey, the English doctor who showed that blood circulates. History proved him wrong. After the defeat, in an 1868 book, Stephens claimed the war had been about constitutional questions and that reporters had misquoted him, but he had let the whole speech be reprinted in his own authorized biography, which wrecked his excuse. The later story that the war was really about states' rights collapses against the secessionists' own words.

cervantes-don-quixote.context_blurb:
Miguel de Cervantes (1547 to 1616) was a Spanish soldier, captive, tax collector and finally novelist. In his late fifties, poor and battered by life, he published Don Quixote, the comic tale of a country gentleman who reads so many old romances of chivalry that he loses his wits and rides out across La Mancha as a knight. It made him famous across Europe.

Out on the dusty plain of La Mancha, Don Quixote sees thirty or forty windmills and declares that they are monstrous giants he must battle and slay. His loyal, down-to-earth squire, Sancho Panza, warns him plainly that they are only windmills, but the knight lowers his lance and charges.

The knight's whole world is make-believe. He wears a barber's brass shaving-basin on his head, convinced that it is the famous helmet of Mambrino. Every knight needs a lady, so he invents Dulcinea del Toboso and praises her endlessly, but she is really Aldonza Lorenzo, a sturdy farm girl from nearby to whom he has scarcely said a word.

When his lance strikes a turning sail, the windmill shatters it and sends horse and rider rolling. Still he will not admit his mistake: an enchanter, the sage Friston, must have changed the giants into windmills to rob him of glory. The scene gave English the phrase tilting at windmills. Cervantes knew real battles. In 1571, in the great naval clash at Lepanto, he fought while sick with fever and was hit by three bullets, one of which crippled his left hand, and ever after he proudly called himself el manco de Lepanto, which means the one-handed man of Lepanto.

On his voyage home in 1575, Barbary pirates seized him and he spent five years as a slave in Algiers, and when one of his four escape plots failed and he was hauled in front of Hassan Pasha, the viceroy, he took the whole blame on himself to protect his fellow captives. His courage won a reprieve, and he was ransomed in 1580. When Part One appeared in January 1605 it was an instant sensation, and Don Quixote is often called the first modern novel; it is among the most translated books on earth.

In 1614 a rival writing as Avellaneda published a fake, unauthorized Part Two using Cervantes's characters, and the insult spurred Cervantes to finish his own authentic Part Two, which appeared in 1615. He died in April 1616, near the date tradition gives for Shakespeare's death.

chaco-canyon-and-pueblo-bonito.context_blurb:
From about AD 850 to 1150, Chaco Canyon in the high desert of today's New Mexico was the ceremonial heart of the Ancestral Puebloan world. Its builders raised great houses of fitted sandstone with hundreds of rooms, the largest being Pueblo Bonito, and laid ruler-straight roads across the land. A long drought in the 1100s helped break the Chacoan world apart.

The Chacoans watched the sky closely. Atop Fajada Butte, sunlight squeezes between three tilted slabs of stone and falls in a narrow sliver across a spiral pecked into the cliff. At about a quarter past eleven on the morning of the summer solstice, this Sun Dagger slices right through the centre of the spiral, while at the winter solstice two daggers frame its outer edges. The artist Anna Sofaer discovered it in 1977, but around 1989 visitors' footsteps shifted a slab and spoiled the alignment for good.

The Chacoans traded far. At Pueblo Bonito, scientists found theobromine, the chemical signature of cacao, in tall cylinder jars, proof that the Chacoans were drinking chocolate carried more than 1,200 miles from Mesoamerica. The same trade brought scarlet macaws and copper bells up from the south.

charlemagne-the-carolingian-empire.context_blurb:
Charlemagne, Charles the Great, became king of the Franks in 768 and conquered most of western and central Europe. In 800 he became the first emperor in the West in over three hundred years. He drove a great revival of learning, though he struggled to write himself, and he could be ruthless toward the peoples he conquered.

On Christmas Day 800, in Rome's Old St Peter's, Pope Leo III crowned the kneeling king, and the crowd hailed him three times as emperor of the Romans, a title no man in the West had held for over three hundred years. His fame reached far beyond Christendom. Around 802 Harun al-Rashid, the caliph of Baghdad, sent him a live Asian elephant called Abul-Abbas, which came by ship as far as Italy, spent the winter at Vercelli, and then walked over the Alps to Charlemagne's court at Aachen. Aachen's hot springs had drawn him to make it his capital, and his biographer Einhard says no one could out-swim him and that a hundred or more people sometimes bathed with him at once.

Einhard also reveals that the king who sponsored so much learning kept writing tablets under his pillow, so that in spare hours he could train his hand to form his letters, but he had begun too late and never wrote well. His crown had a violent start: in April 799 enemies attacked Pope Leo III during a procession in Rome and tried to cut out his tongue and tear out his eyes, but Leo survived, fled to Charlemagne, and a year later crowned him. Not every campaign went well. In August 778 Basque fighters fell on his rearguard in a pass of the Pyrenees, and among the dead Einhard names Roland, governor of the Breton March, a man whose name later grew into France's most famous knightly legend.

Three centuries later the Song of Roland, the oldest great French epic, turned the small defeat into a vast battle: proud Roland refuses to call for help until too late, then blows his ivory horn, the olifant, so hard that his temples burst. Charlemagne's scholars left a quieter legacy. At his palace school, run by Alcuin, a scholar from York in England, scribes developed a clear new handwriting, Carolingian minuscule, which gave us lowercase letters and spaces between words; Renaissance printers revived it, believing it was ancient Roman writing. Around 793 he based all money on one silver penny, twelve to a shilling and 240 to a pound, and Britain kept this pounds, shillings and pence system until 15 February 1971, the switch to decimal money that Britons called Decimal Day.

Einhard claimed the king measured seven of his own feet in height, and in 2010 scientists measuring his shinbone, kept at Aachen Cathedral, found he stood about 1.84 metres, taller than about 99 percent of the men of his time. His conquests had a dark side. In 782 at Verden, after a Saxon revolt destroyed a Frankish army, the Frankish annals report that Charlemagne ordered some 4,500 Saxon prisoners beheaded in one day, the old Roman punishment for oath-breakers. His family, the Carolingians, took their name from his grandfather, Charles Martel, Charles the Hammer, who defeated an invading Muslim army at Tours in 732. Charles's son Pepin the Short became the first Carolingian king in 751.

charles-lindbergh-and-the-age-of-flight.context_blurb:
On 20 May 1927 Charles Lindbergh, a 25-year-old American airmail pilot, took off alone from Long Island, and 33 and a half hours later he landed outside Paris before a crowd of some 150,000. He was the first person to fly solo and nonstop across the Atlantic, he won a $25,000 prize, and overnight he became the most famous man on earth.

His silver, single-engine monoplane was named the Spirit of St. Louis, after the city whose businessmen helped pay for it. The plane was built to his own strange orders: stripped of weight and crammed with extra fuel.

Because a fuel tank filled the nose where a windshield would be, Lindbergh could not see straight ahead, so he watched the way forward through a small periscope mounted on the side, or by tipping the plane to peek out of a side window. He flew the whole 3,600 miles with no co-pilot, and his flight set off an aviation craze across America.

chaucer-s-canterbury-tales.context_blurb:
Geoffrey Chaucer, an English courtier and civil servant of the late 1300s, wrote The Canterbury Tales, the story of a band of pilgrims riding to the shrine at Canterbury and telling tales to pass the time. His pilgrims, from a quiet knight to a crooked miller, form a warm and funny portrait of medieval England. He died before finishing it.

In Chaucer's England the king's court spoke French and churchmen wrote in Latin. Chaucer chose the everyday English of ordinary people, Middle English, and his Tales open with the words Whan that Aprille, followed by April's shoures soote, its sweet showers, one of the most famous beginnings in English. That choice earned him the title Father of English literature.

He loved and mocked his pilgrims alike. The Pardoner preaches against greed, which his Latin text calls the root of all evil, and in the same breath he sells fake holy relics, and his most brazen fraud is a glass jar of bones he swears belonged to a saint, which are really just a pig's bones. His pack also holds a cross of brass studded with false gems and an old pillowcase passed off as the Virgin Mary's veil, and he commits the very sin he preaches against.

chavin-de-huantar-early-andean-culture.context_blurb:
Chavin de Huantar, high in the Andes of central Peru, was a temple centre built from about 1200 BC and busiest from about 900 to 200 BC, long before the Inca. Its religion and art spread across the Andes without any sign of conquest, carried by pilgrims. Its underground stone galleries channelled rushing water and torchlight to fill visitors with awe.

At the dark heart of its stone maze, in a cramped cross-shaped chamber, stands the Lanzon, a granite shaft about fifteen feet tall carved as a snarling man-jaguar god, and its hair and eyebrows are carved as coiled snakes. One of its hands points up and the other down, and pilgrims met it in near-total darkness.

Another carving, the Raimondi Stele, shows a fanged Staff God holding a staff in each hand, and when the slab is turned upside down, his tall headdress becomes a tower of grinning, fanged faces stacked one above another, while his face becomes a smiling reptile. The stele packs in fifty snakes, and Antonio Raimondi recorded it in 1873.

child-labor-and-industrial-working-condi.context_blurb:
In Britain's early industrial age, from about the 1780s to the 1840s, and later in America, children as young as five worked in mines, mills and chimneys, often ten to fourteen hours a day. Their bosses profited from small bodies and cheap wages. Then reformers dragged the facts into the light, and Parliament learned to make child-labour laws stick.

In the coal pits the smallest children, aged five or six, were trappers, working shifts as long as twelve hours, alone and in darkness, opening a wooden ventilation door with a rope each time a coal cart came through. That door kept fresh air moving so the pit did not fill with deadly gas, and eight-year-old Sarah Gooder told inspectors she had to do it without a light and was scared. Master sweeps bought orphan climbing boys, some as young as four, and drove them up flues as narrow as seven inches, and when a frightened boy froze, the master lit a fire of straw under his bare feet or jabbed him with pins. In the cotton and flax mills, children of six or seven worked as scavengers, crawling under the spinning machines while they still ran at full speed to sweep up loose cotton, where one slip meant a crushed hand. In Pennsylvania, breaker boys as young as eight picked slate from rushing chutes of coal with bloody bare hands, because the bosses banned gloves: bare fingers could tell slate from coal by feel and work faster.

Older children worked as hurriers, dragging coal carts called corves along passages so low that they had to crawl, pulled by a chain that ran from a belt round the waist down between the legs. Patience Kershaw, a seventeen-year-old hurrier near Halifax, told the 1842 Commission that the bald patch on top of her head came from shoving the loaded carts, the corves, forward with her head, day after day. Elizabeth Bentley, who went to work in a flax mill in Leeds at the age of six, told Parliament in 1832 that in the busy season her day began at 5 a.m. and ended at 9 p.m., and of those sixteen hours she was given just forty minutes for all her meals. She said girls were beaten with a strap as well as boys. In 1838 at the Huskar pit near Silkstone, Yorkshire, a thunderstorm burst on the surface and its water poured down the drift, drowning twenty-six children, eleven girls and fifteen boys, as they tried to escape. The young Queen Victoria heard of it, and an inquiry followed.

In 1830 Richard Oastler, a Yorkshire land steward, accused the gentlemen who celebrated abolition abroad of overlooking the child workers dying in their own factories, and he branded the system Yorkshire Slavery. Michael Sadler, a Leeds MP, then gathered the children's testimony. Earlier laws had failed because owners ignored them, so the Factory Act of 1833, which kept children under nine out of the textile mills, for the first time sent salaried government inspectors into the mills to enforce it. The 1842 report on the mines shocked respectable Victorians less with its words than with its engraved pictures of women and small children harnessed by chains to coal wagons underground, and Parliament passed the Mines Act that same year. Lord Ashley, later the Earl of Shaftesbury, a devout Christian reformer in the tradition of William Wilberforce, pushed that Act through, banning women, girls and boys under ten from working underground, and working people called him the Poor Man's Earl.

The first medical warning had come long before. In 1775 Percivall Pott, a London surgeon, saw former climbing boys dying in manhood of one rare cancer, soot-wart, and traced it to the soot rubbed into their skin as children, the first proof that a person's job could be the cause of his cancer. His finding helped pass the first Chimney Sweepers Act in 1788.

child-sacrifice-in-the-ancient-near-east.context_blurb:
In the ancient Near East and the Phoenician world, some peoples killed young children as offerings to their gods. The clearest evidence comes from Carthage, in today's Tunisia, where archaeologists found sacred grounds, called tophets after a Hebrew word, packed with thousands of urns of burned infant bones beneath stones dedicated to the gods Baal Hammon and Tanit.

Greek and Roman historians recorded the rite, and the Greek writer Diodorus described a mass sacrifice during a siege of Carthage. Some modern scholars argued the tophets were only cemeteries for babies who died naturally, but most now agree the killings really happened. The ancient Hebrews condemned the practice as one of the worst evils of Canaan and banned it in their law. The Bible places such burnings in the Valley of Hinnom, just outside Jerusalem, Ge-Hinnom in Hebrew, and the place grew so hateful that its name passed into Greek as Gehenna, the word the New Testament uses to picture hell.

The Hebrew scribes even turned the god's name into a verdict. They took melekh, meaning king, and gave it the vowels of boshet, meaning shame, so that the name Molech, or Moloch, reads as the shameful king. A real cursed valley outside Jerusalem became the name of hell itself.

chinampas-the-aztec-floating-gardens.context_blurb:
In the 1400s the Valley of Mexico, where the Aztecs built their capital, Tenochtitlan, was filled by a great shallow lake. To feed one of the densest cities in the world, Aztec farmers raised gardens out of the water itself, growing maize, beans, squash, chilies and tomatoes several times a year. Pieces of this water world survive in Xochimilco, in today's Mexico City.

The Spanish called these garden strips floating gardens, but a chinampa never floated. Farmers staked out a long rectangle of shallow lakebed, wove reeds and branches between the stakes, and piled in alternating layers of mud and rotting plants until a solid bed rose above the water, rooted to the lake bottom. Canals between the plots let farmers paddle canoes to their fields and kept the soil wet all year.

Loose mud beside open water erodes easily, so each plot's border needed anchoring. The construction stakes themselves took root and grew into ahuejote willows, whose roots bound the soil against erosion while their leaves shaded the crops. The willows quite literally held the islands together.

chinese-art-landscape-painting-calligrap.context_blurb:
Chinese art is one of the oldest unbroken traditions on earth. Three forms sit at its heart: calligraphy, the art of beautiful brush writing; ink landscape painting on silk or paper scrolls; and porcelain, whose secret the rest of the world spent centuries trying to copy. Painting, poetry and calligraphy were prized together as the Three Perfections.

Porcelain made one town famous across the world. Jingdezhen, once called Changnan, turned out the world's finest tableware for more than ten centuries, and a popular account holds that as foreign traders repeated its old name, it wore down into the English word china, which came to mean both the country and fine ceramic ware. Landscape painting, shan shui or mountain-water, works by leaving things out. The painter leaves wide stretches of silk bare on purpose, planning the empty spaces as carefully as the inked ones, and the bare silk becomes sky, water and mist.

Around the year 1000, Fan Kuan painted Travelers Among Mountains and Streams, in which one towering mountain fills most of the picture and a tiny mule train creeps along below. He hid his signature among a tree's leaves in the lower right corner, disguised as drooping twigs, and no one noticed it until the scholar Li Lincan spotted it in 1958. Ink painting demands total confidence. Unlike oil paint, a brush stroke of ink on silk can never be erased once it touches the surface, so the painter must commit to every mark without hesitating.

Calligraphy was the highest art of all. In 353 the calligrapher Wang Xizhi dashed off the Orchid Pavilion Preface at a riverside drinking party, and the common character zhi appears in it twenty times, yet he formed it differently every single time. Sober, he could never write it so well again. Europe, meanwhile, could not make true porcelain. In 1712 a French Jesuit, Francois Xavier d'Entrecolles, studied the Jingdezhen kilns with help from Christian workers there and sent the secret of how porcelain was made back to France, one of the earliest cases of industrial spying.

chinese-foot-binding.context_blurb:
For about a thousand years, from roughly the 900s until the early 1900s, Chinese parents bound the feet of their young daughters to keep them tiny. Beginning as young as five, they curled the four small toes under the sole and pressed until the bones broke. Bound women lived in lifelong pain, and many could barely walk.

The goal was a foot no more than three Chinese inches long, about ten centimetres. Such a tiny foot was prized as a woman's greatest beauty and given a poetic name, the golden lotus. Feet even a little larger were given lesser names, and the practice spread from the imperial court down through society.

The fight against it began with small groups of believers. In 1875, in the city of Xiamen, about sixty Christian women, with the missionary John MacGowan at their head, formed the Natural Foot Society, named for the unbound foot they defended. The Chinese reformer Kang Youwei later urged the throne in 1898 to forbid foot binding, and government bans in the 1900s finally ended it.

chinese-four-great-inventions.context_blurb:
Around 1620 the English thinker Francis Bacon named printing, gunpowder and the compass as three inventions that had changed the world, and historians later added paper. All four first appeared in China, between the Han dynasty and the Song, over more than a thousand years. Together they are called China's Four Great Inventions.

Around 105, Cai Lun, an official at the Han court, beat bark, hemp, rags and old fishing nets into a soggy pulp, then flattened the mush and let it dry as thin sheets, inventing paper. Before that, Chinese books were written on heavy strips of bamboo and wood, and a single long book could fill a whole wagonload of bamboo slips. About a thousand years ago Daoist alchemists mixing saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal in search of an elixir of eternal life stumbled instead on a powder that exploded, and its Chinese name, huo yao, still means fire medicine. The earliest Chinese compass, the si nan, was a lodestone spoon that spun on a polished bronze plate until it came to rest pointing south, for Chinese compasses traditionally pointed south, not north.

The world's earliest printed book that carries a date is the Diamond Sutra, a Buddhist text printed from carved woodblocks in 868, some 600 years before Gutenberg, on seven sheets glued end to end into a roll some sixteen feet in length. Between 1039 and 1048 a commoner named Bi Sheng invented movable type, cutting each character into a block of sticky clay as thin as a coin's edge and baking it hard. Gunpowder first went to war in fire arrows and the fire lance, a tube of powder fixed to a pole that spat flames, and a silk banner of about 950 from Dunhuang shows a demon aiming one. For centuries the Chinese did not steer by the compass at all; they used it for feng shui and fortune-telling, lining up houses and graves with the earth's magnetic pull.

The stories behind the inventions can be dark or lucky. Cai Lun later passed along a slander that helped cause a death at court, and in 121, ordered to prison for trial, he bathed, dressed in his finest formal robes and drank poison. The Diamond Sutra survived about 900 years walled up in a cave near Dunhuang among a vast hoard of other manuscripts, until around 1900 the caretaker monk Wang Yuanlu found the sealed library by chance while clearing away drifted sand. In 1088 the scholar Shen Kuo noticed that a magnetised needle did not point exactly at true south but a little to one side, the first recorded measure of magnetic declination.

Movable type had a puzzling fate. Chinese printers kept carving whole pages as single woodblocks for centuries, because Chinese writing uses thousands of different characters, and cutting a full set of type cost far more than carving a page. When the same idea met Europe's alphabet of some twenty-six letters, it exploded.

chinese-revolution-mao-1949.context_blurb:
In 1949 the Chinese Communist Party under Mao Zedong won China's long civil war against the Nationalist government of Chiang Kai-shek. Mao ruled the new People's Republic until his death in 1976. His campaigns, above all the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, killed tens of millions of Chinese, one of the worst records of any ruler in history.

On 1 October 1949 Mao proclaimed the People's Republic from atop Beijing's Gate of Heavenly Peace, to a 21-gun salute. Over the square rose a new red flag carrying five gold stars in its corner, one large and four small, still China's flag today. Chiang Kai-shek refused to surrender and fled across the strait to Taiwan, taking some two million refugees and the bulk of the nation's gold, and made the island his last stronghold.

The road to that gate was long. In the Long March of 1934 and 1935, some 86,000 Red Army soldiers left Jiangxi and trekked some 6,000 miles to Shaanxi, but only a few thousand, perhaps 4,000 to 8,000, reached the end. Its most famous episode is Luding Bridge in 1935, where, the journalist Edgar Snow wrote, the planks had been torn away and 22 commandos swung hand over hand across the bare iron chains under machine-gun fire. In the civil war, numbers decided. In the Huaihai Campaign of 1948 and 1949, the war's largest battle, more than two million peasants pushing wooden wheelbarrows kept the Communist armies supplied as they destroyed about 550,000 Nationalist soldiers equipped with American arms. As defeat neared, on 1 December 1948, after dark, Chiang's men emptied the Bank of China in Shanghai, and a British reporter watched lines of men carrying heavy boxes of gold on long poles across their shoulders to a waiting ship. The slogan every Chinese child learns, that the Chinese people have stood up, is not in Mao's proclamation at all: it comes from a different speech he gave ten days earlier, on 21 September 1949.

Mao's rule soon turned deadly. In his Four Pests campaign, peasants banged pots and drums until the exhausted birds fell from the sky, but sparrows had eaten crop-eating bugs, so locusts and insects swarmed and devoured the harvests. In the Great Leap Forward, launched in 1958, peasants chasing Mao's impossible steel targets melted down their own pots and farm tools in backyard furnaces, which yielded only brittle pig iron that broke under strain. The result was the deadliest famine in history. Even as peasants starved, some so desperate that they ate the dead, Mao's government kept exporting grain abroad, sending it as aid to allies such as Albania and Cuba and selling it for hard currency, while its granaries stayed locked. Estimates of the dead run from about 36 to 45 million. In 1966 Mao launched the Cultural Revolution, and millions of teenage Red Guards waving his little book of quotations dragged teachers and officials into struggle sessions, where crowds screamed at, beat and humiliated them.

The legends have cracked too. Deng Xiaoping, later China's leader, admitted to Zbigniew Brzezinski, an American adviser, that Luding Bridge had been an easy fight against warlord troops armed with old muskets, and that the heroic version was propaganda. Jung Chang and Jon Halliday's 2005 biography, Mao: The Unknown Story, opens by charging that he was responsible for well over 70 million deaths in peacetime, more than any other twentieth-century leader.

christian-and-student-resistance-of-cons.context_blurb:
A few Germans resisted Hitler's dictatorship from the inside, knowing it could cost their lives, and some of the bravest came from Christian and student circles. At the University of Munich, Hans Scholl, his sister Sophie and a few friends formed the White Rose and secretly spread leaflets against the Nazis. The Lutheran pastor Dietrich Bonhoeffer went further still.

The White Rose leaflets told Germans that they would not be silent and named the murder of Jews as a crime against human dignity. One February morning in 1943, Hans and Sophie carried a case of leaflets into the university's main hall, and with the last stack left over, Sophie shoved it over the railing of the top floor so that the pages fluttered down onto the students pouring out of class. A custodian, Jakob Schmid, saw her and held them for the Gestapo. The Nazi judge Roland Freisler sentenced Sophie, Hans and their friend Christoph Probst to death. On the morning of 22 February 1943, minutes before her execution, Sophie looked at the sky and said that the sun was still shining.

Moments before the guillotine fell on him that same day, Hans cried out so loudly that it rang through the prison: Long live freedom! Probst, a young father of three who was studying medicine, had never been baptized, so in his last minutes a Catholic priest baptized him and gave him his first communion.

Bonhoeffer had once leaned toward pacifism, but as Hitler's crimes mounted he came to believe that his faith demanded action, so he joined a secret circle plotting to assassinate Adolf Hitler. Working as cover in military intelligence, he also helped smuggle a group of Jews into Switzerland, and after the failed bomb plot of July 1944 the SS hanged him at Flossenburg on 9 April 1945, two weeks before the camp was freed. Years before, in a 1937 book, he had attacked cheap grace, forgiveness that asks for no repentance and carries no cross, and set against it costly grace, which claims a person's whole life. His death became the test of his words.

christianity-under-roman-rule-and-persec.context_blurb:
In the three centuries after Jesus, Christianity grew from a small Jewish movement into a faith found in every province of the Roman Empire. Christians refused to burn incense to the emperor or swear by Rome's gods, and several emperors answered with waves of persecution: arrests, torture and death in the arena. The faith kept growing until a Christian emperor changed the rules.

In July 64 fire swept through Rome for days, and when people whispered that Nero himself had lit it to make room for his Golden House, he turned the crowd's anger by blaming the city's Christians and having many of them killed. Christians recognised one another by a secret sign, a fish, because the Greek word for fish, ICHTHYS, spelled out the first letters of Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour. Beneath Rome they dug the catacombs, not as hideouts, as legend says, but to bury their dead, since they believed the body would one day rise again. Most Romans burned their dead instead.

Martyrs faced death with startling resolve. Around 107 Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, condemned to the beasts in Rome, wrote ahead begging the Roman Christians not to save him, calling himself God's wheat, to be ground by the beasts' teeth so that he might become the pure bread of Christ. Around 155 the aged bishop Polycarp of Smyrna, ordered to curse Christ, answered that he had served his King for eighty-six years and had never been wronged by him, so how could he blaspheme him now? In 203 Perpetua, a young noblewoman of Carthage still nursing her baby, kept a prison diary, and in it she dreamed of a narrow ladder to heaven, its sides hung with swords and blades, with the serpent coiled at its foot. Lawrence, a deacon of Rome martyred in 258, presented the city's poor as the Church's treasures, and tradition says that, roasted on an iron gridiron, he told his executioners to turn him over because he was done on that side.

Perpetua's pregnant slave Felicity feared being left behind, because Roman law did not allow a pregnant woman to be executed, but she gave birth to a daughter days before the games. Around 197 the North African writer Tertullian argued that every killing won the faith more converts, and he wrote that the blood of the martyrs was the seed of the Church.

In the arena at Carthage, when a nervous young gladiator's first stroke struck bone, the wounded Perpetua took his trembling hand and guided his sword to her own throat. Modern historians have corrected the popular picture. Condemned criminals of all kinds were sent to the beasts, rarely lions, and Perpetua's own group faced a wild cow, a leopard, a bear and a boar. Despite the famous image, historians find no solid evidence that any Christian was martyred in the Colosseum. The last and fiercest persecution began under the emperor Diocletian on 23 February 303, when officials tore down the new church at Nicomedia and burned the Christians' scriptures. Later edicts ordered everyone to sacrifice to Rome's gods, until toleration came in 311 and the Edict of Milan in 313.

cicero-orator-statesman-voice-of-the-rep.context_blurb:
Marcus Tullius Cicero (106 to 43 BC) was a lawyer, philosopher and the greatest orator of Rome. Born into a family with no senators, he rose by talent alone to become consul. He lived through the dying years of the Roman Republic, and his letters and speeches, which survive in great numbers, became the model of Latin style for a thousand years.

After Julius Caesar's murder, Cicero fought to save the Republic from Mark Antony, attacking him in fourteen blistering speeches called the Philippics. In 43 BC Antony had him killed. Antony's soldiers cut off Cicero's head and also his hands, the hands that had written the Philippics, and both were nailed up at the Rostra, the speakers' platform in the Forum where he had given his greatest speeches.

The historian Cassius Dio adds a grim legend: when the head reached Antony, his wife Fulvia took it on her lap, drew out her hairpins and stabbed them into Cicero's tongue, the tongue that had savaged her husband. It was revenge on the voice of the Republic itself.

cincinnatus-the-dictator-who-returned-to.context_blurb:
Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus was a Roman farmer and statesman of the 400s BC whom the Romans held up as the perfect citizen. Rome's law allowed a dictator, one man given total power for a short emergency. Cincinnatus took that power to save his country and then gave it straight back, and his story inspired George Washington.

In 458 BC, when an Aequian army had a Roman force cornered, the Senate chose Cincinnatus as dictator, and its messengers found him at work on his small farm across the Tiber, plowing a field, and asked him to put on his toga to hear the Senate's command.

Granted total command for half a year, he gathered troops, made a night march, defeated the Aequi and made them pass under a yoke of spears, then laid down the dictatorship after only about sixteen days and went back to his plow.

During the American Revolution the painter Benjamin West assured George III that, should Washington win, he would hand back his power and return to his fields, and the King replied that if he did that, he would be the greatest man in the world. On 23 December 1783 Washington did exactly that, resigning his command and riding home to Mount Vernon, and Americans called him the American Cincinnatus.

cleopatra-and-the-end-of-ancient-egypt.context_blurb:
Cleopatra VII (69 to 30 BC) was the last ruler of the Ptolemaic dynasty and the last pharaoh of ancient Egypt. Clever, ambitious and fluent in many languages, she allied herself with the two most powerful Romans of her day, Julius Caesar and then Mark Antony. When she lost, Egypt became a province of Rome.

In 48 BC, barred from the royal palace at Alexandria by her brother's troops, the 21-year-old queen had her servant Apollodorus roll her up inside a bed-sack and carry her in past the guards to Julius Caesar; she tumbled out at his feet, and her daring won him over. Later tellings turned the bed-sack into a carpet.

Her family were outsiders in Egypt. Despite the legend of an Egyptian queen, Cleopatra was Greek by blood, a Macedonian descended from Ptolemy, a general of Alexander the Great who seized Egypt when Alexander died. For almost three centuries the Ptolemies governed from Alexandria, a Greek city, without bothering to learn their subjects' tongue, and Cleopatra was the first of her line to learn to speak Egyptian.

She dealt face to face with Medes, Parthians, Hebrews, Arabs and Ethiopians, rarely needing an interpreter, and Plutarch said her tongue was like a many-stringed instrument, turning to whatever language she pleased. She reportedly spoke about nine. In 41 BC, summoned by Mark Antony to Tarsus, she arrived on a barge with a golden stern, purple sails and silver oars beating time to flutes, dressed as Venus, goddess of love, and Antony was won. Pliny tells how she bet Antony she could give the costliest banquet ever, then dropped one of the world's two biggest pearls into a cup of vinegar, let it dissolve, and drank it down. The tale is probably exaggerated.

Later legend made her the world's great beauty, but the coins struck in Alexandria during her reign show a strong hooked nose and a jutting chin, and Plutarch credited her charm, wit and voice rather than her looks. At the Donations of Alexandria in 34 BC, Antony and Cleopatra parcelled out the eastern provinces among her children and proclaimed Caesarion, her son by Julius Caesar, Caesar's true heir and King of Kings, a direct challenge to Octavian, Caesar's adopted son. In September 31 BC, at Actium off the Greek coast, her sixty or so ships broke away in the middle of the battle and made for Egypt, and Antony abandoned the fight to follow her, so his fleet surrendered.

In 30 BC, rather than be paraded in chains through Rome in Octavian's triumph, she chose death, and the famous story says an asp, an Egyptian cobra, was smuggled to her hidden in a basket of figs. She was found dead on a golden couch in her royal robes, and when a guard burst in asking whether this was well done, her maid Charmion replied that it was extremely well done, and fitting for the descendant of so many kings, then fell dead beside her. Determined to leave no rival standing, Octavian had Caesarion, Julius Caesar's only true son, about seventeen, hunted down, and Arius Didymus, a scholar at his side, egged him on by twisting a line of Homer: it was not good to have too many Caesars. With Caesarion's death, some 3,000 years of pharaohs came to an end.

cliff-palace-at-mesa-verde.context_blurb:
Cliff Palace, on Mesa Verde in southwestern Colorado, is the largest cliff dwelling in North America. Ancestral Puebloans built it in the late 1100s and 1200s beneath a sandstone overhang, with round underground ceremonial rooms and a tall tower. Around 1280 they left it, along with every other cliff village on the mesa, during a long drought.

In December 1888 two cowboys searching for stray cattle on a canyon rim saw, through falling snow, a stone village of some 150 rooms tucked beneath one overhang across the gorge, empty for centuries. They named it Cliff Palace.

The cowboys, Richard Wetherill and Charlie Mason, made their way down into the empty rooms, where they found clay pots and human remains. Among them lay a stone axe head still bound to its wooden handle, looking as though someone had laid it aside moments before, though the village had stood empty for some 600 years. The Ancestral Puebloans had no metal tools, so every blade was shaped stone.

clovis-points-and-the-first-big-game-hun.context_blurb:
About 13,000 years ago, at the end of the last Ice Age, hunters across North America made long, razor-sharp stone spear points now called Clovis points. They are named for Clovis, New Mexico, where in 1929 a 19-year-old, Ridgely Whiteman, found them among mammoth bones. Clovis people were once thought the first Americans, but older sites now show that others came earlier.

The signature of a Clovis point is its flute, a long groove struck from the bottom and stretching a third to half of the way up, which let hunters fit the point into a wooden spear shaft, a trait no later style copies.

Clovis hunters took on mammoths, mastodons and bison. In Arizona, at a place called Naco, a local man, Marc Navarrete, found points while his father dug fossil bones from a dry streambed. There archaeologists uncovered a Columbian mammoth butchered about 12,000 years ago, with eight Clovis spear points still lying in and among its ribs, right where the weapons had struck. The hunt had been frozen in time.

collapse-of-the-classic-maya.context_blurb:
From about AD 250 to 900, the Maya built great stone cities such as Tikal, Palenque and Copan in the lowland jungles of Central America, carved hieroglyphic monuments and kept precise calendars. In the 800s the southern cities stopped building, lost their people and fell silent one by one, and the rule of their divine kings collapsed.

The people did not vanish, only the great cities: millions of Maya descendants still live in the Yucatan, Guatemala and southern Mexico, and about seven million people speak Mayan languages today.

The collapse shows in the stone. The Maya carved about forty dated monuments a year around 750, ten a year by 800 and none by 900. The last Long Count date the Maya ever carved is on Monument 101 at Tonina, from January 909, and after it no Maya city carved a Long Count date ever again, ending a tradition some 700 years old.

Why the cities emptied is still argued. Cores of mud drilled from the bed of Lake Chichancanab, in Mexico's Yucatan, show that the 800s brought a drought so severe that yearly rainfall fell by about half, 41 to 54 percent, and in the worst spells by up to 70 percent. Scholars also blame endless wars between rival cities and soil worn out by too many farmers, and most now see a chain reaction rather than a single cause.

columbus-and-the-voyages-of-1492.context_blurb:
Christopher Columbus, a sailor from Genoa, persuaded King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella of Spain to pay for a voyage west across the Atlantic to reach Asia. In 1492 he reached the Americas instead, though he never admitted it. His four voyages opened the age of European conquest, and for the peoples he met they brought slavery, killing and devastating disease.

His flagship was the Santa Maria, a heavy, slow cargo ship of about 110 tons, sailing with two nimble caravels, the Nina and the Pinta. Before dawn on 12 October his lookouts sighted an island, and because Columbus was sure he had reached the Indies near Asia, he called its people Indians, a mistaken name that stuck to the peoples of the Americas. On Christmas Day 1492 the Santa Maria struck a reef off Hispaniola and was lost, so Columbus built a fort from her timbers, left about 39 men there, and named it La Navidad, Spanish for Christmas. On his next voyage he found it destroyed.

The crossing had tested his crew. In September, far out of sight of land, the ships sailed into the Sargasso Sea, carpeted with floating brown weed, and the frightened sailors feared it would trap their ships and drag them under, though the weed is far too flimsy to snag a ship. By 10 October, after more than a month at sea, the crew was close to mutiny, so Columbus promised to turn back if no land appeared within three days, and two days later land was sighted. Ferdinand and Isabella had offered a pension of 10,000 maravedis a year to the first man to sight land, and Rodrigo de Triana on the Pinta cried out first around 2 a.m., but Columbus took the pension himself, insisting he had glimpsed a faint light the evening before. When Columbus showed the Taino his steel swords, they grasped them by the blades and cut themselves, because they had never seen steel; he also noticed bits of gold in some of their noses.

The story that Columbus was out to prove a round Earth is false, for educated Europeans had known the world was round ever since the ancient Greeks; the American author Washington Irving invented the flat-Earth showdown in his 1828 biography, a scene the historian Samuel Eliot Morison called pure moonshine. Sailing home in February 1493, when a storm off the Azores almost sank the Nina, Columbus sealed a report of his discovery in a waxed cask and threw it overboard, hoping it would drift ashore if he drowned. To his death in 1506 Columbus maintained that he had touched Asia, and the continents were named instead for Amerigo Vespucci, who argued they were a New World; in 1507 the mapmaker Martin Waldseemuller labelled them America. The voyages also joined the germs of two worlds, and smallpox, measles and flu killed roughly 80 to 95 percent of the native peoples of the Americas in the next century and a half, tens of millions of deaths.

Columbus's learned critics were right about what mattered, the Earth's size: Columbus pictured the globe about a quarter too small, so he thought Asia lay only some 3,000 miles west of the Canaries, when the true distance was more than 7,000. In 1495, ruling Hispaniola, Columbus demanded that each Taino older than fourteen deliver, every three months, enough gold to fill a hawk's-bell. When Taino who could not pay fled to the mountains, his men hunted them down and, as the Spanish priest Bartolome de las Casas later recorded, slaughtered them like sheep in a corral.

columbus-s-1492-voyage.context_blurb:
In August 1492 Christopher Columbus, a sea captain from Genoa, sailed west from Palos in Spain with three small ships and about ninety men, backed by Queen Isabella. He meant to reach Asia. He reached the islands of the Caribbean instead, and his first meetings with the Taino people opened a story of trade, conquest and cruelty.

His two smaller ships were fast caravels, the Pinta and the Nina, captained by the Pinzon brothers, while Columbus sailed on the bigger, slower carrack, the Santa Maria, as his flagship. After five weeks at sea, the crew sighted an island before dawn on 12 October; its Lucayan people called it Guanahani, but Columbus knelt on the beach, claimed it for Spain's monarchs and renamed it San Salvador, Holy Saviour.

The islanders were the Taino, and several of their words passed into English, among them canoe, hammock, barbecue, tobacco and hurricane. They welcomed the strangers with parrots, cotton thread and food, and Columbus handed them glass beads and red caps in return, while noticing the bits of gold some wore in their noses. On the night of 24 December, with a cabin boy at the tiller while Columbus slept, the flagship ran onto a reef and was lost, so Columbus built a small fort from her timbers, left 39 men in it, and named it La Navidad, for Christmas.

Columbus was certain he had reached the Indies, the wealthy country around China and Japan, and he clung to that belief until he died in 1506, insisting he had touched the edge of Asia. Spain's monarchs had offered a yearly pension of 10,000 maravedis to the first man to sight land, and at about 2 a.m. on 12 October Rodrigo de Triana on the Pinta cried Tierra!, but Columbus insisted that he himself had spotted a dim light the previous evening, and pocketed the pension. Afraid that his men would panic so far out on the open sea, Columbus kept two logbooks, and the public one he read to the men recorded smaller daily distances to hide how far they had really sailed. Ironically, those fake numbers were closer to the truth.

By his reckoning Japan sat a mere 3,000 miles or so beyond his starting islands, though the true gap is over 7,000, because he had made the Earth far too small, undercounting its circumference by about 25 percent, and stretched Asia too far east. When he returned later in 1493, he found La Navidad burned to the ground and all 39 men dead: they had abused the local Taino, who struck back, led, the accounts say, by the chief Caonabo.

Hunting for gold on Hispaniola, Columbus forced every Taino of about fourteen or older to deliver, every three months, a thimbleful of gold dust, enough to fill a small hawk's-bell, an impossible quota on an island with little gold, and those who failed were brutally punished. Only two days after landing, on 14 October 1492, Columbus had written in his journal that the Taino would make good servants and that with fifty men they could all be subjugated. On his first day he had already seized several Taino to take back to Spain. The friar Bartolome de las Casas later recorded the cruelty, and the Taino population collapsed.

commodore-perry-s-black-ships-open-japan.context_blurb:
For about 250 years Japan's Tokugawa shoguns kept the country almost sealed off from the world, a policy called sakoku, or closed country. Any Japanese who left faced execution. In July 1853 an American naval squadron under Commodore Matthew Perry arrived to force Japan to open its ports, and the shock helped push Japan into rapid modernisation.

On 8 July 1853 Perry's four warships steamed into Edo Bay, their hulls painted black and their funnels pouring black coal smoke, and the astonished Japanese called them the Black Ships, kurofune. Two of them, the steam frigates Susquehanna and Mississippi, needed no sails and could move straight into the wind, even towing the two sailing sloops, which to people who knew only wind-driven ships looked like sorcery. When Perry returned in February 1854 he brought gifts, including a quarter-size steam locomotive running round a ring of track near Yokohama, and since its car was too small to sit in, dignified officials climbed onto its roof and rode it with their robes flying.

Before Perry, the one foreign trading post Japan allowed was run by Dutch merchants on Dejima, a small man-made island in Nagasaki harbour. The panic inspired satire. A comic poem, a kyoka, grumbled that a strong tea called Jokisen kept people awake all night after just four cups, but jokisen also means steamships and four cups also means four vessels, so it really said that four steamships had robbed the country of its peaceful sleep.

common-sense-thomas-paine.context_blurb:
Thomas Paine, an English-born corset-maker, came to Philadelphia in 1774 with a letter from Benjamin Franklin and few prospects. In January 1776, with fighting already under way but most Americans unsure about independence, he published Common Sense, signed only by an Englishman: a short, fiery pamphlet in blunt, plain English arguing for an American republic at once.

It spread like fire. By the time the war for independence ended, Paine claimed, about 500,000 copies were in circulation among only some 2.5 million colonists, many of them read aloud in taverns, though the figure comes from Paine himself and few sales records survive. It helped push Americans toward the Declaration of Independence six months later.

Paine's tone was a scandal, because in 1776 few writers dared to sneer at a ruling monarch. Paine refused to call George III king of America, saying America's true king reigned above and did not make havoc of mankind like a Royal Brute of Britain. Later that year his essays The American Crisis were read aloud to Washington's soldiers.

confucius-confucianism.context_blurb:
Confucius, Kong Qiu, was a teacher and official in the small Chinese state of Lu around 500 BC, when the old Zhou order was collapsing into war. He wandered in search of a ruler who would govern by virtue, and he died disappointed. Yet his teaching about family, duty and goodness shaped China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam for over two thousand years.

His own people called him Master Kong, Kongzi or Kong Fuzi, and the Latin name Confucius was invented by European Jesuit missionaries, whose translation of his works was published in Paris in 1687. He wrote no book himself; his students gathered his remembered sayings into the Analects, whose short passages so often begin with the same three words: The Master said. When his student Zigong asked for one word to live by, he answered reciprocity, and gave the rule: never do to others what you would not want done to yourself, a negative Golden Rule centuries older than its famous Western forms.

From about 498 BC he spent some fourteen years travelling through the states of Chu, Chen, Song and Wei, searching for a prince who would actually use his ideas to govern, and finding mostly indifference. His favourite student was Yan Hui. Yan Hui was so poor that he lived in a mean lane on one bamboo dish of rice and one gourd of drink, yet nothing spoiled his joy, and Confucius praised him for it. When Yan Hui died young, the calm master broke down, crying out twice that Heaven was destroying him, and asked whom he should mourn bitterly if not this man.

Confucius idolised the Duke of Zhou and the sages of the past, and he described himself as one who transmitted the old wisdom but did not create anything new. When Duke Jing of Qi asked how to govern, he answered that the ruler should be a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father and the son a son, because society holds together only when each person lives up to his station. His highest virtue was ren, which a gentleman would rather die than betray, and when asked to define it, he said simply that ren is caring for others. Its root, he taught, is devotion to one's parents. Tracing his own growth, he said that learning became his goal at fifteen, and that at seventy he could follow whatever his heart desired without overstepping what was right.

In 136 BC the Han emperor Wu made Confucian teaching the empire's official doctrine, and it became the heart of the imperial civil-service examination that chose China's officials until 1905. The failed wanderer's words ran the empire for two thousand years. The tradition's Five Relationships, set out fully by his follower Mencius, run both ways: subjects owe their ruler loyalty, and the ruler owes his people real care and good government in return.

constantine-founds-constantinople.context_blurb:
Constantine the Great, Rome's first Christian emperor, decided around 324 that Rome lay too far from the empire's richest and most dangerous lands. He rebuilt the old Greek town of Byzantium, where Europe meets Asia, and in 330 dedicated it as New Rome, though everyone soon called it Constantinople, the city of Constantine.

Legend says he marked out its walls on foot, dragging a spear along the ground, and when an alarmed aide asked how much farther he would go, Constantine replied that he would keep going until the One who led him stopped.

He filled the city with treasures taken from across the empire. In the Hippodrome he set up the Serpent Column, three intertwined bronze snakes cast by the Greeks from the shields of the Persians they defeated at Plataea in 479 BC, which had stood at Delphi for over 800 years. Part of it still stands in Istanbul. Atop a towering porphyry column in his new forum he placed his own bronze likeness, remade as Apollo, or Helios, the sun god, crowned with metal rays facing the rising sun. Legend claimed the rays were forged from the nails of the Crucifixion, a blend of old gods and new faith.

constantine-the-milvian-bridge-and-nicae.context_blurb:
Constantine the Great, born around 272, fought his way to the top of the Roman Empire through years of civil war. In 312 he defeated his rival Maxentius outside Rome after a vision he linked to Christ, and from then on he favoured the Christians. He ended their persecution, called the great Council of Nicaea in 325, and was baptized as he lay dying in 337.

Marching on Rome in 312, Constantine reported seeing at about noon a blazing cross over the sun, with words his whole army saw too, commanding, By this sign, conquer, as the historian Eusebius heard from the emperor himself. So his men marked their shields with the Chi-Rho, in which the Greek letters X and P, chi and rho, overlap: the first letters of Christ in Greek. When Maxentius's army broke and fled over a bridge of boats across the Tiber, the bridge gave way, and Maxentius, dragged down by his armour, drowned in the river. Legends gathered later too. One says that at the Council of Nicaea Bishop Nicholas of Myra, the saint who became Santa Claus, grew so angry at the priest Arius that he struck him across the face, though the tale first turns up about ten centuries later and Nicholas is missing from the council's lists.

Constantine's turn was stunning, because in 303 the emperor Diocletian had begun the Great Persecution, ordering churches torn down and scriptures burned, and Christians tortured and killed. After his vision, Eusebius says, Constantine had a new battle standard made, the labarum: a long gold-covered spear crossed by a bar, crowned with a jewelled wreath around the Chi-Rho. His rival had trusted older oracles. Maxentius consulted the Sibylline Books, which foretold that a foe of Rome would die on 28 October, and, sure they meant Constantine, he left the safety of Rome's walls to fight, and died himself. At Nicaea many bishops bore scars from the persecutions, and the historian Theodoret says Constantine greeted these confessors by kissing their wounds and the empty sockets of their eyes; Rufinus names Bishop Paphnutius of Egypt, who had lost his right eye.

The deeper story is full of puzzles. The two earliest writers disagree about the sign: Eusebius describes a blazing cross that the whole army saw by day, but Lactantius, writing earlier, says it came to Constantine in a dream, telling him to mark God's heavenly sign on his soldiers' shields. In 315 the Senate dedicated the Arch of Constantine, crediting his victory to divine inspiration without ever saying which god, a careful balance between the Christian God and the old gods. Constantine summoned the bishops to Nicaea to end a quarrel over Arius, a priest of Alexandria, who taught that the Son was created, so that there was once a time when the Son did not exist; the council declared the Son of one substance with the Father. Later Christians called Nicaea the Council of the 318 Fathers, though fewer bishops signed, because 318 echoed the servants Abraham led to rescue his nephew Lot in Genesis. Yet in 337 Constantine was baptized as he lay dying, by Bishop Eusebius of Nicomedia, a follower of the Arian movement, the very party Nicaea had condemned.

constitutional-convention-great-compromi.context_blurb:
In the summer of 1787, delegates from twelve of the thirteen states met in secret at the State House in Philadelphia to repair a weak national government. George Washington presided, and James Madison took notes. After four months of argument they produced the Constitution, the oldest written national constitution still in use anywhere in the world.

To keep every word secret, the delegates nailed the windows of their meeting room shut and posted sentries at the doors, and they sweated in wool suits all summer. Benjamin Franklin, 81 and the oldest delegate, was too crippled by gout to walk to the State House, so each day four inmates of the Walnut Street jail carried him there in a sedan chair he had brought back from Paris. When it was over, a Philadelphia woman, Elizabeth Powel, asked him whether the new government was to be a republic or a monarchy, and he answered, a republic, if they could keep it; the exchange survives only in James McHenry's diary.

As the delegates signed, Franklin said he had long wondered whether the half-sun carved on the back of Washington's chair was rising or setting, and now he was happy to know it was rising, not setting. On average the delegates were only about 42, and the youngest, Jonathan Dayton of New Jersey, was just 26 when he signed, 55 years younger than Franklin.

By July the Convention was deadlocked, the big states wanting seats by population and the small states an equal vote each, until two Connecticut delegates, Roger Sherman and Oliver Ellsworth, offered a split: two houses, a House of Representatives by population and a Senate with two votes for every state. This Great Compromise saved the Convention. Rhode Island alone sent no one, so distrustful of any powerful national government that its critics mocked it as Rogue Island, and it was the last state to ratify, in May 1790. Virginia's fiery Patrick Henry also refused to attend, saying he smelt a rat, one in Philadelphia tending toward monarchy. The first draft began with a roll call of all the states, but Gouverneur Morris of Pennsylvania, who gave more speeches than anyone and walked on a wooden peg leg, and he rewrote it to begin with We the People, naming not each state but the United States as one.

The Convention's worst bargain, the Three-Fifths Compromise, pushed by James Wilson and Charles Pinckney, counted three of every five enslaved people toward a state's population for House seats and taxes, and Wilson later disowned his own clause.

James Madison of Virginia came better prepared than anyone, having studied two trunks of books on ancient and modern confederacies that Thomas Jefferson shipped him from Paris, and he brought a ready-made blueprint, the Virginia Plan, and took notes at every session, earning the title Father of the Constitution. Article V protects one deal above all others: no state may lose its equal vote in the Senate without its own consent, which makes equal Senate representation essentially the one rule that can never be amended away.

convivencia-moorish-spain-the-alhambra.context_blurb:
For about seven centuries, Muslim princes ruled much of Spain, and Christians, Jews and Muslims lived side by side in cities such as Cordoba, Toledo and Granada. Later writers called it convivencia, living together. It was real but unequal: Jews and Christians lived as protected but lower-ranked subjects who paid a special tax. Its last great jewel was the Alhambra palace in Granada.

In the Alhambra's Hall of the Two Sisters, the Nasrid sultans built a muqarnas vault, a honeycomb ceiling of some 5,000 small prism-shaped cells circling a star at its centre, so that the dome seems to hang overhead like a sky full of stars. A poem by the court poet Ibn Zamrak, running around the walls, compares the dome to the heavens.

The living-together could turn deadly. In Granada on 30 December 1066, Muslim rioters broke into the palace, murdered Joseph ibn Naghrela, the Jewish vizier, and went on to slaughter the city's Jews: the Jewish Encyclopedia counts about 1,500 families, some 4,000 people, in a single day. Later the Almohad rulers ordered Jews and Christians to convert, flee or die, driving the philosopher Maimonides from Cordoba.

coolidge-prosperity-and-the-limited-gove.context_blurb:
After the First World War, American voters turned to leaders who promised to leave them alone. When President Warren Harding died in 1923, Calvin Coolidge took the oath by lamplight from his own father, a small-town notary, at the family farmhouse in Vermont. Coolidge governed with famous thrift, the economy boomed, and in 1928 he chose not to run again.

One famous line makes Coolidge seem interested in nothing but money. In a 1925 speech he said that the chief business of the American people was business, but in the very next breath he said their chief ideal was idealism and that America was a nation of idealists, the half the famous soundbite leaves out.

His Treasury Secretary, Andrew Mellon, wrote that high tax rates do not necessarily mean large revenue. Mellon lowered the highest income-tax bracket from 73 percent to 25, and according to Cato Institute figures, revenue then rose, by 1928 passing its 1920 level, while the budget ran surpluses and the national debt was paid down. Unemployment fell to about 3 percent in the boom years.

copernicus-and-heliocentrism.context_blurb:
Nicolaus Copernicus (1473 to 1543) was a Polish churchman, doctor, economist and astronomer, born in Torun. He argued that the Earth is not the centre of the heavens; the Sun is, and that the solid ground beneath us is racing through space. Cautious by nature, he held back his great book until he was dying, yet it began the Scientific Revolution.

He did all his work before the telescope existed, for it came about 65 years after his death, so he studied the sky with only his naked eyes and mathematics. One of his first recorded observations came in 1497, while he was a student in Bologna, when he watched with his naked eyes as the Moon passed across Aldebaran, the red eye of the bull in Taurus, and hid it. People objected that if the Earth raced through space we would feel it move, and Copernicus answered that the Earth only looks still because we ride along with it. For his last thirty years he served as a canon of Frombork Cathedral and watched the stars from a tower in the cathedral's defensive wall, still called the Copernicus Tower.

Around 1514 he wrote a short sketch of his idea, the Commentariolus, or Little Commentary, and shared handwritten copies with a few trusted friends instead of printing it. For years he held his great book back, until a young Lutheran from Wittenberg, Rheticus, became his only pupil, lived with him for about two years, and persuaded him to publish his sun-centred theory. Printed in 1543 as De revolutionibus, On the Revolutions, the book was not hidden from the Church: Copernicus dedicated it to Pope Paul III, appealing to the Pope's own skill in mathematics. Legend says that on 24 May 1543 he woke from a coma caused by a stroke, saw his printed book for the first time, and died that same day, though historians call it a dramatic tale.

In the book's most beautiful line he pictured the Sun as a lamp in a beautiful temple, asking who would place that lamp anywhere but the centre, where it can light the whole at once. Copernicus also advised on money, and around 1519, watching debased coins circulate beside full-weight ones, he stated the rule later called Gresham's Law: bad money drives out good. His lost grave was found in 2005 under the floor of Frombork Cathedral, and scientists proved the bones were his by matching their DNA to strands of hair left in one of his books, now at Uppsala University in Sweden.

When the book was printed, the editor Andreas Osiander slipped in an unsigned preface telling readers that the moving Earth was only a calculating device, not a real claim about the world, and readers did not learn until the 1600s that the words were not Copernicus's. For his tomb Copernicus chose humble words, asking God not for the grace given to Saint Paul nor the pardon given to Saint Peter, but only for the mercy Christ showed the robber who was crucified at his side.

copernicus-the-heliocentric-model.context_blurb:
Nicolaus Copernicus (1473 to 1543) was a Polish thinker who argued that the Earth is not the still centre of the universe but one of several planets in motion. He studied in Krakow and Italy, then spent most of his working life as a church official in Frombork, on the Baltic coast, practising medicine and managing church lands as well as watching the sky.

In 1543 his great book appeared in Nuremberg as De revolutionibus orbium coelestium, On the Revolutions, that is the turnings, of the Heavenly Spheres, and its title began the word revolution's journey from meaning a turning sphere to meaning an overturning of ideas. Astronomy was only his spare-time passion: in 1497 his uncle, the bishop Lucas Watzenrode, found him a salaried post as a cathedral canon at Frombork, running the cathedral's affairs, and he held it for life. He was probably never even ordained a priest. At the heart of his book he crowned the Sun with grand titles, calling it the Lamp, the Mind and the Ruler of the Universe, seated as if on a royal throne with the planets circling round it. Legend says a finished copy reached him on his deathbed, but the printing was not quite complete, so what he most likely held were the final printed pages, the front matter, not a bound book.

Around 1514 he had already shared a brief essay, copied by hand, with a few friends, setting out seven bold statements, among them that the Earth is not the centre of the universe and that the Sun is. In 1539 a young Lutheran mathematician, Georg Joachim Rheticus, came to Frombork, became his only pupil for two years, and in 1540 printed the Narratio Prima, the First Account, the first book to announce Copernicus's sun-centred theory of the heavens. Copernicus did not hide the book from the Church: he dedicated it to Pope Paul III, hoping the Pope's love of mathematics would give it a fair hearing, and admitting he had held it back for fear of scorn. His bones were identified in our own century, and in 2010 Poland gave him a hero's reburial in Frombork Cathedral, under a black granite tombstone showing a golden Sun ringed by six planets, his own model.

The printing in Germany was overseen by a Lutheran clergyman, Andreas Osiander, who, nervous about the moving Earth, secretly slipped in an unsigned note claiming it was merely a device for calculation, not the physical truth. Because the note was unsigned, readers long blamed Copernicus for it. When Rheticus found out, he flew into a rage, quarrelled bitterly with the printer and, with Copernicus's friends, demanded a reprint without the fake preface, but the printer refused.

The Church did not ban the book until 5 March 1616, when it went onto the Index of Forbidden Books more than seventy years after it was published. The famous clash came generations after Copernicus was dead. In 2005 archaeologists found a skeleton under Frombork Cathedral, and scientists proved it was his by matching its DNA to two of his hairs still lodged in a book he had owned, now at Uppsala University. Forensic artists even rebuilt his face, broken nose and all.
