copernicus-the-scientific-revolution.context_blurb:
In 1543 Nicolaus Copernicus, a Polish churchman, put the Earth in motion around the Sun. His idea took most of a century to win, because others had to test it: Tycho Brahe measured the sky, Johannes Kepler found the true shape of planetary paths, and Galileo Galilei turned a telescope on the heavens. Their trust in measurement over authority became the Scientific Revolution.

The Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe lost part of his nose in 1566 when he fought his cousin with swords over which of them was the better mathematician, and for 35 years he wore a false nose, which tradition called precious metal but a 2012 chemical analysis showed was really brass. Since ancient times Europeans had placed a motionless Earth at the centre, but Copernicus's book of 1543 placed the Sun at the centre instead and made the Earth one more orbiting planet: the idea called heliocentrism. In January 1610 Galileo turned his new telescope on Jupiter, saw small points of light beside it shift from night to night, counted four, and realised they were four moons circling it, proof that not everything orbits the Earth. Legend says that after the Inquisition forced Galileo to kneel and swear the Earth does not move, he muttered, And yet it moves, though historians doubt he ever said it.

Copernicus was no lone rebel against the Church: he had earned a doctorate in canon law, the law of the Church, and worked as a cathedral canon at Frombork, doing astronomy in his free hours. Tradition says the first printed copy of his book was placed in his hands on his deathbed on 24 May 1543, though the timing was probably coincidence. Galileo shrewdly named Jupiter's moons the Medicean Stars after the Medici family and his former pupil Cosimo II, Grand Duke of Tuscany, who made him court mathematician. In 1633 the Inquisition in Rome found the 69-year-old Galileo strongly suspect of heresy, forced him to take back his teaching, and sentenced him to house arrest for life at his villa near Florence.

Galileo's most decisive proof came when he watched Venus for months and saw it wax and wane, from a tiny full disc to a large crescent, which was impossible in Ptolemy's Earth-centred system, so Venus had to orbit the Sun. Kepler inherited Tycho's measurements and fought what he called his war on Mars, whose orbit refused to fit a circle, until he saw that a planet's true path is an ellipse, a stretched oval with the Sun at one focus. When Kepler's elderly mother, Katharina, was jailed for witchcraft and shown the instruments of torture, Kepler wrote a long legal defence tearing apart each accusation, and won her release.

When Copernicus's book was printed, the theologian Andreas Osiander slipped in an unsigned preface saying the sun-centred model was only a hypothesis that need not be true, and Copernicus's friends were furious. Galileo, a devout Catholic, liked to quote a churchman's saying that the Holy Spirit means to teach us how one goes to heaven, not how the heavens go. Faith and science, he argued, answer different questions.

cort-s-and-the-fall-of-the-aztec-empire.context_blurb:
In 1519 the Spanish adventurer Hernan Cortes landed on the coast of Mexico with roughly six hundred soldiers and a handful of horses and marched inland against the Aztec Empire, ruled from its island capital, Tenochtitlan. Within two years the empire had fallen, brought down by Spanish steel, by native peoples who hated Aztec rule, and above all by disease. Both sides committed horrors.

When the foot soldier Bernal Diaz first saw Tenochtitlan rising from its lake, he later wrote, it seemed like an enchanted vision out of an old romance, and some soldiers asked whether it was all a dream. In the great market of Tlatelolco, Diaz said, more than sixty thousand people came every day to buy and sell, and two days were not enough to see it all. Cortes's voice was an enslaved Nahua woman who spoke Nahuatl and Maya and quickly learned Spanish, baptized Dona Marina and remembered as La Malinche, and Cortes said that after God the conquest was owed to her. On 8 November 1519 the emperor Moctezuma welcomed Cortes with gifts that included two great discs, one of gold and one of silver, and Cortes melted them down for their metal.

Early on, to stop his men sailing back to Cuba, Cortes had loyal men secretly bore holes in ten of his eleven ships to sink them, then blamed shipworms; the famous tale that he burned his ships is a myth first told in 1558. The city of Tlaxcala hated the Aztecs, because the Aztecs forced conquered peoples to hand over their young men, whom the priests at Tenochtitlan then sacrificed. On the Night of Sorrows, 30 June 1520, the Spanish tried to slip out along a causeway, and when the alarm went up, soldiers weighed down by looted gold fell from the causeway into the lake and drowned. That autumn smallpox, a disease never seen in the Americas, arrived with an infected man in a Spanish relief force and gutted the Aztec army and killed between a quarter and a half of the people in the city.

The Spaniards were a minority of the army that took the capital; most of it was tens of thousands of native warriors, Tlaxcalans above all, who hated Aztec rule. To fight on the lake, Cortes had his shipwright Martin Lopez build thirteen small warships at Tlaxcala, then take them apart, carry them piece by piece over the mountains, and rebuild them by the water.

The siege of 1521 was a slow strangling. When Pedro de Alvarado's men cut the aqueduct from Chapultepec, the city was left without fresh water, because the water of Lake Texcoco around it was brackish, too salty to drink. The Aztecs marched captured Spaniards up the pyramid at Tlatelolco to drums and conch shells, and in full view of their comrades the priests cut out their hearts on the altar at the top. The city fell on 13 August 1521, and its last emperor, Cuauhtemoc, was captured on the open water as he tried to slip away across the lake by canoe. Hunting gold, the Spanish tortured Cuauhtemoc by burning his oiled feet, and when the lord of Tacuba beside him groaned, Cuauhtemoc, the story goes, asked whether he thought Cuauhtemoc himself was lying in a bath for pleasure.

creation-of-israel-1948.context_blurb:
In 1948, as the British Mandate over Palestine ended, Jewish leaders proclaimed the modern State of Israel. A United Nations plan of 1947 had proposed separate Jewish and Arab states; Jewish leaders accepted it and Arab leaders rejected it. The war that followed shaped a conflict over land, refugees and sovereignty that continues today.

On 14 May 1948 David Ben-Gurion, head of the Jewish Agency, rose at a museum in Tel Aviv and read Israel's Declaration of Independence in sixteen minutes, declared the State of Israel established, and then adjourned the meeting. When he first struck his gavel, the guests had burst into the anthem Hatikvah. The next day, 15 May, the armies of five Arab neighbours, Egypt, Syria, Jordan, Iraq and Lebanon, invaded the new state, beginning the war Israelis call their War of Independence. Hundreds of thousands of Palestinian Arabs were driven from or fled their homes in the fighting, an event Arabs call the Nakba, the catastrophe.

Just eleven minutes after the declaration, President Harry Truman made the United States the first country to recognise Israel, overruling his Secretary of State, George Marshall, who feared angering the Arab world. The streets filled with dancing, but that night, with the murder of six million Jews in the Holocaust fresh in mind, Ben-Gurion wrote in his diary that he mourned among the joyful.

The ceremonial scroll in the newsreels hid a secret: the calligrapher Otte Wallish had finished only its bottom part, so the scroll was mostly blank and Ben-Gurion was really reading from handwritten notes. It was completed in June. The name Israel was chosen only two days earlier, on 12 May, and the founders dropped Judea and Zion because those names pointed to places, such as Jerusalem, that lay outside the new state's borders.

crimean-war-and-the-charge-of-the-light-.context_blurb:
The Crimean War (1853 to 1856) pitted Russia against Britain, France, the Ottoman Empire and Sardinia, and most of it was fought on the Crimean peninsula in the Black Sea. It was the first war reported home by telegraph and the first widely photographed. It is best remembered for a single doomed charge by British horsemen at Balaclava, in October 1854.

Lord Raglan's order meant the cavalry to recover captured guns on the heights, but when Lord Lucan asked which guns, the messenger, Captain Louis Nolan, swept his arm not toward the heights but down the valley toward the main Russian battery, and some 670 riders charged the wrong target. Nolan was the first man killed, and the brigade lost well over a hundred dead for nothing. A French general watching said it was magnificent, but not war.

Weeks later the poet Alfred Tennyson fixed the disaster in memory with The Charge of the Light Brigade. Its galloping refrain sends the six hundred riding into the valley of Death, with cannon on their right, on their left and in front of them. It became the English-speaking world's great story of brave men destroyed by a muddled order.

cuban-missile-crisis-1962.context_blurb:
In October 1962 the United States discovered that the Soviet Union was secretly placing nuclear missiles in Cuba, about 90 miles from Florida. For thirteen days President John F. Kennedy and the Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev stood at the edge of nuclear war. It remains the closest the world has come, and it ended in a compromise partly kept secret.

On 14 October Major Richard Heyser flew a U-2 spy plane high over Cuba, and his photographs showed nuclear missile launch sites, with Soviet medium-range missiles being assembled. Kennedy sent warships to surround Cuba and stop any ship bringing weapons, but because a blockade is an act of war, he called it a quarantine, a word borrowed from keeping out disease. On live television he warned that any nuclear missile fired from Cuba at any nation in the Americas would be treated as a Soviet attack on the United States, requiring full retaliation against the Soviet Union itself. On 28 October Khrushchev announced over Radio Moscow that the Soviets would dismantle the missiles and ship them home to the USSR, and the United States promised not to invade Cuba.

From 16 October Kennedy's secret advisers, the Executive Committee or ExComm, argued in the White House over two answers: bomb the missile sites and invade the island, or surround it with a ring of warships, which Kennedy chose. On 25 October at the United Nations, when the Soviet ambassador Valerian Zorin stalled, the American ambassador Adlai Stevenson had aides unveil huge blown-up U-2 photographs of the missile sites for the whole Security Council to see. On 27 October, Black Saturday, a Soviet missile shot down the U-2 of Major Rudolf Anderson, the crisis's one American combat death, and he had not even been scheduled to fly that day; he had pushed hard to take the mission.

On 24 October, when word came that Soviet ships had stopped short of the quarantine line, Secretary of State Dean Rusk whispered to McGeorge Bundy that they were eyeball to eyeball and he thought the other fellow had just blinked. In a letter of 26 October Khrushchev warned that the two sides were pulling on a rope in which they had tied the knot of war, and that the harder they pulled, the tighter it would grow. But on Black Saturday a second, tougher letter came from Khrushchev, demanding that the United States also remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey.

The real story was stranger than the legend. When Rusk spoke, the Soviet ships carrying missiles had already turned back the day before and were about 500 miles away, heading home, so his famous showdown never happened. Kennedy's advisers escaped the harder letter with the Trollope ploy: they publicly answered only the softer Friday letter, as if the Turkey demand had never come, while Robert Kennedy secretly promised the Soviet ambassador that the Jupiter missiles would quietly go. Underwater that same day, the Soviet submarine B-59, cut off from Moscow, was being battered by American depth charges, and its captain readied a nuclear torpedo, but Vasili Arkhipov, a senior officer aboard, would not give his consent, realising the Americans were dropping signalling charges to force the sub to surface, not to sink it. The torpedo never fired.

cuban-revolution-fidel-castro.context_blurb:
On 1 January 1959 Fidel Castro, a young Cuban lawyer, overthrew the American-backed dictator Fulgencio Batista after years of guerrilla war, fought alongside his brother Raul and the Argentine doctor Ernesto Che Guevara. Castro soon turned Cuba into a one-party communist dictatorship allied with the Soviet Union, and he ruled it for almost fifty years.

His road to power began with defeat. On 26 July 1953 Castro led about 160 rebels against the Moncada barracks and failed, and at his trial, acting as his own lawyer, he spoke for nearly four hours, ending by telling the judges to condemn him, since it did not matter: history would absolve him. Freed after 22 months, he went to Mexico. In late 1956 Castro and 82 fighters sailed for Cuba crammed into the Granma, a pleasure yacht built for 25, and only about 20 survived the landing. In late 1958 near Santa Clara, Che Guevara's 300 fighters used a captured bulldozer to rip up the railway, derailed an armoured train carrying 3,500 government soldiers, and captured the troops with all their weapons. Within hours Batista fled.

For two years Castro avoided the word communist, but in December 1961 he declared on live television that he was a Marxist-Leninist and would remain one until the end of his life. Che, the romantic face on countless T-shirts, wrote in 1967 that hatred must turn a revolutionary into a violent, selective, cold-blooded killing machine, and at La Cabana fortress he had overseen tribunals that sent men to the firing squad. Cubans voted with their feet. In April 1980, after thousands of Cubans crowded into the Peruvian embassy, Castro opened the port of Mariel to anyone who wanted to leave, and in five months some 125,000 Cubans, nicknamed Marielitos, crossed to Florida by boat. Since 1959 millions of Cubans have emigrated.

cuneiform-the-first-writing.context_blurb:
Writing was invented around 3200 BC in Sumer, in the south of today's Iraq. Its scribes pressed marks into tablets of wet clay, and the system, called cuneiform, was used for some three thousand years by Sumerians, Babylonians, Assyrians, Persians and others. It began not with poetry but with bookkeeping, and hundreds of thousands of tablets survive.

The name comes from the Latin cuneus, meaning wedge, because every cuneiform sign is built from one small shape, a wedge, repeated again and again. Scribes made their marks with a stylus cut from reed, which grew thick in the marshes, and the Sumerian word for the stylus meant tablet-reed. To make each mark, a scribe pressed the stylus straight down into the soft clay and lifted it out again, leaving one little wedge, then pressed again for the next. Fire, which turns scrolls to ash, did the opposite for clay: when cities burned, the fire baked the tablets hard as pottery, which is why about half a million survive. Around 1750 BC a merchant of Ur named Nanni sent the world's oldest known customer complaint to the dealer Ea-nasir, furious that the copper he had been sent was of bad quality. Other buyers complained about Ea-nasir's copper too.

The earliest writing was strikingly ordinary. At Uruk, home of the oldest writing yet found, about 85 percent of the earliest tablets are records of who owed grain and who owed beer, written by temple accountants. The oldest personal name in any writing, Kushim, belonged not to a king but to an accountant tracking barley for a temple brewery, some 135,000 litres of it over 37 months. The first signs were little pictures of what was counted, and the sign for eating was a human head bent toward a bowl. Boys trained in the edubba, the House of Tablets, and a Sumerian poem called Schooldays shows that a student who made careless marks was beaten with a stick.

Writing grew out of counting. Long before writing, Sumerian traders tracked goods with little clay counters and shipped them sealed in a hollow clay envelope, a bulla, after pressing each token into its soft outer skin. When clerks saw that the marks outside already told them everything, they dropped the tokens altogether and kept only the marks, on flat tablets. To write words that cannot be drawn, scribes borrowed a picture for its sound, so the sign for arrow, ti, also wrote til, life. Cuneiform was then forgotten for some 1,500 years. In the 1830s and 1840s the British officer Henry Rawlinson climbed the sheer cliff at Behistun in Persia to copy King Darius's inscription in three languages, with a local boy rigging ropes to take casts of the highest signs, and he cracked the script.

cyril-methodius-and-the-cyrillic-alphabe.context_blurb:
Cyril and Methodius were Greek brothers from Thessalonica who in the 800s carried Christianity to the Slavic peoples in their own language, instead of Latin or Greek. They are honoured as saints by both the Catholic and the Orthodox churches. Today some form of the alphabet named after Cyril writes Russian, Ukrainian, Bulgarian, Serbian and many other languages.

In 863 the Byzantine emperor Michael III sent Cyril north to Great Moravia, whose prince, Rastislav, wanted his people to hear Scripture in Slavic, a language that had never been written. Cyril invented a completely new alphabet from scratch, Glagolitic, the oldest known Slavic script, with 41 letters, the first of them shaped like a cross.

Yet the alphabet called Cyrillic is not Cyril's own. His followers created it later, at the Preslav Literary School in the First Bulgarian Empire, basing it mostly on Greek letters, and they named it after their teacher as an act of homage.

cyrus-field-and-the-atlantic-telegraph-c.context_blurb:
Cyrus Field was a New York paper merchant who in the 1850s became obsessed with laying a telegraph cable across the floor of the Atlantic, from Ireland to Newfoundland, so that messages could cross in minutes instead of weeks. He was no engineer, but he raised the money, hired the experts and refused to quit after costly failures.

In 1858 two warships worked together, the American Niagara and the British Agamemnon. They met in mid-ocean and spliced their two halves of cable together, then steamed off in opposite directions, the Niagara west toward Newfoundland and the Agamemnon east toward Ireland, each paying out cable behind it.

When the first message crossed that August, New York threw a wild party, and its fireworks set the dome of City Hall ablaze. The cable soon fell silent, and after more than a decade of attempts a lasting line was finally laid by the giant steamship Great Eastern. From then on, news and money could cross the ocean in minutes.

cyrus-the-great-and-the-persian-empire.context_blurb:
In the 500s BC a Persian prince named Cyrus ruled Anshan, a minor kingdom in what is now southern Iran. He became Cyrus the Great, founder of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, and he won his wars with cunning as much as with force. He also did something rare for a conqueror: he let beaten peoples keep their gods, and he sent captives home.

In about two decades Cyrus turned that little realm into a superpower that ran from the Aegean shore of Turkey to the Indus River, and when he died in 530 BC it was the biggest empire anyone had ever built. His tricks became legends. Around 546 BC he faced Croesus, king of Lydia, whose horsemen were the terror of the region. The Mede general Harpagus told Cyrus to put his baggage camels in the front line, because horses panic at the smell and sight of camels, and when the Lydians charged, their horses reared in fright and bolted. The dreaded cavalry broke at the Battle of Thymbra.

Babylon was a harder prize, a walled giant far too strong to storm. But the Euphrates ran straight through the city, under its walls. In 539 BC the Persians drew the river down until its bed lay bare, then waded along the exposed riverbed and slipped in beneath the walls. Cyrus's general Gobryas marched in with hardly a fight. Among the captives in Babylon were the Jews, whom King Nebuchadnezzar had carried off from Jerusalem long before, and Cyrus decreed that they could go home to Jerusalem and build their Temple again. The Book of Ezra records that decree, which began the Second Temple.

Cyrus had his victory written on a barrel-shaped clay cylinder, dug up at Babylon in 1879 and now in the British Museum, where he stacks up royal titles and tops them with the oldest Mesopotamian boast of all: king of the world's four quarters, meaning ruler of everything. Herodotus told wilder tales. He says Cyrus set the captured Croesus on a burning pyre, and as the flames rose, Croesus kept crying out the name of Solon, the wise Athenian who had told him never to call any man happy before his death. Curious, Cyrus had the fire put out (in the Lydian version a sudden rainstorm did it) and kept Croesus as an adviser for life. Herodotus also tells how Cyrus died, fighting the Massagetae, nomads of the far northeast. He had killed the son of their queen, Tomyris, with a trap baited with wine, and she swore to give him his fill of blood. When Cyrus fell in battle, Tomyris kept her vow by plunging his severed head into a wineskin filled with blood. These are legends, not proven history. Two centuries later Alexander the Great, who had admired Cyrus all his life, came to the tomb at Pasargadae and found that robbers had smashed the golden coffin and thrown out the body, so he ordered the tomb restored and the robbers punished. It still stands in Iran.

In Isaiah, the Hebrew prophet's book, God speaks to Cyrus directly and calls him the Lord's anointed, mashiach in Hebrew, the word behind messiah, and no other non-Jew in the whole Bible receives that title. Cyrus knew how to win priests, too. He left Babylon's gods standing, and his cylinder claims that Marduk, the chief god of Babylon itself, called Cyrus by name and took him by the hand as a righteous king. The Babylonian priests welcomed him. In 1971 Iran's government hailed the cylinder as the first charter of human rights in the world and presented a copy of it to the United Nations. Historians reject the label as anachronistic; a British Museum curator called it simply a building inscription in the old Babylonian style. It is a striking decree of tolerance, not a modern bill of rights. The Greek soldier Xenophon wrote a whole book, the Cyropaedia, praising Cyrus as the ideal king, and it became a handbook for Western statesmen; Thomas Jefferson kept two copies on his shelves.

d-day-normandy-invasion.context_blurb:
On 6 June 1944, in the fifth year of World War Two, the Western Allies crossed the English Channel and landed in Normandy, on the coast of German-occupied France. General Dwight Eisenhower, the American Supreme Commander, ran the operation, code-named Overlord. Its purpose was to open the second front that would crush Nazi Germany between the Allies in the west and the Soviets in the east.

No invasion from the sea, before or since, has ever been bigger: close to 160,000 men came ashore that one day along some fifty miles of coast. The coast was split into five code-named beaches. The Americans landed at Utah and Omaha, the British at Sword and Gold, and the Canadians at Juno. Most men reached the sand in plywood landing craft that each held 36 soldiers, the work of Andrew Higgins, a stubborn boat maker from New Orleans who turned out more than 23,000 of them. After the war Eisenhower said Higgins was the man who had won the war for them. The worst killing came at Omaha. There steep bluffs looked down on a bare tidal flat with nowhere to hide, Company A of the 116th Infantry was nearly wiped out, some 2,400 men were killed or wounded, and the beach became known as Bloody Omaha.

The night before, paratroopers had dropped behind the beaches. Over Sainte-Mère-Église, John Steele's parachute caught on the church steeple, and wounded in the foot, he hung there pretending to be dead for about two hours while the fight raged below. A dummy of him still hangs from that steeple. On Sword Beach the Scottish piper Bill Millin paraded back and forth across the sand with no weapon, playing Highland Laddie, and German snipers captured later said they had left him alone because they took him for a madman. At Pointe du Hoc, Lieutenant Colonel James Rudder's Rangers climbed sheer cliffs a hundred feet high under machine-gun fire, using ropes, grapnels and long extension ladders borrowed from the London Fire Brigade and mounted on amphibious trucks. Even the date hung by a thread. A storm swept the Channel until the weatherman Group Captain James Stagg spotted a short break, and after one day's delay Eisenhower launched the whole invasion with the words "OK, we'll go."

Two hidden achievements made the landings work. The first was a lie told on a grand scale, Operation Fortitude. Across from Calais, in southeast England, the Allies created a phantom army under the famous General George Patton and let German planes photograph it. Its tanks were rubber balloons pumped full of air and its landing craft were dummies, but from above the whole fake force looked real. The second was a harbour. An army cannot be supplied across open sand for long, and the Allies held no French port. So British and American engineers built two artificial harbours, the Mulberries, and towed them across the Channel in pieces: concrete caissons, floating roadways and breakwaters made of old ships sunk on purpose.

The deception succeeded beyond all hope. The planners had hoped to fool Hitler for a fortnight, but he was so sure the real blow would fall at the Pas-de-Calais that he kept his reserves away from Normandy for about seven weeks. Eisenhower had prepared for disaster too. In case the landings failed, he wrote a statement for the press saying that any blame was his alone. He first wrote that the troops had been withdrawn, then struck out that passive line and rewrote it in the first person, saying that he himself had withdrawn the troops, so that the responsibility fell on him. He carried the unused note in his wallet.

dahomey-benin-human-sacrifice-altars.context_blurb:
In the 1700s and 1800s two West African kingdoms, Dahomey (in today's Republic of Benin) and Benin (in today's southern Nigeria), ran strong states with royal courts, armies and long-distance trade. Their kings also killed people in great public sacrifices, mostly war captives and condemned criminals. European visitors wrote down what they saw, and archaeology has confirmed it.

At Abomey, Dahomey's capital, King Agaja made the killings a yearly royal festival around 1730, and it went on until France conquered Dahomey in the 1890s. The Fon people called it the yearly head business. English visitors named it the Annual Customs, and also the Watering of the Graves, because its central rite was killing victims to honour and serve Dahomey's dead kings. The Fon believed those dead kings still held council in an unseen world. When the king wanted to send them news, he whispered his message into the ear of a condemned prisoner, and then his men cut the prisoner's throat so that the man's spirit would carry the words to the ancestors. In 1863 Britain sent the explorer Richard Francis Burton to King Gelele to protest the killings.

Benin's turn came in February 1897, when a British expedition took Benin City. In the Oba's palace the soldiers found the famous cast heads now called the Benin Bronzes, each topped by a carved elephant tusk on a raised altar. The expedition surgeon, Dr. Felix Norman Roth, wrote that the heads and their tusks were caked with dried human blood, and that bodies of the sacrificed lay around the palace. Commander R. H. Bacon called his book about it Benin: The City of Blood. The same court that made the beautiful art used it on these altars; both belong to one honest record.

dante-s-divine-comedy.context_blurb:
Dante Alighieri was a poet and politician of Florence whose enemies drove him into exile in the early 1300s. On the road he wrote the Divine Comedy, a long poem in which he himself travels down through Hell, up the mountain of Purgatory and into Paradise, meeting real popes, emperors and sinners. His picture of the afterlife has shaped Western imagination for seven centuries.

His first guide is Virgil, the great poet of ancient Rome. Over the gate of Hell the travellers read an inscription saying the gate was made by divine Power, highest Wisdom and primal Love, and will last forever. Its last line orders everyone who passes through to abandon all hope. In Italian it reads Lasciate ogne speranza, voi ch'intrate. At the bottom of the pit, Satan stands frozen to the waist in ice, a giant with three faces, chewing a traitor in each mouth. The middle mouth holds Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus, stuffed in head-first so that only his legs kick outside, while the two men who murdered Julius Caesar hang from the other two mouths.

Dante wrote the poem not in Latin but in the Tuscan speech of ordinary people, and his Tuscan became the base of modern standard Italian, which is why he is called the Father of the Italian Language. In the poem's design Virgil stands for human reason, which can lead a soul through Hell and up Purgatory, but as a virtuous pagan he cannot enter Heaven, so at its border he turns back and a new guide, a woman Dante had loved since boyhood, takes over.

Dante also used the poem to settle scores. He set the journey at Easter 1300 but wrote it between about 1308 and 1321, and Pope Boniface VIII, his enemy in the feud that exiled him, was still alive in 1300. Dante damned him anyway, among the simonists, churchmen who sold holy offices for money. In a fiery pit the dead Pope Nicholas III, stuck upside down, hears Dante's footsteps, mistakes him for his successor, and asks whether Boniface is already standing there, years before his time. With one wrong guess, Dante sends a living pope to Hell.

daoism-laozi.context_blurb:
Daoism is one of China's great native traditions, first a philosophy and later a religion, built around the Dao, or Way: the deep pattern of nature that a wise person follows instead of forcing. Its founder, by tradition, is a sage of the 500s BC credited with a tiny book of rhymed sayings, the Tao Te Ching (also spelled Dao De Jing), one of the most translated books on earth.

The sage's name, Laozi, is really a title of respect meaning Old Master, from lao, old, and zi, master; tradition says his family name was Li and his given name Er. He was no hermit or warlord but a humble official who looked after the archives of the Zhou kings, the royal librarian in all but name. As the Zhou kingdom decayed, says the legend, he gave up on it and rode west. At the Hangu Pass the gatekeeper Yin Xi saw that he was a sage and would not let him through until he wrote down his wisdom, so Laozi composed the entire Tao Te Ching right there and then rode away forever. The book has only about 5,000 characters. In Chapter 64 it gave the world the proverb that even a thousand-mile journey starts with a single step; the Chinese literally says it starts beneath your feet.

The book loves paradox. Laozi praises water as the softest, most yielding thing in the world, which still wears down the hardest stone, because it patiently settles into the lowest places. His great teaching is wu wei, literally not-doing, which does not mean laziness: it is effortless action that goes with the grain of the moment, the way a swimmer moves with the current instead of fighting it. He prizes things in their natural state. His image for that state is pu, the uncarved block, a lump of raw wood before any carver shapes it, because once you cut it into something, its wholeness is gone. The same idea runs his politics. In Chapter 60 he says that governing a great country is like cooking a small fish: poke and stir it too much and you ruin it. Legend says Confucius, as a young man, came to the old sage to ask about ritual. He left amazed, telling his pupils that Laozi was like a dragon, a beast that rides the clouds and cannot be pinned down.

The book's famous opening line is a paradox about words: any Dao you can put into speech is not the eternal Dao. In other words, if you can fully explain the Way, you have not got the real thing. Chapter 11 says a wheel, a clay pot and a room are useful for the same reason: the empty space inside, the hollow hub that lets the wheel turn, the hollow that holds water, the open room you live in. Many people link Daoism with yin and yang, dark and light. Yet in all 81 chapters Laozi names the pair together exactly once, in Chapter 42, where all things carry yin on their backs and embrace yang.

Who wrote it? The oldest life of Laozi, written by the historian Sima Qian around 100 BC, offers several conflicting stories and admits its own doubt, and many modern scholars now think there may never have been a single Laozi, seeing the book as a gathering of sayings from many hands. Others still hold to one author. Whoever he was, his followers raised the old librarian higher than any sage: by the second century AD he was worshipped as Taishang Laojun, the Most High Lord Lao, a god counted among the supreme deities of Daoism, the Three Pure Ones. In 166 AD the Han emperor Huan offered him sacrifices.

darwin-and-evolution-by-natural-selectio.context_blurb:
Charles Darwin was an English naturalist who, at twenty-two, sailed around the world on the Royal Navy survey ship HMS Beagle, a voyage that lasted five years. What he saw, above all on the Galapagos Islands off Ecuador, led him to an idea that would remake biology: that species are not fixed forever but change over long ages through natural selection.

He nearly missed the boat. Captain Robert FitzRoy believed he could read a man's character in his face, and he almost turned Darwin down because the shape of Darwin's nose seemed to him to show a lack of energy. Darwin later joked about his narrow escape. On the Galapagos he met black marine iguanas crawling over the volcanic rock and swimming in the surf. He thought them so hideous that he called them imps of darkness in his notes. He kept tossing one into the sea, and each time it swam straight back to the same spot on shore.

Back in England he began to think the unthinkable. In a private notebook in 1837 he drew a little branching sketch of species splitting from shared ancestors, the first tree of life, and over it he wrote two cautious words: I think. The birds he brought home helped. In March 1837 the bird expert John Gould studied Darwin's Galapagos specimens and told him that the varied birds he had taken for unrelated kinds were in fact one closely related group of finches, differing from island to island. On the islands themselves it had been the mockingbirds, not the finches, that first stirred his doubts.

Afraid of the uproar, Darwin kept his theory to himself. He had sat on it for some twenty years when, in 1858, a letter came from Alfred Russel Wallace, a younger British naturalist in the Malay Archipelago, with an essay setting out nearly the same idea. To share the credit fairly, papers by both men were read to the Linnean Society of London on 1 July 1858, and On the Origin of Species followed in 1859.

darwin-and-on-the-origin-of-species.context_blurb:
In the 1830s Charles Darwin, a young naturalist from England, sailed around the world aboard HMS Beagle, collecting fossils, plants and animals. Back at his country house in Kent he spent more than twenty years turning what he had seen into a theory: that living things descend from common ancestors and slowly change through natural selection. In 1859 he published it as On the Origin of Species.

The Galapagos Islands gave him his sharpest clues. Nicholas Lawson, the islands' vice-governor, met Darwin on Floreana and told him he could name any giant tortoise's home island just by the shape of the animal's shell. On lush highland islands the shells were domes; on dry islands they curved up at the front like a saddle, so the tortoise could stretch its neck to reach high plants. Around 1837, back in London, Darwin sketched the first tree of life in a secret notebook, a branching diagram of species splitting apart over long ages, and above it he wrote only two hesitant words: I think.

The Galapagos finches told the same story: some eighteen species came from a single ancestor, and as the birds on different islands took to hard seeds, insects or cactus, their beaks grew into different tools for each food. Big crushing beaks cracked seeds; slender ones caught insects.

Darwin knew how his idea would sound in an age that believed every species had been made fixed and separate. In 1844 he wrote to his friend Joseph Hooker that admitting species can change felt like confessing a murder. Shy and often ill, he left the public fighting to his friend Thomas Henry Huxley, nicknamed Darwin's Bulldog. At Oxford in 1860, when Bishop Samuel Wilberforce asked whether Huxley's monkey ancestor was on his grandfather's side or his grandmother's, Huxley is said to have replied that he would sooner descend from an ape than from a man of great gifts who used them to mock serious science. Accounts of the exact words differ, so the exchange lives on as legend.

What finally forced Darwin into print was a letter. In 1858 Alfred Russel Wallace, ill with malaria on a faraway island in Indonesia, mailed Darwin an essay that set out almost exactly his own theory, which Wallace had worked out entirely by himself. Darwin's friends arranged for both men's papers to be read together at the Linnean Society on 1 July 1858. Neither man was there.

declaration-of-independence-1776.context_blurb:
In the summer of 1776, more than a year into the war with Britain, the Second Continental Congress met in Philadelphia and cut the thirteen American colonies loose from the British crown. Thomas Jefferson, a 33-year-old Virginia lawyer, drafted the document that explained why. Its ideas about equal rights and government by consent have echoed through freedom movements ever since.

Its opening creed declares that all men are created equal and endowed by their Creator with rights that cannot be taken from them, among them life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. John Hancock, the president of Congress, signed in the middle of the page in letters far bigger than anyone else's, which is why Americans still say "put your John Hancock here" when they mean sign here. Congress had actually voted for independence on July 2, 1776, when twelve colonies approved Richard Henry Lee's motion and New York abstained; July 4 is when it approved the wording that explained the vote. The document has a mystery too. Near the bottom left of the original sits a handprint that appeared sometime between 1903 and 1940, and the National Archives admits that nobody knows whose it is or how it got there.

A legend says Hancock signed big so King George III could read his name without spectacles. It cannot be true, because the signed parchment stayed in America and no signed copy ever went to Britain. In fact no one signed on the Fourth. The clerk Timothy Matlack first had to hand-letter the official parchment, and most of the 56 delegates added their names on August 2, 1776. Today many of those names have nearly vanished. In the 1820s, to make William Stone's official facsimile, workers pressed damp paper or cloth onto the parchment again and again to lift its ink for copying, and on untanned skin even that little moisture pulled the ink away. On July 4, 1826, fifty years to the day after independence, Jefferson died, and John Adams, who died hours later not knowing his old rival had gone first, is said to have murmured Thomas Jefferson survives.

The heart of the Declaration is an argument about power. A government's rightful power, it says, comes only from the consent of the people it governs, so when a government turns destructive of their rights, the people may alter it or abolish it and set up a new one. Jefferson reshaped an idea of the English philosopher John Locke, who in 1689 had said government exists to protect life, liberty and estate, meaning property, and Jefferson swapped property for the pursuit of happiness. In this logic rights come first and government exists only to secure them. So liberty is a natural, negative right: a freedom to act and pursue your own good that nobody else may block, not a claim on another person's labour or property.

The document's great contradiction was slavery. Jefferson's draft attacked King George for the slave trade, a market where men were bought and sold, but Congress cut the passage, and Jefferson blamed the delegates of South Carolina and Georgia, along with Northern merchants who profited from the trade. Congress made 86 changes and struck about a quarter of his text. In 1852 Frederick Douglass, born enslaved, spoke in Rochester on the fifth of July and called the Declaration the ring-bolt that holds the chain of the nation's destiny, while he denounced slavery as making a sham of American freedom. He attacked the hypocrisy, not the principle, holding America to its own promise, as Lincoln and later Martin Luther King would do.

decolonization-of-india-1947.context_blurb:
In August 1947 Britain gave up its rule over India after nearly two centuries. British India was split in two: a Hindu-majority India and a Muslim-majority Pakistan, a partition that Muhammad Ali Jinnah's Muslim League demanded over the objections of Mahatma Gandhi. Freedom came with one of the largest and bloodiest mass migrations in history, and its scars still mark the region.

The last viceroy, Lord Mountbatten, pulled independence forward by almost ten months and picked 15 August because it was the second anniversary of Japan's surrender to him in World War Two, his own day of victory. At the stroke of midnight Jawaharlal Nehru, the first prime minister, told the Constituent Assembly that while the world slept, India would wake to freedom, and he called the moment India's tryst with destiny. His handwritten draft shows that he first wrote date with destiny, then crossed out date and wrote tryst above it.

The man who drew the new border, the London lawyer Sir Cyril Radcliffe, arrived on 8 July 1947 having never set foot in India, and he had about five weeks and badly outdated maps to divide the homes of 400 million people. Roughly 15 million people fled across his line, about 5.5 million Hindus and Sikhs into India and some 5.8 million Muslims into Pakistan, and one to two million were killed. Mobs on every side attacked refugee columns. Some refugee trains pulled into their stations in dead silence, with every passenger already murdered, and people called them ghost trains. On 22 September 1947 attackers killed about 3,000 Muslim refugees on a single train at Amritsar.

The British held back the Radcliffe Line until 17 August, two days after independence, so millions celebrated their freedom without knowing which country they lived in. Sickened by what his line had done, Radcliffe burned his papers and maps, refused the 40,000 rupees he was owed, left India and never spoke publicly about the partition again.

A few people held back the killing. In the Punjab the British had 55,000 soldiers and still faced huge riots, while Calcutta stayed calm as Gandhi fasted and prayed there, so on 26 August Mountbatten wrote to Gandhi and called him a one-man boundary force. The women of Partition suffered a particular cruelty. Kidnappers seized somewhere between seventy-five and a hundred thousand women, and a joint India-Pakistan recovery program brought back about 30,000 of them between 1948 and 1956, but it often sent rescued women back across the border against their own wishes.

diderot-s-encyclopedia.context_blurb:
Denis Diderot was an 18th-century French writer who, with the mathematician Jean le Rond d'Alembert, edited the Encyclopédie, a giant reference work that set out to gather all human knowledge, from science and philosophy to the crafts of ordinary trades. It meant to teach readers to think for themselves about religion and government, and that made it dangerous.

The volumes began appearing in the 1750s. In 1759 King Louis XV revoked its licence and the Pope condemned it, but Diderot and his writers simply carried on in secret, and the volumes kept coming. By 1789 some 25,000 sets had been sold across Europe.

Diderot, who had once been jailed for his own writing, also had a cleverer weapon: the renvois, or cross-references, which sent a reader from one article to another. A censor could strike out any sentence he found, but he could not police the gap between two entries, so Diderot set two harmless-looking articles side by side and let the reader draw the forbidden conclusion that was never printed. The censors guarded the words on the page, not the paths a reader followed. Diderot died in 1784, five years before the French Revolution that his book helped to inspire.

diocletian-and-the-splitting-of-the-empi.context_blurb:
Diocletian ruled the Roman Empire from AD 284 to 305, after half a century of civil wars, murdered emperors and foreign invasions had nearly torn it apart. He reorganised its provinces, its money and its army, and he launched the last and worst imperial persecution of the Christians. Above all, he decided that the empire was too big for any one man to guard.

His answer was the Tetrarchy, from the Greek tetra, four, and archy, rule: a rule of four, in which two senior emperors and their two younger heirs each guarded a quarter of the empire. Diocletian kept the East, with Galerius as his junior Caesar, while Maximian held the West with Constantius. That split between East and West foreshadowed the day Rome would divide for good.

Then Diocletian did what no emperor before him had done. On 1 May 305 at Nicomedia he abdicated of his own free will and retired to a great walled palace on the Adriatic coast, at Split in modern Croatia, and planted a vegetable garden. His four-man system soon broke down in civil war, and old colleagues begged him to take power again. A late Roman history tells that he refused them, saying that if they could only see the cabbages he had grown with his own hands, they would never ask such a thing. The story is told as legend, but his palace still stands at the heart of the city of Split.

diogenes-the-cynic-and-the-barrel.context_blurb:
Diogenes of Sinope was a Greek philosopher of the 300s BC and the most famous of the Cynics, whose name comes from the Greek word for dog, because they tried to live like strays, with almost no property, pride or manners. He made his bed in a big clay storage jar on a Corinth street and turned his whole life into street theatre aimed at the rich and the pompous.

Even a conqueror got no bowing from him. When Alexander the Great came to see him and promised him whatever he wished, Diogenes, lying in the sun, asked only that the king step aside a little and stop blocking his sunlight. Alexander is said to have remarked that if he were not Alexander, he would wish to be Diogenes, and Diogenes replied that if he were not Diogenes, he too would wish to be Diogenes.

Philosophers fared no better. Plato had won applause in Athens for calling man a featherless animal that walks on two feet. Diogenes answered with a plucked chicken: he carried it into Plato's lecture room, held it up, and cried out that here was Plato's man. Nothing Diogenes wrote survives, and every story comes from collections made centuries later. Yet his idea that what truly matters lies inside your own mind passed to the Stoics, who built a great philosophy on it.

donatello-and-ghiberti-early-renaissance.context_blurb:
In the early 1400s the city of Florence launched the Renaissance in art, and two of its sculptors, Lorenzo Ghiberti and Donato di Niccolò, known as Donatello, led the way. They brought back the lifelike human figures of ancient Greece and Rome, and their work, still on show in Florence, trained the generation that produced Michelangelo.

In 1401 Ghiberti won a famous competition to make bronze doors for the Baptistery, the eight-sided church that faces Florence's cathedral, and he spent half a century on two sets. The second set, for the east side, took him some 27 years: ten gilded bronze panels of Bible stories. Michelangelo later called those doors the Gates of Paradise, and the name has stuck to them ever since. Ghiberti slipped his own small portrait into the frame, a bald man of about sixty wearing a pleased little smile.

Around 1440 Donatello cast a bronze David, a boy standing naked over Goliath's severed head, and it was the first nude figure made to stand free on its own since the Romans, a gap of nearly a thousand years. No wall or pillar holds it up. Cosimo de' Medici most likely ordered it, and it stood on a column in the courtyard of the Medici Palace; today it is in the Bargello museum in Florence.

doolittle-raid.context_blurb:
In April 1942, four months after Pearl Harbor, American spirits were low and Japan believed its home islands were out of reach. Lieutenant Colonel Jimmy Doolittle led sixteen B-25 bombers off the deck of the carrier USS Hornet to bomb Tokyo and other Japanese cities. It was a one-way trip: the big planes could not land back on a carrier, so they flew on toward China.

To fly that far, the crews stripped out every spare pound, including the real gun turret in the belly. To frighten off enemy fighters coming in from behind, they fixed two broomsticks painted black into the tail cone of each bomber as fake machine guns. Most of the raiders crash-landed in China or came down in the sea. Chinese resisters smuggled most survivors to safety, though the Japanese captured some crews.

The bombs did little damage, but the shock was huge. Back in Washington, reporters wanted to know where the bombers had taken off, and the Hornet's part had to stay secret. With a grin, President Franklin Roosevelt told them the planes had come from Shangri-La, the secret mountain paradise of the novel Lost Horizon. The raid also pushed Japan's commanders to strike at Midway, where they met disaster two months later.

dunkirk-evacuation.context_blurb:
In May 1940 German armies broke through into northern France and trapped the British Expeditionary Force, with many French and Belgian troops, against the Channel coast around the French port of Dunkirk. Over nine days the Royal Navy and a fleet of civilian boats carried them home to England under constant bombing. The rescue meant that Britain could fight on.

Vice-Admiral Bertram Ramsay ran the rescue from a room tunnelled under Dover Castle, where a dynamo, an electric generator, hummed in the corner, and so the plan was called Operation Dynamo. It ran from 26 May to 4 June. The Navy had too few warships for the job. So hundreds of small craft crossed to help, many crewed by civilians: fishing smacks and cockle boats, Thames pleasure cruisers, car ferries and lifeboats, remembered ever since as the little ships of Dunkirk. Somewhere between 860 and 930 vessels took part, and about 240 were lost. The smallest was the Tamzine, an open fishing dinghy less than fifteen feet long, which survives today, kept by London's Imperial War Museum.

German bombs had wrecked the harbour, so ships could not tie up in the usual way. Captain William Tennant, the Navy's man in charge on shore, marched the men out along the East Mole, a long, thin breakwater of concrete and timber that was never built for ships, and used it as a pier. Nearly 200,000 men left from the Mole, far more than from the open beaches. Overhead, Stuka dive-bombers screamed down. Their air-driven sirens, nicknamed the Jericho Trumpet, were built to make the dive itself a weapon of terror. Yet one soldier, Alfred Baldwin, remembered long lines reaching out into the water without any pushing or shoving, as if the men were waiting for a bus.

At the start, Churchill and his advisers feared that no more than twenty or thirty thousand men could be saved, and only about 8,000 got away on the first day. In the end about 338,000 escaped, some 198,000 British and 140,000 French and Belgian soldiers, more than eleven times the gloomiest guess. The men came home, but the army left behind nearly all its guns, vehicles and tanks, some 2,472 guns and close to 65,000 vehicles. On 4 June Churchill called it a miracle of deliverance in the House of Commons, but he warned members not to mistake it for a victory, because evacuations do not win wars. The same speech promised that Britain would fight on the beaches and never surrender.

The hidden story explains how it was possible. On 24 May, with German tanks close enough to crush the trapped armies, Hitler confirmed a halt order, first urged by General von Rundstedt, which stopped the panzers short of Dunkirk for about two days and gave the Allies time to organise. Many rescued men grumbled that the Royal Air Force had abandoned them, yet its pilots flew over 3,500 missions and lost some 145 planes, meeting the German bombers well inland, out of sight of the men on the sand. On the Mole, the Canadian commander James Campbell Clouston served as pier-master, shipping out some two thousand men every hour. When frightened men surged toward one ship, he drew his revolver and calmly warned them that he had six shots, that he was a decent shot, and that the lieutenant behind him was better still. On 2 June Stukas sank his boat; he gave up his place in the only dinghy and died in the cold water with his men. The last stand belonged to the French, whose rearguard held the shrinking ring around the port to the end, and after the last ships had gone on 4 June, about 40,000 French soldiers were left behind as prisoners.

easter-island-rapa-nui-moai.context_blurb:
Rapa Nui, which Europeans call Easter Island, is a small volcanic island far out in the South Pacific, one of the loneliest inhabited places on earth. Polynesian voyagers settled it around AD 1200, and their descendants carved nearly a thousand giant stone figures called moai from the island's volcanic rock: long-faced statues of their honoured ancestors.

Almost every standing moai has its back to the ocean, because the islanders set up their ancestors to protect the living, so the statues face inland toward the villages they guard. They stood on platforms near the coast, many miles from the quarry where they were carved.

How did people without wheels or big animals move statues weighing many tons? The islanders' oral tradition always gave a simple answer: the moai walked. For years outsiders called that a myth. Carl Lipo and Terry Hunt, two archaeologists, put the story to the test with a replica weighing 4.35 tons: eighteen people with three ropes rocked the upright statue from side to side so that it waddled forward, the way you might walk a refrigerator across a kitchen, and it covered 100 meters in 40 minutes. One rope on each side did the rocking, and one behind kept the statue leaning forward. The moai's wide, D-shaped base and slight forward lean turn out to be exactly the shape that makes walking possible, just as the islanders had said for generations.

edmund-burke-and-the-conservative-critiq.context_blurb:
Edmund Burke was an Irish-born member of the British House of Commons in the 1700s and one of the great speakers of his age. He defended the American colonists, Irish Catholics and the people of India against abuses of power, yet he is remembered as the father of modern conservatism, because of the stand he took against the French Revolution of 1789.

In 1790 Burke published Reflections on the Revolution in France, warning that abstract theories, cut loose from history and inherited institutions, would end in blood. He sneered that the radicals would let learning be trampled by a swinish multitude, and England's own radicals, far from hiding, took up the insult with pride: in 1793 James Parkinson answered Burke with a pamphlet from the Swinish Multitude. Thomas Paine, whose Common Sense had helped stir the American Revolution, hit back in 1791 with Rights of Man, which sold about 100,000 copies and accused Burke of letting the dead rule over the rights and freedom of the living. Mary Wollstonecraft mocked his love of tradition as worship of the rust of antiquity.

Burke grieved over the mob's insults to Queen Marie Antoinette, writing that he had expected ten thousand swords to leap from their scabbards for her, but chivalry's age had passed, and the age of sophisters, economists and calculators had taken its place. As France slid toward terror, he turned to theatre: on 28 December 1792, in a debate in the Commons, he flung a real dagger onto the floor of the House, warning that French principles would bring French daggers to Britain. He claimed that 3,000 such daggers were being made in Birmingham, and the cartoonist James Gillray drew the Dagger Scene.

His enemies called him a hypocrite for backing the American rebels and attacking the French. Burke answered that the two revolts were opposites: the Americans were claiming the English rights they had inherited, while the French were throwing away every inheritance in the name of abstract reason. Society, he wrote, is a partnership of the living, the dead and those yet to be born, and liberty is safest in careful, gradual reform. In 1790, nine years before Napoleon seized power, Burke predicted that some popular general, skilled at winning over the soldiers, would draw every eye to himself, and that whoever truly commanded the army would become master of France. Napoleon made himself ruler in 1799 and crowned himself emperor in 1804.

edward-jenner-and-the-smallpox-vaccine.context_blurb:
Edward Jenner was a country doctor in Gloucestershire, England, in the late 1700s, when smallpox killed or scarred huge numbers of people. He knew the farm lore that milkmaids who caught cowpox, a mild disease of cattle, hardly ever caught smallpox, and in 1796 he set out to test it. His experiment founded vaccination.

A milkmaid named Sarah Nelmes had caught cowpox from a cow called Blossom, whose hide is still on show today in the library of St George's, a medical school in London. Jenner took matter from a cowpox blister on Sarah's hand and rubbed it into small cuts on the arm of James Phipps, the eight-year-old son of his gardener. Eight weeks on, Jenner infected the boy with real smallpox on purpose, a test no doctor would be allowed to run today. Phipps did not fall ill, and over the rest of his life he was exposed to smallpox more than twenty further times without ever catching it. In thanks, Jenner gave the Phipps family a cottage free of rent, and James came to his funeral in 1823.

The new method took its name from the cow: vaccine comes from vacca, the Latin word for cow, because the protection came from cowpox caught from cattle. Jenner's booklet of 1798 spread the idea across Europe. Cartoonists mocked him, drawing patients sprouting little cows from their arms, but within two centuries vaccination had driven smallpox out of the wild entirely.

egyptian-achievements-calendar-medicine-.context_blurb:
Ancient Egypt lasted some three thousand years, from about 3100 BC to the Roman conquest in 30 BC. Beside its tombs and temples it built up a body of practical science that Greece and Rome inherited. Its scribes, doctors and surveyors handed down exact knowledge for centuries, in a land stable and rich enough to keep learning.

Start with the calendar. Egyptian astronomers split the year into twelve months of thirty days, which came to only 360, so they added five extra days at the end of the year to reach 365, the basic shape of the year we still keep. Those five were called the epagomenal days, and through Julius Caesar's reform the Egyptian year became the base of the Western calendar.

Egyptian doctors were famous across the ancient world. The oldest surgical text we have is a doctor's casebook of 48 injuries from around 1600 BC, now called the Edwin Smith Papyrus. In one case a doctor looked into a man's cracked skull and wrote the first known account of the brain, saying its wrinkled surface looked like the corrugations in molten copper. He was describing the folds that cover every human brain.

Geometry came from mud. Each year the Nile flood wiped out the boundaries between fields, and surveyors called rope-stretchers marked them again with a rope tied in twelve evenly spaced knots, which, stretched taut as a three-four-five triangle, makes a perfect right angle. They used the Pythagorean rule centuries before Pythagoras, and thanks to such corners the base of the Great Pyramid is a nearly perfect square.

egyptian-art-and-the-pyramids-of-giza.context_blurb:
For some three thousand years Egyptian artists and builders followed the same rules, making art for the gods, the pharaoh and the dead, built to last forever. Their greatest work stands on the Giza plateau near Cairo: three pyramids and the Great Sphinx, raised about 4,500 years ago as royal tombs and their guardian. Their richest treasure came out of a tomb far to the south.

The largest of the three, the Great Pyramid, was raised around 2560 BC as the tomb of the pharaoh Khufu, from more than two million great stone blocks, and for some 3,800 years nothing built by human hands stood taller. In front of the pyramids crouches the Great Sphinx, carved from one ridge of limestone, with the body of a lion and the head of a man, its face a pharaoh's. It is about 73 meters long and 20 meters high. In November 1922 the archaeologist Howard Carter chipped a hole into the sealed tomb of the boy-king Tutankhamun in the Valley of the Kings, peered in by candlelight, and when his patron Lord Carnarvon asked whether he could see anything, Carter replied, "Yes, wonderful things!" That polished line comes from his later book; his diary put it more plainly.

The pyramid age had begun a century before Giza at Saqqara. There the pharaoh Djoser's Step Pyramid, six giant terraces stacked like stairs, became the first large building in the world made of cut stone. The Great Pyramid looks rough and stepped today, but when new it was sheathed in smooth, polished white limestone that shone in the sun. An earthquake in 1303 loosened many of those casing stones, and Cairo's rulers carted them off to build mosques and forts. Painters showed a person in a composite pose, with the head and legs seen from the side but the eye and shoulders seen from the front, so that every part appeared as clearly as possible. That is why one eye stares out of a sideways face. Tutankhamun's mummy wore a death mask made of solid gold, some ten kilograms of it, inlaid with blue lapis lazuli and other stones.

Djoser's designer, Imhotep, is the earliest architect whose name has come down to us, and long after his death Egyptians worshipped him as a god. Size showed rank, a rule called hierarchical scale: a god or the pharaoh loomed largest, officials and family were smaller, and servants and captives smallest of all. The gold mask suffered a modern blunder. In 2014 workers at Cairo's Egyptian Museum broke its braided beard off by accident and stuck it back with quick-setting epoxy glue, leaving it crooked. Experts fixed it properly with beeswax, and eight employees were disciplined. A favourite story blames Napoleon's soldiers for the Sphinx's missing nose, but drawings made some sixty years before he came already show it gone, and the leading account blames a Sufi, Muhammad Sa'im al-Dahr, who smashed it in the 1300s in protest because people were worshipping the statue.

Two last puzzles belong to Giza. Khufu's son Khafre built the second pyramid a generation later, a little shorter than his father's, yet it looks taller, because he set it on bedrock about ten meters higher up the plateau. It even keeps a cap of its original smooth casing. A thousand years after the Sphinx was carved, a prince named Thutmose fell asleep in its shadow after hunting, and the Dream Stele between its paws records the legend that the statue promised to make him pharaoh if he cleared away the sand that buried it. The prince did become king, as Thutmose IV.

egyptian-gods-and-the-book-of-the-dead.context_blurb:
The ancient Egyptians worshipped many gods of nature, cities and death, and their religion cared above all about the afterlife. They placed scrolls of spells, prayers and instructions in their tombs to guide the dead through the underworld, past judgment and into eternal life. Today we call those scrolls the Book of the Dead, and its scenes still shape how the world pictures Egypt.

The great myth begins with a murder. The god Osiris was killed by his jealous brother Set, and Plutarch, a Greek author, says Set then tore the corpse into fourteen pieces and scattered them the length of Egypt. When the pieces were gathered, the jackal-headed god Anubis embalmed the body, inventing the art of mummification, and Osiris became the first mummy. Osiris rose again and became king of the underworld. Painters gave him green skin, the colour of new plants sprouting from the earth, because he was the god of life returning after death. Sometimes they painted him black, like the rich mud the Nile leaves behind.

The sun faced death too. Each night the sun god Ra sailed his boat through the underworld, where the giant serpent Apophis, chaos itself, tried to swallow it, and each morning the sun rose because Ra had beaten him once more.

Every soul faced a trial. At the final judgment Anubis laid the heart of the dead on a great balance, against a single ostrich feather, the Feather of Ma'at, goddess of truth. Thoth, the ibis-headed scribe of the gods, stood ready with his reed pen to write down the result and report it to Osiris. A heart as light as the feather won eternal life. A heart dragged down by evil was thrown to a monster that devoured it, and the soul was wiped out of existence forever, a death worse than dying. That monster was Ammit, the Devourer of the Dead, built from Egypt's three great man-eaters: a crocodile's head, a lion's forequarters and a hippopotamus's hindquarters.

Before the weighing, the soul stood before 42 judges, one for every district, or nome, of Egypt, and swore to each one that it was innocent of a particular crime. This list of denials, such as I have not stolen, is called the Negative Confession. Egyptians feared their own hearts might tell on them, so over a mummy's heart they laid a heart scarab, a dark stone charm shaped like a beetle and carved with a spell ordering the heart not to bear witness against its owner. Even paradise had a catch, since the gods might call the dead out to labour in the fields. So tombs were packed with little mummy-shaped figures called shabti, whose spell made each one answer, "Here I am!" when summoned, and march off to work in its owner's place.

The German Egyptologist Karl Richard Lepsius coined the name Book of the Dead in 1842; the Egyptians called these texts the Spells of Coming Forth by Day. Some of the spells are over 4,000 years old. The finest copy known, a scroll about 78 feet long made around 1250 BC, belonged not to a king but to Ani, a royal scribe of Thebes, and the British Museum bought it in 1888. Even a working scribe could be sent into the afterlife with the whole book of spells.

einstein-and-relativity.context_blurb:
Albert Einstein was a German-born Jewish physicist who, while still a junior clerk in the Swiss patent office, rewrote our picture of space, time and gravity. His theories of relativity showed that clocks and rulers depend on how you move, and that gravity is the bending of space itself. In the 1930s Nazi Germany drove him into exile, and he spent his last years at Princeton.

The world remembers his face best from 1951: on his 72nd birthday, worn out from smiling for cameras, he stuck out his tongue at the photographer Arthur Sasse, and that snapshot is now among the best-known photographs in the world. He loved it and ordered prints for friends.

In 1905, aged 26 and a mere technical expert, third class, he wrote four papers in his spare time that each remade a corner of physics, and scientists call it his miracle year, in Latin annus mirabilis. One of them gave the world E = mc², which says that mass and energy are one and the same thing in two disguises, and because the speed of light squared is so huge, a pinch of matter holds enormous energy. That principle powers the Sun and the atomic bomb. In May 1919 Arthur Eddington, a British astronomer, photographed stars beside the Sun during a total eclipse from the island of Principe, and their light had been bent off its straight path, just as Einstein had predicted. Overnight Einstein became the most famous scientist in the world.

Relativity made him a star, but when he won the Nobel Prize in Physics for 1921, the committee thought it too new and too disputed, so it honoured his law of the photoelectric effect instead. He lectured on relativity at the ceremony anyway. Time itself runs slower for anything moving fast, so if one twin rockets away near the speed of light and comes home, the traveller is now younger than the twin who stayed on Earth. His later life had strange turns. When Einstein died in 1955, the pathologist Thomas Harvey secretly kept his brain without the family's permission, cut it into about 170 pieces and stored them in jars for over forty years. In 1952 the new state of Israel asked him to become its president, and he declined, saying he lacked the knack and the experience for dealing with people.

General relativity grew from one picture. In 1907, sitting at his desk in the patent office, he had what he called the happiest thought of his life: a person falling freely does not feel his own weight, so gravity and acceleration must be one and the same. Your phone's GPS still depends on him: satellite clocks gain about 38 microseconds a day, and if engineers stopped correcting for it, your position on the map would drift off by several miles every day.

Einstein also imagined lightning striking a railway at two points at once for a man standing beside the track, and showed that for a passenger speeding past on a train, one strike comes before the other, because whether two things happen at the same moment depends on how you are moving. In general relativity gravity is no invisible rope: a heavy body like the Sun bends the space around itself, and even light, which weighs nothing, follows that curve. The physicist John Wheeler summed it up: matter tells space how to curve, and space tells matter how to move.

election-of-1800-peaceful-transfer-of-po.context_blurb:
In 1800 President John Adams, a Federalist, lost to Thomas Jefferson, leader of the Democratic-Republicans, after one of the nastiest campaigns in American history. A flaw in the original rules then left Jefferson tied with his own running mate, Aaron Burr, at 73 electoral votes each, so the House of Representatives had to choose, with each state casting a single vote.

In February 1801 the House deadlocked through 35 ballots over six days, while partisans talked openly of force and two states put their militias on alert. Every vote mattered. Maryland's Joseph Hopper Nicholson was gravely ill, yet he had himself carried to the Capitol on a stretcher so that he could keep voting for Jefferson; without him, Maryland would have gone to Burr. Delaware's lone congressman, James Bayard, held his whole state's vote, and after seeking assurances from a Jefferson ally, he stopped voting for Burr and abstained on the 36th ballot, which broke the deadlock and made Jefferson president.

The real achievement was what happened next. Adams and the Federalists handed power peacefully to their bitter rivals, the first time in American history that one party gave way to another. In much of the world such changes came by coup or civil war. Jefferson called it a revolution, but a quiet one, and the Twelfth Amendment of 1804 fixed the flaw that had caused the tie.

eli-whitney-cotton-gin-and-interchangeab.context_blurb:
Eli Whitney was a young Yale graduate from New England who went south in 1793 to work as a tutor and, on a Georgia plantation, built a small wooden machine that pulled the sticky green seeds out of short-staple cotton. His cotton gin remade the economy of the American South, and it deepened slavery at the very moment many Americans hoped slavery would fade.

By hand, Whitney said, nobody could clear the seeds from more than a pound in a day, while his hand-cranked gin, worked by one person, cleaned about fifty pounds. Yet Whitney earned almost nothing from it, because the machine was so simple that blacksmiths and planters made copies of their own instead of paying his fees. At one point he had some sixty lawsuits running at once. Cheap cleaning made cotton enormously profitable, so planters planted much more of it and purchased many more enslaved people to grow and pick it, and the number held in slavery rose from about 700,000 in 1790 to about 4 million by 1860.

Burned by the gin, Whitney turned to making muskets for the army, promising parts so uniform that any piece would fit any gun. The idea was not new: in 1785 the French gunsmith Honoré Blanc dismantled fifty musket locks, jumbled the parts together and reassembled working locks at random, and Thomas Jefferson, then the American ambassador in France, watched him do it. In January 1801 Whitney put on a show of his own for President John Adams and the incoming President Jefferson, building musket locks out of a jumbled heap of parts. Historians now believe the show was rigged, because Whitney's surviving muskets carry secret matching marks that pair each part with one particular lock, marks no one would need if the parts truly fitted any gun. The historian Merritt Roe Smith concluded that Whitney deliberately fooled the officials. Still, the dream of standard parts grew into the American System of Manufacturing.

eli-whitney-s-cotton-gin-and-its-consequ.context_blurb:
In 1793 the inventor Eli Whitney, visiting a Georgia plantation, built a simple hand-cranked machine to clean short-staple cotton, the kind that grew across the whole inland South but clung to its sticky green seeds. Before the gin, picking out those seeds by hand was brutally slow, and Whitney said he had never seen anyone clean more than a pound in a day.

His gin did the work of fifty people: a turning cylinder studded with short wire hooks dragged the fibre through slots too narrow for the seeds, and one machine cleaned about fifty pounds a day. Short-staple cotton, barely profitable before, suddenly became the richest cash crop in the world.

Many Americans, Whitney among them, had hoped that slavery would slowly die out, since tobacco was exhausting the soil and earning less every year. The gin did the opposite: once upland cotton could be cleaned fast and cheaply, planters spread cotton west across the Deep South and beyond the Mississippi, and the demand for enslaved labour grew enormously. The number of enslaved people in the United States rose from about 700,000 in 1790 to over three million by 1850, and cotton output leapt from about 3,138 bales in 1790 to some 3.8 million in 1860. A machine built to save labour ended by spreading forced labour, and it helped set the country on the road to civil war.

elizabeth-i-england-s-golden-age.context_blurb:
Elizabeth I, daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn, ruled England from 1558 to 1603, a reign of forty-five years remembered as a golden age. She inherited a small kingdom torn between Protestants and Catholics, and she left behind a sea power whose theatres staged Shakespeare. She survived plots, a Spanish invasion and her own cousin's claim to her throne.

Her start was dangerous: her mother, Anne Boleyn, had been beheaded in the Tower of London when Elizabeth was two, and in 1554 her half-sister, Queen Mary, sent Elizabeth to that same fortress as a suspected traitor. Tradition says she balked at stepping ashore through the river entrance later called Traitors' Gate. As queen she never married, and when courtiers begged her to give the realm an heir, she told them she was already bound to a husband: the kingdom of England. So she became the Virgin Queen, and in 1585 Sir Walter Raleigh named England's first American colony Virginia in her honour. The tale of his cloak spread over a puddle for her is unproven folklore. Her sea captains grew rich on Spain. From 1577 to 1580 Francis Drake plundered Spain's American ports, crossed the Pacific and limped home in the Golden Hind, the first Englishman to circumnavigate the globe.

The quarrel with King Philip II of Spain turned to war. In April 1587 Drake slipped into the harbour of Cádiz, set fire to dozens of Philip's ships at anchor, and boasted that he had singed the Spanish king's beard, delaying the invasion by a year. In the summer of 1588 the Spanish Armada, about 130 warships, sailed to conquer Protestant England. Legend says that when it was sighted on 19 July, Drake was playing bowls on Plymouth Hoe and declared there was time enough to finish the game and still beat the Spaniards, though no record from the time backs the tale. At the army's camp at Tilbury, Elizabeth told her soldiers that her body might be a weak and feeble woman's, but she had a king's heart and stomach, and a King of England's at that.

Off Calais the Armada lay packed in a tight crescent, and at midnight the English sent eight burning fireships drifting into it; no Spanish hull burned, yet the terrified crews hacked through their anchor cables and scattered in panic. The battle of Gravelines followed. Storms then wrecked many fleeing ships off Scotland and Ireland, and England struck a victory medal giving the credit to God, its Latin motto saying that he blew with his winds and the enemy were scattered. Philip is said to have grumbled that he had sent his ships against men, not against the elements.

Elizabeth's cousin, the Catholic Mary, Queen of Scots, was her prisoner and her rival. Elizabeth's spymaster, Sir Francis Walsingham, allowed the captive Mary to send secret letters in code, hidden inside the wooden bung that stopped a barrel of beer, so that his codebreakers could read every one. The letters trapped Mary in the Babington plot of 1586 to murder Elizabeth. At Fotheringhay Castle in 1587 the nervous executioner needed three blows, and when attendants lifted Mary's skirts they found her little dog hiding there, refusing to leave her. Elizabeth had signed the death warrant, but afterwards she claimed she never meant it to be sent, and she had her secretary William Davison fined and locked in the Tower for sending it.

In religion she wanted a middle way after decades in which rulers of both faiths had burned their enemies: everyone had to attend the Church of England, but she had no wish, she said, to make windows into the souls of men. She would not hunt quiet Catholics for their private beliefs. A late painting, the Rainbow Portrait, shows her gripping a rainbow beneath a Latin motto, her golden cloak embroidered all over with eyes and ears, a sign that the queen saw and heard everything in her realm.
