empire-of-ghana-the-land-of-gold.context_blurb:
Long before the modern country took its name, the Empire of Ghana ruled the southern edge of the Sahara, in what is now Mauritania and Mali, from around the 700s to the 1000s AD. It grew rich by controlling the trade across the desert: gold from the south, salt from the north. Arab writers described a king so rich that even his dogs wore golden collars.

The southern lands dug up gold but had no salt, while the Sahara had salt in plenty, so salt could fetch its own weight in gold. People need salt to live, and the hot south had none of its own. Deep in the desert, at the mining town of Taghaza, people cut blocks of rock salt and built their houses and even their mosque out of them, with roofs of camel hide.

Ghana was not even the kingdom's own name: in the Soninke language ghana meant warrior king, the title of its rulers, while the Soninke called their land Wagadu. Foreign traders heard the title and named the whole country after it.

The king guarded his wealth with secrets and laws. No outsider knew where the gold mines lay, so the two sides traded by silent barter: salt traders spread their wares on the ground, beat a drum and went away, then the gold people came, left some gold next to whatever they wished to buy, and withdrew in turn. The two sides never met. To keep gold scarce, the king claimed every gold nugget found in his mines for the crown and left only the gold dust to the people, as al-Bakri, an Arab geographer, wrote down in 1068.

Al-Bakri described stranger customs too. The crown passed not to the king's son but to his sister's son, because the people could always be sure that a son of the king's sister truly shared the royal blood. When a king died, his people buried him under a huge timber dome, on carpets, among his weapons, jewels, food and drink. They sealed inside with him, still alive, the men who had served his meals, and then heaped earth over the dome into a hill. A Soninke legend explained the gold itself: a huge black snake called Bida dwelt in a deep well, and each year the people handed him the loveliest young woman among them, so that he would shower Wagadu with gold. In the 1000s invasions from the north and shifting trade routes weakened Ghana, and power moved south to the new empire of Mali.

english-common-law-the-jury-and-innocent.context_blurb:
Medieval England tried suspects in ways that look strange today: by plunging them into blessed water or making them carry red-hot iron, trusting God to reveal the truth. Over centuries English kings, churchmen and lawyers replaced those ordeals with trial by a jury of neighbours, and they built the ideas that the accused must be heard and is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

In the ordeal of cold water, the accused, tied to a rope, went down into a pool that a priest had consecrated. Sinking proved innocence, because the holy water had accepted the body, while floating meant the blessed water had refused a guilty person; the rope kept the innocent from drowning. In the ordeal of hot iron the accused carried a glowing iron bar three paces, his burnt hand was bandaged, and three days later a priest unwrapped it to judge the wound: clean and healing meant innocent, festering meant guilty.

Kings began to build something new. In 1166 King Henry II's Assize of Clarendon ordered the sheriff of every district to gather twelve trusted local men, who swore before the king's travelling judges to name everyone they suspected of robbery, murder or theft. These twelve were accusers, not judges, the ancestor of today's grand jury. A trial needed the prisoner's own plea, so a prisoner who refused to plead could be pressed under heavy stones until he spoke. Giles Corey, an old man of Salem, endured it for two days in 1692, and whenever his tormentors demanded a plea, he answered with two words: more weight. By dying without a verdict, he kept his land for his heirs.

Then in 1215, at the Fourth Lateran Council, Pope Innocent III forbade priests to bless the iron or the water, and without that blessing the ordeal could no longer call down God's judgment, so within a few years it collapsed. England replaced it by letting twelve men weigh the evidence. The same year King John's barons forced him to seal Magna Carta, and in Clause 39 the king promised that no free man could be jailed without a lawful verdict from his equals or the law of the land, words that passed into the due-process guarantees of the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments of the American Constitution.

Around 1300 the French church lawyer Johannes Monachus pointed out that even God, facing Adam after the forbidden fruit, did not simply condemn him but questioned him first, asking where he was and who had told him he was naked, and so held a kind of trial. If even God heard Adam before judging, Monachus argued, no earthly judge may do less. From his argument came the crisp Latin maxim that everyone is presumed innocent until proven guilty. Many people think it is in Magna Carta; it is not.

enigma-and-bletchley-park-codebreaking.context_blurb:
In World War Two, British codebreakers at Bletchley Park, a country estate north of London, cracked the messages of Nazi Germany's Enigma, an electric cipher machine that scrambled every letter through spinning rotors. Their secret intelligence, code-named Ultra, helped hunt U-boats and win battles, and it stayed secret for some thirty years after the war.

Bletchley's most famous mind, the mathematician Alan Turing, suffered so badly from hay fever that each June he cycled to work wearing a military gas mask to keep out the pollen. He also chained his tea mug to a radiator. Fearing that paper money would be worthless if Britain lost, Turing turned his savings into two silver bars and buried them in the woods, then recorded the hiding place in a code that after the war even he could not crack, and the silver was never found. At its peak about 9,000 people worked at Bletchley, and roughly three out of every four were women, among them some 700 Wrens who ran the clattering code-breaking machines in shifts. All of them kept silent for decades. In May 1941 a young officer, David Balme, climbed down into the sinking German submarine U-110 and brought up its Enigma machine together with its codebooks, left behind by the fleeing crew. The Navy let the sub sink so the Germans would never learn of the capture.

The first break came from Poland. In 1932 the mathematician Marian Rejewski, who had never seen a real Enigma, worked out the complete internal wiring of all its rotors from intercepted messages and mathematics alone, in about ten weeks. On 25 July 1939, five weeks before the war began, Polish codebreakers met British and French officers at Pyry, in the woods outside Warsaw, and gave them working copies of Enigma and their methods for breaking it, the foundation of all Bletchley's work. German operators helped by being predictable, signing off nearly every message with Heil Hitler, so codebreakers could guess those letters, a known scrap of text they called a crib.

The machine could be set up in some 159 quintillion ways each day, and the bulk of that power lay not in the spinning rotors but in the plugboard, which swapped pairs of letters and did more to protect a message than an extra rotor would have done. Yet Enigma had a fatal flaw: a reflector, working like a mirror, sent each signal back through the rotors, so no letter could ever come out of the machine as itself, and codebreakers threw out every line-up of a guessed word that put a letter opposite its own match. Turing's bombe machine did not decode messages: starting from a crib, it ran through all 17,576 rotor positions in some twenty minutes, discarding wrong ones by finding contradictions, to find the day's settings, after which people could read every signal sent that day.

Rejewski's tool was permutation group theory, the mathematics of shuffling symbols, and one theorem he relied on was later nicknamed by the cryptologist Cipher Deavours the theorem that won the Second World War. Abstract algebra, not spycraft, had cracked the machine. Sir Harry Hinsley, who wrote the official history of British intelligence in the war, judged that without Ultra the fighting would have lasted about two years longer, perhaps three, possibly four.

enlightened-despots.context_blurb:
In the later 1700s a handful of European monarchs, above all Frederick the Great of Prussia, Catherine the Great of Russia and Joseph II of Austria, ruled as absolute sovereigns while styling themselves philosopher-kings. They wrote to Voltaire and Diderot, reformed laws and schools and eased some religious persecution, but they never gave up any of their own power.

At Potsdam Frederick built a one-floor retreat for flute playing and philosophy, and he named it Sanssouci, French for without care. He asked to be buried there beside his greyhounds. In 1750 Voltaire came to live at his court, but the friendship soured, and when Voltaire griped that he had to wash the king's dirty linen by polishing the king's awkward French poems, Frederick remarked that you squeeze an orange and toss away its peel. Voltaire fled in 1753. German tradition calls Frederick the Potato King, who supposedly guarded a royal potato field so that peasants would think the crop precious and steal it, but historians doubt he ever ate a potato himself, and say the legend has won out over the facts. Germans had grown potatoes since 1647, yet visitors still leave them on his grave.

Catherine the Great rescued Diderot from his debts by buying his whole library, letting him keep the books as her paid librarian, and paying his salary fifty years in advance. In 1767 she issued her Nakaz, or Instruction, which drew on Montesquieu and Beccaria, spoke against torture and even questioned serfdom, and it made her famous across Europe as an enlightened ruler. Yet serfdom spread in her reign, and in the years after Pugachev's great revolt she gave the nobles even more power over their serfs, which historians see as the basic flaw of such reform: what a ruler grants, a ruler can simply take back. Rights that a people secure for themselves do not vanish at a monarch's whim.

Joseph II issued some 6,000 decrees in ten years, freeing serfs and granting religious toleration, but the Hungarian nobles forced him to cancel nearly all of it, and he wrote his own epitaph: here lies a ruler who, despite his best intentions, failed in everything he tried. Only his toleration edict and the end of serfdom outlived him.

enlightenment-ideas-in-the-american-foun.context_blurb:
The Americans who declared independence in 1776 and wrote the Constitution in 1787 drew on the European Enlightenment: John Locke on natural rights, Montesquieu on dividing power. They braided those ideas with their Protestant Christian faith and long experience of governing their own colonies, and they built a republic for people who, in their view, were capable of both greatness and mischief.

In June 1776 Congress chose a Committee of Five to prepare a declaration, and the five handed the writing to their youngest member, the 33-year-old Thomas Jefferson. His first draft called its truths sacred and undeniable, but Benjamin Franklin crossed out those words and made the truths self-evident, turning a claim of faith into a claim of reason that any thinking person could see. Locke had named life, liberty and property as the rights government must guard; Jefferson kept the first two and put in place of property something larger, the pursuit of happiness. From Montesquieu, writing in 1748, the founders took the idea that a free state divides its power three ways, into making the laws, carrying them out and judging them: the legislative, executive and judicial branches.

Jefferson leaned on a Virginian too. Three weeks before the Declaration, Virginia adopted a Declaration of Rights drafted by George Mason, whose promise of happiness and safety Jefferson followed closely, and he kept a copy at his elbow as he drafted. The historian John Ferling says nothing influenced Jefferson more. Locke had taught that a people need not endure a destructive government, and the Declaration echoed him: when a government turns destructive of those ends, the people have the right to alter it or abolish it. Jefferson's draft also attacked King George for the slave trade, calling it a war on human nature, but Congress cut the passage, and Jefferson later wrote that it was struck out to please South Carolina and Georgia, which still wanted to import enslaved people.

That was the founding's deepest contradiction: the man who wrote that all men are created equal enslaved more than 600 people over his lifetime, and about a fifth of the new nation's people were enslaved. Counting the founders' citations, the political scientist Donald Lutz found that Montesquieu led all the secular writers, ahead even of the legal scholar William Blackstone, but the Bible was quoted more than any of them. In Federalist No. 47 James Madison called Montesquieu the oracle always consulted on dividing power, and warned that gathering every power into one set of hands is the very definition of tyranny. In 1788 Madison, writing with Alexander Hamilton and John Jay under the name Publius in The Federalist Papers, opened Federalist No. 51 by observing that if men were angels, government would not be needed at all. Since men are not angels, he argued, ambition must be made to counteract ambition.

Madison did not trust strict separation alone: in Federalist No. 48 he scorned written limits as mere parchment barriers that power would ignore, so the framers let the branches check one another with tools such as the veto and judicial review. Even the happiness phrase had Lockean roots, though not in his political writing: Locke's remark linking the pursuit of happiness to liberty comes from his Essay Concerning Human Understanding, a book about how the human mind comes to know things. Jefferson had in mind a purposeful, virtuous life, but the Declaration offers only the freedom to chase happiness, not a promise that anyone will catch it: a negative right, freedom from interference, not a good the government owes you.

erasmus-christian-humanism.context_blurb:
Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam was a Dutch priest and the greatest Christian humanist of the early 1500s, a master of Greek and Latin and the most widely read author in Europe. He wanted to reform the Catholic Church from within by sending readers back to the earliest texts of Scripture, and when Martin Luther split the Church, Erasmus was caught between the two sides.

In 1509, staying at the London house of his friend Thomas More, he wrote In Praise of Folly in about a week, and its Latin title, Moriae Encomium, secretly puns on More's Latin name, Morus. In the book Folly herself, in a jester's cap, praises herself and mocks the pompous of the age. In 1516 he urged that Scripture be put into every common language, wishing that the farmer might sing it as he guides his plough and the weaver hum it to the rhythm of his shuttle.

That same year he did what no printer had done: he published the New Testament in its original Greek, with his own fresh Latin translation in a column beside it. Johann Froben printed it at Basel, and Erasmus built it by comparing old handwritten copies. He left out one verse, 1 John 5:7, a favourite proof of the Trinity, because no Greek manuscript he could find contained it, but after critics howled, a lone Greek manuscript with the verse turned up, and he added it to his third edition in 1522 while noting his doubts. That manuscript had apparently been copied by a friar from the Latin.

Critics blamed him for Luther's revolt, jeering that he had laid the egg that Luther hatched. In 1523 Erasmus replied that he had laid a hen's egg, but Luther had hatched a bird of quite another breed. At last, in 1524, Erasmus published On Free Will, arguing that a person's will can still choose to accept or resist God's grace, and in 1525 Luther answered with On the Bondage of the Will, insisting that the will is enslaved to sin and saved by grace alone. Erasmus stayed a Catholic to the end, respected by both sides and fully trusted by neither.

eratosthenes-measures-the-earth.context_blurb:
Eratosthenes was a Greek scholar who ran the great Library of Alexandria in Egypt in the 200s BC. He wrote on poetry, history, geography and mathematics, mapped the known world and devised a sieve for finding prime numbers. Around 240 BC he measured the size of the whole Earth with a stick, a shadow and some geometry.

He knew that at noon on midsummer's day the Sun shone straight down a deep well at Syene, far to the south, so that nothing there cast a shadow. At that same hour in Alexandria an upright stick threw a shadow leaning some 7.2 degrees, which is exactly one fiftieth of a full circle, so the two cities had to lie a fiftieth of the way around the Earth. He took the distance between them, about 5,000 stadia, and multiplied by fifty to reach 250,000 stadia, a figure close to the true distance around the planet.

Eratosthenes was not proving the Earth round: educated Greeks already knew it was a sphere, and he set out to measure how big that ball was. Shadows that differ from place to place only make sense on a curved world, which is why his method worked. The modern tale that people before Columbus believed in a flat Earth falls apart before a Greek librarian who measured the globe more than two thousand years ago.

eratosthenes-measures-the-earth-s-circum.context_blurb:
Eratosthenes was a Greek mathematician and geographer who ran the Library of Alexandria in Egypt around 245 BC and tutored the children of Pharaoh Ptolemy III. Using nothing but sunlight, a stick and geometry, he worked out the size of the whole Earth, and schoolchildren around the world still repeat his experiment today.

His starting point was a strange fact about Syene, today called Aswan: at midday on the longest day of the year the Sun stood directly overhead, so its light fell straight to the bottom of a deep well and lit the water there, and an upright stick cast no shadow.

At noon that same day in Alexandria, hundreds of miles north, a stick's shadow leaned about 7.2 degrees, exactly one fiftieth of a circle, so the two cities lay a fiftieth of the way around the globe, and the road between them was a fiftieth of the Earth's circumference. Royal surveyors called bematists had paced that road at 5,000 stadia. Fifty times 5,000 gave about 250,000 stadia, roughly 40,000 kilometres, within a few percent of the true figure. The Greeks had worked out that the Earth was round, and roughly how big, long before the Middle Ages.

euclid-and-the-elements-geometry.context_blurb:
Euclid was a Greek mathematician who taught in Alexandria around 300 BC. Almost nothing is known of his life, but his textbook, the Elements, gathered Greek geometry and number theory into thirteen books and built it all, one checkable step at a time, from a few definitions and starting rules. Schools taught from it for more than two thousand years.

A legend, written down by the philosopher Proclus some seven centuries later, says King Ptolemy I grew weary of proof after proof and asked for a shortcut, and Euclid told him there was no royal road to geometry. Even a king had to walk the same path as everyone else.

In Book IX Euclid proved that the primes never run out: suppose you had a complete list, multiply all of them and add one, and the new number must have a prime factor that is not on your list, so no list can ever hold them all. The proof is still taught today.

The fifth of his starting rules, about parallel lines, felt clumsy, and for over two thousand years mathematicians failed to derive it from the other four, until three mathematicians of the 1800s, Gauss, Bolyai and Lobachevsky, found that you could reject it outright and still build a geometry that never contradicts itself. That non-Euclidean geometry later helped Einstein describe curved space.

european-resistance-movements.context_blurb:
Across Nazi-occupied Europe in World War Two, ordinary people organised resistance: they printed underground newspapers, hid Allied airmen, sabotaged German transport and spied for the Allies. Many were tortured and shot by the Gestapo. Two of the most striking stories come from Scandinavia, where small groups of people did enormous things.

In Norway the Germans held the Vemork plant, the only factory in occupied Europe making heavy water for a German atomic-bomb program. On the night of 27 February 1943, Joachim Roenneberg led a handful of Norwegian commandos on skis to Vemork, and they blew up the only store of heavy water the plant had. They destroyed about 500 kilograms of it without firing a shot or losing a man, and Roenneberg then skied more than 200 miles to neutral Sweden. The British called it the most successful sabotage mission of the war.

In Denmark the danger fell on the Jews. A German diplomat, Georg Duckwitz, secretly warned the resistance of a roundup planned for the Jewish New Year. In October 1943 Danish fishermen, doctors, priests and police smuggled about 7,200 Jews across the strait to neutral Sweden in fishing boats, saving more than 95 percent of Denmark's Jews. Nineteen-year-old Henny Sinding ferried some 300 people on the lighthouse boat Gerda III.

european-union-the-euro.context_blurb:
After World War Two, leaders such as Robert Schuman, Konrad Adenauer, Alcide De Gasperi and Jean Monnet set out to bind Europe's old enemies so tightly together that another war between them would be impossible. Their coal and steel pact of 1951 grew into the European Union of 1993, and in 1999 most members launched a shared currency, the euro.

The Austrian artist Robert Kalina, who won the contest to design the banknotes, invented every bridge on them, in seven styles from Classical to modern, so that no nation's real landmark would be favoured over another's and none would take offence. Later a Dutch artist, Robin Stam, built all seven bridges for real in the town of Spijkenisse, near Rotterdam.

The euro began as an accounting currency on 1 January 1999 and reached people's wallets as coins and notes on 1 January 2002. Its deeper problem lies in its design: one central bank in Frankfurt sets a single interest rate for twenty countries, while each runs its own budget, taxes and pensions, and one rate cannot suit every economy at once. Economists call this a monetary union without a fiscal union.

everest-hillary-and-tenzing.context_blurb:
Mount Everest, on the border of Nepal and Tibet, is the highest point on Earth, and for decades it had killed those who tried to climb it. In 1953 Colonel John Hunt's British-led expedition laid siege to it, and on 29 May two of its men reached the top: Edmund Hillary, a New Zealand beekeeper, and Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa who had climbed higher on Everest than almost anyone.

They spent only about fifteen minutes on top. Tenzing, a Buddhist, scooped out a hollow in the snow and buried a small offering for the mountain gods: some sweets, a bar of chocolate and biscuits. Beside it Hillary buried a small crucifix that John Hunt had given him.

Back down, reporters kept asking which man had stepped on top first, but the two climbers and Hunt had agreed never to say, treating the summit as the whole team's achievement. To a mountaineer, Hillary said, it hardly mattered who set foot there first. Only years later did Tenzing's autobiography reveal that Hillary had been first. The news reached London in time for the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II, and the two men stayed friends for life.

ezana-of-aksum-ethiopian-christianity.context_blurb:
In the 300s AD Aksum, a trading kingdom of the Ethiopian highlands, prospered from the ships of the Red Sea, and around 340 its king, Ezana, made it one of the first Christian states in the world. Africa had Christian kings centuries before most of Europe, and the Ethiopian church that grew from Ezana's choice is still alive today, with its own language, Ge'ez, and its own calendar.

Before his conversion Ezana's royal inscriptions called him the son of Mahrem, the Aksumite war-god, much like the Greek Ares. The historian Rufinus says Christianity came by shipwreck: attackers killed everyone aboard a merchant ship from Tyre at an Aksumite port except two boys. One of them, Frumentius, rose at the royal court, tutored the young Ezana, was made the first bishop of Aksum in Alexandria, and is honoured by Ethiopians as Abba Salama, Father of Peace.

You can watch the change on Ezana's own money: his first coins showed Almaqah, the moon-god, as a disc and crescent, but later ones bore a Christian cross instead, possibly the first cross on any coin in the world. A later inscription drops the old gods altogether and calls on the Lord of Heaven.

fall-of-berlin-and-hitler-s-death.context_blurb:
In April 1945, after nearly six years of war, the Soviet Red Army closed in on Berlin, the capital of Nazi Germany. Adolf Hitler hid far underground in the Führerbunker, beneath the Reich Chancellery, while boys and old men fought in the streets above. Within three weeks Hitler was dead and his Third Reich had fallen, but Berlin's suffering did not end.

Hitler last saw daylight on his 56th birthday, 20 April, when he stepped out into the ruined garden of the Chancellery and pinned Iron Crosses on Hitler Youth boys, some only twelve years old, who were about to be sent against Soviet tanks. Just after midnight on 29 April he married his longtime companion Eva Braun, with Joseph Goebbels and Martin Bormann as witnesses, and they were husband and wife for less than two days. Hitler doubted that his cyanide capsules were real poison, so his doctor, Werner Haase, tested one on Hitler's German shepherd, Blondi, and the dog died. On the afternoon of 30 April Eva Braun bit a capsule and Hitler shot himself, and his aides, obeying his standing order, carried the bodies into the garden, soaked them in petrol and set them alight while Soviet shells fell. The fire left only charred fragments, which fed rumours for decades that he had escaped. The Soviets later tore down the ruined Chancellery, and today the bunker site lies under an ordinary parking lot behind an apartment block, left unmarked for decades so that it would never become a Nazi shrine.

In those last days Soviet soldiers fought their way onto the Reichstag roof and raised their flag around 22:40, while German troops still held the floors beneath them. The day after Hitler's death, Magda Goebbels drugged her six children with morphine and killed them with cyanide in their sleep, and witnesses say she then sat down to a game of solitaire before she and her husband took their own lives. In a farewell letter to her grown stepson she wrote that the world coming after Hitler and National Socialism would not be worth living in, and that her children were too good for the life that would follow.

The bunker had long since lost touch with reality. On 22 April Hitler learned that the relief attack he had pinned his hopes on, under Felix Steiner of the SS, had never been launched, and he raged and conceded, for once, that Germany had lost, yet he went on moving little flags on his map for divisions that no longer existed. His last hope was General Walther Wenck's 12th Army, ordered to abandon its front against the Americans and break through to Berlin, but Wenck never reached the city and instead held open an escape route for civilians and soldiers fleeing west, then surrendered to the Americans. Even the famous picture of the Red Army's flag above the Reichstag was a staged shot, taken in May by Yevgeny Khaldei, who scratched a second wristwatch off one soldier's arm before it was published, because two watches would have shown the world that Red Army men were looting.

The battle had opened before dawn on 16 April, when Marshal Georgy Zhukov switched on 143 giant searchlights to blind the Germans on the Seelow Heights, but the light scattered in the smoke and haze and silhouetted his own advancing soldiers as targets for German gunners. Since the bodies had burned to fragments, the Soviets confirmed Hitler's death on 11 May through his teeth: Käthe Heusermann, who had assisted his dentist, described his distinctive gold bridgework from memory, and it matched the remains. Soviet soldiers raped women across the conquered city on a vast scale, and drawing on Soviet files released after the Cold War, the historian Antony Beevor put the number at no fewer than 100,000 in Berlin alone and perhaps two million across the Soviet zone. Beating Hitler did not free the east: Stalin's army stayed, Moscow set up a one-party state, and eastern Germany vanished behind the Iron Curtain into communist rule, delivered from one tyranny into another.

fall-of-constantinople-1453.context_blurb:
In the spring of 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II, only twenty-one, laid siege to Constantinople, the great Christian city on the Bosphorus and capital of the Eastern Roman, or Byzantine, Empire. Its last emperor, Constantine XI, had about 7,000 defenders against an army of 50,000 or more. The city's fall shocked Christian Europe and helped spark the Renaissance.

When the city fell on 29 May, after fifty-three days of siege, the Roman Empire itself came to an end, for the Byzantines called themselves Romans, and Roman rule in that city had lasted about 1,100 years. The victory earned Mehmed the title Fatih, the Conqueror. On land the city sheltered behind the Theodosian Walls, a triple line of ramparts with a moat sixty feet wide, raised by a Roman emperor in the 400s and long thought unbreakable. By sea, a giant iron chain with links about two feet long floated on logs across the mouth of the Golden Horn, the harbour on the city's north side, and kept the Ottoman warships out.

Mehmed's answer to the walls came from Orban, a Hungarian gunsmith who had first offered his giant cannon to the Byzantine emperor, but the emperor could not pay for it. So Orban built the Basilica for Mehmed, a bronze monster about 27 feet long that hurled stone balls of some 600 pounds, with a barrel so wide that a grown man could crawl inside. It took sixty oxen and over 400 men to drag it to the walls. The chain still held, so one April day Mehmed had his men drag dozens of warships overland on a road of greased logs, over the hill behind Galata, and slide them into the harbour behind the chain, to the defenders' horror.

The Genoese captain Giovanni Giustiniani Longo led the defence of the land walls, bringing some 700 Genoese of his own, and when he was badly wounded in the final assault and carried off the wall, panic spread and the defence collapsed. Constantine XI would not flee: eyewitnesses say he tore off his imperial purple so that he would look like any common soldier and plunged sword in hand into the battle, and his body was never found. Mehmed rode straight to Hagia Sophia, the vast domed church built in the 500s, the largest in Christendom, claimed it as the greatest prize of his conquest and had it turned into a mosque. He made the city his new capital in place of Edirne.

Greek scholars escaped to Italy carrying ancient Greek manuscripts, giving Italians the original texts of Plato and Aristotle and helping to spark the Renaissance. In 1468 Cardinal Bessarion gave 482 Greek books to Venice, the core of its great library. Bitter quarrels had weakened the city. Many Byzantines rejected union with the Catholic West that might have brought rescue, and the historian Doukas quotes the official Loukas Notaras saying he would rather see the Turkish turban in the City than the Latin mitre, though the line may be invented. The Greeks refused to accept that their last emperor had vanished for good, so legend made him the Marble Emperor: an angel turned Constantine to stone and hid him beneath the city, where he sleeps until he wakes to win it back.

fall-of-constantinople-1453-2.context_blurb:
On 29 May 1453 the Ottoman Turks stormed Constantinople, the walled Christian city on the Bosphorus that had defied armies for more than a thousand years. Their sultan, Mehmed II, was twenty-one, and he brought new weapons and new tricks against an empire that had shrunk almost to its capital. Orthodox Christians still remember the day with grief.

The conquest made Mehmed's name forever: the Turks call him Fatih, the Conqueror. His great weapon was the Basilica, a bronze cannon about 27 feet long built by the gun-maker Orban, whose barrel was so wide that a grown man could crawl into it, and which hurled stone balls of over 600 pounds. Orban had gone first to the Byzantines, who could not afford him. The city's weak side was its harbour, the Golden Horn, so the defenders closed its mouth with a huge iron chain strung across floating logs and guarded by warships. The last emperor, Constantine XI Palaiologos, refused to flee, and tradition says he threw off his imperial purple and charged into the breach like an ordinary soldier. His body was never identified.

One night in April Mehmed had his men lay a road of greased timbers over the hills behind the Genoese colony of Galata and haul some 70 or 80 ships overland into the Golden Horn, behind the chain. On the final night Mehmed sent his army against the walls in three waves: the expendable irregulars, then the Anatolian regulars, and last his elite household troops, the Janissaries, who cracked the worn-out defence. In Hagia Sophia, the great domed church, Mehmed caught a soldier prising up marble paving to steal and stopped him, saying the plunder and the captives belonged to the soldiers, but the city's buildings belonged to him. Then he had the call to prayer sounded and made the church a mosque.

The Genoese captain Giovanni Giustiniani had held the land walls for weeks with the 700 men he brought, but in the final assault he was badly wounded and carried off to a ship, and when his Genoese saw him go, they followed and the defence broke. He died of the wound on 1 June. Before the siege the official George Sphrantzes had secretly counted the city's fighting men and found only 4,773 Greeks and some 200 foreigners; even with Giustiniani's Genoese and other volunteers, the defenders numbered about 7,000 against 50,000 to 80,000 Ottomans. Fleeing scholars carried Greek manuscripts and learning west to Italy, Cardinal Bessarion alone gathering some 800 Greek manuscripts that he later gave to Venice, and this flood of books and teachers helped feed the Renaissance.

The emperor's end is a mystery. Most accounts say Constantine died sword in hand, but the Venetian eyewitness Nicolo Barbaro wrote that the emperor hanged himself when the Turks broke through the San Romano gate. A later legend from the chronicler Doukas blamed the whole disaster on a small back gate, the Kerkoporta, left open by accident so that about fifty Turks slipped in, but Doukas was not there, no such gate has been found, and historians reject the tale. Walking through the half-empty city, Mehmed did not boast but recited an old Persian verse in which a spider hangs the curtains in the palace of the Caesars and an owl keeps watch from its towers. He cut the three-day sack short, because little was left to take.

fall-of-france-1940.context_blurb:
In May 1940 Nazi Germany struck France and the Low Countries, and in six weeks it beat what had looked on paper like the strongest army in the West. France signed an armistice in June, and Britain was left alone in Western Europe against Hitler for a year. French doctrine had failed, not French courage.

France had built the Maginot Line, a line of massive concrete forts facing Germany, but the Germans never broke it: they went around its northern end through Belgium and left its guns facing the wrong way. The main panzer thrust came through the Ardennes, a hilly forest that French commanders thought the thick woods and the Meuse River made impassable to tanks, so they barely defended it, and on 13 May the panzers crossed the Meuse at Sedan. General Erich von Manstein's plan, the Sickle Cut, rested on a trick called the matador's cloak: a showy attack into Belgium and Holland drew the best Allied armies north, while the real blow swung behind them through the Ardennes and cut them off from the sea.

Trapped at Dunkirk, the British and many French soldiers were rescued by the Royal Navy and a surprise fleet of civilian craft, fishing boats, yachts and pleasure steamers, which crossed the Channel to lift about 338,000 men off the beaches. On 22 June Hitler took his revenge: he had the very railway carriage in which Germany had signed its armistice in 1918 pulled from its museum and set back on the same spot in the Forest of Compiègne, and France surrendered inside it. The Germans occupied the north and west, a collaborating regime ruled the south from Vichy, and General Charles de Gaulle fought on from London.

fall-of-the-romanovs-and-rasputin.context_blurb:
Tsar Nicholas II, the last emperor of Russia, and his German-born wife, Alexandra, had four daughters and one son, Alexei, who had hemophilia: his blood would not clot, so even a bruise could kill him. In desperation Alexandra turned to a wandering Siberian holy man, Grigori Rasputin, and his hold over the royal family helped bring the dynasty down.

When Alexei lay near death from bleeding, Rasputin assured the weeping mother that God had heard her prayers and the boy would live, and when the bleeding stopped, she came to believe that God had sent him to save her son. Books and films call him the Mad Monk, but he was never a monk at all: born a peasant in the Siberian village of Pokrovskoye in 1869, he was a self-taught wanderer who was never ordained.

His drinking, his women and his sway over appointments scandalised the court, above all during World War One, when Nicholas left to lead the army. In December 1916 a band of nobles led by Prince Felix Yusupov invited Rasputin to a cellar room in the Yusupov Palace and fed him cakes and wine laced with cyanide, and by Yusupov's own story the poison seemed to have no effect at all, so they shot him. A legend grew of an unkillable mystic who shrugged off poison and bullets and drowned only under the river ice. But the autopsy found not a speck of poison in him, just alcohol, along with three gunshot wounds, and a close-range shot to the forehead had killed him.

Within three months the Romanov dynasty collapsed in the February Revolution. In July 1918 Bolshevik gunmen murdered the whole family in a basement room of the Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, and the first bullets glanced off the four princesses because more than a kilogram of diamonds and jewels had been sewn into their corsets. For most of the century a claimant named Anna Anderson insisted to be the escaped Grand Duchess Anastasia, until DNA tests in 1994 showed she was Franziska Schanzkowska, a Polish factory worker who had gone missing. In 2007 two more bodies were found near Yekaterinburg, matched by DNA to the family, proving that no child escaped.

fall-of-the-western-roman-empire-476.context_blurb:
By the 400s AD the western half of the Roman Empire was crumbling, ruled from Ravenna by puppet emperors whom Germanic generals propped up, while the eastern half stayed strong. In 476 the last western emperor, a boy, was pushed off his throne, and nobody replaced him. Historians such as Edward Gibbon mark that year as the fall of Rome in the West.

The boy was called Romulus Augustulus, and by coincidence his names echoed both Romulus, the legendary founder of Rome, and Augustus, its first emperor. His real name was simply Romulus; Augustulus was a mocking nickname meaning little Augustus, the little emperor, for a child who held the grandest title in the world and none of its power.

The real ruler was his father, Orestes, a general who seized power around 475 and set his son on the throne as a puppet, perhaps at about fifteen. Orestes had hired Germanic soldiers, Heruli, Sciri and others, who demanded a third of the land of Italy to settle on, and when he refused, they rose against him and killed him. Their general, Odoacer, marched into Ravenna on 4 September 476 and deposed the boy emperor, the date historians give for the Western Empire's end. A Roman chronicle, the Anonymus Valesianus, says Odoacer was moved by the boy's youth and beauty and spared his life. He sent Romulus to live in a fortress-villa on the coast near Naples, the castellum Lucullanum, with a yearly pension of 6,000 solidi. Rome itself did not vanish: its eastern half, governed from Constantinople, kept the Roman name for almost another thousand years, until that great city fell to the Turks in 1453.

Orestes had a startling past, for years earlier he had served as personal secretary to Attila the Hun, Rome's deadliest foe. Odoacer refused to make himself emperor: he shipped the western crown and purple robe east to Emperor Zeno in Constantinople and called himself only king of Italy, a sign that the West no longer needed an emperor of its own. Odoacer's end came in 493, when Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths, killed him himself at a feast in Ravenna meant to seal their peace, and legend says Theodoric then looked at the corpse and marvelled that the man had not a bone in his body.

Many Romans had felt the real fall decades earlier, in 410, when Alaric and the Visigoths sacked Rome itself, and far off in Bethlehem the grieving scholar Jerome wrote that the city which had captured the whole world had now been captured itself. 476 was only the quiet, legal date. Rome changed shape rather than dying: Roman law grew into the foundation of Western law, the Church took over its organisation, and everyday Latin slowly turned into French, Italian and Spanish.

families-of-instruments-and-the-orchestr.context_blurb:
The modern Western symphony orchestra sorts its instruments into four families: strings, woodwinds, brass and percussion. It grew to its present size between the 1600s and the 1800s as composers such as Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven wrote for ever larger forces. To teach children those families, the Russian composer Sergei Prokofiev wrote Peter and the Wolf, a story in which every character has an instrument of its own.

The bird is a flute, the cat a clarinet, grumpy Grandfather a bassoon, Peter the whole string section, and the duck is the oboe, which goes on quacking faintly at the end because the hasty wolf swallowed her whole and alive. Listen closely and you can hear her still inside him.

To make the wolf sound big and frightening, Prokofiev gave him three French horns playing together, brass instruments sounded by buzzing the lips into a cup-shaped mouthpiece. By the time the story ends, a child who has listened has met all four families.

faraday-maxwell-and-the-conquest-of-elec.context_blurb:
Michael Faraday, the son of a poor blacksmith, born near London in 1791, became the greatest experimenter of his age, and James Clerk Maxwell, a Scot born in 1831, became its greatest mathematical physicist. Between them they showed that electricity, magnetism and light are one force, and nearly every power station, motor and phone today rests on their work.

Faraday left school at fourteen to be apprenticed to a bookbinder, and he taught himself science by reading the very books he was paid to bind. He never learned advanced mathematics, yet the unit of electrical capacitance, the farad, is named in his honour. Maxwell was curious from the cradle: before he was three he pestered his family about doors, locks, streams and bells, forever asking what the go o' that was, meaning how it worked.

Fame never changed Faraday: he turned down a knighthood from Queen Victoria and twice refused to lead the Royal Society, saying he would remain plain Mr Faraday until the end. He also refused, on moral grounds, to help make poison gas for the Crimean War. In 1861 Maxwell made the first true colour photograph by photographing a tartan ribbon three times, through red, green and blue filters, and combining the three images.

In August 1831 Faraday wrapped two coils of wire around opposite sides of an iron ring, and when he switched on the current in the first, the meter needle on the second coil, which had no battery, twitched: a changing magnetism had made an electric current. That is electromagnetic induction, the principle behind every generator, and the ring is still on show at the Royal Institution.

Around 1862 Maxwell used his equations to calculate how fast an electric wave should cross empty space, and the answer matched the measured speed of light, so he concluded that light itself is an electromagnetic wave. He died before anyone made such waves, but in 1887 the German physicist Heinrich Hertz created them in his lab and reportedly called them useless, and within a decade they had become radio.

fdr-and-the-new-deal.context_blurb:
Franklin Delano Roosevelt became president in March 1933, in the worst depths of the Depression: a quarter of American workers had no job, banks were failing every day and the economy had shrunk by about a third. His answer was the New Deal, a flood of federal programs that changed what Americans expect from their government, and that critics warned would cost them their liberty.

In his first inaugural address he tried to steady a frightened nation by telling it that the only thing it had to fear was fear itself, a line often credited to his adviser Louis Howe. Two days later he ordered every bank in America closed for a few days, a bank holiday, while Congress passed the Emergency Banking Act to reopen them under federal watch. In his first fireside chat he told listeners that a reopened bank was safer than a mattress, and about a billion dollars in hoarded cash came back. His Civilian Conservation Corps put nearly three million jobless young men to work planting trees and building parks for $30 a month, but the Corps mailed $25 of every $30 directly to each man's family.

Sixteen dams of the Tennessee Valley Authority, spread over seven poor Southern states, brought electric lights to backcountry farms that had never had electricity. The cost was real too: the first dam, Norris Dam, flooded a valley and forced nearly 3,000 people from their homes. His Labor Secretary, Frances Perkins, had made history in 1933 as the first woman ever to sit in a U.S. Cabinet, and she fought harder than anyone for the Social Security Act of 1935, receiving one of the pens Roosevelt used to sign it.

The Works Progress Administration put 8.5 million Americans to work on roads and bridges, but it also hired out-of-work writers and artists, who painted 2,566 murals and wrote guidebooks to every state. Social Security's first monthly payment went out in 1940 to Ida May Fuller, a retired teacher from Vermont, who had paid only $24.75 in payroll tax, lived to 100 and collected $22,888.92. Roosevelt admitted the payroll tax was political armour, so that no politician could ever scrap the program.

The Supreme Court fought back. In 1935 a Brooklyn poultry firm run by the Schechter family challenged the National Industrial Recovery Act, and in what became known as the Sick Chicken Case the justices unanimously threw the act out, ruling that it handed the president lawmaking power he could not hold. In February 1937 an angry president proposed letting himself name an extra justice for each justice past seventy who stayed on, up to six more, which would have swelled the Court from nine to as many as fifteen. Critics called it court-packing, and it died in the Senate that July.

Meanwhile Justice Owen Roberts, a swing vote, upheld a state minimum-wage law in March 1937, and the humorist Cal Tinney, punning on a stitch in time, called it the switch in time that saved the nine. Records show Roberts had already voted that way in private, weeks before the plan, so the timing may be coincidence. In his State of the Union of 1944, Roosevelt argued that needy men are not free men and proposed a Second Bill of Rights that would promise every American work, a decent house, doctors' care and schooling. That same year Friedrich Hayek, an Austrian economist in London, answered in The Road to Serfdom that central planning erodes freedom even when its aims are good, because every promised good must be taken from somebody, and a plan can only work by overriding those who resist. Americans have argued over those two cases ever since.

fdr-s-wartime-leadership.context_blurb:
Franklin Delano Roosevelt led the United States through the Depression and then the Second World War, from 1933 until his death in April 1945, less than a month before Germany surrendered. He worked closely with Winston Churchill and more warily with Joseph Stalin, and he turned American factories into the Allies' greatest weapon. He also made grave mistakes.

He was the only president elected four times, breaking the tradition George Washington began in 1796 when he stepped down after two terms, that no president would serve more than two; the 22nd Amendment of 1951 later made the limit law. In a fireside chat in December 1940 he promised to keep American soldiers home and beat Hitler with factories, flooding Britain with planes, ships and tanks as democracy's great arsenal.

Britain had run out of money, so Roosevelt sold Americans on lending arms with a picture: if your neighbour's house is on fire, you lend him your garden hose to put it out and do not haggle over the price, and he gives it back afterward. That image sold Lend-Lease, which shipped about $36.5 billion in war supplies by 1945. Polio had paralysed his legs in 1921, and he hid it so well that one biographer named it his splendid deception: he learned to swing forward a few steps in steel braces, and reporters agreed that no photographs of him in his wheelchair would be taken.

Drafting his address after the attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941, he crossed out the words world history at the end of his line about the date of the attack and wrote infamy instead, so that the day would live in infamy. The draft in his own hand survives.

On 19 February 1942 Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066, which named no group, yet it was used to force about 120,000 Japanese Americans out of their West Coast homes and into incarceration camps, a dark mark that historians judge harshly.

federalist-papers-hamilton-madison-jay.context_blurb:
The Federalist Papers are 85 essays that Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay published in New York newspapers in 1787 and 1788 under the shared pen name Publius, urging Americans to ratify the new Constitution. Hamilton wrote most of them and Madison some of the deepest, and the Supreme Court still quotes them today.

The essays explain why the Constitution splits and balances power. In Federalist No. 51 Madison admitted that people are no angels, so he gave each branch of government both the means and the motive to resist the others, setting ambition against ambition so that selfishness would check itself. He tied the interest of each officeholder to the rights of his office, so that every branch would guard its own ground.

Madison also faced the danger of faction, groups of citizens chasing their own interest against the common good. In Federalist No. 10 he argued that faction cannot be abolished without destroying liberty, which feeds it as air feeds fire, so the safest design is a republic spread over a large and varied people, where factions multiply and check one another and no single one can seize control. A small republic, he warned, is easier for one faction to capture. The essays were collected as a book during the ratification fight and have never gone out of print.

feudalism-lords-vassals-fiefs.context_blurb:
After Charlemagne's empire broke apart in the 800s, Europe held together not through a central state but through a web of personal promises between warriors and landholders. A lesser man swore loyalty to a greater one and received land to feed his household, owing armed service in return. Historians call this system feudalism, and it ran on sworn trust rather than paperwork.

The bond began with a ceremony. In homage the vassal knelt bareheaded and unarmed and placed his clasped hands between his lord's, and as the lord closed his hands around them, the kneeling man became wholly his lord's man. The posture showed submission; the enclosing hands promised protection. Then, before the watching household, the lord kissed him on the mouth, so that everyone had witnessed the oath. The land the vassal received was his fief: he kept what it earned, governed the peasants who worked it and could leave it to his sons, and in exchange he owed his lord military service, usually as an armoured knight on horseback.

Custom set the terms. The smallest standard English fief, a knight's fee, was sized to support one knight with his family, servants, warhorses and armour, and he owed his lord 40 days of fighting a year. The cap kept nobles from leaving their own lands too long. A knight who would rather not ride to war could pay scutage instead, shield-money, from the Latin scutum, and England's Henry II levied it seven times in thirty years, hiring with it soldiers who answered to him alone.

The bond ran both ways. In 1020 Fulbert, the bishop of Chartres, set out a vassal's duties in a famous letter, but he added that the lord owed his faithful vassal the same in return, and a lord who failed him would rightly be judged guilty of bad faith. In England a king turned the whole web toward himself. In the summer of 1086 William the Conqueror summoned some 170 leading landholders to Old Sarum and made every one of them swear loyalty straight to the king, above any lesser lord, an act remembered as the Oath of Salisbury. It came the same month the Domesday Book survey was finished.

fijian-ritual-cannibalism-its-end-at-chr.context_blurb:
In the islands of Fiji, in the South Pacific, ritual cannibalism was part of warfare well into the 1800s: victorious chiefs ate slain enemies in ceremonies bound up with honour, revenge and religious belief. Methodist missionaries who arrived from the 1830s recorded such feasts. Within a single generation, Christian conversion ended the practice.

The feasts followed strict rules. A chief or priest in a sacred tapu state could not lay his hands on the cooked body of a dead foe, so attendants fed him with a long-pronged wooden fork carved for that one grim purpose. Fijians called it the iculanibokola, the fork for the human victim.

The great turn came through one chief. Seru Epenisa Cakobau, a chief who had eaten men slain in his wars, accepted baptism from the missionary James Calvert in 1854, and when he won the Battle of Kaba a year later, he pardoned his captured enemies and spared their lives instead of killing and eating them. His conversion led tens of thousands of Fijians to Christianity. The last known ritual killing came in 1867, when the missionary Thomas Baker and seven companions were killed and eaten, and in 2003 the village involved held a public ceremony of apology to his descendants.

first-political-parties-federalists-vs-d.context_blurb:
The men who founded the United States distrusted political parties, which they called factions, and George Washington warned against them in his Farewell Address. Yet the first American parties grew up inside Washington's own cabinet. The followers of Alexander Hamilton became the Federalists, and those of Thomas Jefferson and James Madison became the Democratic-Republicans.

Treasury Secretary Hamilton and Secretary of State Jefferson split over the reach of the national government: Hamilton wanted a powerful central state, commerce and manufacturing and a loose reading of the Constitution, while Jefferson wanted strong states, a farming republic and a strict reading. Their quarrel, not an election, created the parties. Over dinner at Jefferson's lodgings in June 1790, the three men struck a bargain: Hamilton got the federal government to take over the states' war debts, and in return the Virginians won the permanent national capital on the Potomac River, the future Washington, D.C.

By 1791 the two camps each had a newspaper to fight with, and when the poet Philip Freneau's National Gazette, the Republicans' paper, hammered the administration, Washington privately fumed about that Rascal Freneau. The Federalists had John Fenno's Gazette of the United States. The party press had turned a cabinet feud into a national fight, and the two-party pattern it began has outlasted both parties.

fleming-and-the-discovery-of-penicillin.context_blurb:
Alexander Fleming was a Scottish bacteriologist at a London teaching hospital, St Mary's, who, as a doctor in World War One, had watched soldiers die of infected wounds that no medicine could cure. In 1928 he stumbled on penicillin, the first antibiotic, but it took a team at Oxford, and a race during World War Two, to turn his find into a drug that saved millions.

In September 1928, back from a summer holiday, he was sorting a pile of forgotten dishes in his untidy lab when he noticed one with a patch of bluish mould, and legend says he murmured, "That's funny." Around the mould lay a clear ring where the bacteria had been killed off, because the mould was making something that destroys germs. Before he named it penicillin in March 1929, after the mould Penicillium, Fleming called the germ-killing liquid simply mould juice. The rare spore had most likely drifted up through an open door from the lab one floor below, where the Irish mould expert C. J. La Touche was working.

Fleming could not purify the substance or keep it stable, so his paper sat almost ignored for a decade, until Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford took it up in 1939 and made penicillin a real medicine. Mould needs a wide surface to grow on, so they turned their lab into a makeshift factory, using biscuit tins, pie dishes, bath tubs, milk churns and hospital bedpans. Gallons of broth gave a fingernail's worth of the drug. On 25 May 1940 they infected eight mice with deadly streptococci and gave penicillin to four of them, and by next morning the four treated mice were alive and the four untreated ones were dead.

On 12 February 1941 an Oxford policeman, Albert Alexander, so badly infected that he had lost an eye, became the first person treated with penicillin, and within a day his fever fell and the infection began to heal. The drug was so scarce that his doctors collected his urine, recovered the penicillin from it, since about 80 percent passed straight through him, and injected it again, but the supply still ran out, and he relapsed and died on 15 March. That year Florey and Norman Heatley crossed to the United States to have the drug made in bulk, and in case the Nazis invaded Britain, they rubbed the mould spores into the linings of their coats so that the strain could never be lost. At a government lab in Peoria, Illinois, a worker nicknamed Moldy Mary Hunt brought in the best mould of all from a local market, growing on a mouldy cantaloupe, and its strain became the ancestor of mass-produced penicillin.

In March 1942 a New Haven patient, Anne Miller, near death from an infection of the blood, was the first patient penicillin truly rescued, and the tablespoon of it flown in for her was half of all the penicillin then in the United States. Accepting his Nobel Prize in December 1945, Fleming warned that people who underdose themselves would expose their microbes to amounts too small to kill them, and so make the germs resistant to penicillin. Norman Heatley, who built the methods and equipment that turned penicillin into a usable drug, was left off that Nobel Prize because he was a chemist, not a doctor, but in 1990 Oxford gave him an honorary Doctorate of Medicine, said to be its first for a non-physician.

florence-nightingale-and-modern-nursing.context_blurb:
Florence Nightingale was an upper-class Englishwoman, born in 1820, who trained as a nurse against her wealthy family's wishes. In 1854, during the Crimean War, she led a small band of nurses to the British army hospital at Scutari, where filthy wards and backed-up sewers were killing more soldiers than enemy weapons. Her reforms of cleanliness and record-keeping cut the death rate sharply.

Each night, when the doctors were asleep, she made her rounds of the wards by the light of a small lamp, and the grateful soldiers called her the Lady with the Lamp. The Times wrote of a ministering angel with a little lamp in her hand, and in 1857 the poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow fixed the image in verse. Her real lamp survives in a museum.

Back in Britain she spent fifty years pushing to reform army medicine, hospitals and nurse training, often from her sickbed. To convince doubtful officials that filth and disease, far more than battle, had killed most of the soldiers, she invented a coloured statistical diagram, the coxcomb or Nightingale rose: twelve wedges, one for each month, with great blue areas for deaths from disease and red ones for deaths from wounds. The huge blue wedges made the truth impossible to miss, and they shrink after her reforms. In 1859 she became the first woman elected a Fellow of the Royal Statistical Society.

foreign-allies-lafayette-von-steuben-fra.context_blurb:
The American Revolution was not won by Americans alone. Foreign volunteers and allies proved vital: the young French nobleman the Marquis de Lafayette, the Prussian drillmaster Baron Friedrich von Steuben and, from 1778, the kingdom of France itself, whose navy, money and soldiers helped win the final victory at Yorktown in 1781.

Lafayette landed in July 1777, a rich nineteen-year-old eager to fight, and although Congress distrusted foreign officers, it gave him a major general's rank, partly because he offered to serve without pay. He came to love Washington like a father, and back in France he named his newborn son Georges Washington de Lafayette.

Benjamin Franklin sent von Steuben over billed as a lieutenant general of Frederick the Great, but the title was largely invented: his real top rank had been captain and aide-de-camp. Even his title of baron was puffed up. Reaching the frozen camp at Valley Forge in February 1778, he was appalled to find that soldiers barely knew how to fight with their bayonets and used them instead to roast beefsteak over their campfires. He drilled them into a disciplined army that could charge with the bayonet.

France joined the war after the American victory at Saratoga. When Yorktown fell, the French admiral de Grasse, himself six foot two, hosted the even taller Washington aboard his flagship, kept throwing his arms around him, and called him mon petit général, my little general.

fort-sumter-and-the-outbreak-of-the-civi.context_blurb:
Fort Sumter was a brick federal fort on an artificial island at the mouth of Charleston Harbor, South Carolina. After South Carolina and other Deep South states seceded in the winter of 1860 to 1861, Major Robert Anderson held it for the Union, and Confederate forces under General P. G. T. Beauregard demanded he surrender. The Civil War began here.

At 4:30 in the morning on 12 April 1861 the Confederate batteries opened fire, and over 34 hours they hurled more than 3,000 rounds, among them hot shot, iron balls heated in furnaces until they glowed red, which set the fort's wooden barracks ablaze. Anderson's men held out, short of food and powder, until he surrendered with honour.

Not one soldier died in the bombardment, but after Anderson surrendered, his men began a 100-gun salute to the flag, a spark set off a pile of cartridges, and the explosion killed Private Daniel Hough, the first soldier to die in the war. Hundreds of thousands would follow him.

Anderson took the fort's 33-star flag home with him instead of surrendering it, and on 14 April 1865, with Charleston retaken, he came back and raised that same flag over the ruined fort, weeping that restoring it had been the cherished wish of his heart.

founding-of-tenochtitlan-eagle-on-the-ca.context_blurb:
The Aztecs, who called themselves the Mexica, told how their ancestors wandered south from a mythical northern homeland, Aztlan, guided by their war god. In 1325 they founded the city of Tenochtitlan on marshy ground in the middle of Lake Texcoco, and over two centuries they built it into the capital of an empire that ruled most of central Mexico when the Spanish arrived.

Their god had told them to settle where they saw an eagle perched on a prickly-pear cactus, and that founding sign still sits at the centre of Mexico's national flag and coat of arms. An old story became a living national symbol.

On today's flag the eagle grips a snake, and most people assume the snake was always there. Yet the earliest Aztec drawings, among them the opening page of the Codex Mendoza, have an eagle and a cactus but no serpent; the snake first appears around 1576, some fifty years after the conquest. The likeliest explanation is that later artists misread a glyph beside the eagle's beak, the atl-tlachinolli, a sign of water and fire that stood for sacred war. The famous serpent is an addition from after the Spanish conquest.

founding-of-the-united-nations-1945.context_blurb:
The United Nations came into being in October 1945, after World War Two had killed some sixty million people, to try to prevent another such war. Fifty Allied governments drafted its charter at a conference in San Francisco, and it replaced the League of Nations, which had failed in the 1930s. Its headquarters stand in New York.

The name came first: President Franklin Roosevelt coined it, and on 1 January 1942 twenty-six Allied countries at war with Germany, Italy and Japan signed a Declaration by United Nations in Washington. That was years before the organisation itself existed.

The charter set up a Security Council with five permanent members, Britain, China, France, the Soviet Union and the United States, and gave each a veto, so that one no from any of the five stops a resolution dead, however many others vote yes. The great powers settled this at Yalta in early 1945; they would join only a body that could never force them to act against their will. The veto was the price of their joining, and it has often paralysed the Council. In 1968, when Soviet tanks crushed the Prague Spring in Czechoslovakia, ten Council members voted to condemn the invasion and order the troops out, but one Soviet no was enough to sink the resolution, and the tanks remained. The same had happened in 1956 over Hungary.

four-great-inventions-paper-printing-com.context_blurb:
China gave the world four great inventions: paper, printing, the compass and gunpowder. Each was in everyday use in China for centuries before it reached Europe, and each, once it spread, changed the world. Behind them stand named people: a court official, Daoist alchemists, diviners, a printer and a scholar who noticed what no one else had.

Around AD 105 the Han court official Cai Lun perfected paper: he pounded old rags, hemp, tree bark and worn-out fishing nets into a wet mush, spread it thin on a screen to drain, and dried it into cheap, smooth sheets. Paper made from scraps could spread to everyone. Gunpowder came by accident around 850, when Tang-dynasty alchemists seeking a drink that would make them immortal mixed saltpeter, sulfur and charcoal, and its Chinese name, huo yao, still means fire medicine. Printing came early too: a copy of the Diamond Sutra, a Buddhist scripture printed from wooden blocks and found in a sealed cave library at Dunhuang, carries the date 11 May 868, making it the oldest printed book in the world that bears a date.

The alchemists believed they were brewing the potion of eternal life, but their mixture exploded. By 1132, at the siege of De'an, Chinese soldiers fought with the fire lance, a bamboo tube fixed to a pole that blasted flame and smoke into the enemy's face, the direct ancestor of the gun. The emperor made Cai Lun a marquis, but around 121, caught up in a palace scandal and ordered to stand trial, he bathed, put on his finest robes and drank poison rather than face disgrace. The compass began as magic, not navigation: around 100 BC Han diviners spun a south-pointing spoon, a ladle carved from lodestone, on a bronze board, and used it to line up tombs and buildings with unseen cosmic forces.

The earliest text describing a gunpowder recipe, from the 800s, is a Daoist warning to alchemists never to mix sulfur, saltpeter and honey, because the smoke and flames had burned their hands and faces and even burned down whole houses. China guarded the secret of paper for centuries, until 751, when an Abbasid Arab army beat a Tang army at the Battle of Talas in Central Asia and captured Chinese prisoners who knew the craft; soon the first paper mill in the Islamic world rose at Samarkand. From there paper reached Europe. In 1900 a Daoist monk, Wang Yuanlu, found a walled-up door in one of the Mogao caves at Dunhuang, and behind it lay a lost library of about 40,000 manuscripts, among them the printed Diamond Sutra.

Around 1040, four centuries before Gutenberg, a commoner named Bi Sheng invented movable type, carving each character into sticky clay as thin as a coin's edge and baking it hard so the pieces could be set, printed and used again. He chose clay because wood warped. In his Dream Pool Essays of 1088 the scholar Shen Kuo gave the first clear description of a magnetic needle compass, and he was the first to record that the needle does not point exactly along the true north-south line but leans slightly to the east, the effect now called magnetic declination.

franco-prussian-war-and-the-capture-at-s.context_blurb:
The Franco-Prussian War of 1870 and 1871 pitted Emperor Napoleon III's France against a coalition of German states led by Prussia and its chancellor, Otto von Bismarck. Bismarck wanted a war that would weld the German states into one empire under the Prussian king, and he arranged a quarrel that let France declare war first. Prussian railways, artillery and staff work crushed the French within weeks.

On the first day of September 1870 the French army lay trapped at Sedan, in a valley ringed by German guns, and when Napoleon III raised the white flag, a reigning emperor was taken prisoner on the battlefield together with his whole army, something unheard of in modern Europe. Some 104,000 soldiers and 558 cannon went into captivity with him; he later died in exile in England.

To crown the victory, Bismarck staged the birth of the new German Empire on French soil: on 18 January 1871 Wilhelm I was proclaimed Kaiser in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles, the showpiece of France's old royal palace. The Treaty of Frankfurt then took Alsace-Lorraine from France, a grievance that festered until 1914.

frederick-douglass-and-the-abolitionists.context_blurb:
Frederick Douglass, born enslaved in Maryland around 1818, died in 1895 the most famous Black American of his century. He taught himself to read, escaped to the North, and became an abolitionist speaker, newspaper editor, author and adviser to presidents. He argued that America's founding promises were worth keeping, and that keeping them meant freedom for all.

Like most enslaved children he never knew his birthday, so as a free man he chose 14 February, because his mother had called him her Little Valentine. In Baltimore his master, Hugh Auld, forbade anyone to teach him, saying reading would spoil a slave, so Frederick traded his bread to hungry poor white boys in the street in return for reading lessons. He called it buying the bread of knowledge. With half a dollar earned shining boots he bought The Columbian Orator, a schoolbook whose dialogue between a master and a slave, in which the slave argues so well that he wins his freedom, taught the boy how to argue for his own freedom.

As a teenager he was sent to work for Edward Covey, a notorious slave-breaker, and when Douglass fought back and wrestled him for nearly two hours, Covey never whipped him again; Douglass called that fight the turning point of his life as a slave. On 3 September 1838 he escaped from Baltimore by train and steamboat to New York in under a day, slipping past slave-catchers disguised as a free Black sailor in a red shirt and sailor's hat, carrying a friend's seaman's papers. Anna Murray, a free woman who became his wife, had sewn the outfit. In New Bedford the abolitionist Nathan Johnson gave the runaway Frederick Bailey a new surname to fool the slave-catchers, borrowing it from the heroic clan of Douglas in Sir Walter Scott's poem The Lady of the Lake. In 1847 he launched an antislavery weekly in Rochester, New York, and named it The North Star, after the star runaways followed through the dark to freedom. He sat for more than 160 photographs, more than any other American of the 1800s, even Lincoln, and in almost all of them he stares at the camera unsmiling, because he would not give anyone the grinning, contented slave of racist caricature.

In 1852 Rochester invited him to give its Fourth of July oration, and he gave it a day late, on 5 July, telling the crowd that the Fourth was theirs, not his, while some three million people were held as slaves. Yet he called the Declaration the ringbolt of the nation's destiny and its principles saving principles, and he urged his listeners to stand by them against all enemies, whatever the cost. His old mentor William Lloyd Garrison had publicly set fire to the Constitution, calling it a covenant with death, but Douglass studied it, broke with Garrison and argued that, rightly read, it was a glorious liberty document, a weapon to use against slavery. In March 1865, when police turned him away from Lincoln's second inaugural reception because he was Black, Douglass got word inside, and Lincoln called out across the crowded room, here comes my friend Douglass, and asked what he thought of the speech. Lincoln told him no man's opinion mattered more to him.

galileo-and-the-telescope.context_blurb:
Galileo Galilei was an Italian mathematician and professor who, in 1609, heard of a Dutch spyglass and built a far better one of his own. Turning it to the night sky, he saw things no human had ever seen, and they convinced him that the Earth goes around the Sun. That conviction brought him before the Roman Inquisition in 1633.

In late 1609 he aimed his telescope at the Moon and, from the long shadows on its face, saw that it was not the flawless sphere of the old teaching but a rugged world covered in mountains and craters. He even estimated that its peaks rose about four miles. In January 1610 he studied Jupiter from a Padua rooftop for several nights, and four specks of light kept moving with the planet: four moons orbiting Jupiter, the first ever found circling another world. We call them Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. In March 1610 he rushed his discoveries into print in Venice in a slim book, Sidereus Nuncius, The Starry Messenger, the first book of science based on telescope observations.

Hoping for a rich patron, he named Jupiter's moons the Medicean Stars after the Medici family, rulers of Florence, and the flattery worked: Grand Duke Cosimo II made him court philosopher and mathematician. He turned the telescope on the Milky Way, the faint white band across the night sky, and found that it was made of countless faint stars, too dim and crowded for the naked eye to split apart.

In the constellation Orion, where the naked eye shows about nine stars, his lens revealed about 80. The sky was far fuller than anyone had imagined. Saturn puzzled him: it seemed to have bumps on both sides, three bodies almost touching, and when the bumps vanished in 1612 he could not know that he had glimpsed the edges of its rings, turned edge-on to Earth. In 1633, forced before the Roman Inquisition to deny that the Earth moves around the Sun, he is said to have muttered as he rose, And yet it moves, in Italian Eppur si muove, but the story first appeared in print in 1757 and is almost certainly a legend.

Watching Venus night after night, he saw it pass through crescent, half and full phases like the Moon, which was impossible in the old Earth-centred system of Ptolemy, proving that Venus circles the Sun. On 22 June 1633, about 69 and ailing, he knelt in a white penitent's gown at the convent of Santa Maria sopra Minerva and swore to abjure, curse and detest the belief that the Earth moves.

The trial was about pride and politics as well as astronomy. Pope Urban VIII, once Galileo's friend, had asked him to include his own favourite argument in his book of 1632, and Galileo put it in the mouth of the dim character Simplicio, whose name means simpleton and who loses every argument, so the Pope felt mocked and never forgave him. Confined for life to his villa near Florence and going blind, he still finished Two New Sciences, smuggled out and printed abroad in 1638, which laid the foundations of the science of motion that Isaac Newton later built on. He died in 1642.
