kingdom-of-kongo.context_blurb:
The Kingdom of Kongo grew up in the late 1300s along the lower Congo River, near the Atlantic coast of today's Angola and Democratic Republic of the Congo. When Portuguese sailors arrived in the 1480s, they found a strong kingdom ruled by a king called the Manikongo from his capital, Mbanza Kongo. Its king Nzinga a Nkuwu soon became a Christian and took the name Joao I.

When Afonso, the king's son, fought Mpanzu a Kitima, his half-brother, for the crown around 1509, his men were outnumbered. Afonso's court chroniclers told how Saint James appeared above the battlefield with five horsemen from heaven and sent the enemy running, and the scene was added to the kingdom's coat of arms. It is a legend, told by his own court.

Afonso I became a devout Catholic king who learned to write Portuguese and wrote letters to the kings of Portugal and to the pope. But Portuguese slavers were raiding his lands. In 1526 he wrote to King Joao III of Portugal pleading for an end to it, because every day the traders were kidnapping his people: children of the country, sons of his nobles, even members of his own family. A baptized king was begging a Christian ally to stop carrying off his subjects, and the slave trade went on to weaken his kingdom.

kingdom-of-kush-nubia-mero.context_blurb:
South of Egypt, up the Nile in today's Sudan, lay Nubia, the land the Egyptians called Kush. For two thousand years it traded and fought with Egypt, sometimes as its subject and once as its master. Its kings built pyramids, ruled Egypt for a century, and later, from their city of Meroe, defied the Roman Empire itself.

Nubian archers had a fearsome name all over the ancient world, so the Egyptians named their southern neighbour Ta-Seti, the Land of the Bow. Nubian fighters called the Medjay even became the elite police of Egypt. Around 728 BC the Nubian king Piye led his army downriver and made himself master of Egypt, and his family ruled it as the 25th Dynasty, the line remembered as the Black Pharaohs. For once, Nubia ruled Egypt instead of the other way round. Nubia's kings and queens were buried under pyramids of their own, small, narrow and sharply pointed, rising at about 70 degrees, far steeper than the gentle slopes at Giza. Sudan, ancient Nubia, has some 200 to 255 of them, more than twice Egypt's total and more than any other country on Earth, and the royal field at Meroe alone holds over 200.

Kushite pharaohs such as the warrior king Taharqa wore a pair of cobras on the brow, set next to each other, instead of the single Egyptian cobra, one snake for Nubia and one for Egypt. The furnaces of Meroe, which later became the Kushite capital, poured out so much iron that black slag heaps rose around the town, and British explorers nicknamed it the Birmingham of Africa, after their own iron-making city. Meroe's scribes created an alphabet of their own, the earliest writing known from Africa south of the Sahara, and today scholars can sound out every one of its 23 signs yet still cannot translate what most of the inscriptions say. The language itself remains mostly a mystery.

Taharqa appears by name in the Hebrew Bible, as Tirhakah, king of Cush, marching out against the Assyrian king Sennacherib while Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem. Centuries later a Kushite queen took on Rome. Queen Amanirenas of Kush marched some 30,000 soldiers against Roman Egypt around 25 BC, and the Greek geographer Strabo described her as a mannish woman, blind in one eye. Her warriors pulled down a bronze statue of the emperor Augustus at a frontier fort, sawed off its head, carried it home to Meroe and buried it under the front steps of a temple, so that everyone who walked in would tread on the emperor's face. The archaeologist John Garstang dug up this Meroe Head in 1910, and it is now in the British Museum.

The Nubian kings left vivid records of themselves. After taking the city of Hermopolis, Piye had it carved on his victory stela that what pained his heart most was not any other crime of the beaten prince Nimlot but that Nimlot had let his horses starve. Piye loved horses so much that four favourites were buried standing near his own pyramid at El-Kurru. Modern visitors were less respectful. In 1834 the Italian treasure-hunter Giuseppe Ferlini broke into the pyramids of Meroe by blowing their tops off with explosives, wrecking some 40 of them, and found the gold jewellery of Queen Amanishakheto. When he tried to sell it, Europeans refused to believe that such fine work could have been made in Africa.

knights-chivalry-the-code.context_blurb:
In medieval Europe the fighting elite were knights, armoured horsemen trained from boyhood and bound by a code called chivalry. It laid duties on them toward their lord, their faith and the people too weak to defend themselves. The code was a noble ideal; real knights lived up to it sometimes, and sometimes broke it horribly.

A boy began training at about seven as a page in a lord's household, learning manners and riding. At about fourteen he became a squire, a knight's working apprentice who carried his shield and lances and looked after his armour and horses. The true badge of a knight was not his sword but his spurs, gilded for knights, silver for squires and tinned for pages, which is why earning knighthood was called winning your spurs. In peacetime knights trained and showed off at tournaments. In the joust, the most glamorous event, two mounted knights galloped head-on along a fenced course, the lists, each aiming to splinter his lance against his rival or unseat him. A lady watching from the stands might hand her chosen champion a favour, a ribbon, sleeve or veil of hers that he tied on and carried into the fight in her honour.

The night before his knighting, a squire bathed to wash away his sins and then knelt alone until dawn in a dark church, guarding his weapons on the altar, a rite called the vigil of arms. Next came the accolade, a light stroke of a sword blade, laid flat across the neck or shoulders, and tradition said it was the last blow he should ever take without hitting back. When the priest blessed a new knight's sword, he charged him above all to defend the weak and the poor, people who could not defend themselves. Squires practised the lance charge at the quintain, a pivoting post with a target shield at one end of its arm and a weighted sack at the other: strike the shield off-centre and the sandbag swung round and knocked the rider off his horse. A knight's warhorse, the destrier, was a huge trained stallion so precious that it was spared the journey: a groom led it to the field while the knight rode a lesser horse, and he climbed onto it only when the fighting began.

William Marshal, whom an Archbishop of Canterbury called the greatest knight who ever lived, once took so many blows at a tournament that his battered helmet stuck fast, and he had to kneel at a blacksmith's anvil while the smith hammered and prised it off. He claimed he captured 500 knights for ransom in his career. Suero de Quinones, a Spanish knight who called himself a prisoner of love, defended a bridge against every comer through a whole month of 1434, a pas d'armes, and he wore an iron collar every Thursday until 300 lances had been broken. Tournaments could kill. When France's King Henry II jousted at a celebration in 1559, his opponent's lance shattered and a splinter slid through the slit of his visor, pierced his eye and drove into his brain. He died after ten days of agony, and France gave up jousting. Mercy was the ideal, yet at Agincourt in 1415, with the battle still undecided, King Henry V of England ordered his men to kill the French prisoners they had already taken, though ransoming captured knights was the usual, profitable custom. Knights spoke of honour even as they burned villages: the code was a goal, not a guarantee.

korea-three-kingdoms-goryeo-joseon.context_blurb:
Korea's long history runs through great dynasties: the Three Kingdoms, then Goryeo, which gave the English name Korea, then Joseon, which ruled from 1392 to 1910. Goryeo and Joseon gave the world two remarkable gifts of the written word: printing with metal type, and one of the cleverest alphabets ever designed.

In July 1377 monks at Heungdeok Temple in Cheongju printed a Buddhist book, the Jikji, with reusable letters cast in metal, seventy-eight years before Gutenberg's Bible, and no older book printed from movable metal type survives anywhere. In 1443 King Sejong the Great of Joseon created Hangul, Korea's own alphabet, and named it Hunminjeongeum, the correct sounds to teach the people, because he wanted common folk, and not just scholars, to be able to read.

The shapes of its letters are pictures of the mouth and tongue forming each sound: the letter for m is a square like closed lips, and the letter for k traces the back of the tongue rising to close off the throat. You can see how to say each letter in the way it is drawn.

Of the Jikji's two volumes, only the second still exists, far from Korea: around 1900 the French diplomat Victor Collin de Plancy bought it in Seoul, and today it sits in the National Library of France in Paris. Sejong raised talent wherever he found it: Jang Yeong-sil, born a palace slave, joined the king's circle of scientists, and in 1441 he built the world's first standardized rain gauge, along with water clocks and sundials.

Not everyone welcomed the new letters. In 1444 the Confucian scholar Choe Manri and six others petitioned Sejong that only barbarians invented their own script and that Ming China would mock Korea for it, but the king kept his alphabet and spread it anyway.

korean-berlin-spy-drama-espionage.context_blurb:
During the Cold War, from the late 1940s to 1991, the United States and the Soviet Union fought a hidden war of spies. Divided Berlin was its busiest battlefield, with agents of both sides working within walking distance of each other, and the tools of the trade included trick coins, poisons and codenames. Some of the strangest stories came out only decades later, when secret files were opened.

A newspaper boy in Brooklyn fumbled a nickel one day in June 1953, and it broke apart: someone had hollowed out the coin to hide a microphotograph of a coded message inside. Years later the FBI cracked the code with help from Reino Hayhanen, who defected, and the trail led to the Soviet spy Rudolf Abel. When the Soviets shot down the American pilot Francis Gary Powers in his U-2 spy plane in May 1960, he carried a hollow silver dollar from the CIA hiding a needle tipped with saxitoxin, a deadly poison drawn from shellfish, so that he could kill himself rather than be caught, but he refused to use it. On 10 February 1962 the two sides swapped prisoners on the Glienicke Bridge, which links West Berlin with Potsdam: Powers walked west, and the KGB colonel Rudolf Abel walked east, which is why it is called the Bridge of Spies.

Kim Philby climbed to a senior post in MI6, Britain's own secret service, all the while working for the Soviets, and in 1951, learning that Donald Maclean and Guy Burgess, fellow agents recruited with him at Cambridge, were close to arrest, he tipped them off so they could flee to Moscow. Philby himself defected in 1963; the group became known as the Cambridge Five. Julius Rosenberg was executed in 1953 and for decades his supporters said he had been framed, but the decoded Venona cables, intercepted Soviet wartime messages that the American government made public in 1995, named him by his codename, LIBERAL, and showed him running a spy ring. Scholars still debate how far his wife Ethel was involved.

korean-war-the-38th-parallel.context_blurb:
When Japan surrendered in 1945, the Americans and the Soviets split Korea, Japan's former colony, into two zones along the 38th parallel of latitude. By 1948 the line divided two rival states, Kim Il-sung's communist North and Syngman Rhee's South. In 1950 the North invaded, and three years of war left millions dead and the peninsula still divided.

In August 1945 two young American colonels, one of them the future Secretary of State Dean Rusk, had roughly thirty minutes to split the country, so they used a National Geographic map and picked the 38th parallel, meaning it to be temporary. Before dawn on 25 June 1950 some 135,000 North Korean troops stormed across the line, led by Soviet-built T-34 tanks that the South had almost nothing to stop. By late summer the South's army was squeezed into a pocket around the southeastern port of Pusan, and the United Nations voted to send troops to defend South Korea under the American general Douglas MacArthur.

The first American ground unit to fight, Task Force Smith, only 540 men with light weapons, faced roughly 5,000 North Korean soldiers backed by 36 tanks at Osan in July 1950 and was overrun, but its seven-hour stand bought time the South badly needed. In September 1950 MacArthur gambled on a landing at Inchon, far behind enemy lines, although its extreme tides gave ships only a few hours at high water before they were stranded in the mud. The gamble worked and broke the war wide open.

Then China entered the war, and on 27 November 1950 about 120,000 Chinese soldiers surrounded some 30,000 UN troops, mostly from the 1st Marine Division, at the Chosin Reservoir, in cold near 30 below zero that jammed rifles and froze plasma solid. Told that Chinese troops had closed in all around his Marines, Colonel Lewis "Chesty" Puller answered that they had been hunting the enemy for a while and had finally found him; being surrounded, he said, simplified the problem. As the division fought some 70 miles through mountain passes to the sea, a reporter asked General Oliver P. Smith whether the Marines were retreating, and Smith snapped that it was no retreat at all: they were simply attacking in another direction. At the port of Hungnam that December, one cargo ship built for just 12 passengers, the SS Meredith Victory, crammed in more than 14,000 Korean refugees and sailed three days to safety without losing a soul, while five babies were born on board. It remains the largest rescue ever made by a single ship.

The shooting stopped on 27 July 1953, when commanders signed an armistice at the village of Panmunjom, but it was only a ceasefire, never a peace treaty, so the two Koreas are technically still at war across the heavily mined DMZ. As late as the early 1970s the North produced more per head than the South, but the South's Miracle on the Han River changed everything, and today the average South Korean is over fifty times richer, roughly $35,000 a year against about $640. From space the gap is plain: NASA's night photographs show the South blazing with light and the North almost black, except for one glowing dot, its capital, Pyongyang.

kristallnacht.context_blurb:
On the night of 9 to 10 November 1938, Nazi stormtroopers and civilian mobs, directed by the propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels, attacked Jewish shops, homes and synagogues across Germany and annexed Austria. They killed more than a hundred Jews, and the regime sent some thirty thousand Jewish men to concentration camps. The pogrom took its name from the shattered window glass that glittered in the streets next morning.

The Nazis claimed it was the public's spontaneous anger at the killing of a German diplomat, Ernst vom Rath, in Paris by a young Polish Jew. The mobs set more than 1,400 synagogues on fire, and German firefighters came, but their orders were to let the synagogues burn and protect only the neighbouring buildings owned by non-Jews. About 7,500 Jewish businesses were smashed and looted the same night.

Then Hermann Goring's government made the victims pay: it fined the Jewish community one billion Reichsmarks as an atonement payment, forced Jewish owners to repair their own shops, and seized the insurance money they were owed. The people who had been robbed were punished for the crime done to them. From that night on, the Nazi state moved from legal persecution into open violence.

kublai-khan-the-yuan-dynasty.context_blurb:
Kublai Khan, grandson of Genghis Khan, finished the Mongol conquest of China and in 1271 declared himself first emperor of a new dynasty, the Yuan, ruling from Dadu, where Beijing stands today. For the first time, foreigners ruled the whole of China. His dazzling court drew envoys from across the Old World, among them, by his own account, the Venetian merchant Marco Polo.

Polo amazed his readers with coal, a black rock the Chinese dug from the hills and burned; it gave out heat longer than any log, while Europeans still warmed their homes with wood. He also described Chinese shoppers buying whatever they needed with paper money, notes called chao, while Europeans still lugged about heavy coins of gold and silver. It was one of the world's first paper currencies used across a whole country.

Kublai also kept a second palace at Xanadu, his summer capital, made of bamboo and gilded cane and braced by more than 200 silk cords, and Polo marvelled most that the whole building could be taken apart and carried off wherever the Khan commanded. Kublai twice sent vast fleets against Japan, and both times storms smashed them; the 1281 armada, about 140,000 men aboard some 4,400 ships, was torn apart and at least half the men drowned, and the grateful Japanese named those storms kamikaze, the divine wind.

The conquerors ruled the conquered harshly. Kublai's government ranked all its subjects in four legal classes, with Mongols on top and the Southerners, the Chinese of the conquered Song lands, at the bottom, and the two lowest classes got harsher punishments for the same crime and were forbidden to own weapons or to keep dogs and hunting eagles. Venetians nicknamed Polo's book Il Milione, The Million, for its tall tales, and the historian Frances Wood has argued he may never have reached China at all, since he never mentions the Great Wall, tea or chopsticks. Nor does he mention foot-binding, and Wood suggests he may have borrowed from Persian guidebooks and other travellers.

kublai-khan-the-yuan-marco-polo.context_blurb:
Kublai Khan, the grandson of Genghis Khan, completed the Mongol conquest of China in the late 1200s, the first foreigner to rule the whole country. The Venetian merchant Marco Polo claimed to have served at his court for years, and the book Polo dictated back in Italy gave medieval Europe its first detailed picture of Chinese wealth, cities and inventions, some of them almost unknown in the West.

In 1271 Kublai named his new dynasty Yuan, a word taken from the I Ching, China's ancient book of wisdom, meaning the origin, the primal source. In 1279 his navy destroyed the last Song forces at Yamen, and all China was his.

Polo had grown up knowing only firewood, so he was astonished to see the Chinese pull black stones from the earth and burn them to heat their houses: coal, a fuel almost unknown in Europe. Twice, in 1274 and 1281, Kublai's invasion fleets were wrecked off Japan and countless soldiers drowned, and the Japanese believed twin typhoons had saved them, storms they named kamikaze, the divine wind.

Kublai paid for goods and labour with paper banknotes, and Polo reported that they were made from the fine white inner bark of the mulberry tree, the thin layer between the wood and the rough outer bark. Polo also described a fireproof cloth called salamander, which Europeans thought was the skin of a lizard living in flames, but he reported that it was really dug out of the rock and spun into thread: asbestos, cleaned by throwing it into the fire. Kublai reportedly sent a bolt of it to the Pope in Rome.

labor-unions-and-the-early-reform-moveme.context_blurb:
The Industrial Revolution packed Britain's workers into mills and onto farms they did not own. They had no vote, they could be fired at will, and the courts treated their unions as conspiracies. In the 1830s and 1840s ordinary working men fought back with unions, mass petitions and angry pamphlets, and out of that struggle grew modern labour politics.

In 1833 the ploughman and Methodist preacher George Loveless and five other farm labourers in the Dorset village of Tolpuddle formed a society and swore not to work for less than ten shillings a week, as farmers pushed their pay down toward six. Legend says they met under a great sycamore on the village green, which still grows there, though court testimony shows the oath was really sworn in Thomas Standfield's cottage. The government struck back hard: in March 1834 the six were sentenced to seven years' transportation and shipped to Australia as convicts.

Forming a union was not itself the charge; the court convicted them for the secret oath of loyalty they had sworn to their society, using a 1797 act aimed at mutinous sailors. James Brine was set to dig holes for fence posts with no shoes on his feet, and then to wash sheep for seventeen days while standing in cold water up to his breast. Five of the men were held on rotting prison hulks off Portsmouth, swept by cholera and smallpox. In 1838 William Lovett drew up the People's Charter, six demands for reforming Parliament that became the program of the Chartist movement, and five of them, from a vote for every man over 21 to the secret ballot, are now British law, but yearly elections for Parliament were never adopted.

Feargus O'Connor, a Chartist leader, boasted in 1848 that his petition carried 5,736,000 names, but the Commons clerks counted barely two million and found joke signatures such as Victoria Rex and Mr. Punch, which made it a laughingstock. The genuine 1842 petition, a roll six miles long with 3,315,752 names, the Commons had refused even to hear. In an angry 1830 letter to a Leeds newspaper, the Tory reformer Richard Oastler began the fight to limit the working day to ten hours and titled it Yorkshire Slavery, because children in the Bradford mills, he said, had it worse than slaves in the West Indies. The Ten Hours Act of 1847 finally capped the day for women and young workers.

Economic historians call the long stretch before 1830, when output per worker climbed far faster than pay, Engels' pause, and they find it ended after 1830 as the capital behind each worker, the machines and tools he worked with, kept growing. Real pay for working men about doubled over the four decades from 1810, and hours fell, which suggests that more capital and higher productivity, not protest alone, lifted wages.

lalibela-s-rock-hewn-churches.context_blurb:
In the highlands of northern Ethiopia around 1200, King Gebre Mesqel Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty had eleven churches carved out of the solid volcanic rock. He meant them as a New Jerusalem for Ethiopian Christians at a time when Muslim conquest made the journey to the real Jerusalem hard. Linked by rock-cut tunnels and courtyards, they are still used for Ethiopian Orthodox worship some 800 years later.

The builders stacked no stones at all: they chiselled a deep trench all the way around a block of bedrock to free it from the mountain, then hollowed the block out from its roof downward into a finished church, with columns, windows and naves. Each church is really a giant sculpture, sunk below ground level, with its roof at the height of the original surface.

The last of the eleven, Bete Giyorgis, the House of Saint George, was cut from one enormous block so precisely that, seen from the rim of its pit, its roof forms a perfect cross pressed into the earth. It stands in a courtyard about 72 feet square and 36 feet deep, and its roof is carved with a pattern of nested crosses, all from the same single piece of rock.

las-casas-the-salamanca-school-and-the-d.context_blurb:
In the early 1500s Spanish settlers conquered the Caribbean islands and forced the Taino and other Native peoples to labour for them, working huge numbers to death. A handful of Spaniards, most of them Catholic friars, fought back with sermons, books and law, and none fought harder than Bartolome de las Casas. Their claim, that every human being has rights by nature, became a root of modern international law.

In 1516 Cardinal Cisneros, who governed Spain as regent, made Las Casas Protector of the Indians, a new royal office that paid him 100 pesos a year and gave his campaign official standing. Las Casas insisted that Native peoples could be won by preaching alone. To prove it, he led a band of friars, carrying no weapons, into a Guatemalan region that soldiers had nicknamed Tuzulutlan, the Land of War, and they won it over so peacefully that it was renamed Verapaz, True Peace.

Las Casas knew the system from inside: in his early years in the islands, first Hispaniola and then Cuba, he had held an encomienda, a royal grant of Native labourers forced to work his land, and he even owned African slaves. In Advent of 1511, Antonio de Montesinos, a Dominican, preached to the settlers of Hispaniola that they stood in mortal sin for their cruelty, and he asked whether the Taino they were working to death were not men with rational souls. The outraged colonists demanded that he take it back, and he refused. The Spanish burned the Taino chief Hatuey at the stake in Cuba in 1512 for leading the resistance. When a friar promised him heaven if he accepted baptism and said that good Spaniards went there too, Hatuey answered, by Las Casas's account, that he preferred hell if heaven meant spending eternity beside such cruel men. Cuba remembers him as its first national hero.

In 1514, while preparing a sermon, Las Casas read in the book of Sirach that an offering from stolen goods is blemished, because the poor man's life depends on the bread of the needy, and he freed his labourers and never turned back. Early on he made a terrible suggestion, to spare Native workers by bringing in enslaved Africans instead, but in his History of the Indies he admitted he soon repented, because enslaving Africans was exactly as unjust as enslaving Indians. In his Short Account, a book of 1552 written to shock Prince Philip, he recorded that Spaniards hanged Native people thirteen at a time, in honour, they said, of Christ and his twelve Apostles, and lit fires beneath them.

The scholars carried the fight into law. At the University of Salamanca, the Dominican professor Francisco de Vitoria told his students in 1539 that the Indians were true owners of their land, just as Christians were of theirs, and that not even the Pope could hand that land to someone else. His idea of a law binding all nations made him a father of international law. Never before had Europeans held a public hearing on whether a defeated nation possessed any rights, but in 1550 the Emperor Charles V called one at Valladolid. Juan Gines de Sepulveda, a humanist scholar, argued for three hours, and Las Casas answered by reading his reply aloud for five days straight. Sepulveda called the Native Americans natural slaves, drawing on Aristotle's notion of people fit by nature only to obey, but even before the hearing the universities of Salamanca and Alcala, the greatest in Spain, refused to license his book, Democrates Alter, for printing. The judges never gave a verdict. The Jesuit Francisco Suarez pushed Salamanca's thinking furthest: in On Laws, in 1612, he rejected the divine right of kings and argued that power passes from God first to the whole people, so a ruler holds it only because the people agree to be governed, and they may depose a tyrant.

lascaux-altamira-cave-paintings.context_blurb:
During the last Ice Age, many thousands of years ago, people in what are now southwestern France and northern Spain crept deep into limestone caves and painted horses, bison, bulls and deer on the rock with charcoal and ochre. The two most famous caves are Lascaux in France and Altamira in Spain, and young people found both of them.

On 12 September 1940, four teenage boys in the woods of southwestern France followed their dog, Robot, down a hole under an uprooted tree and found Lascaux, its walls covered with animals painted some 17,000 years ago. The first boy down was eighteen-year-old Marcel Ravidat.

At Altamira, the discovery came from a child. In 1879 eight-year-old Maria, daughter of Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola, was small enough to look straight up, and she spotted a herd of bison painted across the cave roof. When her father presented the bison to scholars at a congress in 1880, they called him a fraud, because the paintings were far too skilful and too well preserved to have been made by Ice Age people. Sautuola died in 1888 still disbelieved, and in 1902 his loudest critic, Emile Cartailhac, publicly admitted his mistake. Both caves were later closed to ordinary visitors because their breath was damaging the paint.

later-crusades-the-sack-of-constantinopl.context_blurb:
The knights of the Fourth Crusade meant to win back Jerusalem by striking first at Muslim-held Egypt. But the crusaders owed the Venetians a fortune for their ships, and they turned aside toward a richer target. What they did there horrified Christian Europe and split Eastern and Western Christians more bitterly than ever.

In April 1204 the crusaders, who never fought a single Muslim army, stormed Constantinople, capital of the Christian Byzantine Empire and the largest and richest Christian city in the world, and spent three days looting and killing. They crowned one of their own, Baldwin of Flanders, as emperor instead of restoring a Byzantine ruler. Eight hundred years later, in 2004, Pope John Paul II formally apologized for the sack.

The plunder went west, much of it to Venice. The most spectacular prize was a team of four life-size horses in gilded bronze, which the Venetians ripped from the Hippodrome, the city's chariot-racing stadium, and mounted on St. Mark's Basilica above its entrance. They are the only bronze four-horse team to survive from the ancient world. To ship them, workers cut off the horses' heads and later hid the cuts with collars, which you can still see.

latin-american-independence-bolivar-and-.context_blurb:
Between about 1810 and 1825, almost all of Spain's vast American empire broke away and became independent republics. Two generals led the fight: from the north Simon Bolivar, born in Venezuela to a rich Creole family, and from the south the Argentine Jose de San Martin. Together they drew much of the modern map of South America.

Bolivar's wars freed what became Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Panama and Bolivia, which is named after him, and grateful people gave him one sweeping title that stuck to him until he died: the Liberator.

In 1817 San Martin took his Army of the Andes about 500 kilometres over frozen mountain passes to surprise the Spanish in Chile, a feat historians compare to Hannibal crossing the Alps into Italy. The crossing took 21 days at heights averaging 3,000 metres. To haul soldiers, cannon and stores across the high passes he relied on about 9,000 mules, far more than his 1,600 horses, and roughly a third of his 4,000 soldiers were lost on the way.

In 1819 Bolivar led some 2,400 soldiers across flooded plains and over an icy pass the royalists believed impassable, and on 7 August he destroyed their army at the Battle of Boyaca, taking about 1,800 prisoners, their commander among them. Three days later he entered Bogota.

In July 1822 the two liberators met in secret at Guayaquil, with no witnesses and no record kept, and quarrelled over the new nations' future: Bolivar wanted republics on the American model; San Martin wanted kingdoms with constitutions, each under a prince brought from Europe, and he even proposed one as King of Peru. Soon afterward San Martin handed everything to Bolivar and left South America for good. But the single great state of Gran Colombia that Bolivar dreamed of broke apart, and weeks before he died of tuberculosis in December 1830 he wrote bitterly that America was ungovernable and that whoever serves a revolution ploughs the sea.

lavoisier-and-modern-chemistry.context_blurb:
Antoine Lavoisier, a French nobleman of the 1700s, is called the father of modern chemistry. He brought the balance into the laboratory, weighing everything before and after each experiment, and so turned an old craft into an exact science. He named oxygen and hydrogen and showed that in a chemical change matter is neither created nor destroyed.

The leading theory of his day held that anything burning gives off an invisible fire-stuff called phlogiston, so a burned thing should come out lighter. Lavoisier heated a metal inside a sealed vessel with his balance ready, and the burned metal turned out heavier than it had been, because it had joined with oxygen from the air. The phlogiston theory never recovered.

Lavoisier had also worked as a collector of the king's taxes, and that made him an enemy of the Revolution. During the Reign of Terror, on 8 May 1794, the revolutionary tribunal sent him to the guillotine at the age of 50, just after his father-in-law, Jacques Paulze. The next day the mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange said that it had taken them only a moment to cut off that head, but a hundred years might not be enough to produce another like it.

lawrence-of-arabia-and-the-arab-revolt.context_blurb:
In June 1916, in the middle of the First World War, Hussein bin Ali, the Sharif of Mecca, led the Arabs in revolt against their Ottoman Turkish rulers, trusting British promises of an independent Arab kingdom afterward. A shy British officer and former archaeologist, T. E. Lawrence, joined the revolt as a liaison, fought beside Hussein's son Faisal, and became famous as Lawrence of Arabia.

Aqaba's big Ottoman guns faced the water, ready for any attack by ship. So in 1917 Lawrence and the Howeitat chieftain Auda abu Tayi rode hundreds of miles across the open desert and struck the town from the land, where it had no defences. The march began on 9 May with about 45 camel riders and swelled to some 1,000 as tribes joined, Auda's charge won the decisive fight inland, and Aqaba surrendered on 6 July.

The Arabs did not know they had already been betrayed. Mark Sykes of Britain and Francois Georges-Picot of France had drawn up a secret deal in May 1916, the Sykes-Picot Agreement, which divided the Ottoman Arab lands between the two of them as their own spheres, contradicting the independence promised to the Arabs. The Arabs learned of it only when the new Soviet government published the text in late 1917, and its lines helped shape the borders and grievances of the modern Middle East.

lemaitre-the-priest-who-proposed-the-big.context_blurb:
Georges Lemaitre, a Catholic priest from Belgium, was also a decorated artillery officer of the First World War and a trained astrophysicist. In 1927, working from Einstein's own equations, he showed that the universe is expanding, and he reasoned backward that it must once have been packed into a single super-dense primeval atom. He is the father of the idea we now call the Big Bang.

Einstein was not convinced at first. At a Brussels conference in 1927, Einstein heard Lemaitre out and told the priest that his sums were right but his physics was abominable. He came round: in 1933, after hearing Lemaitre present the theory in California, Einstein stood and applauded, calling it the most beautiful explanation of creation he had ever heard.

Lemaitre was just as careful with his own Church. In 1951 Pope Pius XII said the Big Bang appeared to confirm the Genesis account of creation, but Lemaitre held that science must never be used to prove or disprove a matter of faith, and in private he talked the Pope out of saying so again. Shortly before he died in 1966, he learned that Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson had detected the cosmic microwave background, the faint afterglow that confirmed his idea.

lenin-s-red-terror-and-the-founding-of-t.context_blurb:
In October 1917 Vladimir Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in Russia, and almost at once they turned terror on anyone they counted an enemy: nobles, priests, officers, factory owners, rival socialists and peasants. Lenin himself built the secret police, ordered the shootings and founded the prison camps. Stalin later enlarged the system, but its foundations were laid in Lenin's first years.

Six weeks after taking power, in December 1917, Lenin founded the Cheka, a political police force headed by Felix Dzerzhinsky, and the later Soviet secret police, the KGB among them, grew out of it. Asked by a Moscow newspaper in July 1918 what the Cheka was for, Dzerzhinsky answered frankly that it stood for organised terror, which he called an absolute necessity in a revolution. In late August 1918 Fanny Kaplan, a member of the rival Socialist Revolutionary party, shot Lenin outside a Moscow factory, and she told her Cheka interrogators that she did it because she considered him a traitor to the Revolution. The Cheka shot her days later, and the attack gave the regime its excuse to declare the Red Terror.

On 5 September 1918 the government's decree On Red Terror called for mass shooting and told the Cheka to protect the republic by isolating class enemies in concentration camps, so the camps began under Lenin, not Stalin. That August, Lenin had cabled officials in Penza to hang at least a hundred kulaks, the better-off peasants, in public so that people for miles around would see and tremble, and he ended with a postscript: find some tougher people. The Cheka official Martin Latsis told his agents not to look for evidence of what a prisoner had done: the first question was what class he came from, and that alone should decide his fate. Guilt was decided by birth, not by any deed.

In 1923 the secret police opened their first big camp inside an ancient monastery on the Solovetsky Islands in the freezing White Sea, and its Russian initials, SLON, spell the everyday Russian word for an elephant. New prisoners stepping off the boats at Solovki heard the commander of the camp warn them that there was no Soviet power here, only Solovetsky power, meaning not even Soviet law could protect them. Sekirka, a former church on a hilltop at the top of 365 wooden steps, served as the camp's harshest punishment cell, and there guards made prisoners perch motionless on a thin pole, feet dangling above the floor, for up to 18 hours.

The regime struck at faith and at the villages alike. Bolshevik soldiers beat Metropolitan Vladimir of Kiev, the first bishop they killed, and pulled him out of his monastery in January 1918 to shoot him, and as they led him away he asked God to forgive the men who were killing him. By early 1919 they had killed 18 bishops and more than 100 priests. When Tambov's peasants revolted in 1921 against the requisitions that were emptying their barns, Mikhail Tukhachevsky, commanding the Red Army there, was cleared to use poison gas on the rebels hiding in the forests, calculated to seep through the trees and kill everyone there. The Bolsheviks also seized tens of thousands of villagers as hostages, about 1,000 children among them.

Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, in his history of the camps, The Gulag Archipelago, followed the system back to Lenin's decrees in the first months of the revolution, and argued that Stalin only made it bigger.

leonardo-da-vinci.context_blurb:
Leonardo da Vinci, born in 1452 near Florence, was a painter, sculptor, engineer, anatomist and inventor, and first-rate at all of them. He finished only a handful of paintings, among them the Mona Lisa and the Last Supper, but he filled thousands of notebook pages with machines, bodies, birds and rivers. He died in France in 1519, the model of what we call a Renaissance man.

Leonardo was the son of the wealthy notary Ser Piero and a young peasant woman, Caterina, and because he was a child born out of wedlock, he could neither follow his father's profession nor enter a university, so he taught himself by looking hard at the world. As a teenage apprentice to Andrea del Verrocchio, he painted one small kneeling angel in his master's Baptism of Christ, and the biographer Giorgio Vasari claims it outshone anything Verrocchio had painted, so the master put down his brush and never painted again. Vasari tells it as legend, though Verrocchio's painting does seem to stop around then.

His private notebooks look like code, because every letter is reversed and each line travels leftward, but hold a page up to a mirror and it reads normally. Historians agree on the simplest reason for this mirror writing: Leonardo was left-handed, and writing from right to left kept his hand from smudging the ink he had just put down. His to-do lists mix ordinary errands with strange research jobs, and around 1510 he ordered himself to describe the woodpecker's tongue.

The Mona Lisa's hazy softness, called sfumato, comes from as many as thirty transparent glazes, each thinner than a hair, which he often blended with his bare fingers. Yet the Mona Lisa became world-famous only in 1911, when Vincenzo Peruggia, a handyman who had worked at the Louvre, stole it by hiding it under his smock. To lay out the room in the Last Supper, he drove a nail into the wet plaster at Christ's right temple and stretched strings from it like rays, so that the whole painted room converges on Christ's head. The tiny nail hole is still there. Around 1490 he drew the Vitruvian Man, a figure inside a circle and a square, and noted a rule you can test on yourself: a man's arms, stretched wide, measure as much as his height.

Around 1485 he sketched a pyramid-shaped linen parachute, and in 2000 the skydiver Adrian Nicholas built one exactly to his plans and jumped from 10,000 feet: it worked, carrying him gently down. Around 1495 he planned a mechanical knight, full-size and armoured, moved by concealed gears, cables and pulleys, that could sit, stand, turn its head and raise its visor, and it is often called the West's first humanoid robot. The roboticist Mark Rosheim rebuilt it from the sketches in 2002, and it moved.

To learn how the heart's valves snap shut, he poured wax into an ox heart, made a glass model from the cast, and pumped water full of grass seeds through it so he could watch how the flow swirled. He concluded that little whirlpools close the valve, and scans proved him right in 1968 and again in 2014. Finding fossil seashells high in the mountains, where most people said Noah's Flood had left them, he studied how they lay in their layers and concluded that the mountains had once been the floor of the sea, slowly lifted over ages.

leonardo-da-vinci-michelangelo.context_blurb:
Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo Buonarroti were the two giants of the Italian Renaissance, and they could not stand each other. Leonardo, born in 1452, was the elder, a painter, engineer and scientist who filled notebooks with machines and anatomy. Michelangelo, born in 1475, was sharp-tongued and devout, and he saw himself first of all as a carver of stone.

Leonardo wrote his notes backward, every letter flipped and every line running right to left, a style called mirror writing, probably because he was left-handed and it kept his hand out of the wet ink. Around 1508 Pope Julius II ordered Michelangelo to paint the vast ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, and he protested that painting was not his art, because he was a sculptor. He had never painted a fresco before. In his most famous scene, the Creation of Adam, God reaches down from a cloud toward the first man, and their fingers almost touch, with a small gap of about three-quarters of an inch left between them.

Leonardo dreamed all his life of human flight, studied birds and bats, and drew hundreds of designs for machines with flapping wings, called ornithopters, though he never built one that worked. In 1501 Michelangelo began his David on a block of Carrara marble about seventeen feet tall that workers called the Giant, which had stood unused for some 35 years because two sculptors before him had begun cutting it and then abandoned it, judging it too faulty to carve. In 1911 Vincenzo Peruggia, who had helped build the Mona Lisa's glass case, hid overnight in the Louvre, took the painting down on a Monday when the museum was closed, and walked out with it wrapped inside the white smock he wore for work.

As a young man seeking work from Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan, Leonardo wrote a letter boasting of bridges, cannons, war machines and tunnels, and only at the very end, almost as an afterthought, did he mention that he could also paint. Earlier sculptors such as Donatello had shown David as the winner standing over Goliath's head, but Michelangelo chose the moment before the fight: David tense and alert, sling on his shoulder, watching the giant. Bramante wanted to dangle the Sistine platform on ropes; Michelangelo refused and designed his own wooden scaffold. He painted on his feet with his arms stretched over his head for four years, and the picture of him lying on his back is a myth.

To paint bodies perfectly, Leonardo dissected some 30 corpses by candlelight, and from them he produced the first true drawing of an unborn baby folded up in its mother's womb. He painted the Last Supper on a dry wall with experimental paints instead of true fresco in wet plaster, and it was already decaying by 1517, less than twenty years after he finished it; today fewer than half of his original paint survives.

On the night of 15 August 1943 a British bomb hit the building in Milan, and the roof and two walls fell, but the wall with the painting survived, shielded by sandbags piled against it beforehand. Michelangelo's Pieta, Mary holding the dead Jesus, finished in 1499 when he was 24, is the only work he ever signed: Vasari says he cut his name into Mary's sash in a rage after hearing visitors credit it to a rival, and then, ashamed, vowed never to sign another work. Around 1504 Florence set the rivals against each other, hiring both to paint giant battle scenes in the Palazzo Vecchio, Leonardo the Battle of Anghiari and Michelangelo the Battle of Cascina, but both men abandoned their murals unfinished.

leonardo-da-vinci-mona-lisa-and-last-sup.context_blurb:
Leonardo da Vinci (1452 to 1519) was an Italian painter, engineer, anatomist and inventor who finished only a handful of paintings. Two of them are among the most famous in the world: the Last Supper, painted on the wall of a monks' dining hall in Milan, and the Mona Lisa, the portrait of a smiling Florentine woman that hangs in the Louvre in Paris.

Leonardo was left-handed, and in his notebooks, more than 7,000 pages of which survive, he wrote backward, every letter reversed as in a mirror, so the lines run from right to left. Around 1495, in the Last Supper, he froze one shocking instant: just after Jesus warns the twelve that one among them is about to betray him, every apostle bursts out in shock and argument. Earlier painters had shown them sitting calmly. The Last Supper covers most of a wall, roughly 460 by 880 centimetres. Visitors to the Louvre are often startled to find the Mona Lisa surprisingly tiny, a poplar panel only about 30 by 21 inches, smaller than a poster. Until 1911 the Mona Lisa was simply one more picture in the Louvre's halls, but then Vincenzo Peruggia stole it and kept it hidden for over two years, and the worldwide newspaper frenzy over the theft made it the most famous painting on Earth.

Her face appears to change mood while you watch, because Leonardo blurred every edge of her face, leaving no hard outline anywhere, a method called sfumato, from fumo, the Italian word for smoke. He described it as blending colours without lines or borders, the way smoke drifts. In the Last Supper, Judas, who will hand Jesus over that very night, leans back alone into shadow, clutching a little money bag, the silver he was paid. In the 1490s Leonardo sketched an aerial screw, a spiral rotor designed to twist its way straight upward, about 450 years before the helicopter, whose rotors work in much the same way. He also drew a pyramid-shaped linen parachute on a wooden frame, and in July 2000 Adrian Nicholas, a skydiver, built one exactly to the design, jumped from 10,000 feet, and floated gently to the ground.

Leonardo set the painting's single vanishing point at Jesus' head, in the centre, so every line of the ceiling and side walls slants toward it and pulls your eye straight to him. True fresco binds colour into wet plaster. Leonardo, who liked to work slowly and change his mind, painted the Last Supper in tempera and oil on a dry wall instead, and the paint never gripped the wall. It began flaking off while he was still alive, and the decay was noted by 1517. In 1652 the monks of the monastery cut a doorway through the bottom of the wall to reach their kitchen faster, erasing the painted feet of Jesus.

Leonardo, who dissected some 30 corpses, also worked out that tiny swirling eddies of blood help snap one of the heart's valves shut, and science confirmed it only in the late 1960s, about 450 years later.

lewis-and-clark-sacagawea.context_blurb:
In 1804, soon after Thomas Jefferson bought the vast Louisiana Territory from France, he sent his secretary Meriwether Lewis and Lewis's army friend William Clark west with a small party called the Corps of Discovery. They were to map the land, record its plants and animals, meet its Native peoples and find a water route to the Pacific. They reached the ocean late in 1805 and came home in 1806.

One member of the Corps was not a person at all: Seaman, a big black Newfoundland dog that Lewis had bought for $20, who caught squirrels, dragged a deer from a river and barked the men awake whenever a grizzly or buffalo wandered close. At Fort Mandan, in today's North Dakota, the Corps took on a French-Canadian interpreter, Toussaint Charbonneau, and his young Shoshone wife, Sacagawea, who gave birth to a son there in 1805.

On 7 November 1805 Clark scrawled in his notebook, in his famously rough spelling, that the "Ocian" was in view, and wrote of his joy, but he was fooled: the open Pacific still lay some twenty miles beyond the broad, wave-tossed mouth of the Columbia. Clark adored Sacagawea's baby, Jean-Baptiste, whom he nicknamed Pomp, and on the way home in July 1806 he named a tall sandstone rock rising over the Yellowstone Pompy's Tower and cut his signature and the date into the rock, where they survive today.

In August 1805, needing horses to cross the Rockies, the Corps met a band of Shoshone, Sacagawea's own people, from whom she had been stolen as a girl, and at the sight of their chief, Cameahwait, she sprang to her feet and danced: he was her own brother. That family tie won the Corps the horses it needed.

Earlier, on 14 May 1805, a squall struck one of the boats and Charbonneau panicked at the rudder, but Sacagawea, her baby on her back, kept her head, leaned out over the water and snatched back the journals, the medicine and the scientific instruments before the current took them, all of them irreplaceable. Lewis praised her courage, and five days later the captains named a river after her.

liberation-of-paris.context_blurb:
In August 1944, after four years of Nazi occupation, Allied armies broke out of Normandy and closed on Paris. The French Resistance rose up inside the city, and General Eisenhower let General Jacques Leclerc's Free French armoured division race in, with American troops close behind. On 25 August the city was free, and almost undamaged.

The first soldiers into the heart of the city, on the night of 24 August, were a company nicknamed La Nueve, The Nine, and about 146 of its roughly 160 men were Spanish Republicans who had lost their civil war to Franco, fled into exile and joined the Free French to fight fascism again. They named their half-tracks after battles they had lost in Spain, such as Teruel and Ebro.

Hitler had ordered General Dietrich von Choltitz, commanding the city, to leave Paris a field of ruins, and Choltitz had his men mine the Seine bridges, but he refused to set off the charges and surrendered on 25 August, so the city stood. The legend that Hitler shrieked down the phone asking whether Paris was burning rests mostly on Choltitz's own memoir. That same day Charles de Gaulle spoke without notes at the Hotel de Ville, building from Paris outraged, broken and martyred to a final cry: But Paris liberated! He had fled the city in June 1940.

liberation-of-the-camps.context_blurb:
In the last months of the war in Europe, Allied armies advancing from east and west broke into the Nazi concentration and death camps. Soviet troops reached Majdanek in July 1944 and Auschwitz in January 1945; American and British troops entered Buchenwald, Dachau and Bergen-Belsen that spring. What the soldiers found changed how they thought about the enemy forever.

Ohrdruf was the first Nazi camp American troops reached, and three generals, George Patton, Dwight Eisenhower and Omar Bradley, toured it together on 12 April 1945. In a shed lay some thirty corpses dusted with lime, and beside it a pyre of bodies lay half burned. Patton, famous for his toughness, was so sickened by the sight and smell that he threw up against the wall of a building and would not go into the shed.

Eisenhower went through every part of the camp. In a letter to George Marshall, he explained that he had done it deliberately, so that if anyone ever claimed these horrors were only propaganda, he could give firsthand evidence that they were real. Allied commanders also made local German civilians walk through the camps, and the soldiers' photographs and films became evidence at the Nuremberg Trials.

lincoln-s-assassination.context_blurb:
On the evening of 14 April 1865, Good Friday, President Abraham Lincoln went to see a comedy at Ford's Theatre in Washington. John Wilkes Booth, a bitter Confederate sympathizer, shot him there, and Lincoln died the next morning. Booth meant his shot to be one blow in a plot to destroy the whole Union government in a single night.

Booth, aged 26, was no stranger off the street: he came from the celebrated Booth acting family and was one of the most famous and admired stage actors in America, which is why he could move through Ford's Theatre unquestioned. The war was all but over, because on 9 April, five days earlier, General Robert E. Lee had surrendered to General Ulysses S. Grant at Appomattox. The policeman assigned to guard the door of Lincoln's box, John Frederick Parker, had left his post, by most accounts for a tavern, so Booth simply walked in. Booth knew the play, Our American Cousin, by heart, and he timed his shot to its biggest laugh line, so that the roar of the audience would cover the gunshot. At about 10:14 he fired one ball behind Lincoln's left ear from a small Philadelphia Deringer pistol that held only a single shot. Booth jumped down to the stage, his spur snagging a flag on the railing, and cried out to the audience the Latin words sic semper tyrannis, meaning thus always to tyrants, the state motto of Virginia.

Soldiers carried the dying president to a boarding house across the street, where his long body lay slanted across a bed that was too small, and when he died at 7:22 the next morning, Edwin Stanton, the Secretary of War, is said to have declared that now he belonged to the ages. Some who were there heard angels rather than ages.

Booth's plan was to strike down Lincoln, his Vice President and his Secretary of State in the same hour that night, sending Lewis Powell after Secretary of State William Seward and George Atzerodt after Vice President Andrew Johnson. Atzerodt lost his nerve, and only Booth succeeded. Four conspirators were hanged together on 7 July 1865, among them Mary Surratt, who kept the boarding house where the plotters met, and she was the first woman the federal government ever executed. Her guilt has been argued ever since.

Powell forced his way into Seward's house and stabbed him again and again in his bed, but Seward lived, because a metal brace for a jaw he had broken days earlier in a carriage accident turned the knife. Twelve days after the shooting, soldiers trapped Booth in a Virginia tobacco barn set on fire around him, and Sergeant Boston Corbett, ordered to take him alive, shot him in the neck; paralyzed on a farmhouse porch, Booth stared at his hands and whispered, useless, useless. In a strange twist, about a year earlier Booth's brother, the great actor Edwin Booth, had grabbed Robert Todd Lincoln, the president's son, by the collar and hauled him to safety as he slipped toward a moving train on a crowded Jersey City platform.

linear-perspective-in-art.context_blurb:
Linear perspective is the geometric trick that lets a painter turn a flat panel into a space you feel you could walk into. Florentine artists worked it out in the early 1400s, and the architect Filippo Brunelleschi is usually credited with the first clear demonstration. Within a century, painters such as Masaccio, Piero della Francesca and Leonardo had made it the normal way to build a Western picture.

Its key is a single point on the horizon: every line that runs away from the viewer, such as the edges of a tiled floor, is aimed at that spot, the vanishing point, just as railway tracks seem to meet in the distance.

Around 1413 Brunelleschi showed off the method with a small painting of the Baptistery, Florence's eight-sided church. Instead of painting a blue sky, he laid down burnished silver that reflected the real sky, so that, as his biographer Antonio Manetti wrote, actual clouds and birds drifted across the picture, carried along by the wind. To prove the panel perfect, he bored a tiny hole right through it; the viewer looked through from the back while holding a flat mirror in front, so that the reflected painting lined up perfectly with the true building beyond it. The hole was as small as a lentil on the painted side and flared to the width of a coin behind.

linnaeus-and-biological-classification.context_blurb:
Carl Linnaeus was an eighteenth-century Swedish botanist and physician who gave the living world its filing system. Before him, naturalists described each plant or animal in long, muddled Latin phrases. Linnaeus gave every species just two Latin names, a genus and a species, and fitted them into a neat set of nested ranks in his great book Systema Naturae. Naturalists still use his method today.

He also did something bolder than any earlier naturalist had tried: he set humans firmly among the animals, in the same group as apes and monkeys, and gave our species the name Homo sapiens, meaning wise man.

His plant system grouped flowers by the number of their stamens and pistils, which he likened to husbands and wives. When a critic in St. Petersburg, Johann Siegesbeck, damned the system as loathsome harlotry, Linnaeus took revenge as only a namer of plants could: he named a small, sticky, ugly weed Siegesbeckia after him, forever. He died in Uppsala in 1778, still Sweden's most celebrated scientist.

lise-meitner-and-the-discovery-of-nuclea.context_blurb:
Lise Meitner was an Austrian-Jewish physicist who spent some thirty years in Berlin as the scientific partner of the chemist Otto Hahn, bombarding heavy elements with neutrons. In 1938, after Nazi Germany swallowed Austria, she fled with almost nothing to Sweden. That winter she solved the great puzzle of her career, and the way the credit was handed out has stung ever since.

Hahn and his assistant Fritz Strassmann wrote to her that uranium struck by neutrons seemed to turn into barium, an element about half its size. At Christmas 1938 Meitner walked in the snow with her nephew, the physicist Otto Frisch, and sitting on a log the two of them realised that the uranium nucleus had split in two, and they calculated the energy it set free. Frisch asked a biologist what the splitting of a living cell was called, learned that it was fission, and borrowed the word for the splitting atom. They published their explanation in Nature early in 1939.

When the Nobel committee gave its Chemistry prize for the discovery of fission in 1944, the award went to Otto Hahn alone, and Meitner, who had explained the process and named it with Frisch, was left out entirely. Many called it grossly unfair. In 1982 element 109 was named meitnerium in her honour.

locke-natural-rights-and-the-philosophic.context_blurb:
John Locke's Two Treatises of Government, published without his name in 1689, gave the clearest statement in English of natural rights: people are born free and equal, they hold rights that no government creates, and governments exist to protect those rights with the people's consent. The American founders drew on him so heavily that the Declaration of Independence often reads like Locke in shorter form.

Locke defined political power as the right to make laws, even laws carrying the death penalty, and he insisted that it exists only for the public good. A government may rule you only with your consent, he argued, and that consent comes in two kinds: express consent, a clear act such as an oath, which turns you into a full citizen, and tacit consent, the silent agreement you give just by residing in a country and travelling its roads. A ruler holds power only in trust, like someone hired to do a job, and when people quarrel over whether he has betrayed that trust, Locke answered that the people shall be the judge, since only the one who gives the trust can say whether it is kept. Locke turned the word rebel on its head: a ruler who attacks his own people's rights is the true rebel, because he has dragged everyone back into the state of war, and resisting him is self-defence.

Locke wrote the whole book against Sir Robert Filmer's Patriarcha, which claimed that kings inherited their power father to son from Adam. The doctrine Locke set out to demolish was the one Filmer defended: that kings rule by divine right, holding a power God had granted to Adam and his heirs. Against the defenders of kings, Locke held that our rights to life, liberty and property are no gift of the crown: they come first, before any government exists, and governments are invented afterward to protect them. When a ruler turns tyrant and no earthly judge will hear the people's case, Locke said they still have one last remedy, the use of force, which he called an appeal to Heaven. A century later Jefferson wrote in the Declaration that governments get their just powers from the consent of those they govern, the very source Locke had named.

Labour makes things yours, Locke said, as the apples you pick become your own, but with one limit: you may take from what nature holds in common only where enough, and as good, is left for others. Neither Locke nor Jefferson thought one unjust law justified a revolution; people should bear small wrongs patiently. The Declaration allows a people to throw off a government only when abuses come one after another in a long train, all pursuing the same object, and so reveal a design of tyranny.

People long assumed Locke wrote the book to defend England's Glorious Revolution of 1688 after the fact, but the historian Peter Laslett showed that he wrote most of it around 1679 to 1681, years before the revolution, which makes it a call to overthrow a king still on his throne. That is why he never admitted writing it. The First Treatise begins by calling slavery so wretched a condition for a human being that no Englishman, let alone a gentleman, could plead for it, yet Locke himself held investments tied to the slave trade, a contradiction scholars still debate.

louis-pasteur-germ-theory-and-vaccines.context_blurb:
Louis Pasteur, born in 1822 in Dole, the son of a tanner, became the most famous scientist in nineteenth-century France. His work followed one thread: invisible living things, microbes, cause spoiling and disease that people had long blamed on the air itself. From that idea came pasteurization, the first laboratory vaccines and a treatment for rabies.

Pasteur was a chemist by training, not a medical doctor, so every time he treated a sick person he gambled his reputation. He first showed that microbes, not mere age, were turning France's wine and beer sour, and he rescued them with pasteurization, patented in 1865: gentle heating to about 55 to 60 degrees, short of boiling, which killed the microbes without spoiling the taste. The same trick later made milk safe. To kill the old belief that life springs up by itself in lifeless broth, he boiled broth in a flask whose long glass neck was bent into a swan's S-shaped curve: air could get in, but dust and microbes settled in the bend, and the broth stayed clear for months. Tip the flask so the broth touched the dusty bend, and within days it teemed with life.

Around 1879 his assistant Charles Chamberland forgot a culture of chicken-cholera germs over the summer break, and the stale germs barely sickened the hens, which then survived fresh, deadly ones: the accident had produced the first laboratory-made vaccine. Pasteur called all his shots vaccines, from the Latin vacca, cow, to honour Edward Jenner, who decades earlier had protected people from smallpox with cowpox. His most famous public test came at Pouilly-le-Fort in 1881: he vaccinated a flock of sheep against anthrax, left others unprotected, then gave every animal a deadly dose, and two days later more than 200 onlookers saw each vaccinated sheep alive and grazing while the unprotected ones lay dead.

For rabies, he first had to capture the germ. He leaned over a chained, maddened dog and sucked up drops of its saliva through a glass tube in his mouth, because rabies is carried in saliva. Then he took rabbits killed by rabies, removed their spinal cords and dried them in flasks for as long as fourteen days, since every extra day of drying weakened the material. In July 1885 a mother brought him her nine-year-old son, Joseph Meister, bitten fourteen times by a rabid dog, and after 13 injections, starting with the weakest cord, the boy lived, the first person in history rescued from rabies. When villagers killed the dog, which belonged to the grocer Theodore Vone, they opened it to be sure it was rabid and found its stomach crammed with straw, grass and splinters of wood, the crazed appetite of the disease. The second patient, that October, was Jean-Baptiste Jupille, a fifteen-year-old shepherd who had grappled barehanded with a rabid dog to protect five younger children, and a bronze statue of him wrestling the dog stands today in the Institut Pasteur's garden.

Meister grew up to be gatekeeper of the Institut Pasteur, and a popular legend says that in June 1940, when the Germans took Paris, he killed himself rather than open Pasteur's tomb for them, though his granddaughter and historians say he died in despair, wrongly believing his family had been captured.

louisiana-purchase-1803.context_blurb:
In 1803 the United States under President Thomas Jefferson bought the Louisiana Territory from Napoleon's France, a vast stretch of land from the mouth of the Mississippi north to Canada and west to the Rocky Mountains. Fifteen states, or parts of them, were later carved from it. The sale happened mostly because of what had gone wrong for Napoleon.

Napoleon hoped to rebuild French power in the Americas around Saint-Domingue, the sugar island we call Haiti, but a revolt by the island's slaves and yellow fever destroyed the army he sent under General Charles Leclerc, Napoleon's own brother-in-law, and killed Leclerc himself. Without Haiti, Louisiana was worthless to him, and a new war with Britain was coming.

Jefferson's envoys, Robert Livingston and James Monroe, had orders to buy only New Orleans, but Napoleon's finance minister, Barbe-Marbois, offered them the entire Louisiana Territory, the whole colony, far more than they were allowed to buy. They signed before he could change his mind. For about $15 million the United States got some 828,000 square miles, roughly three cents an acre, and the deal doubled the size of the country overnight. Jefferson worried whether the Constitution let him buy land at all, but the Senate approved, and Lewis and Clark set out the next year to explore it.

luther-s-bible-vernacular-scripture.context_blurb:
In 1521, at the Diet of Worms, Martin Luther refused to take back his teachings and was declared an outlaw whom anyone could kill without penalty. His protector, Frederick the Wise of Saxony, staged a fake kidnapping on Luther's road home and hid him in the Wartburg, a mountain castle. There Luther began the German Bible that put Scripture into ordinary people's hands.

To stay hidden he let his hair and beard grow, put away his monk's habit and lived as a knight, Junker Jorg, Knight George, and in about eleven weeks he translated the whole New Testament from Greek into German. The complete Bible took longer, with help from Hebrew and Greek scholars, and by Luther's death in 1546 some 200,000 copies had spread in hundreds of editions.

Jacob Grimm, one of the two brothers who gathered the famous fairy tales, praised the translation's almost miraculous purity and called Luther's German the kernel and foundation of modern High German, because it did so much to set the standard for the language.

machiavelli-the-prince.context_blurb:
Niccolo Machiavelli, born in Florence in 1469, rose through the Florentine republic's service as a diplomat and organiser of its citizen militia. In 1512 the Medici family seized Florence back by force, and Machiavelli, a committed republican, lost everything. In exile on his farm he wrote The Prince, a short, cold handbook on how a ruler takes and keeps power.

Early in 1513 the Medici jailed him for 22 days on suspicion of plotting against them and tortured him with the strappado, hoisting him by a rope tied to his wrists behind his back and dropping him six times, but he confessed to nothing. An amnesty for the election of the Medici pope Leo X set him free.

On the farm his days went in trapping birds and squabbling over cards with villagers, but each evening, he told his friend Francesco Vettori, he put on courtly robes and stepped in his imagination into the ancient courts of the great men of old, asking the dead writers why they had acted as they did. In The Prince he taught that a ruler must play two beasts at once, a fox and a lion: the fox to spot the traps and the lion to frighten off the wolves. Pure force gets trapped, and pure cunning gets mauled.

His model of a new ruler was Cesare Borgia, who sent a ruthless lieutenant, Remirro de Orco, to tame the Romagna and then, once the people hated Remirro, had him cut in two and left in the square at Cesena with a bloody knife beside him, so the blame fell on the dead man. Machiavelli dedicated the book to Lorenzo, the young Medici who ruled Florence, hoping to win back his post, but a story says Lorenzo barely glanced at it, because another visitor had brought him two hunting dogs that same day. He died in 1527 without regaining office. Machiavelli never actually wrote that the ends justify the means; those words are nowhere in the book, and the closest he came was saying that in the actions of princes, people judge by the result.

machu-picchu.context_blurb:
High on a steep ridge in the Peruvian Andes, above the Urubamba River, the Inca built Machu Picchu around 1450 as a royal estate for their great ruler Pachacuti. It holds terraced fields, temples, a central plaza, fountains fed by mountain springs and some of the finest Inca stonework anywhere.

In the 1530s the Spanish conquerors looted and wrecked Inca cities across Peru, but they never found Machu Picchu, so its temples and houses survived untouched, which is why it is better preserved than almost any other Inca site. By the 1600s its builders had abandoned it, and the jungle crept over its buildings.

In 1911 the Yale historian Hiram Bingham made himself famous for finding the lost city, but when he reached the terraces he found local Quechua families already farming them and living there, and another explorer, Agustin Lizarraga, had reached the site in 1902. The city had never really been lost to the people who lived around it.

magellan-s-circumnavigation.context_blurb:
In September 1519 Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese captain sailing for Spain, set out with five ships and about 270 men. Portugal's king had refused to back him, so Spain's young King Charles I did. Three years later a single battered ship came home, having sailed right around the world for the first time in history, but Magellan was not aboard.

Going around the world was not what Magellan set out to do: he meant to reach the Spice Islands, the Moluccas, by sailing west, so that Spain could break Portugal's grip and buy cloves straight from where they grew. In the winter of 1520, at Port San Julian far down the coast of South America, his men marvelled at the tall local people, whom Magellan called Patagao, and by legend the region's name, Patagonia, means the land of people with big feet. The fleet found its passage at the continent's tip in October 1520, a strait 350 miles long that now bears Magellan's name. While the ships were still fighting their way through it, the crew of the San Antonio mutinied and secretly sailed home to Spain, abandoning the expedition and carrying off much of its food.

In November 1520 Magellan led the remaining ships out into a vast, calm ocean that no European had crossed, and because they met no storms, he named it the Pacific, the peaceful sea. It was far bigger than anyone had guessed. The crossing took about 98 days, and when the biscuit ran out and the water turned rotten, the starving sailors soaked the ox-hides that protected the rigging in the sea, heated them on the embers and ate them, along with sawdust and rats. Without fresh food they fell sick with what we now call scurvy, and Antonio Pigafetta, the expedition's diarist, wrote that the men's gums swelled up over their teeth until they could not eat; nineteen died.

Magellan's end came on 27 April 1521, in a fight on the Philippine island of Mactan, where he waded ashore in armour with about fifty men against some 1,500 warriors led by Chief Lapulapu, and a spear through his unarmoured leg brought him down in the surf. His body was never returned to his men. The Basque captain Juan Sebastian Elcano took command of the last ship and brought it home, finishing the first voyage around the world. Of the five ships that sailed, only the Victoria returned to Spain; even the flagship Trinidad never made it home. When the Victoria reached Seville on 8 September 1522, only 18 starving men were aboard, out of the roughly 270 who had set out.

The voyage left two strange proofs that the world is round. When they put in at Cape Verde in July 1522, the crew's logbook, kept every day for three years, said Wednesday while the islanders insisted it was Thursday: by always sailing west around the globe, the crew had gained a whole day, the first real proof of what became the International Date Line. Magellan's interpreter, an enslaved man from Malacca named Enrique, may have beaten everyone around the world. Carried east to Europe years before, he now sailed west with Magellan. At Limasawa in the Philippines in March 1521, the local people understood his Malay, which meant he had travelled right round the globe to a place where his own language was spoken.

magna-carta-1215.context_blurb:
In June 1215 King John of England, hated by his barons, was forced to accept a long charter limiting his own power: Magna Carta, the Great Charter. Most of it dealt with narrow feudal grievances, and it was cancelled within weeks. Yet reissued again and again, it became a founding stone of English liberty and of constitutional law across the English-speaking world.

John's troubles began abroad: in 1204 he lost Normandy and his family's French lands to King Philip II of France, and the heavy taxes he wrung from his barons for a failed reconquest bred fury. In August 1213 Archbishop Stephen Langton read the barons a forgotten charter that Henry I had granted at his coronation in 1100, giving them a written precedent on which to build their own demands. On 17 May 1215 the rebel barons seized London, the capital, while the king was away, leaving John little choice but to bargain. In June the two sides met on neutral open ground, the meadow of Runnymede beside the River Thames between Windsor and Staines, as the charter itself records. John never signed Magna Carta with a quill; like every medieval king, he made it binding by pressing his great wax seal into it. The charter ran as one unbroken block of 63 provisions, and the clause numbers people quote today were added by editors long after John's reign.

Clause 39, the most quoted of all, protected every free man from arrest, prison, loss of land or exile unless his peers judged him lawfully or the law of the land allowed it, and that judgment by one's peers grew into trial by jury. Clause 40 bound the crown never to sell justice to anyone, nor to deny it or delay it, and it is one of the few clauses still on the British statute book. But about ten weeks after Runnymede, Pope Innocent III, whose vassal John had made himself, declared the charter shameful, illegal and void forever, because the king had been forced into it. In October 1216, fleeing a French invasion, John tried to cross the Wash, a stretch of tidal sands and quicksand on the east coast, and tradition says the incoming sea engulfed part of his baggage train, including the crown jewels, which have never been found. Days later, on the night of 18 to 19 October 1216, John died of dysentery at Newark Castle. His nine-year-old son became Henry III, and the boy's regents reissued the charter to win the barons back.

The most radical clause, 61, set up a council of 25 barons who could seize the king's castles and lands if he broke the charter and did not repair the wrong within 40 days, which in effect gave legal cover to rebels taking up arms against their king. It was dropped from the very first reissue. Clause 39 protected only free men, a thin slice of England's people, while the unfree majority, the villeins, were tied to their lords' estates and left outside its protection. The version that lasted was not John's: Henry III reissued a settled charter in 1225, and in 1297 Edward I made it statute law, the version that lived on in English law. Even a humble order to rip out the fish-weirs, traps that were silting up the Thames, the Medway and other rivers, survived as law into the 1960s, long after the grand clauses were gone.
