mahabharata-ramayana-epics.context_blurb:
The Mahabharata and the Ramayana are the two great Sanskrit epics of ancient India, shaped over many centuries from older spoken tales and still retold across South and Southeast Asia. The Mahabharata tells of a feud between two families of royal cousins, the Pandavas and the Kauravas, that ends in a vast war. The Ramayana tells how Prince Rama rescues his wife Sita from Ravana, the demon king of Lanka.

The Mahabharata is the longest poem ever composed, some 100,000 verses and 1.8 million words, roughly ten times as long as Homer's Iliad and Odyssey put together. It is about four times the length of the Ramayana. Ravana carries Sita off to his island fortress of Lanka, and Rama's army of monkeys and bears cannot follow across the sea. But the mighty monkey Hanuman, son of the wind god Vayu, prays, swells to a giant's size and leaps the whole ocean to Lanka in a single bound from the top of Mount Mahendra.

When Ravana's demons catch Hanuman spying and set his oil-soaked tail alight to shame him, he bounds from roof to roof and sets fire to all of Lanka, sparing only the grove where Sita is held. In the Mahabharata, King Yudhishthira, eldest of the five Pandava brothers, gambles away everything in a rigged game of dice, even his wife, Queen Draupadi, and when Prince Dushasana tries to strip her before the court, Krishna makes her sari endless, so it unwinds and unwinds until Dushasana collapses.

Brahma, the creator, had granted Ravana a boon: no god and no demon could ever kill him. In his pride Ravana never bothered to ask for safety from mere mortals, and that gap in his boon is why Rama, only a man, can kill him in the end.

On the eve of the great battle of Kurukshetra, the warrior Arjuna talks with his charioteer, who is the god Krishna, and that dialogue is the Bhagavad Gita. The patriarch Bhishma held a boon that let him decide for himself when he would die. Arjuna's arrows brought Bhishma down at Kurukshetra, and so many of them stood in his body that they held him off the ground, so he lay suspended on a bed of arrows for weeks, teaching Yudhishthira, until the holy season of Uttarayana came.

mandate-of-heaven-zhou-dynasty.context_blurb:
In 1046 BCE a Chinese army under King Wu crushed the Shang dynasty and set up a new one, the Zhou. The new rulers had to explain why toppling a king backed by the heavens could be right, and their answer shaped Chinese politics for more than two thousand years: a ruler who governed badly could lose his right to rule.

According to the Duke of Zhou, Heaven gives power to a virtuous ruler and withdraws it from a cruel one, and this heavenly grant became known as the Mandate of Heaven, or Tianming. The Shang had fallen, he said, because Heaven had already rejected them. The Zhou themselves outlasted every other Chinese dynasty, ruling for about 800 years until 256 BCE, though their real power faded long before the end.

To make the last Shang king the very image of a ruler Heaven had abandoned, the Zhou blackened his memory and renamed him Zhou, a character meaning the grimiest strap on a horse's saddle. The Han scholar Wang Chong already dismissed the lurid tales about him as the victors' propaganda.

Centuries later Mencius, asked by the king of Qi whether killing the tyrant Zhou of Shang had been the murder of a king, replied that he had heard of the execution of a mere fellow called Zhou, but never of a ruler being slain, because a cruel tyrant is no true king. The Mandate's boldest idea was that Heaven speaks through ordinary people: the Book of Documents says that Heaven sees as the people see and hears as the people hear, so a king who loses his people's loyalty has already lost Heaven. Floods, famines and revolts could be read as Heaven's verdict, and Mencius taught that the people matter most and the ruler least.

manhattan-project.context_blurb:
The Manhattan Project was the top-secret American effort in the Second World War to build an atomic bomb before Nazi Germany could. At its peak it employed more than 125,000 people and cost some two billion dollars. Under the physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, its scientists at Los Alamos, New Mexico, built the first atomic weapons in 1945 and opened the nuclear age.

It began with a warning: in August 1939 the Hungarian physicist Leo Szilard wrote a letter to President Franklin Roosevelt, signed by Albert Einstein, cautioning that Nazi Germany might beat America to an atomic bomb. At Los Alamos, Richard Feynman, a young physicist, passed idle hours learning to open the locked safes that held the bomb's secrets, and one safe opened to 27-18-28, the first digits of the mathematical constant e, 2.71828. The German-born refugee physicist Klaus Fuchs worked on making the plutonium bomb implode, and all the while he was passing what he knew of the bomb to Soviet intelligence through a courier named Harry Gold; he was caught only in 1949.

Oppenheimer named the first test Trinity, and it took place on a barren stretch of New Mexico desert that old travellers had called Jornada del Muerto, the Journey of the Dead Man. While they waited, the scientists ran a betting pool on the size of the explosion, and I. I. Rabi, arriving last, took the only number left, 18 kilotons, which turned out almost exactly right, so he won. At 5:29 on the morning of 16 July 1945 they set off the Gadget, a steel ball of explosives and plutonium perched on a steel tower 100 feet tall, and the blast turned the tower to vapour, so that only the stumps of its legs remained. The fireball melted the desert sand around it into a crust of faintly radioactive, light-green glass, later named trinitite. The test's director, the physicist Kenneth Bainbridge, turned to Oppenheimer and told him bluntly that now they were all sons of bitches. Twenty years later Oppenheimer said that, watching the fireball, he had remembered words from the Bhagavad Gita, a sacred Hindu text, in which the speaker says he has become Death, the destroyer of worlds. His brother Frank, standing beside him at the test, remembered Robert's real words in the moment as much plainer: it worked.

Little Boy, the Hiroshima bomb of 6 August 1945, worked like a gun barrel, shooting one lump of uranium into a second. Fat Man, which fell on Nagasaki on 9 August, used plutonium instead and worked by implosion: a carefully timed shell of explosives squeezed a plutonium ball inward. Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, found guilty of giving the Soviets atomic secrets, were executed at Sing Sing prison in June 1953, the only American civilians ever put to death for espionage in peacetime. Years later Ethel's brother, David Greenglass, admitted that he had lied on the stand about her typing the spy notes.

manorialism-the-medieval-peasant.context_blurb:
In medieval Europe most people lived on manors, farming estates owned by a lord, with fields, meadows, woods, a mill and a village of peasant households. Most peasants were serfs: not slaves, but bound to the land, owing the lord labour, crops and fees in return for strips of land of their own. It was a hard life, and sometimes the villagers pushed back.

Breaking northern Europe's heavy, wet clay took a great iron-shod plough that only a team of eight oxen could drag, so families that owned only two had to pool their animals with the neighbours just to plough at all. That is one reason peasant farming was so communal. Before a serf could tend his own crops, he owed week-work: two or three days of unpaid labour every week, and more at harvest, on the demesne, the part of the manor the lord kept for himself.

At a serf's death the lord claimed a death-tax called the heriot, the dead man's best beast, his finest ox or cow, and the church often claimed the second-best as well, so a grieving family lost its two most valuable animals at once. Peasants also had to grind their grain at the lord's mill and pay him a share of the flour. Abbot Richard of St Albans, around 1331, confiscated about eighty hidden hand-mills from the townspeople and had the millstones cemented into the floor of the abbey parlour as a lasting humiliation. Fifty years later, on 12 July 1381, the Peasants' Revolt reached St Albans, and the townsfolk tore those millstones out of the abbey floor, broke them into pieces and handed the fragments round as trophies.

Slowly, farming grew richer. Villages learned to rotate three fields, one sown with winter grain, one with beans and peas and one left resting, and with no notion of chemistry, they had hit on real science: the beans and peas were returning nitrogen to the soil that the grain had worn out. The extra food helped the population grow and towns spread around the years 900 to 1000.

mansa-griots-african-oral-tradition.context_blurb:
Across West Africa, especially in the Mande-speaking lands of the old Mali Empire, history was kept not in books but in trained memory. Hereditary musician-historians called griots, or jeli, carry a community's family lines, wars, births and deaths in song, and a griot could even speak hard truths to kings. The epic of Sundiata, founder of the Mali Empire in the 1200s, has passed from griot to griot for over seven hundred years.

As he recites, a griot often plays the kora, a harp-lute with 21 strings whose body is a halved gourd with a cowhide face; the strings were traditionally made from fishing line. A griot is a living library who carries unwritten history line by line.

Because nothing was written down, an old griot's death means the loss of everything he carried, and a famous Mandinka saying puts it plainly: when one of them dies, it is as though a whole library has gone up in flames. The Malian writer Amadou Hampate Ba gave the best-known version of the idea to a UNESCO conference in 1960. Some of West Africa's most famous modern singers still come from griot families.

mansa-musa-and-the-mali-pilgrimage.context_blurb:
In the early 1300s Mansa Musa was king of Mali, a West African empire that controlled the gold fields of the upper Niger and the trade routes across the Sahara. In 1324 he began the hajj, the pilgrimage of Muslims to Mecca, with a caravan so rich that it shook the economy of Egypt and carried his fame all the way to Europe.

His title, mansa, meant ruler or emperor, literally the king of kings. In Egypt, Musa explained how he had come to the throne, and the scholar al-Umari wrote it down. Musa's predecessor, he said, was sure the Atlantic must end somewhere and sent 200 ships to find its far shore. Only one came back, and its captain reported that the rest had been swallowed far out at sea by a mighty current flowing like a river through the open ocean. That king then sailed off himself with 2,000 ships and never returned, and so Musa became king. It is told as legend.

At the head of his procession walked five hundred attendants, each carrying a staff of pure gold weighing four to six pounds. Behind came some 80 to 100 camels, each loaded with about 300 pounds of gold dust, in a caravan of perhaps 60,000 people. A later legend says that every Friday of the journey he had a brand-new mosque built wherever he happened to be.

In Cairo he showered every emir and official at the sultan's court with loads of gold, and so much poured in that he crashed the price of gold across Egypt. Gold there had always fetched at least 25 silver dirhams per mithqal, but after his visit a mithqal sold for 22 or less, and al-Umari, collecting stories in Cairo around 1340, found it had stayed cheap for about twelve years. Told to kiss the ground before the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad, Musa at first refused, then bowed while declaring aloud that he made obeisance to God who created him. On the way home the richest king in the world ran short of money and borrowed gold from Cairo's merchants at a steep rate, which drew gold out of the market and helped push its price back up.

Back home around 1325 he ordered the Djinguereber Mosque built at Timbuktu, and with no stone quarries anywhere near, his builders raised it in mud brick. Under his patronage Timbuktu became a city of scholars around its Sankore mosque, and in its markets books were among the most valuable goods for sale. In 1375 the Majorcan mapmaker Abraham Cresques painted him on the great Catalan Atlas, enthroned and crowned in the middle of West Africa, holding out a big gold nugget toward a camel rider, and called him the richest and noblest king of those lands.

mansa-musa-the-mali-empire.context_blurb:
In the early 1300s Mansa Musa ruled the Empire of Mali, a vast West African realm that held the goldfields of the upper Niger and the trading cities on the southern edge of the Sahara. His pilgrimage of 1324 and 1325, with thousands of followers and camels loaded with gold, made him the first ruler from south of the Sahara to become famous across the Middle East and Europe.

In the Mandinka language mansa meant king or emperor, so his name simply means King Musa. Musa told the Egyptians that the king before him, often called Abu Bakr II, would not believe the Atlantic had no far shore, so he gave up his throne and sailed west with some 2,000 vessels and never returned, and that is how Musa became king. Modern historians suspect Musa may simply have pushed him aside, so the tale is told as legend.

Mali's wealth came from trading its plentiful gold for salt, which the south badly lacked and prized like treasure, while at the desert town of Taghaza the stuff lay so thick that houses, and even the mosque, were built of salt slabs. The traveller Ibn Battuta saw people there cut salt into pieces and spend it as money. To guard the secret of his real mines at Bambuk and Bure, Musa spread the rumour that in Mali gold grew up out of the ground like a plant. About two-thirds of the gold in the medieval Mediterranean came from West Africa.

In 1324 Musa crossed the Sahara on the hajj, the pilgrimage Muslims hope to make at least once, to the holy city of Mecca in Arabia, a trek of some 2,700 miles. When the caravan neared a city, 500 men marched in front of the king, each carrying a gold staff weighing about six pounds, followed by riders with red-and-gold flags. In Cairo the Mamluk sultan expected him to kiss the floor on his knees, and Musa at first refused; then, on a companion's whispered advice, he bowed, declaring that his reverence went to the God who had made him.

His gifts of gold in Cairo were so lavish that the metal's price collapsed. When al-Umari, an Arab writer, came to Cairo about twelve years later, gold there was still cheap: a mithqal that had never sold below 25 silver dirhams now fetched 22 or fewer. On the journey home the great king actually ran out of cash, and to pay his way across the Sahara he had to take loans of gold from the merchants of Cairo, 50,000 dinars from one man alone. About fifty years after his pilgrimage, the Majorcan mapmaker Abraham Cresques drew him on the 1375 Catalan Atlas, crowned, with a sceptre in one hand and a giant gold nugget held out in the other toward a camel-riding merchant.

Back home he raised the Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu from banco, an earthen mud brick, and nearly seven centuries later it still stands. Timbuktu grew rich on gold, yet the traveller Leo Africanus reported that the most profitable merchandise in the city was books, manuscripts carried south across the Sahara. Online lists now crown Musa the wealthiest human who ever lived, but the historian Hadrien Collet and others point out that the old maps called him richest only in his own region, and that his true fortune is impossible to calculate. He was staggeringly rich; the famous number is simply made up.

mao-s-great-leap-forward-cultural-revolu.context_blurb:
Mao Zedong led the Chinese Communists to victory in 1949 and ruled China until his death in 1976. Two of his campaigns, the Great Leap Forward of 1958 to 1962 and the Cultural Revolution that began in 1966, killed tens of millions of his own people. The first caused the deadliest famine ever recorded; the second turned China's young people against teachers, parents and the Party itself.

In 1958 Mao ordered China to wipe out sparrows for eating grain seed, and whole cities hammered pots, pans, gongs and drums without pause, so the birds had nowhere to settle and fell from the sky exhausted. With the sparrows gone, insects swarmed the fields and ate far more of the crops, and around 1960, persuaded by the bird scientist Tso-hsin Cheng, the leaders had to import some 250,000 live sparrows from the Soviet Union. Mao also wanted China to outproduce Britain in steel, so peasants built backyard furnaces in their fields and, with no scrap iron, threw in their woks, cooking pots and kitchen knives and even their iron hoes and ploughs, producing useless pig iron and leaving nothing to farm with. Officials faked enormous harvests to please Mao, and one propaganda photo showed a boy perched on a field of wheat, as if the stalks were thick enough to hold him, when he was really standing on a hidden table.

At the Lushan Conference in July 1959, Defence Minister Peng Dehuai alone dared tell Mao that the Great Leap was starving the countryside, and Mao threw him out of power, branding him a right-opportunist, a warning to every official who might tell the truth. At a secret meeting in Shanghai that March, Mao had told officials to take as much as one third of the grain, and the historian Frank Dikotter, quoting Party archives, records that he said it was better to let half the people die so that the other half could eat their fill. Even as roughly 30 to 45 million people starved, the government shipped about 7 million tons of grain abroad in 1959 and 1960, selling it for hard currency or giving it away as foreign aid. In Xinyang, in Henan province, about a million of 8.5 million people died around 1960, many at the doors of Party granaries that were full of grain the officials were forbidden to hand out.

Under Mao almost everyone was expected to carry Quotations from Chairman Mao, the Little Red Book, and recite from it daily; around a billion copies had been printed by 1966, and misquoting it could bring punishment. In 1966 Mao launched the Cultural Revolution and sent gangs of teenage Red Guards to smash the Four Olds: old customs, old habits, old culture and old ideas. At struggle sessions the Red Guards made their victims kneel in tall paper dunce caps and hold the jet plane for hours, arms wrenched up behind them while their heads were forced down. Liu Shaoqi, who had been president of China, was labelled the nation's chief capitalist roader, battered at struggle meetings and allowed to die untreated in a prison in Kaifeng in 1969. From 1968 the Party sent some 17 million city teenagers Down to the Countryside for years of farm labour, and one of them, a teenage Xi Jinping, later rose to rule China.

marbury-v-madison-judicial-review.context_blurb:
Marbury v. Madison was the 1803 Supreme Court case that gave American courts one of their greatest powers. In the last hours of John Adams's presidency, William Marbury was appointed a justice of the peace, but his signed commission never reached him. Thomas Jefferson's new Secretary of State, James Madison, refused to deliver it, and Marbury sued.

The chief justice who heard the case, John Marshall, had a hidden tie to it: as Adams's outgoing Secretary of State, he was the very official who had failed to get Marbury's commission delivered before Jefferson's people took over. Marshall was in a trap: ruling against Marbury would bless the government ignoring the law, but ordering Madison to deliver would invite Jefferson to defy the Court.

So Marshall held that Marbury had a right to his commission but that the statute letting him sue in the Supreme Court broke the Constitution, and in surrendering that minor power the Court won a mighty one: the power to declare a law passed by Congress void when it conflicts with the Constitution. This is judicial review, and Marshall's words still guide it: no act of the legislature that goes against the Constitution can be valid.

marco-polo-the-silk-road-to-cathay.context_blurb:
In the late 1200s the young Venetian Marco Polo set out east along the Silk Road with his father and uncle, and he spent nearly a quarter of a century serving Kublai Khan, ruler of the Mongol empire and of China, which Europeans called Cathay. He saw cities bigger than any in Christendom and inventions Europe had never heard of, and his book of wonders amazed and puzzled readers back home.

He described a strange fuel the people of Cathay dug in lumps from beds in the mountains and burned to heat their homes, black stones that stayed alight all night: coal, almost unknown in Europe. Kublai paid for things with sheets of mulberry bark pressed flat and stamped with his red seal, and since he could spend tree bark as treasure, Polo said the Khan had mastered the alchemists' secret. When the Polos finally headed home, the Khan gave them a golden tablet, a paiza about a foot long, warning that anyone who failed to honour its bearers would be killed, and it worked as a passport that commanded horses, food and lodging across the whole empire.

In 1298, a prisoner of war in Genoa after a naval defeat, Polo told his adventures aloud to his cellmate Rustichello of Pisa, a writer of Arthurian romances, who wrote them down. When he lay dying in Venice in 1324, friends at his bedside urged him to confess, for his soul's sake, that his book was full of lies, and he answered that he had not told half of what he saw. It is remembered as tradition rather than a recorded quotation.

marconi-radio-and-broadcasting.context_blurb:
Guglielmo Marconi was a young Italian inventor who believed that the invisible electromagnetic waves Heinrich Hertz had produced in 1887 could carry signals across miles of countryside without any wire. Italian officials ignored him, so he took his idea to Britain. By 1899 he was sending messages across the English Channel, and his wireless soon became standard on ocean ships, famously calling rescuers to the sinking Titanic in 1912.

On 12 December 1901, on Signal Hill in Newfoundland, Marconi and his assistant George Kemp flew a wire aerial on a kite and caught a signal fired from Cornwall, some 2,000 miles away across the Atlantic: the letter S in Morse code, three faint dots, repeated over and over. They had chosen S because three quick dots were the easiest pattern to pick out of the static; some later scientists doubted whether he really heard it.

Soon radio carried more than code: on Christmas Eve 1906, operators at sea, used to nothing but clicking Morse, heard a man's voice and the sound of a violin, as Reginald Fessenden broadcast from Brant Rock, Massachusetts, playing O Holy Night on his violin, singing and reading from the Bible.

marcus-aurelius-the-philosopher-emperor.context_blurb:
From AD 161 to 180 Rome was governed by Marcus Aurelius, the last of the so-called Five Good Emperors and the nearest thing Rome ever had to a philosopher king. He spent much of his reign fighting Germanic tribes along the Danube while plague and war drained the empire. In spare hours he wrote down private reflections in a notebook that became one of the most-read books of ancient philosophy.

As a boy, Marcus Annius Verus so charmed the old emperor Hadrian with his seriousness that Hadrian punned on his family name, Verus, meaning true, and called him Verissimus, the truest. Marcus said the greatest gift of his life came from the philosopher Rusticus, who lent him the discourses of Epictetus, a teacher born a slave, and so the Stoic philosophy passed from a former slave to the ruler of the world.

When plague and endless war drained the treasury, he refused to load his suffering people with heavier taxes and instead auctioned off palace treasures in Trajan's Forum, even the silk robes woven with gold that belonged to his wife, to pay his soldiers. In the war against the Quadi, the men of the Thundering Legion were parched and trapped when rain suddenly poured down, and the historian Cassius Dio says they caught it in their mouths, shields and helmets and drank and fought at the same time. Dio put the rain down to Harnouphis, an Egyptian magician, but the Christian writer Tertullian claimed it came because Christian soldiers in the legion had prayed for it.

When the general Avidius Cassius rebelled on a false rumour that Marcus had died and was then killed by his own officers, a centurion brought Marcus the rebel's head, but Marcus would not even glance at it and ordered it buried, for he had hoped to show Cassius mercy. Over the centuries some twenty bronze emperors went into the melting pot for coin, but medieval Christians spared the great bronze horseman of Marcus because they mistook him for Constantine, Rome's first Christian emperor. Marcus broke the custom of the Five Good Emperors, who had chosen heirs by adoption on merit, by leaving the throne to his own son, Commodus, one of Rome's worst emperors.

Marcus wrote his notebook on campaign: a line in its first book places him among the Quadi beside the river Granua, in a soldier's tent on the battlefront, in what is now Slovakia. Though he was a Roman emperor and a native Latin speaker, he wrote the Meditations in Greek, the language of philosophy. He never meant anyone to read it and gave it no title; copyists later added the Greek heading Ta eis heauton, meaning To Himself. The famous poster line about our deeds echoing in eternity is not his at all: it was written for Gladiator, a big Hollywood film of 2000 about a fictional Roman general named Maximus. His real lines are plainer: stop arguing about what a good man should be, and be one.

marie-curie-and-radioactivity.context_blurb:
Marie Curie, born Maria Sklodowska in Warsaw in 1867, grew up in a Poland that Russia, Germany and Austria had divided between them. She became the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, discovered two new elements with her husband, Pierre, and gave a name to the strange energy that pours out of certain atoms. That energy made her famous, and in the end it killed her.

In the 1880s the University of Warsaw would not admit women, so Maria and other Polish women studied in the Flying University, secret evening lessons that moved from home to home to escape the police. She later worked as a governess to pay for her sister Bronya's studies in Paris, then followed her there and graduated first in physics at the Sorbonne.

In Paris, Marie and Pierre found that pitchblende ore gave out more radiation than all the pure uranium inside it could explain, and they reasoned that hidden, more powerful new elements must be in the rock. Marie coined a new word for what elements such as uranium were doing as they gave off invisible rays: radioactivity. In 1898 they announced the first new element, and Marie named it polonium after her homeland, Poland, which had been erased from the map, a defiant act of patriotism. Radium followed that December.

Proving that radium existed took her about four years of boiling and stirring roughly seven tons of ore with an iron rod nearly as big as herself, and in 1902 it yielded a mere tenth of a gram of pure radium chloride. They worked in a leaky wooden shed with no ventilation, and when the German chemist Wilhelm Ostwald visited, he said it looked like something between a horse stable and a shed for potatoes. She loved to slip into the workroom at night to see her tubes of radium glowing on their own in the dark, like faint fairy lights.

She won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903, shared with Pierre and Henri Becquerel, and the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1911, and she is still the only person ever to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. She refused to patent her method of isolating radium, so that every laboratory and hospital could use it free, even though it left her too poor to buy radium herself. In the First World War she equipped some twenty vehicles with X-ray apparatus and drove them to the battlefields, so that surgeons could locate bullets and shrapnel, and the soldiers called them the petites Curies, the Little Curies.

She carried glowing radium in her pockets and kept it in her desk with no idea of its danger, and she died in 1934 of aplastic anaemia, brought on by years of radiation from the very element she had found. In 1995, when France moved her remains to the Pantheon in Paris to lie among the nation's great minds, her body was still radioactive, and she was found to have been buried in a lead-lined coffin. She was the first woman laid there for her own achievements.

marshall-era-economic-miracles-japan-wes.context_blurb:
After the Second World War, West Germany and Japan lay in ruins, yet within a generation both had become industrial giants, in what people called economic miracles. American Marshall Plan aid helped, but much of the recovery came from within: freer markets, high saving and skilled workers. In West Germany the turning point came from one economist, Ludwig Erhard.

Under price controls, German shopkeepers hid their goods rather than sell them at the official prices, and a black market thrived. One Sunday in June of 1948, while Allied generals still governed, Erhard abolished the controls on his own authority. When the American general Lucius Clay warned him that his advisers called it a terrible mistake, Erhard told him not to listen to them, because his own advisers told him the same thing.

By the next morning, goods that had been hoarded for years were back in the shop windows, and the black market melted away, because merchants could at last sell at real prices. West German industrial output jumped from about half of its 1936 level in May 1948 to more than three-quarters by December, and the Wirtschaftswunder, the economic miracle, had begun.

marshall-plan.context_blurb: The Marshall Plan was a massive American economic-aid program for post-war Western Europe named after Secretary of State George Marshall, who proposed it in a famous speech at Harvard University in June 1947. By the summer of 1947 the economies of Western European countries had still not meaningfully recovered from the Second World War. Industrial production, agriculture, housing, and ordinary consumer goods were all catastrophically below pre-war levels, winters were brutal, and American officials in Washington were increasingly worried that economic desperation might push France, Italy, Greece, or other countries into pro-Soviet politics. Marshall's plan offered large grants and loans — eventually totaling around thirteen billion dollars, a huge sum in 1948 money — to be used by the recipient countries for whatever reconstruction they considered most important, as long as they coordinated with each other. Sixteen Western European countries accepted. The Soviet Union and the Soviet-occupied countries of Eastern Europe refused on Stalin's orders. The money, together with sound domestic policy choices in the recipient countries, helped produce the Western European Economic Miracle of the 1950s. The Marshall Plan is often cited as one of the most successful foreign-aid programs in American history and as a defining act of American Cold War generosity.

martin-luther-the-95-theses.context_blurb: Martin Luther was a 16th-century German Augustinian friar and professor of Bible whose public protest against indulgences in 1517 cracked the religious unity of Western Europe. He was born in 1483 in Saxony, the son of a copper miner who had scraped money together to send his bright boy to law school. Luther abandoned law in his early twenties for the monastic life, took vows in the Augustinian order, and after further study became a professor at the small new university of Wittenberg. His quarrel with the Church began over the aggressive selling of indulgences in nearby Saxon towns and quickly escalated into a wider attack on Rome. The Church excommunicated him. The emperor summoned him to Worms in 1521 and ordered him to take back everything he had written; he refused. On the way home a protective German prince hid him in a mountain fortress, where he grew out his hair and beard, took a false identity, and worked on a German translation of the Christian Scriptures. The reform movement he set in motion was no longer his personal fight by the end — it had grown into a continent-wide upheaval — but his writings on grace, Scripture, and faith remain foundational for every Protestant tradition that would follow. He died in 1546.

martin-luther-the-protestant-reformation.context_blurb: Martin Luther was a German monk and professor of theology who, in 1517, publicly protested the sale of indulgences — printed documents that preachers were peddling across Germany with the pitch that Church-authorized payments could change a departed loved one's fate after death. Luther argued, with growing fury, that salvation came from God's grace through faith alone and could not be bought or earned by any human act. His 95 Theses were a professor's debate challenge, written in Latin, but a printer translated them into German, cheap pamphlets flew off the presses, and within a few years half of Germany was reading Luther and the Pope had excommunicated him. Hauled before Emperor Charles V at the Diet of Worms, Luther refused to take any of it back and was declared an outlaw whom any man could lawfully kill. A friendly prince hid him in a castle in disguise under an invented alias, where he worked at a furious pace on a vivid everyday German version of a central Christian text that ordinary people could read for themselves without needing a priest and a Latin dictionary. The Reformation he set off split Western Christianity for good, and shaped the political and religious map of Europe for centuries after.

marx-engels-and-the-communist-manifesto-.context_blurb: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels were two young German thinkers who, in the winter of 1847-1848, were asked by a small revolutionary club in London to write a short declaration of its principles. Marx was a brilliant, abrasive, poor former newspaper editor and philosopher living in exile with his wife Jenny and a growing family; Engels was the son of a German textile manufacturer who had been running one of his father's cotton mills in Manchester and had seen firsthand the conditions of British industrial workers. The pamphlet they produced, the Communist Manifesto, appeared on the eve of a wave of revolutions that would sweep most of Europe in 1848. It was short, scorching, and quotable, and it argued that modern industrial capitalism had split society into a tiny class of owners and a huge class of wage-workers, and that the only cure was a revolution by the workers that would abolish private property in the means of production. The questions ahead cover the opening image of the pamphlet, Marx's family nickname, its famous closing call, an earlier draft Engels had written, the revolution in Europe that began the week it appeared, the long work that was Marx's real life's labor, the women closest to the two men, one of Marx's recurring physical complaints, an early English translator's awkward wording, the death of one of Marx's children, a famous scientist Marx admired, Marx's line about religion, his view of what drives history, and his famous instruction to philosophers. It matters because these ideas, worked out by two scribblers in reading rooms, would in the next century inspire regimes — in the Soviet Union, Communist China, Cambodia, and elsewhere — whose attempts to put them into practice killed somewhere around a hundred million people; the Manifesto is where that story begins.

mary-anning-the-fossil-hunter-of-lyme-re.context_blurb: Mary Anning was born in 1799 in the small English seaside town of Lyme Regis on the Jurassic coast of Dorset, where the eroding cliffs are packed with fossils laid down about 200 million years ago. Her father was a poor cabinetmaker who topped up his income by selling curiosities to tourists, and he died when Mary was eleven, leaving the family deep in debt. Mary and her brother Joseph kept the fossil business going. Over the next three decades, armed with a hammer, a basket, and an uncanny eye for which lumps in the rock were worth digging out, Mary unearthed one spectacular ancient creature after another from the dark Jurassic shale, including early examples of several whole kinds of giant extinct reptile that had never been seen in one piece before. She reconstructed them, cleaned them, drew them, and sold them, mostly to wealthy gentleman naturalists and university men who then wrote the scientific papers, named the specimens, and often forgot to credit her. The Geological Society of London would not admit women; neither would most universities. She was Dissenter, poor, and self-taught, and she worked a dangerous shoreline where a landslide killed her dog and almost killed her. By the end of her life, however, the scientific men of London had quietly recognised what they owed her and raised a small annuity to support her when illness ended her climbing. The tongue-twister about seashells by the seashore that modern readers sometimes connect to Anning is widely discussed online, and the story behind it is worth looking up for yourself.

mary-wollstonecraft-and-women-s-rights.context_blurb: Mary Wollstonecraft was an 18th-century English writer and one of the earliest serious thinkers to argue that the women of her time were being deliberately prevented from fully exercising their reason. Born in 1759 to a shiftless and sometimes violent father, she scraped together an education on her own, worked as a governess, and eventually became a writer in radical London circles. In 1792 she published A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, which argued that women are not naturally silly or weak but become so because their society trains them to be. The book landed in the middle of the French Revolution debates and was both celebrated and attacked. Wollstonecraft had an unconventional personal life — an affair, an illegitimate daughter, a suicide attempt, and finally a happy marriage to the philosopher William Godwin — and died in 1797 shortly after giving birth to her second daughter, who grew up to be Mary Shelley, the author of Frankenstein. For almost a century afterward Wollstonecraft was remembered mostly as a scandal, but by the late 1800s her book was being read seriously again and she is now treated as a founder of modern argument about women's rights.

mauryan-empire-ashoka-the-great.context_blurb: The Mauryan Empire, which flourished from around 322 BC to 185 BC in India, was the first great empire to unify most of the subcontinent under a single ruler. It was founded by the shrewd Chandragupta Maurya, who seized power in the aftermath of Alexander the Great's withdrawal from northwestern India. His empire reached its peak under his grandson Ashoka in the 3rd century BC. Ashoka was initially a conquering warrior like his grandfather and father, but after an especially bloody campaign in the eastern coastal kingdom of Kalinga — in which, by his own later account, over a hundred thousand people died — he underwent a moral conversion to Buddhism and spent the rest of his long reign trying to govern by principles of nonviolence, religious tolerance, and public welfare. He carved his famous edicts into stone pillars and polished rocks across the subcontinent, in several languages, communicating directly with his subjects about the moral life he wanted them to live. He sent Buddhist missionaries abroad as far as Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia, and the Hellenistic kingdoms of the Mediterranean world. The Mauryan state did not long survive him, but Ashoka himself is one of the rare rulers in world history remembered not for how much he conquered but for what he refused to conquer.

maya-astronomy-and-the-long-count-calend.context_blurb: The ancient Maya of southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, and western Honduras developed one of the most sophisticated astronomical and calendrical traditions anywhere in the ancient world. Working from stone platforms aligned to the rising points of specific stars and planets, their astronomer-priests kept meticulous observations of the movements of the Sun, the Moon, and especially the planet Venus over centuries, and they tracked eclipses and seasons with precision. Their calendar system interlocked several cycles at once: a 260-day ritual calendar, a 365-day solar calendar, and a long-count calendar that counted days outward from a mythological starting date far in the past. The long count ran in giant cycles whose end dates were used to mark cosmic transitions. One such end date fell in late December 2012, which is why there was a wave of popular (and completely baseless) New Age panic in the early 21st century about a Maya-predicted end of the world. The actual Maya would have been puzzled; the end of a long-count cycle was simply the beginning of the next long-count cycle, not an apocalypse. The sophistication of their observations without any optical equipment is still breathtaking.

maya-writing-and-the-dresden-codex.context_blurb: The Maya were the only pre-Columbian people in the Americas known to have developed a fully phonetic writing system that could record any sentence in their spoken language. Their script is a hybrid of logographic signs — one sign per word — and syllabic signs for the individual sound-units of their speech, with over 800 known signs recorded on stone monuments, painted pottery, and folded bark-paper books. The system was used for well over a thousand years, from before the Classic era until the Spanish conquest. The arriving Spanish friars, led by Bishop Diego de Landa in the 16th century, deliberately burned nearly every Maya book they could find, considering them devilish; only four pre-conquest Maya codices are known to have survived to the modern period. One of them, now kept in Dresden, Germany, is an elaborate astronomical and divinatory manuscript covering Venus tables, eclipse tables, and ritual calendars. Modern decipherment of the Maya script took nearly two centuries of frustrated effort, and only in the 1960s and 1970s did Russian and American scholars finally crack the code. We can now read the stone-carved history of the Maya kings in real detail for the first time since the 16th century.

mccarthyism-the-red-scare.context_blurb: In the late 1940s and early 1950s, in the opening years of the Cold War and in the aftermath of several high-profile cases of actual Soviet espionage in the United States, a broad anti-communist mood swept American politics and culture. The Republican senator Joseph McCarthy of Wisconsin became the most visible political figure of this period after his 1950 claim, in a speech in Wheeling, West Virginia, that he had in his hand a specific list of communists in the State Department. McCarthy used his Senate subcommittee for several years to accuse government officials, military officers, intellectuals, and private citizens of secret communist sympathies, often with little or no evidence, and he destroyed many careers before his colleagues finally censured him in late 1954 after his accusations against the United States Army. In parallel, the House Un-American Activities Committee held similar hearings in Hollywood and elsewhere, producing a blacklist of film-industry employees. The underlying concern about Soviet espionage was not fabricated — Alger Hiss, the Rosenbergs, Klaus Fuchs, and the Cambridge Five were all real cases, and the Venona decrypts later confirmed much of the intelligence picture — but the political techniques of accusation without due process gave the whole period a bad reputation. The term McCarthyism now stands in English for exactly that kind of accusation.

mecca-the-kaaba-and-the-hajj.context_blurb: Mecca is the holiest city of Islam and the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad. At the center of its Great Mosque stands the Kaaba, a cubic stone shrine draped in black cloth that Muslims believe was first built by Abraham and his son Ishmael as the first house of worship to the one God. Every Muslim who is physically and financially able is expected to make at least one pilgrimage — the hajj — to Mecca in a lifetime, following the pattern laid down by the Prophet Muhammad on his own farewell pilgrimage, and the central ritual at the Great Mosque is walking seven times around the Kaaba counterclockwise. Pilgrims put on simple white garments called ihram during the hajj, honoring the equality of all believers standing before God. Set in one corner of the Kaaba is a dark stone that pilgrims try to touch or kiss as they pass — tradition says the angel Gabriel gave it to Abraham — and the full hajj also takes pilgrims east of the city to stand on the plain of Arafat on a single appointed afternoon, in one of the largest annual gatherings on earth, and to stone three pillars at Mina that represent the devil tempting Abraham to disobey the command to sacrifice his son.

medieval-jewish-life-persecution.context_blurb: For most of the Middle Ages, Jewish communities lived in Christian Europe as a protected but second-class people, allowed to practice their faith, forbidden most trades, pushed into money-lending because Christians were not supposed to charge interest, and expelled, taxed, massacred, or protected by whichever king happened to need their money most urgently that year. In Muslim Spain and in parts of Christendom, Jewish scholars and physicians thrived; one great Jewish philosopher of the 12th century, born in Spain and ending his career as a doctor to the sultan of Egypt, wrote works on philosophy, medicine, and Jewish law that scholars of three faiths read in translation and still read today. Elsewhere, Jewish communities were pushed into particular streets, forced to wear distinguishing badges, blamed for plagues and for the murder of Christian children, and sometimes killed in mass violence by their neighbors. The story follows both sides of this life, the extraordinary scholarship and the brutal persecution, including the particular word that was first invented in Italy for the enclosed areas Jewish communities were forced to live in, and the quiet continuity of a people who kept their learning, their language, and their worship alive through all of it.

medieval-knight-s-arms-armor.context_blurb: A fully armored knight of the later Middle Ages was one of the most expensive weapons any medieval economy produced, a man who carried a tailored shell of articulated steel plates over mail, trained from boyhood to move and fight in it, and could cost a village's yearly income just to equip. Every joint of his harness was hinged, and every surface was shaped to turn away a blade or an arrow. He wore armor from his crown down to the piece that protected his feet, with every limb and every vital organ shielded by a specific named part. His shield, painted bright with his family's heraldic design, had to serve a very practical identification purpose that is one of the quietest and most ingenious legacies of medieval design, and the rules the medieval heralds developed about which colors could sit next to which other colors are still studied by graphic designers today. The story covers the gear, the painted signs that distinguished one armored shape from another on the battlefield, the long training needed to wear and use the whole outfit, and the famous legendary blades and surprising practical details of how a man actually armored up and climbed on a horse to ride to war.

medieval-medicine-the-calendar-daily-lif.context_blurb: Medieval doctors inherited an elaborate theory from Greek and Arabic writers, in which the body was ruled by four fluids whose balance set your temperament and your health, and most of their treatments, bleeding, purging, special diets, carefully timed to the stars, were aimed at putting those fluids back in balance. Barbers doubled as surgeons, performing minor surgery and pulling teeth; monks ran hospices and infirmaries; and women did most of the actual day-to-day doctoring in a village, as midwives, herbalists, and household healers. The medieval year was marked out by saints' days, by church bells for the hours, and by regular quarterly payments to one's local lord that fell on specific feast days. Modern researchers combing through surviving medieval manuscripts have occasionally stumbled on remarkable surprises hidden in the recipes, including one thousand-year-old English salve that, when carefully recreated by modern biologists, turned out to have a genuinely useful effect on a stubborn modern bacterial problem. The story covers the humors, the calendar, the barbers and the midwives, and the odd flashes of genuine medical knowledge hidden inside a world without germ theory. It also covers the moment one later French army surgeon stumbled by accident onto a wound treatment that worked better than the fiery cautery method his training had told him was correct, and watched his patients recover in front of his eyes.

medieval-universities-scholasticism.context_blurb: In the 12th and 13th centuries, Europe grew a new kind of institution: a self-governing community of masters and students that eventually came to be called by the Latin word for a whole corporate body. In Paris the professors ran their community, in Bologna the students did; and in both towns and in a growing list of others, young men from across Christendom took vows, lived rough in rented rooms, studied the seven liberal arts and then medicine, law, or theology, and defended their ideas in long formal debates in front of their teachers. The method they built was called scholasticism, and its signature was a careful, patient, rigorous handling of opposing arguments before giving an answer, step by step, like a court case. The greatest of their teachers used this method to try to reconcile Christian faith with the newly rediscovered Greek philosophy. The story covers the famous teachers, the student riots that sometimes shut whole towns down, the tavern brawls, the strange instruments they used to study the stars, the complicated question of who got to grant degrees, and the quiet discipline of patient debate that still runs under almost every modern classroom today. Modern degree ceremonies, academic gowns, the division of a university into faculties, the Latin names of its degrees, and the whole idea of a self-governing community of scholars with its own courts all come down to us in a direct line from these medieval guilds of masters and students.

medieval-women-s-lives-roles.context_blurb: Medieval women lived under heavier legal and social restrictions than their fathers and brothers, and yet the record is full of women who ran estates while their husbands went on crusade, who held thrones in their own right, who dominated particular trades in their towns, who founded and ran great monasteries, who wrote books of visions and theology and courtly conduct, who argued publicly with popes, and who occasionally changed church law by force of their personal argument. One extraordinary 12th-century German abbess corresponded with emperors. A powerful French-born queen of two realms rode east on crusade with her own retinue, scandalizing some of the men on the expedition. A pioneering 15th-century French widow became the first woman in Europe known to have earned her living primarily by writing. The story covers both the limits women faced and the women who climbed over them, from the queens and the saints and the writers down to the ordinary village brewer, the midwife, and the merchant's wife running the shop while her husband was away. The story covers queens who went on crusade and widows who went into business, abbesses who corresponded with popes and ordinary village women who ran small trades in the shadow of the local parish church, and it refuses the easy modern caricature that medieval women were simply silent and shut away.

mendel-and-the-birth-of-genetics.context_blurb: Gregor Mendel was an Augustinian friar in a monastery in Brunn, in what is now the Czech Republic, who in the 1850s and 1860s ran an enormous and painstakingly careful breeding experiment in the monastery's garden. He crossed thousands of plants over multiple generations, tracking a handful of easily visible traits — height, pod shape, seed color — and counting what happened in the offspring. From those counts he worked out that inheritance is not a smooth blending of the parents but comes in discrete units — what we now call genes — that pass intact through generations and recombine according to predictable mathematical ratios. Mendel published his results in 1866 in a local scientific journal; the paper sank almost without a trace, and he spent the rest of his life as a busy abbot and died in 1884 largely unknown as a scientist. Thirty-five years after his paper appeared, three different European biologists, working independently, rediscovered his ratios in their own experiments, dug up his old paper, and realized that a monk in Moravia had already solved the problem. The questions ahead cover the specific garden plant he worked with and the famous confident thing he once said about his future. It matters because what he discovered became the foundation of modern genetics, and the backbone of twentieth-century biology, medicine, and agriculture.

mendel-and-the-foundations-of-genetics.context_blurb: Gregor Mendel was an Austrian Augustinian friar and later abbot who, in a small plot behind his monastery in Brunn in Moravia (now Brno in the Czech Republic), spent eight patient years in the 1850s and 1860s crossbreeding ordinary garden pea plants. He picked peas because he could watch sharply contrasting traits — round seeds versus wrinkled, yellow versus green, tall plants versus short — pass from one generation to the next. He grew tens of thousands of plants, kept meticulous counts of every offspring, and did the arithmetic. Out of this came two of the deepest laws in biology: that each parent passes on one of two separate heritable 'factors' for each trait, and that different traits are shuffled independently when they are passed on. He published his results in 1866 in the proceedings of the local natural-history society in Brunn, and almost nobody read them. Mendel became abbot shortly afterwards, got bogged down in a long dispute with the Austrian government over monastery taxes, and died in 1884 without ever learning that he had founded a whole science. Around 1900 three different botanists — Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns, and Erich von Tschermak — came up with essentially the same laws independently, each dug back into the old literature, and each stumbled on the forgotten Brunn paper. They had the honesty to say so publicly. Mendel's name has carried the field ever since.

mexican-independence-and-father-hidalgo.context_blurb: In 1810 New Spain — the enormous Spanish colony stretching from the modern American Southwest down through most of today's Mexico and Central America — was still ruled from Madrid, and had been for roughly three centuries. The social order was built on a strict hierarchy running from Spanish-born officials at the top, down through American-born Spaniards (Creoles), mixed-race people (castas), and the vast indigenous and enslaved African populations at the bottom. In the countryside north of Mexico City, in the parish of Dolores, lived a sixty-year-old Creole priest named Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla. Hidalgo had read Enlightenment books, taught his parishioners new trades to lift their poverty, and quietly joined a group of Creole conspirators plotting against the colonial regime. On September 16, 1810, warned that the plot had been discovered, Hidalgo rang the church bell before dawn and called his parishioners together to launch an uprising. The questions ahead cover the name Mexicans still give that call to arms and the figure Hidalgo chose to carry as his banner. His army swelled into tens of thousands within weeks, fought and marched and faltered, and Hidalgo himself was captured and executed the following year. It matters because that morning in Dolores is the one Mexicans still celebrate every September as the beginning of their nation — the moment a parish priest took a huge country out of three hundred years of colonial rule.

michelangelo.context_blurb: Michelangelo Buonarroti was a Florentine sculptor who also painted, drew, built, and wrote poetry, and he did all of them at the highest level that his age had seen. He lived from 1475 to 1564, far longer than most of his contemporaries, and worked for a long line of popes who alternately adored and infuriated him. He grew up near the stone quarries of Carrara, where he said he had drunk marble dust with his wet-nurse's milk, and he always considered sculpture his true vocation, even when a pope dragged him by force onto a scaffold to paint a ceiling. His finished works were already treated as miracles in his lifetime: a free-standing marble figure of a biblical hero cut from a long-abandoned block in Florence, a Pieta in Saint Peter's with every fold of Mary's robe polished smooth as skin, the Sistine Chapel ceiling, the Last Judgment on the altar wall of the same chapel, and the dome of the new Saint Peter's basilica itself. He was a difficult man — proud, lonely, sometimes paranoid, driven by a severe private faith — and he fell into bitter quarrels with rivals and patrons for most of his life. He died in Rome at the age of eighty-eight, still at work on a sculpture, and his body was later smuggled quietly out of the papal city to be buried in his beloved Florence.

michelangelo-sistine-ceiling-and-david.context_blurb: Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475 to 1564) was an Italian Renaissance sculptor, painter, architect, and poet who worked in Florence and Rome during one of the greatest artistic flowerings in human history. He trained as a sculptor and considered sculpture his true calling, though he was repeatedly dragged into painting commissions by patrons whose power he could not refuse. His sculpture includes several figures that are among the most-reproduced images in Western art: an enormous marble figure of the biblical hero David, carved in his twenties from a block of marble Florentine sculptors had declared impossible, and a famous grieving mother with her dead son in St. Peter's in Rome. His painting commissions include the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Rome, where he spent four years lying and standing on scaffolding in the 1510s painting hundreds of figures from the opening chapters of the book of Genesis across the vault, and later the Last Judgment on the altar wall of the same chapel. In the last decades of his life he was also chief architect of the new St. Peter's Basilica. He wrote fine sonnets, lived frugally, served nine popes, and died in Rome at the age of 88. He is one of the handful of individuals in the Western tradition routinely called a universal genius.

ming-china-zheng-he-s-treasure-fleets-th.context_blurb: The Ming dynasty of 14th- to 17th-century China is one of the great flowerings of Chinese civilization, following the collapse of the Mongol Yuan and preceding the rise of the Manchu Qing. The Ming emperors moved the capital north from Nanjing to Beijing and built the enormous palace complex at the center of the city, with its courtyards, its gilt-roofed throne halls, and its surrounding moat, from which the dynasty was quietly ruled for over two centuries. Civil servants were selected through the famous examination system; porcelain-making, silk weaving, and printed book publishing reached new heights; and the Great Wall as we see it today was substantially rebuilt in the stone-and-brick form by Ming engineers. In the early 15th century, the Ming also sponsored a series of enormous overseas voyages under the Muslim eunuch admiral Zheng He, whose treasure fleets of hundreds of ships, including some of the largest wooden vessels ever built, sailed through Southeast Asia, India, Arabia, and the East African coast, exchanging ceremonial gifts and establishing diplomatic contact. The voyages were abruptly ended in the 1430s by a change in imperial policy — the court decided they were too expensive and too unsettling — and China turned inward for the next few centuries while European ships were just beginning to venture out.

ming-dynasty-the-forbidden-city.context_blurb: The Ming dynasty ruled China from 1368 to 1644, after overthrowing the Mongol Yuan dynasty, and marks a return to native Chinese rule after a century of foreign domination. The founder of the Ming, Hongwu, was a destitute peasant and former Buddhist monk who rose through the ranks of anti-Yuan rebel armies and ended up on the imperial throne, which is one of the great social-ascent stories in Chinese history. His son, the Yongle emperor, moved the capital from Nanjing in the south to Beijing in the north and built there a vast imperial palace complex that is still called the Forbidden City. Covering around 180 acres and containing hundreds of surviving buildings, the Forbidden City housed Ming and later Qing emperors and their enormous court staffs for nearly five centuries, until the last Qing emperor was deposed in 1912. The Ming is also the dynasty of the famous Zheng He treasure-fleet voyages, of the great flowering of Ming blue-and-white porcelain that was traded all over Eurasia, of the civil-service examination system at its mature form, and of the substantial rebuilding of the Great Wall in the stone-and-brick form that modern visitors see today. Ming authority finally collapsed in the mid-17th century under a mix of peasant rebellion, fiscal crisis, and northern invasion.

ming-voyages-of-zheng-he.context_blurb: Zheng He was a Chinese Muslim eunuch who, in the early 1400s, commanded seven staggering state-sponsored naval expeditions for the Ming dynasty. His fleets dwarfed anything Europe had afloat — hundreds of ships, tens of thousands of sailors and soldiers, and treasure junks on a scale that European captains two or three generations later would have found almost impossible to imagine. He sailed across the Indian Ocean to the Arabian coast and East Africa, received tribute from local rulers, and once brought back a wondrous foreign animal that courtiers at the imperial court delightedly re-identified as a creature out of ancient Chinese religious legend. Then a new emperor and a new faction decided the voyages were extravagant and distracting; the fleets were tied up and rotted at anchor, the great shipyards were closed, and a later Ming official is said to have made sure the technical records of what Zheng He had done were suppressed in a way that saved later emperors from the same temptation. China turned inward just as Europe was learning to sail out, and the exact gap between the two reversals is one of the great what-if questions of world history, endlessly argued over by economists and historians.

moctezuma-ii-and-the-spanish-conquest-of.context_blurb: Moctezuma II was the Aztec ruler, or Great Speaker, who was running the Aztec Triple Alliance's empire out of the capital Tenochtitlan when a small Spanish expedition under Hernan Cortes landed on the Gulf coast of Mexico in April 1519. Over the course of the next two years the Aztec state collapsed from the combined pressure of Spanish steel and gunpowder, horses, Spanish diseases to which the native population had no immunity, and — most important militarily — tens of thousands of Indigenous warriors from Tlaxcala and other city-states who hated Aztec rule and allied with the Spanish against them. Moctezuma was taken captive inside his own palace, held as a human hostage while the Spanish and their allies maneuvered against the city, and killed under disputed circumstances during a riot. The Aztecs elected successors and fought on, and Tenochtitlan fell only after a brutal siege that destroyed much of the city in August 1521. Cortes's lieutenant and chronicler Bernal Diaz del Castillo wrote one of the great firsthand accounts of the whole campaign, and his book is still the richest surviving window into what the fall of the Aztec Empire looked like from the inside.

mongol-empire-genghis-khan.context_blurb: In the early 13th century, a man known to history as Genghis Khan unified the fractious tribes of the Mongolian steppe under his personal leadership and then launched one of the most devastating sequences of conquest in human history. From roughly 1206 to the end of the century under his successors, Mongol armies conquered China, Persia, Central Asia, parts of Eastern Europe, Russia, Baghdad, and almost everything else between them, building the largest contiguous land empire ever assembled. The campaigns killed many millions of people and depopulated whole cities that had refused to surrender — Baghdad fell in 1258 with staggering slaughter, and the Mongols are said to have thrown so many books from the libraries into the Tigris that the river ran black with ink for days. The empire later fragmented into regional khanates and gradually assimilated into the cultures of the lands it had conquered: Islam in the west, Chinese administration in the east. The Mongols also opened up the Silk Road to safe travel in a period called the Pax Mongolica, during which the Mongol-held routes let goods, ideas, people — and probably the Black Death — flow across Eurasia on a scale not seen before. Genghis Khan's descendants include a significant fraction of modern Central Asian men by direct genetic descent.

mongol-threat-to-europe-subutai-1241.context_blurb: In the mid-13th century, a Mongol army under a brilliant veteran general swept out of the steppe, smashed one Christian army in Poland and another in Hungary within two days of each other, and found no force left in central Europe capable of standing against it. The Mongols fought with mounted archery, careful coordination between units, a sophisticated signal system, and tactical tricks that European heavy cavalry simply could not match. Chroniclers in both the Catholic and Orthodox lands at the time thought the end of the world had come, and the pope began desperately writing letters trying to find out who these people were and whether any messenger could reach the court of their Khan. Then, in a sudden stroke of luck no one in Europe understood at the time, the Mongol princes packed up their army and rode home. The reason lay thousands of miles away in the Mongol homeland, in a political development inside the Mongol royal family that mattered far more to the invaders than any Christian army ever could. The story covers the invasion, the tactics, the panic in Europe, and the specific chance event that saved western Christendom from a conquest that no western army of the time could have stopped.

monitor-versus-merrimack-ironclads.context_blurb: In early March 1862, during the American Civil War, the world of naval warfare changed in a single week in Hampton Roads, Virginia. The Confederacy had raised the burned hulk of a captured U.S. steam frigate from the mud of Norfolk harbor, armored its sides with iron plates, mounted guns in a sloped casemate, and sent it out as a new kind of ship — the ironclad CSS Virginia, which Northerners kept calling by its old wooden name of Merrimack. On its first day out it rammed and sank one Union wooden warship, set another ablaze, and seemed about to break the Union blockade. That night the Union's own hastily built experimental ironclad arrived — a strange low-slung craft designed by the Swedish engineer John Ericsson, with a single revolving gun turret on an almost-submerged deck. The questions ahead cover the vivid nickname Union sailors gave this odd little ship on sight, and what happened to a key weapon the Confederate ironclad used in its first day's attacks. The two ships fought to a draw the next morning in the first battle between ironclad warships in history. It matters because that one duel announced the end of the age of the wooden sailing warship — within a few decades every major navy would be building iron and steel ships with armored sides and rotating turrets.

montesquieu-and-separation-of-powers.context_blurb: Montesquieu, whose full title was Charles-Louis de Secondat, Baron de la Brede et de Montesquieu, was an 18th-century French judge and political philosopher who gave the modern world one of its most important political ideas. In 1748, after decades of work and travel, he published The Spirit of the Laws, a huge book that tried to understand how different kinds of government rise and fall, and what makes a country free. His most influential argument was that liberty is best preserved when the power to make laws, the power to enforce laws, and the power to judge laws are placed in different hands, so that each can check the others. His other great concern was the way the climate, customs, and inherited habits of a people shape its politics, which he argued no abstract system of government could ignore. Montesquieu lived quietly in the French countryside between trips to Paris, running an inherited estate and writing in a book-lined tower. He died in 1755. A generation later the men writing the United States Constitution would quote him more often than anyone except perhaps the Bible, and his central idea was built directly into the American government.

monteverdi-and-the-birth-of-opera-palest.context_blurb: Opera — a staged dramatic work set entirely to music — was invented in Italy around the year 1600 by a group of Florentine composers and theorists who were trying to recover what they thought ancient Greek drama had sounded like. The experiments produced the earliest surviving operas, including works by Jacopo Peri and Giulio Caccini. The composer who first brought the new form to full artistic maturity was Claudio Monteverdi (1567 to 1643), whose 1607 opera telling the story of a Greek legendary singer descending into the underworld to retrieve his dead wife is still regularly performed four hundred years later. Monteverdi later moved to Venice, where he wrote more operas, and the form took off: Venice built the first public opera houses in the 1630s, open to anyone who could pay for a ticket, and opera became a wildly popular European entertainment over the following two centuries. In the generation before Monteverdi, the Catholic Counter-Reformation composer Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina had quietly perfected the earlier polyphonic Mass tradition, writing music of extraordinary clarity that has been treated as the model of pure sacred polyphony ever since. Monteverdi and Palestrina between them bookend the moment when European music moved from a mostly church-centered tradition into a world that had both great sacred music and the new secular dramatic art of opera.

mosque-architecture-minaret-dome-mihrab.context_blurb: A mosque is a Muslim house of prayer, and most mosques around the world share a few common features that follow directly from the obligations of Islamic worship. A dome often marks the main prayer hall, both for acoustics and for a sense of enclosed sacred space. A tall slender tower called a minaret rises alongside, from which the five daily calls to prayer have traditionally been chanted out over the surrounding city, a tradition going back to a freed Ethiopian slave named Bilal who had been one of Muhammad's earliest companions and had the loudest and most beautiful voice. Inside the prayer hall, a wall niche called the mihrab marks the direction of Mecca, which Muslims are required to face when they pray, so that when a congregation lines up behind the imam all are oriented toward the Kaaba no matter where in the world they happen to be. The whole plan is spacious and open: there are no pews, no statues, and no central altar, and the floor is usually covered in rich carpets because the worshippers kneel directly on it, pressing their foreheads to the ground in a posture of absolute surrender that is also the literal meaning of the word 'Islam.'

mound-of-empires-end-atlantic-slave-trad.context_blurb: The transatlantic slave trade, which forcibly carried millions of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic between the 16th and 19th centuries, was built on top of a far older West and Central African internal slave trade that had operated for many centuries before European ships ever arrived on those coasts. African kingdoms, including Ghana, Mali, Songhai, Benin, Dahomey, Kongo, and the Asante confederacy, had long traded in captives taken in local wars and sold them north across the Sahara to the Islamic Mediterranean world or east to the Red Sea trade. When Portuguese ships began arriving on the West African coast in the mid-1400s, they plugged into these existing networks and shifted a growing share of their output west, across the Atlantic, to the sugar plantations and silver mines of the Americas. The African side of the trade was run by African merchants and African rulers who sold captives to European traders on the coast; European traders rarely penetrated far inland and almost always bought from existing suppliers. This fact is not an excuse for anyone involved in the trade; it is just the historical shape of it. The eventual abolition of the Atlantic trade in the early 1800s, led by evangelical Christian campaigners in Britain, was a Western moral breakthrough with few parallels in world history.

mozart-the-prodigy-composer.context_blurb: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (1756 to 1791) was an Austrian composer who was performing in European courts and composing original music by the age of five, who wrote his first opera at twelve and his first mature symphonies as a teenager, and who in his short thirty-five-year life produced an immense body of operas, symphonies, concertos, chamber music, sacred works, and keyboard music that stands at the center of the Western classical canon. He was taken on long concert tours across Europe as a child by his demanding musician father, performed for kings and empresses, and settled in Vienna in his mid-twenties, where he had chronic trouble managing money and chronic brilliance in managing music. His operas with the Italian librettist Lorenzo Da Ponte — The Marriage of Figaro, Don Giovanni, Cosi fan tutte — are three of the greatest ever written and are still performed constantly today. His last opera, The Magic Flute, premiered just weeks before his death. He died suddenly in late 1791 of an illness historians still debate, left unfinished a Requiem Mass commissioned anonymously by a mysterious stranger, and was buried in a common grave. His reputation only grew after his death. He is probably the single composer whose work most people have heard, often without knowing it.

mozart-vs-salieri-the-poisoning-myth-vs-.context_blurb: A persistent legend, popularized by Alexander Pushkin's 1830 verse-play and by Peter Shaffer's 1979 play Amadeus and the Oscar-winning 1984 film based on it, holds that Mozart's older Viennese contemporary and rival Antonio Salieri (1750 to 1825) poisoned Mozart out of jealousy over Mozart's superior genius. The legend is not true. Mozart and Salieri were both working composers in Vienna during the 1780s and early 1790s, and they were professional rivals in the normal sense that most composers in a shared city were, but there is no credible contemporary evidence that Salieri had anything to do with Mozart's death. Mozart's death in 1791 was almost certainly from a natural illness. Salieri lived another thirty-four years, taught several of the greatest musicians of the next generation (including Beethoven, Schubert, Liszt, and Hummel), and in his senile old age was tormented by rumors circulating in Vienna that he had killed Mozart. The myth survived because it made a satisfying story about mediocrity envying genius. Historians today have mostly rehabilitated Salieri's professional reputation. He wrote serviceable operas, trained most of the Beethoven-and-Schubert generation, and bore no responsibility for the premature death of his more famous younger colleague.

muhammad-and-the-origins-of-islam.context_blurb: Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570, orphaned young, and grew up in a merchant society where his reputation for honesty was so famous that his neighbors called him al-Amin, 'the trustworthy,' long before he claimed any prophetic mission. He married a wealthy older widow named Khadija, whose caravan business he had been managing, and she became his first wife and his first convert through the hardest early years of his teaching. Muslims hold that in the year 610, during a retreat on Mount Hira outside Mecca, the angel Gabriel came to him with the first words of what Muslims understand to be the Qur'an — the direct and uncreated speech of God — revealed to Muhammad over about twenty-three years. Persecution in Mecca grew so dangerous that in 622 Muhammad and his followers made a secret migration to the oasis town of Yathrib, soon renamed Medina ('the City'), and that journey, called the Hijra, is the event the Islamic calendar is still dated from today. From Medina the new community grew into a political and military power, returned to Mecca a few years later largely in peace, and by the time of Muhammad's death in 632 most of the Arabian Peninsula had accepted the new faith.

mummification-and-the-afterlife.context_blurb: The ancient Egyptians developed over the course of thousands of years one of the most elaborate funerary traditions in human history, driven by the central Egyptian conviction that the preservation of the body was essential to the continuing life of the soul in the afterlife. Egyptian embalmers removed the internal organs, which were preserved separately in canopic jars, dried the body with a specific natural salt for about forty days, treated it with resins and perfumed oils, wrapped it in many layers of linen bandages, placed amulets within the wrappings, and finally sealed it inside successive coffins — often nested — with a face mask covering the head. The whole process took around seventy days for a wealthy client. Burial goods accompanying the mummy included food, furniture, weapons, servants in model form, and papyrus scrolls containing spells to help the deceased navigate the underworld. The practice continued for over three thousand years with gradual changes in technique and iconography. Thousands of ancient Egyptian mummies survive today in museums, archaeological collections, and still-sealed tombs. Modern analytical techniques including CT scanning and DNA analysis have been applied to many of them to understand ancient Egyptian health, diet, kinship, and disease, which turns the mummies into unexpectedly rich scientific resources.

mussolini-and-fascist-italy.context_blurb: Benito Mussolini was an Italian politician who, in the political chaos following the First World War, built the Fascist movement out of a mix of nationalism, hostility to Marxism, veterans' resentment, and street violence. In October 1922, during the famous March on Rome, King Victor Emmanuel III invited Mussolini to form a government rather than resist the Fascist march with the Italian army. Over the following several years Mussolini turned a coalition cabinet into a one-party dictatorship. Fascist Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935, intervened on Franco's side in the Spanish Civil War, allied formally with Nazi Germany in the Pact of Steel in 1939, and entered the Second World War on the German side in June 1940 after France had already fallen.
