Italian military performance in the war was poor; Mussolini's armies lost in North Africa, Greece, East Africa, and the Balkans, and had to be repeatedly bailed out by German forces. In July 1943, after the Allied invasion of Sicily, Mussolini was arrested by Italian authorities and Italy switched sides. Mussolini was rescued by German commandos and installed as puppet ruler of a northern Italian collaborationist regime. In April 1945 Italian partisans captured, executed, and hung his body upside down in a Milan square. Fascist Italy ended with him.

nato-vs-warsaw-pact.context_blurb: The North Atlantic Treaty Organization was founded in April 1949 by the United States, Canada, Britain, France, and several smaller Western European states as a defensive military alliance against the possibility of Soviet aggression in Western Europe. The treaty's core provision stated that an armed attack on one member would be treated as an attack on all. West Germany joined NATO in 1955, and in response the Soviet Union organized its Eastern European satellite states into a parallel defensive alliance called the Warsaw Pact, named after the city where its founding treaty was signed. For the next thirty-six years, the two alliances faced each other across the Iron Curtain in central Europe, with hundreds of thousands of troops permanently stationed near the border, nuclear weapons deployed on both sides, and recurring crises in Berlin, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, and Poland. The Warsaw Pact dissolved in 1991 following the collapse of communist governments across Eastern Europe. NATO survived the end of the Cold War, admitted most of the former Warsaw Pact states as new members over the following two decades, and currently includes thirty-two member states. Its article defining an attack on one as an attack on all has been invoked exactly once in its history, in support of the United States after the attacks of September 11, 2001.

navajo-code-talkers.context_blurb: During the Pacific War, the United States Marine Corps recruited several hundred Navajo men to serve as battlefield communications specialists, using the Navajo language — which had never been systematically written down and which almost no non-Navajo speakers knew — as the basis for a secure field code. Navajo is a complex Native American language with sounds and grammatical structures very different from English, Japanese, or any other language the Japanese code-breaking services would have resources trained to attack. The Navajo recruits developed a specialized vocabulary of Navajo words substituting for military terms the base language did not naturally have (iron fish for submarine, metal turtle for tank, and so on), memorized the vocabulary, and operated the radios in combat. The Code Talkers served in every major Marine operation in the Pacific from Guadalcanal onward and were in heavy use at Iwo Jima, where several Code Talkers worked around the clock during the first days of the invasion. The code was never broken by the Japanese. The entire program was kept classified for decades after the war, which meant the Code Talkers could not talk publicly about their own service. In 2001, Congress awarded gold medals to the original Code Talkers, acknowledging a crucial contribution that had been quietly carried for over fifty years.

nazi-ghettos-warsaw-ghetto-uprising.context_blurb: After the German conquest of Poland in 1939, the Nazi regime began forcing the Jewish populations of Polish cities into sealed urban districts called ghettos, in preparation for later deportation to the extermination camps. The Warsaw Ghetto, the largest, was sealed off in November 1940 with over four hundred thousand Jews packed into a small walled area that normally held perhaps 160,000 people. Starvation and disease killed tens of thousands within the ghetto in the following two years. In the summer of 1942 the Germans began deporting the ghetto's inhabitants to the Treblinka extermination camp, where they were killed on arrival. By early 1943 only about sixty thousand Jews were left in the ghetto. On April 19, 1943, when the Germans entered the ghetto to begin the final deportation, the Jewish fighters of the Jewish Combat Organization and the Jewish Military Union, led by the twenty-three-year-old Mordechai Anielewicz, resisted with homemade weapons and smuggled firearms. The Germans eventually crushed the uprising only by systematically burning the ghetto to the ground over four weeks of brutal fighting. The uprising inspired other smaller Jewish armed revolts in Vilna, Bialystok, Treblinka, Sobibor, and Auschwitz-Birkenau over the following year, and it is remembered as a defining moment of Jewish resistance to the Holocaust.

nazi-ideology-and-the-nuremberg-laws.context_blurb: The Nuremberg Race Laws of September 1935 turned the Nazi Party's anti-Semitism from street violence into state law. The two statutes stripped German Jews of equal legal standing and criminalized any marriage or romantic relationship between a Jew and a non-Jewish German. Nazi ideology taught that the German people were a racially pure 'Aryan' nation whose blood was being contaminated by Jewish presence, and in the four years that followed the Nazi state built an elaborate legal machinery to classify Germans by their grandparents in order to tell who was 'really' which. Children were given school textbooks and anti-Semitic picture books that taught them to spot Jews as if they were a hidden danger among their neighbors. On the night of November 9-10, 1938, Nazi party thugs smashed Jewish shops, synagogues, and homes across Germany and Austria in a nationwide pogrom now remembered by a chilling one-word name; the Nazi state then punished the Jewish community collectively for the damage its own thugs had done. All of this was the ideological runway from which the Holocaust would take off beginning in 1941. The Nuremberg Laws themselves would be entered as evidence after the war at the Nuremberg war-crimes tribunals, where the surviving leaders of the regime that had passed them were tried for the crimes those laws had made legal.

nazi-soviet-molotov-ribbentrop-pact.context_blurb: In August 1939, less than two weeks before the German invasion of Poland that started the Second World War in Europe, Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union signed a formal non-aggression pact. The pact was negotiated and signed in Moscow by the German foreign minister Joachim von Ribbentrop and the Soviet foreign minister Vyacheslav Molotov. On its public face, the pact simply committed the two countries not to attack each other for ten years. A secret protocol attached to the pact divided Eastern Europe between the two signatories into spheres of influence: Germany would get western Poland, the Soviet Union would get eastern Poland, the Baltic states, Finland, and parts of Romania. The pact shocked the world, since the two regimes had been ideological enemies, with Nazi Germany officially anti-communist and Soviet Russia officially anti-fascist, and it specifically removed the possibility of a Western-Soviet alliance against Germany that the British and French had been halfheartedly exploring. The pact lasted less than two years. In June 1941 Hitler broke it with his massive invasion of the Soviet Union. The pact's existence was publicly denied by the Soviet Union throughout the Cold War and officially acknowledged only in 1989, five decades after it had been signed.

nazi-soviet-pact-of-1939.context_blurb: In the summer of 1939 Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union — the two bitterest ideological enemies in Europe — stunned the world by signing a non-aggression pact. Josef Stalin had spent much of the decade warning that fascism was the deadliest enemy of socialism, and Adolf Hitler had built his career on anti-Bolshevism, so Western diplomats had assumed the two could never reach a deal; Stalin's foreign minister Vyacheslav Molotov and Hitler's foreign minister Joachim von Ribbentrop proved them wrong, signing the agreement in Moscow on August 23 at a dinner where the two sides toasted each other with grim enthusiasm. The public text of the pact promised only that neither state would attack the other for ten years, but there was a secret protocol attached — one the Soviet Union would deny existed for the next fifty years — in which Hitler and Stalin privately settled their accounts over the independent countries of eastern Europe. Nine days later Hitler invaded Poland from the west, and seventeen days after that the Red Army invaded Poland from the east. The war Stalin had helped arrange turned on him in June 1941, when Hitler broke the pact and sent three and a half million soldiers into the Soviet Union — and Stalin, who had refused for weeks to believe the warnings, was for a moment stunned into silence.

negative-rights-vs-positive-rights-what-.context_blurb: The rights listed in the American Declaration of Independence — life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness — are what later political theorists call negative rights. A negative right is a right to be left alone by others, including by the government: a right not to be killed, a right not to be imprisoned without cause, a right not to be prevented from pursuing your own vision of the good life as long as you do not harm anyone else. Negative rights do not require anybody else to actively give you anything; they only require everyone else to refrain from attacking you. A positive right is a right to have something provided by somebody else: a right to housing, a right to healthcare, a right to a job. Positive rights require the active labor and resources of other people to deliver what they promise. The founders' rights were explicitly negative in form, which is one reason the United States Constitution and the Bill of Rights are mostly a list of things the government may not do rather than a list of things the government must provide. The deeper claim behind the word unalienable is that negative rights are built into what a human being is, by the Creator, and no government can hand them to anyone or take them away.

nero-caligula-and-the-mad-emperors.context_blurb: After the death of Augustus, the Roman Empire was ruled by a line of related emperors called the Julio-Claudian dynasty, and two of them became infamous as cautionary examples of what absolute power can do to an unstable man. The first, who ruled briefly from AD 37 to 41, had been a popular young prince while his father served as a general in the German wars; his childhood nickname came from the little army boots he had worn around the camps. In office he became wildly cruel and extravagant and was finally murdered by his own bodyguards. The second, who ruled from AD 54 to 68, was Augustus's great-great-grandson and started out well enough under careful tutors, but as he aged he grew paranoid, murderous, and theatrical, performing on stage like a professional actor and treating serious state business as a sideshow. Rome famously suffered a huge fire during his reign, and he blamed and executed a scapegoat group with gruesome public cruelty. He died running from his own officers, saying the world was losing an artist. The two of them became the archetypes everyone else was measured against when later writers wanted to describe a tyrant losing his mind.

new-weapons-of-wwi.context_blurb: World War I turned Europe's industrial muscle on itself and produced a wave of terrifying new weapons that transformed battle forever. In April 1915 the Germans opened canisters of poison gas along the Ypres salient, and the heavy cloud rolled across no-man's-land into French colonial trenches, killing men by the hundreds and setting off a race in gas and gas-masks that would see mustard gas, phosgene, and other horrors deployed by both sides. In September 1916 the British sent out the first battlefield tanks — strange armored boxes that could crawl over trenches and rolled wire. In the air, both sides worked out how to mount machine guns on their new fighter planes in a way that could fire straight ahead through the spinning propeller without shredding the blades, a problem the Dutch designer Anthony Fokker solved for the Germans with an elegant mechanical device. Along the ground the machine gun itself mowed down whole lines of attackers walking across open ground, and by 1918 the shape of modern mechanized war — gas, tanks, aircraft, automatic weapons — was almost all in place, waiting for the engineers of the next war to perfect it. The casualties these weapons produced were on an industrial scale: whole generations of young men in Britain, France, Germany, and Russia were killed, maimed, or psychologically broken.

new-world-crops-potato-maize-tomato.context_blurb: Thousands of years before Europeans arrived, indigenous farmers in the Western Hemisphere bred a stunning array of foods from wild plants that would eventually reshape every cuisine on Earth. Three in particular changed Europe and Asia almost beyond recognition. One root crop could feed more people per acre than any European grain and grew in cold, thin, mountainous soil where wheat would not; after a slow start — European farmers eyed it with suspicion for a century because its above-ground parts belong to a plant family some of whose relatives are notoriously toxic — it became the staple of Ireland, Prussia, and much of eastern Europe. A tall golden grain long farmed on the plains, often planted together with beans and squash in a traditional companion-planting system, became the backbone of African, Italian, and southern U.S. cooking. A bright red fruit the Italians at first eyed with suspicion is now so central to Italian cuisine that it is hard to picture pizza or pasta without it. All three left their birthplace during the great post-Columbus exchange of plants and animals, and all three were on dinner tables worldwide within two centuries. Their global success is one of the clearest answers to the question of what humanity actually gained from the collision of the Old World and the New.

north-africa-and-el-alamein.context_blurb: The North Africa campaign of the Second World War ran from 1940 to 1943 across the desert of what is now Libya and Egypt, with Italian and German Axis forces fighting British Commonwealth and later American and Free French Allied forces for control of the Suez Canal and the oil of the Middle East. The German commander was the gifted general Erwin Rommel, whose maneuvering tactics with his Afrika Korps earned him the nickname the Desert Fox. In the autumn of 1942, after a series of back-and-forth campaigns across the desert, British Commonwealth forces under General Bernard Montgomery decisively defeated Rommel at the Second Battle of El Alamein in Egypt. The battle was one of the first major Allied victories of the war on land. A few days later, American and British forces landed in French-held Morocco and Algeria in Operation Torch, catching the Axis forces in Tunisia between two Allied armies. By May 1943 all Axis forces in North Africa had surrendered, with over two hundred and fifty thousand prisoners captured — a loss comparable to Stalingrad for the German war effort. The Allied victory in North Africa cleared the way for the invasion of Sicily and then Italy later in 1943.

north-korea-the-prison-state.context_blurb: The Democratic People's Republic of Korea, the northern Korean state established in 1948 under Soviet-backed communist leader Kim Il-sung, has become one of the most closed and most repressive regimes in the world. For over seventy-five years, three successive generations of the Kim family — Kim Il-sung, his son Kim Jong-il, and his grandson Kim Jong-un — have ruled the country under a Stalinist system reinforced by a bizarre family cult of personality, with the founder's embalmed body kept on permanent display in the capital Pyongyang like Lenin's. The country runs a system of political prison camps where entire families, including children, are imprisoned for the alleged offenses of a single relative. Thousands die in these camps every year, and some have operated continuously for over fifty years. Famine during the mid-1990s killed somewhere between hundreds of thousands and three million North Koreans while the regime diverted resources to its military and its nuclear weapons program. North Koreans who successfully defect to the south describe a system of total information control, mandatory propaganda ceremonies, caste-like classifications of citizens by family political history, and executions for watching foreign television. North Korea is one of the clearest ongoing moral indictments of twentieth-century communism, and the regime shows no signs of reforming.

nuclear-arms-race-mad.context_blurb: The United States first developed and used atomic weapons at the end of the Second World War in 1945. The Soviet Union, aided by espionage against the American Manhattan Project, tested its own atomic bomb in 1949, far earlier than most American analysts had expected. The two superpowers then raced each other through the development of the far more destructive thermonuclear hydrogen bomb in the early 1950s, and through the development of intercontinental ballistic missiles that could deliver nuclear warheads from one superpower's territory to the other's in roughly thirty minutes. By the 1960s both sides had assembled nuclear arsenals large enough to effectively destroy each other's societies. This stalemate was often described by the acronym MAD, for Mutually Assured Destruction, and the uneasy logic held that neither side would start a nuclear war because retaliation was certain. The arsenals continued to grow through the 1970s and 1980s, with ultimately tens of thousands of warheads on each side, until a series of arms-control treaties beginning with the SALT agreements of the 1970s and continuing with the START treaties of the 1990s brought the totals down. Several close calls — crises, false alarms, misinterpreted radar signals — have survived in declassified records to remind us how close MAD came to collapsing.

nuremberg-trials.context_blurb: In November 1945, six months after Germany's surrender, an international military tribunal set up by the Allies at the German city of Nuremberg began the trial of twenty-two of the senior surviving leaders of the Nazi regime for crimes against peace, war crimes, and crimes against humanity. The chief prosecutor was the United States Supreme Court Justice Robert H. Jackson, who had taken a leave of absence to lead the American team. The trials ran for nearly a year, used both documents captured from German archives and testimony from survivors, and produced convictions on various charges for most of the defendants; twelve were sentenced to death and hanged in October 1946. A parallel series of twelve subsequent trials prosecuted lower-ranking Nazi officials — doctors who had conducted human experiments, judges who had enforced Nazi racial laws, SS officers, industrialists — over the following years. A separate International Military Tribunal for the Far East, held in Tokyo, tried Japanese wartime leaders on similar charges. The Nuremberg Trials established in international law the principle that individual officials can be held personally responsible for crimes against humanity, even when they claim to have been following orders. The idea has shaped international justice and the modern International Criminal Court.

olmec-civilization-and-the-colossal-head.context_blurb: The Olmecs are generally regarded as the mother culture of Mesoamerica, the first great civilization in that part of the world. They flourished in the humid lowland rainforest of what is now the Mexican Gulf Coast from roughly 1500 BC to 400 BC, in a region that no later Mesoamerican civilization would use as a political center. They built large ceremonial centers at San Lorenzo and La Venta with earthen platform mounds, carved jade figurines, and worked soft greenstone into exquisite small objects. Their most famous works, though, are the enormous basalt sculptures of human heads — portraits probably of specific rulers — carved from boulders that had to be dragged more than fifty miles overland from the nearest basalt source. The heads weigh many tons each, wear a distinctive helmet-like headgear, have strongly individualized faces, and are a baffling technical achievement for a culture without metal tools or wheels. The Olmecs' art, their ritual ballgame, their pantheon, their calendar, and their chocolate-drinking all passed down to the Maya, the Toltecs, and the Aztecs who followed them, which is why we treat Olmec civilization as the common root of the whole Mesoamerican tradition.

operation-barbarossa.context_blurb: On June 22, 1941, Nazi Germany invaded its former pact partner the Soviet Union in the largest military operation in human history, code-named Operation Barbarossa. Three million German soldiers plus hundreds of thousands of Finnish, Romanian, Hungarian, Italian, and Slovak allies crossed the border along a 1,800-mile front, aiming to destroy the Soviet state before winter. German armored columns advanced hundreds of miles into Soviet territory in the first six months, encircling and destroying huge Soviet armies. The Germans came within sight of Moscow in late 1941 but were turned back in brutal winter weather by a Soviet counteroffensive and by the first serious signs of German overstretch. The war on the Eastern Front dragged on for nearly four more years and became the deadliest ground theater in human history, killing somewhere around twenty-seven million Soviet soldiers and civilians along with several million Germans. The Soviet winter counteroffensive at Moscow, the Soviet victory at Stalingrad in late 1942 and early 1943, and the enormous tank battle at Kursk in the summer of 1943 broke the German army. From then on the Red Army steadily pushed west, finally reaching Berlin in late April 1945. The Eastern Front broke Nazi Germany militarily.

origins-of-parliament-the-english-common.context_blurb: Over the course of the 13th century, English kings who needed money for their wars began summoning not only their great lords and bishops but also elected representatives from the shires and the market towns to a formal assembly whose Norman-French name simply meant a place where people came to speak. One powerful rebel earl, who had married into the royal family and quarreled with the king, briefly held his captured royal brother-in-law hostage and expanded the assembly in a way that pointed clearly toward the common-born lower chamber of a modern parliament. He was eventually run down and killed in battle by the heir to the throne, in a fight where even his own son could not reach him in time with reinforcements, but the idea he helped plant kept growing. Within a few decades, English kings had accepted that major taxation needed the consent of this new body, and over the following centuries the lower and upper chambers slowly turned from an occasional royal tool into a permanent part of English government. Modern parliaments all over the world trace a line back to this prickly English experiment in binding kings to the voices of their subjects. The story covers the quarrel, the battle, the famous shout from the royal brother-in-law hiding in a mill, and the moment the dead rebel's grave quietly became a secret pilgrimage site for the English common folk who had hoped he was going to speak for them against the king.

parthenon-and-the-greek-architectural-or.context_blurb: The classical Greek temple is one of the most-copied building forms in human history, and the specific vocabulary of columns, capitals, and friezes that Greek architects worked out between the 7th and 5th centuries BC is still being used by builders today. The Greeks developed three main architectural orders, each with its own column proportions, its own capital design at the top, and its own moldings. The most famous example of classical Greek temple architecture is the great marble temple on the acropolis of Athens, built in the mid-5th century BC under the leadership of Pericles during the city's golden age. Its architects were Iktinos and Kallikrates. Its sculptural program was overseen by Phidias, the greatest Greek sculptor of the classical age, who directed teams of carvers to produce friezes, pediments, and metopes that are still studied as high points of the Greek achievement. The temple also housed inside it an enormous gold-and-ivory statue of the city's patron goddess, over thirty feet tall, which is lost to history. The three orders were taken over by the Romans, who used them on nearly every public building across their empire, and through the Romans they entered the Renaissance, the Neoclassical movement, and the modern Western public-building tradition.

pasteur-germ-theory-and-vaccines.context_blurb: Louis Pasteur was a French chemist, born in 1822, whose work across the second half of the nineteenth century helped establish that many diseases are caused by microscopic organisms — and that those organisms can be deliberately weakened and used to protect people and animals against the diseases they cause. He was not the first person to suggest a 'germ theory' of disease, but he was the one whose careful experiments, dramatic public demonstrations, and gift for persuading governments and the press convinced most of the medical and scientific world. His career was built on a running fight with an older view called spontaneous generation, which held that microscopic life could arise fresh from broth or decaying matter. The questions ahead cover his famous public outdoor demonstration of a livestock vaccine, the first time he used an experimental vaccine on a human child who had been exposed to a terrifying infectious disease, what visitors to a research institute built in his honor can still see, the clever glassware experiment with which he answered his spontaneous-generation rivals, and a modern historical charge that one of his most celebrated triumphs was less original than he claimed. It matters because germ theory and vaccination together are among the few single ideas in human history that have measurably added decades to the average human life.

paul-revere-s-ride-lexington-and-concord.context_blurb: On the night of April 18, 1775, two silversmiths-turned-messengers from Boston, Paul Revere and William Dawes, rode out of the city on separate routes to warn the Massachusetts militia that British troops were marching west out of Boston to seize rebel-held military stores at Concord and probably to arrest the patriot leaders Samuel Adams and John Hancock, who were staying in Lexington. By the time the British column reached Lexington at dawn on April 19, local militia under Captain John Parker were drawn up on the village green. Shots were exchanged — nobody has ever quite established which side fired first — and eight militiamen were killed. The British column marched on to Concord, where more militia had gathered, found most of the military stores already moved, and skirmished at the North Bridge. On the long march back to Boston, thousands of militia from surrounding towns swarmed the retreating British column, firing from behind stone walls and farm buildings. The British made it back to Boston but took heavy casualties. The day became the opening battle of the American Revolution, and Paul Revere's night ride, immortalized decades later by a famous Longfellow poem, became one of the founding scenes of the American story.

pearl-harbor.context_blurb: On the morning of Sunday, December 7, 1941, carrier-based aircraft of the Imperial Japanese Navy launched a surprise attack on the United States Pacific Fleet moored at Pearl Harbor on the island of Oahu in Hawaii. The attack came in two waves and lasted less than two hours. It sank or damaged most of the American battleships at anchor, destroyed hundreds of American aircraft on the ground, and killed around 2,400 American sailors, soldiers, Marines, and civilians. The American aircraft carriers, which the Japanese had hoped to catch at anchor, had been at sea when the attack came and escaped undamaged. The attack was intended by the Japanese planners to buy time for Japan to consolidate its planned conquests across Southeast Asia and the Western Pacific. Its political effect was the opposite. The attack unified an American public that had been deeply divided about involvement in foreign wars, and the following day President Franklin Roosevelt asked Congress for a declaration of war against Japan, which Congress passed with only one dissenting vote. Nazi Germany declared war on the United States a few days later. The United States had entered the Second World War, and the war against Japan continued for nearly four more years.

pericles-and-the-golden-age-of-athens.context_blurb: Pericles was a 5th-century BC Athenian aristocrat, general, and political leader who dominated Athens during the city's most spectacular period — the generation after the Greek victory over Persia and before the long war with Sparta. He was elected to the chief Athenian military office year after year for most of three decades. Under his leadership, Athens turned its anti-Persian league into a tribute-paying maritime empire, financed a huge rebuilding program on the Athenian acropolis including the greatest temple of the age, patronized the tragedians and philosophers whose work still defines the Greek achievement, and settled into direct democracy as a working form of government. His famous funeral oration for the Athenian war dead at the start of the Peloponnesian War — preserved by the historian Thucydides, who had heard it in person — is one of the great statements of what a free self-governing people can be. Pericles died in 429 BC of the plague that struck Athens in the second year of the war, and after his death the city's leadership passed to less skillful hands. Classical Athens never quite had another figure like him.

phillis-wheatley-poet-of-the-founding-er.context_blurb: Phillis Wheatley was a young African girl who was kidnapped from somewhere in West Africa, probably Senegambia, around the age of seven, transported to Boston in 1761 on the slave ship Phillis (from which she was given her first name), and purchased by a Boston merchant and his wife as a house slave. The Wheatley family, who were unusual for their time, taught her to read and write both English and Latin and quickly recognized a remarkable literary talent. By her teens she was writing accomplished poetry in the style of her 18th-century English contemporaries, and in 1773 she became the first African American and the first enslaved person in the English-speaking world to publish a book of poetry, titled Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral. The book had to be printed in London, in part because colonial American publishers refused to believe a young enslaved African woman had actually written the poems. Wheatley was emancipated shortly after her book appeared, married a free Black man in Boston, bore three children (all of whom died in infancy), and died herself in poverty in 1784 at around the age of thirty-one. George Washington had praised her verse. Her life is one of the most extraordinary stories of the founding era.

phoenician-sea-traders-and-tyre-s-purple.context_blurb: The Phoenicians were a seafaring Semitic people whose homeland was a string of city-states along the eastern Mediterranean coast of what is now Lebanon, Syria, and northern Israel. From roughly 1200 BC through the fifth century BC, Phoenician merchants dominated eastern Mediterranean shipping, trading from one end of the sea to the other and establishing colonies as far west as the Atlantic coast of Spain and Morocco. Their most famous colony, Carthage in modern Tunisia, would eventually become a Mediterranean superpower in its own right. The Phoenicians were best known for several specific products of their trade. One was a particular purple dye extracted at enormous labor from a specific sea snail native to their coast, which produced a deep reddish-purple color so expensive it was reserved for royalty and the clothing of senior officials; the dye gave its name to a Greek word for red and eventually to the Phoenicians themselves. Another was glass; the Phoenicians were among the earliest systematic glass producers in the Mediterranean. The Phoenicians also carried the alphabet across the Mediterranean, where the Greeks adopted and modified it into the common ancestor of nearly every alphabet now in use in Europe and the Americas. Their home cities were eventually conquered by the Persians and later by Alexander the Great.

picasso-and-cubism.context_blurb: Pablo Picasso (1881 to 1973) was a Spanish painter and sculptor who moved as a young man to Paris and became the single most influential artist of the 20th century. In the first decade of the century, working closely with the French painter Georges Braque, he developed a radical new way of representing objects in painting that broke them into geometric facets and showed them from multiple viewpoints at once on a single flat surface. This method became known as Cubism, and it was the key moment in the Western abandonment of straightforward pictorial perspective that had ruled painting since the Renaissance. Picasso went through many styles across his very long career — a melancholy Blue Period, a warmer Rose Period, Cubism, Neoclassical figures in the 1920s, Surrealist-influenced work, late free-wheeling painting in his seventies and eighties — and he was prolific in painting, sculpture, ceramics, prints, drawings, and stage design. His 1937 painting Guernica, done in response to the German-Italian bombing of a small Spanish town during the Spanish Civil War, is one of the most famous political paintings ever made. His personal life was volatile and his treatment of several of the women in his life was by all accounts cruel, and his legacy is now routinely argued over on moral as well as artistic grounds. His art still fills major museums worldwide.

pizarro-and-the-conquest-of-the-inca.context_blurb: Francisco Pizarro was an aging, illiterate Spanish adventurer from the hog-farming town of Trujillo who, after years of failed probing voyages down the Pacific coast of South America, finally landed in Inca territory in 1532 with only a tiny band of men. He walked straight up into the mountains to meet Emperor Atahualpa, who had just come out on top of a long and devastating political fight whose character and length were themselves a crucial piece of what gave Pizarro his opening. At a tense meeting in the town of Cajamarca, a Spanish friar demanded Atahualpa submit to the Pope and the Spanish king; the emperor refused. Pizarro's hidden gunners opened fire, cavalry rode into the unarmed royal retinue, and by nightfall the emperor was a prisoner. Atahualpa offered a staggering ransom to buy his freedom; the Spanish collected it, melted it down, and then killed him anyway. Pizarro went on to seize the Inca capital of Cuzco, and years later was murdered in his own house by rival Spaniards squabbling over the loot. The Inca state he toppled had been, until very recently, one of the largest and best-organized political structures on Earth, and the strange story of how a few hundred men brought it down fascinated European readers for centuries afterwards.

pizarro-and-the-spanish-conquest-of-the-.context_blurb: Francisco Pizarro was a Spanish adventurer who, with a tiny force of fewer than two hundred men, destroyed the Inca Empire of Peru between 1532 and 1533. He had heard rumors in Panama of a wealthy Andean civilization to the south, and he and his companions set out to find it. They arrived at the extremely bad time, for the Inca, of a brutal civil war that had just ended between two half-brothers claiming the imperial throne, with the winner, Atahualpa, still consolidating control. Pizarro met Atahualpa with a show of friendship in the mountain town of Cajamarca in late 1532, then ambushed him, slaughtered his unarmed retinue, and held the emperor hostage for an enormous ransom in gold and silver that the Inca duly collected and paid. The Spanish then killed Atahualpa anyway, marched on the capital of Cusco, installed a puppet ruler, and spent the following decades fighting Inca resistance and each other over the loot. Smallpox, which had reached the Andes just before Pizarro and killed the previous Inca ruler and his heir, did more damage to the empire than the Spanish ever could have on their own. The whole episode is one of the most brutal and consequential collisions in human history.

plato-the-academy-and-the-republic.context_blurb: Plato was a 4th-century BC Athenian aristocrat who became the most influential philosopher of the ancient world. As a young man he was devoted to the older philosopher Socrates, and after Socrates was executed by the Athenian democracy in 399 BC, Plato set himself to writing dialogues featuring his master in conversation with contemporaries. He founded a school just outside Athens, on grounds dedicated to a local hero, that gave later Western languages a word still in use for high learning. Over the next forty years he wrote a long series of philosophical dialogues on nearly every subject the Greeks cared about: justice, courage, love, beauty, piety, knowledge, art, politics, mathematics, and the nature of reality. His most famous book is a long dialogue imagining an ideal city-state built on strict justice and ruled by philosophers; the book has been admired, imitated, attacked, and repudiated ever since. His student Aristotle disagreed with him on nearly every major question, and the two of them between them set the agenda for Western philosophy for the next two thousand years. The 20th-century British philosopher Alfred North Whitehead famously said that all of Western philosophy is a series of footnotes to Plato.

polar-exploration-amundsen-peary-shackle.context_blurb: In the roughly thirty years on either side of 1900 — the so-called 'Heroic Age' of polar exploration — small teams of men on skis, with sledges and dog teams or ponies, raced each other to the two ends of the Earth. The Norwegian Roald Amundsen was the most ruthlessly competent of them, a cold-eyed planner who prepared obsessively, learned from Inuit survival craft, and won the race to the geographic South Pole in December 1911, beating the British Royal Navy captain Robert Falcon Scott by about a month. All five of Scott's men died on the return journey, roughly eleven miles short of their next food depot, in weather so bad that one of them famously walked out of the tent into a blizzard rather than slow the others down. The American Robert Peary claimed in 1909 to have reached the North Pole, a claim that is still disputed. The Anglo-Irish explorer Ernest Shackleton, having failed to reach the South Pole first, set out instead to cross the whole Antarctic continent in 1914-16; his expedition ran into terrible trouble before they ever set foot on the continent, and the story of how he brought every single one of his twenty-seven men home alive is one of the great survival epics of modern times. The era essentially ended with the aircraft, which could overfly the poles in hours instead of years and spoiled the whole kind of adventure.

policy-of-appeasement-and-munich-1938.context_blurb: By 1938 Adolf Hitler had already remilitarized the Rhineland and absorbed Austria, and in the summer of that year he demanded that Czechoslovakia surrender a strip of its borderland to Germany, where several million ethnic Germans lived. The British prime minister Neville Chamberlain, a 69-year-old provincial industrialist who had come to the premiership determined to avoid another world war, flew three times across Europe to meet Hitler in person — a kind of personal diplomacy no British prime minister had ever attempted — and finally brought back from a four-power conference in Munich in late September a signed agreement in which Britain, France, and Italy handed Hitler what he wanted at the expense of the Czechoslovak state. Chamberlain stepped off his plane at Heston Aerodrome waving the signed paper and declared he had secured, in a famous phrase, exactly the opposite of what the next twelve months would prove. The Czechoslovak president Edvard Benes had resigned in protest; his successor Emil Hacha was summoned to Berlin six months later and coerced into formally handing over the rest of his country overnight. Winston Churchill denounced the agreement in the House of Commons as a surrender, and when war did come in September 1939 Chamberlain's reputation never recovered.

polynesian-wayfinding-settling-the-pacif.context_blurb: Between roughly 1500 BC and AD 1300, the Polynesians settled the vast triangle of the Pacific Ocean reaching from Hawaii in the north, to New Zealand in the southwest, to Easter Island in the southeast — an area several times the size of the entire United States, almost all of it ocean. They did it in double-hulled sailing canoes, provisioned with chickens, pigs, dogs, breadfruit, taro, and yams, and they did it by reading the ocean itself. Polynesian navigators learned by apprenticeship to read the stars at night, the direction and length of ocean swells beneath their canoes, the flight patterns of seabirds, the colors of water, cloud shapes forming over invisible islands, and dozens of other subtle environmental cues. They did not use magnetic compasses, charts, or chronometers, and yet they repeatedly found tiny specks of land hundreds and thousands of miles across empty water. The art of Polynesian wayfinding nearly died in the 19th and 20th centuries as Western navigational technology took over, but a small group of Micronesian masters, especially the Caroline Islands navigator Mau Piailug, preserved it, and in the 1970s a Hawaiian canoe called the Hokule'a sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti by traditional methods, proving that the old knowledge still worked and setting off a Polynesian cultural revival that is still going.

pompeii-and-the-eruption-of-vesuvius-79-.context_blurb: In the late summer of AD 79, a volcano in the Bay of Naples on the west coast of Italy erupted catastrophically and buried several nearby Roman towns, including Pompeii and Herculaneum, under meters of ash and rock. The event killed thousands of people and preserved an entire slice of ordinary Roman life — houses, bakeries, graffiti, mosaics, workshops, meals half-eaten on tables, and the bodies of the dead frozen in place — exactly where they fell. The eruption was described in a letter by a young Roman named Pliny the Younger, whose uncle (a famous naturalist) died trying to help in the rescue. His letters are the only eyewitness account of the eruption that survives, and they describe the famous cloud of ash shaped like a certain Mediterranean tree. Nearly two thousand years later, archaeologists have slowly uncovered the buried towns, and techniques invented in the 1800s let them cast the shapes of the dead in the hollows the ash left behind. Pompeii has become our clearest window into daily Roman life because its destruction was so sudden that almost nothing was taken away or tidied up before it froze in time.

potos-silver-mountain.context_blurb: In 1545 a shepherd on an Andean peak in what is now Bolivia built a small fire to warm himself through a freezing night, and in the morning saw a thin stream of melted silver running out from under the coals. The mountain, Cerro Rico, turned out to be the richest silver deposit the world had ever seen. The Spanish Crown drove a boomtown of up to 160,000 people onto a thin-aired slope higher than any major city in Europe, and for two centuries the stamped silver coins minted there were the first truly global currency, spent from Manila to Antwerp to Boston. Spanish writers of the age piled lavish nicknames on the place, and ordinary Spanish speech even picked up a phrase meaning 'as rich as that one city.' The men who dug the silver out, pressed into service under a system of state-enforced rotating labor service that had deep local roots long before the Spanish adopted and brutalized it, called the same mountain by a far grimmer nickname that captured what the work actually cost; by some estimates it swallowed millions of lives over its working life, through cave-ins, mercury poisoning in the refining sheds, and the sheer altitude.

prague-spring-1968.context_blurb: In the spring and summer of 1968, Czechoslovakia under its reform-minded Communist Party leader Alexander Dubcek embarked on a program of political liberalization that promised, in Dubcek's famous phrase, socialism with a human face. Censorship was relaxed, public political debate opened up for the first time in two decades, and Czech and Slovak citizens briefly experienced something close to normal civic life. The Soviet Union and its hardliner Warsaw Pact allies were deeply alarmed. In August 1968, Soviet, East German, Polish, Hungarian, and Bulgarian forces invaded Czechoslovakia overnight to put a stop to the reforms. The Czechoslovak army did not resist; ordinary civilians instead stood in the streets, confronted the invading tanks, and tried to argue the soldiers out of their mission. Hundreds of people were killed in the aftermath, and the reforms were systematically rolled back. Dubcek was eventually removed and the hardliner Gustav Husak installed in his place. The 1968 invasion was an enormous propaganda defeat for Soviet communism in Western Europe and helped sever the few remaining ties between Western European communist parties and Moscow. Czechoslovakia itself did not escape Soviet-style rule for another twenty-one years, when the Velvet Revolution of 1989 finally brought it democracy and later divided it into the Czech Republic and Slovakia.

pre-columbian-monumental-art-maya-aztec-.context_blurb: The civilizations of the pre-Columbian Americas produced some of the most spectacular large-scale art and architecture in human history, often without wheels, draft animals, or iron tools. The Maya of lowland Central America built hundreds of stepped stone pyramid-temples, royal palaces, and ritual ball courts across their city-states, decorating them with carved stelae telling the hieroglyphic histories of their divine kings. The Aztecs of central Mexico built the enormous twin-shrined Templo Mayor in the center of their capital Tenochtitlan, carved the massive Sun Stone, and sculpted hundreds of ritual objects in a style whose intensity still unsettles modern viewers. The Olmecs along the Gulf of Mexico carved enormous individualized stone heads of their rulers from basalt boulders dragged dozens of miles overland from distant mountains. Far out in the South Pacific, the people of the small island of Rapa Nui carved enormous stone human figures — massive heads and torsos with long solemn faces — and dragged them across their island to a line of ceremonial platforms along the coast. All of these traditions produced monumental sculpture and architecture at a scale that European observers in the 16th and later centuries had trouble believing was really the work of the local population. Modern archaeology has confirmed over and over that it was.

prince-henry-the-caravel-and-navigation-.context_blurb: Prince Henry of Portugal, nicknamed the Navigator by much later writers, was a younger son of King John I and brother of the future King Edward of Portugal. He lived from 1394 to 1460, and from the Portuguese Atlantic coast at Sagres he patronised, financed, and personally pushed a long campaign of seaborne exploration down the western coast of Africa. He never captained a ship himself; the voyages were made by captains in his service, backed by his revenues as governor of the Order of Christ. In his lifetime Portuguese ships rediscovered the Madeira Islands, reached the Azores, and finally forced their way past a dreaded African cape that had defeated every previous captain, opening the rest of the continent's western coast to further exploration. The ships that made this possible were a new kind of light, shallow-draught vessel of a design that could point much higher into the wind than any older European craft, and the navigators used improved versions of older instruments to measure the Sun's noon altitude for latitude as they sailed into unfamiliar southern waters. By the time Prince Henry died, his sailors had reached Sierra Leone; a generation after his death Portuguese ships had rounded the southern tip of Africa and found the sea road to India. Several of the most familiar stories about Prince Henry — the kind told in older schoolbooks about an institute he supposedly ran at Sagres — have been quietly dismantled by careful modern historians.

prince-henry-the-navigator-sagres.context_blurb: Prince Henry of Portugal, the king's third son, never captained a ship himself and never sailed much farther than a short hop down his own coast. What he did, from the 1420s until his death in 1460, was bankroll an age. From a windswept Portuguese cape he gathered mapmakers, Arab geographers, Jewish mathematicians, veteran sea captains, and shipwrights, and sent small Portuguese vessels one after another a little farther down the long African coastline. Each captain pushed past the headland the previous captain had reached, charted the water, brought back notes on winds and currents, and sometimes brought back enslaved Africans too, which is one of the darker inheritances of his project. By the time Henry died his ships had reached modern Sierra Leone, Portuguese sailors trusted the Atlantic as no Europeans ever had, and the ocean-going vessel that would carry Columbus, Dias, and da Gama had been quietly perfected in the shipyards he funded. The men who later made the famous named voyages all stood on groundwork he had put down a generation earlier. Prince Henry showed, maybe for the first time in European history, how much a committed royal patron with a long-term plan and a research institute of his own could change the shape of what humanity thought possible.

prince-shotoku-early-japan-yamato-nara.context_blurb: Prince Shotoku was a 7th-century AD Japanese imperial regent — formally serving under his aunt the empress Suiko — who is traditionally credited with laying the foundations of the Japanese imperial state. He ruled during the Asuka period, just as Japan was being transformed by massive cultural borrowing from Tang China and the Korean kingdoms. Shotoku promoted the adoption of Buddhism, which had recently arrived in Japan, built major temple complexes including the famous Horyu-ji with its ancient wooden pagoda still standing today, promulgated a seventeen-article moral and administrative constitution for his officials, and sent official embassies directly to the Sui dynasty in China to study its government. He is remembered as one of the great statesmen of early Japan, though some modern scholars have questioned how many of the deeds traditionally attributed to him were really his and how many were later invention. The following Nara period, named after the imperial capital at Nara from 710 to 794, consolidated the Chinese-style imperial state Shotoku had helped set in motion, built the great seated bronze Buddha at Todai-ji, and launched the long Japanese tradition of adapting continental Asian learning into native forms.

prohibition-and-the-gangster-era.context_blurb: In January 1920 the Eighteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution took effect, banning the manufacture, sale, and transportation of 'intoxicating liquors' across America, and for fourteen years the country tried to go dry. Americans mostly refused — demand for alcohol stayed high, and the trade simply went underground, giving rise to hidden drinking establishments in city back-rooms, bootleggers who smuggled liquor in from Canada and the Caribbean, and organized criminal gangs that fought one another for the money. The most notorious of these gangsters was Al Capone, who ran Chicago from a suite at the Lexington Hotel and whose men gunned down seven members of a rival gang in a North Side garage on Valentine's Day 1929 in a mass killing that shocked the country. A federal strike force led by a young Prohibition agent named Eliot Ness kept raiding Capone's breweries, but it was actually a different federal case, built on a wholly separate line of evidence, that finally sent Capone to prison on Alcatraz. President Franklin Roosevelt and Congress repealed Prohibition in 1933 by passing the Twenty-first Amendment, the only amendment in American history that undid another amendment. The organized criminal networks the dry years had financed, however, did not go away.

ptolemy-and-the-geocentric-universe.context_blurb: Claudius Ptolemy was a Greek-speaking astronomer, mathematician, and geographer who worked in Roman Alexandria around 150 AD. He gathered up centuries of Babylonian and Greek observations of the sky and bundled them into a single enormous mathematical textbook, in Greek, that set out a complete working model of the heavens. In his model the Earth stood motionless at the centre of the universe, and everything else — Sun, Moon, planets, fixed stars — moved around it on nested circular paths. To make the circles actually match the wandering motions real observers saw, Ptolemy stacked several clever geometric adjustments on top of the simple picture, each with its own technical name in later astronomy textbooks. His system was mathematically ingenious and good enough to predict eclipses and planetary positions for well over a thousand years. The book was translated into Arabic in the ninth century, where it picked up a short new nickname that stuck with it in every language afterwards, and then into Latin in medieval Spain, where it dominated European astronomy until Copernicus. Ptolemy also wrote a landmark Geographia that mapped the known world using latitude and longitude, and the standard treatise on ancient optics. He was not himself an observer of the first rank; he was a brilliant systematiser of other people's data.

pythagoras-and-his-theorem.context_blurb: Pythagoras was a 6th-century BC Greek thinker from the island of Samos who ended up founding a religious-philosophical-mathematical community in a Greek colony in southern Italy. The group he founded was secretive, lived a shared ascetic life, believed in the transmigration of souls, had strict rules including a famous rule against eating beans, and treated mathematics as a form of religious contemplation. The theorem that still bears his name — the one relating the three sides of a right triangle — may actually have been known in some form in older civilizations like Babylon, but the Pythagoreans gave it a strict proof and attached it to a much bigger idea: that numbers are the hidden structure of reality. The Pythagoreans are also credited with the discovery that musical intervals correspond to simple ratios of string length, which was one of the first times a precise mathematical pattern was shown to underlie a physical phenomenon. Pythagoras himself wrote nothing that survives, and almost everything we know about him comes from later writers. His followers were persecuted and scattered, but their blend of math, music, and metaphysics flowed into Plato and from Plato into the whole Western tradition.

qin-shi-huang-china-s-unification.context_blurb: After centuries of civil war between competing Chinese states during the Warring States period, in 221 BC a brutally efficient ruler from the western state of Qin finished off his rivals and declared himself the First Emperor of a unified China. He is known to history by the title Qin Shi Huang, which means roughly the First Qin Emperor. He abolished the old feudal states, divided the empire into administrative districts, standardized the Chinese script into a single written form, standardized weights, measures, and even axle widths for carts so that they would fit the same ruts in the roads. He connected and extended the existing frontier walls of the northern states into an early version of what would centuries later become the Great Wall. His administration was ruthless; he suppressed dissenting schools of philosophy, buried alive hundreds of Confucian scholars according to tradition, and burned books across the empire. He also commissioned a vast underground mausoleum for himself in which, among countless other treasures, an entire buried army of life-sized terracotta soldiers, horses, and chariots was placed to guard him in death — rediscovered by Chinese farmers digging a well in 1974. The Qin dynasty collapsed within a few years of the first emperor's death, but his unification of China survived him, and every later Chinese dynasty built on his template.

queen-victoria-and-the-british-empire-at.context_blurb: Queen Victoria of the House of Hanover came to the British throne in 1837 at the age of eighteen and reigned until her death in 1901. During her sixty-four years as queen, Britain built the largest empire in human history — a quarter of the land surface of the globe and nearly a quarter of its population — and the Industrial Revolution reshaped British life more thoroughly than any century before. She married her German cousin Prince Albert in 1840, had nine children with him, and through their marriages wove the British royal family into most of the continent's thrones. After Albert's early death in 1861 she withdrew from much of public life for a long time before returning to it as a symbol of national continuity. The questions ahead cover the clever argument about where to put a giant iron-and-glass exhibition hall during her 1851 Great Exhibition, two famous nicknames the public gave her, how passers-by once intervened during an assassination attempt against her, and the way one such attempt reshaped the English law of criminal insanity. It matters because 'Victorian' became shorthand for a whole British century — moralistic, confident, industrial, and imperial — whose debates about progress, poverty, and empire the world is still having.

quetzalcoatl-the-feathered-serpent.context_blurb: Quetzalcoatl, whose name in the Nahuatl language of the Aztecs means roughly feathered serpent, was one of the great divine figures of Mesoamerican religion. He was imagined as a plumed, scaly serpent god associated with the morning star, wind, learning, priesthood, and the civilizing arts of agriculture and writing. He appears in various forms across Mesoamerican history, under different names in different cultures. The Maya worshipped a feathered serpent god Kukulkan at Chichen Itza, whose temple is deliberately designed so that at the spring and fall equinoxes a snake-shaped shadow slides down its staircase. The Toltecs centered a cult of Quetzalcoatl at their city of Tula and told stories of a legendary priest-king of the same name who left in disgrace. The Aztecs told a related story in which the god departed by sea toward the east and would someday return. The Spanish conquistadors later convinced themselves, perhaps with Aztec encouragement, that this old legend had led the Aztecs to mistake them for the returning god, but modern scholars treat that part of the story as a self-flattering myth the Spanish constructed afterward. The feathered serpent himself was older and bigger than any of these specific moments.

quipu-the-inca-knotted-string-records.context_blurb: The Inca Empire ran a vast and complicated bureaucracy across a thousand-mile long swath of the Andes without a conventional writing system. Instead the Inca state kept its records on quipus — bundles of cords of different colors, with carefully placed knots of different kinds at specific intervals along each cord. A trained quipu reader, called a quipucamayoc, could record and recall information about census populations, tribute obligations, state storehouses, military rosters, calendars, and historical events, all encoded in the arrangement of knots and the colors and lengths of cords. The Spanish, when they arrived, were astonished at what the quipu-readers could reconstruct from a bundle of knotted strings, and some early Spanish administrators used quipus as valid legal records in court. Thousands of quipus survive in museum collections, and modern researchers can decode the numeric information encoded in the knots — large numbers in a base-ten system, with position of knots indicating place value. Whether the quipus also encoded narrative information, as some Spanish accounts suggest, is still debated. The Inca ran one of the ancient world's largest organized states using what was essentially a three-dimensional knotted spreadsheet.

ramesses-the-great.context_blurb: Ramesses II, often called Ramesses the Great, was an Egyptian pharaoh of the Nineteenth Dynasty who ruled for nearly sixty-seven years in the thirteenth century BC and is remembered as one of the most powerful pharaohs of the New Kingdom period. He conducted a long and famous military campaign against the Hittite Empire in Syria, including the great Battle of Kadesh around 1274 BC — a chariot battle so important that both sides claimed to have won, and the surviving Egyptian-Hittite peace treaty signed afterward is one of the oldest formal international treaties whose text has come down to us. Ramesses was also a prolific builder. He constructed or added to temples all over Egypt, including the vast temple complex at Karnak, the huge mortuary temple called the Ramesseum on the west bank of the Nile at Thebes, and the astonishing rock-cut temples at Abu Simbel in the far south of Egypt, carved directly into the sandstone cliffs with enormous seated statues of himself at the entrance. He fathered an enormous number of children, lived to about ninety, and outlived many of his heirs. Some scholars have proposed Ramesses II as the pharaoh of the Hebrew Exodus, though the identification is far from certain and scholarly debate continues.

rape-of-nanjing.context_blurb: During the Second Sino-Japanese War, the Imperial Japanese Army captured the Chinese capital of Nanjing (then usually spelled Nanking in English) in December 1937. Over the following six weeks, Japanese soldiers conducted one of the worst mass atrocities of the twentieth century against the city's defeated garrison and the surrounding civilian population. Estimates of the Chinese dead range widely — most mainstream Chinese and international historians place the total somewhere between 100,000 and 300,000 killed, with widespread mass rape of Chinese women by Japanese soldiers, systematic looting, and arson across the city. The atrocity was documented at the time by several Western missionaries, journalists, and businessmen who had stayed in the city and who established a safety zone that saved tens of thousands of Chinese civilian lives. One of them, a German Nazi Party member named John Rabe, became one of the main protectors of Chinese civilians during the massacre, in a strange historical irony. Japanese nationalist writers have repeatedly tried to deny the scale or the systematic character of the massacre in the decades since the war, and it remains a sharp historical wound between modern China and modern Japan. Several of the Japanese military officers responsible were tried and executed by the postwar Tokyo War Crimes Tribunal.

raphael.context_blurb: Raffaello Sanzio, usually called Raphael in English, was a High Renaissance Italian painter who died tragically young and was adored almost without rival in his short lifetime. He was born in Urbino in 1483 to a court painter who gave him his first training, lost both parents in his boyhood, and apprenticed with the painter Perugino before moving on to Florence as a young man. In Florence he studied the two great masters working in the city at that moment, and his own portraits and Madonnas quickly began to rival theirs. Pope Julius II called him to Rome in 1508, and the next twelve years were a continuous whirlwind: huge frescoes for the pope's own apartments, including a famous fresco of a gathering of all the greatest ancient Greek philosophers, altarpieces, portraits of cardinals, and the oversight of a huge studio of apprentices. He died on his thirty-seventh birthday in April 1520, almost certainly of fever, and the city of Rome went into real mourning — cardinals and ambassadors standing in the streets, and the pope himself reportedly reduced to tears. He was buried in the ancient Pantheon, where his tomb sits still, carrying an epitaph that credits him with having outmatched Nature herself at her own game. Later ages treated him for a long time as the perfect painter, the one no student could hope to surpass, and his gentle Madonnas and clear-eyed philosophers have never gone out of the Western visual bloodstream.

reagan-s-evil-empire-the-coalition-that-.context_blurb: Ronald Reagan was elected the 40th president of the United States in 1980 and reelected by a landslide in 1984. He came into office with an explicit intention of winning the Cold War rather than merely containing it. In 1983 he gave a famous speech in Orlando, Florida, to the National Association of Evangelicals in which he called the Soviet Union, in blunt and widely criticized terms, an evil empire — a phrase that outraged much of the American foreign-policy establishment but delighted Soviet dissidents, who later said it had restored their confidence that someone in the West still understood the actual nature of their regime. Reagan combined moral clarity about communism with large increases in American military spending, support for anti-communist movements from Afghanistan to Poland to Nicaragua, and the development of advanced defensive missile technology that strained Soviet resources trying to match. He also, importantly, developed over the second half of his presidency a working personal relationship with the Soviet reformer Mikhail Gorbachev, who became general secretary in 1985. The coalition Reagan led — in cooperation with Margaret Thatcher of Britain, Pope John Paul II, and various European allies — contributed significantly to the fall of the Soviet bloc in 1989 to 1991, within just a few years of his second term.

reason-deism-and-religion-in-the-enlight.context_blurb: The Enlightenment is often painted as a war between reason and religion, but the reality is messier and more interesting. Many of the great thinkers of the 1600s and 1700s — Newton, Pascal, Locke, Boyle, Faraday later — were deeply religious, convinced that the universe was the orderly handiwork of a lawgiving Creator and that studying it was a form of worship. Others, including Voltaire and Thomas Jefferson, drifted into Deism, a half-way position that accepted a Creator who had set the universe going but doubted miracles, revelation, and the Christian claims about Jesus. A few, especially in revolutionary France, went all the way into atheism and tried to invent new, secular replacements for religion. In England and America, Christianity and the Enlightenment largely coexisted; in France, they went to war. The relationship between faith and reason during this period shaped the modern world, including the American founders' commitment to religious liberty and their refusal to establish any one church as a state religion. The ideas that came out of this long argument are still being argued over today, which is itself a sign of how big the questions were.

reconstruction-and-the-reconstruction-am.context_blurb: Reconstruction is the roughly twelve-year period after the American Civil War, from 1865 to 1877, in which the United States tried to decide what it had just become. Four million formerly enslaved people were suddenly free; eleven former Confederate states were out of the Union and had to be let back in; the plantation economy was ruined; and the federal government for the first time had to answer, in law, what it meant to be a citizen. Congress wrote three Constitutional amendments — often called the Reconstruction Amendments — and passed a wave of civil rights legislation. For a short time Black men voted in large numbers across the South, were elected as sheriffs, state legislators, and members of Congress, and sent the first Black Americans to the United States Senate. Then white terror organizations, Supreme Court decisions, and the political bargain that ended Reconstruction gradually undid most of it, ushering in a long era of segregation and systematic voter suppression. The questions ahead cover what each of the Reconstruction Amendments actually did, a broken promise about land for freed people, a notorious night-riding organization and the strange title given to its first leader, a pre-war Southern politician's biography, violent episodes used to intimidate Black voters, legal fights over racial classification and public accommodations, dodges invented to keep Black men from the ballot, a famous dissent that rejected those dodges, and a line from Frederick Douglass about the ballot. It matters because the arguments and amendments of Reconstruction remain the legal and moral backbone of American civil rights to this day.

redrawing-the-map-of-europe.context_blurb: The peace settlements that ended World War I redrew the map of Europe more thoroughly than any treaty since 1815. Four old multinational empires went out of existence — Germany lost her monarchy, and the Russian, Austro-Hungarian, and Ottoman empires broke up altogether — and over the next several years negotiators at Paris, Trianon, Saint-Germain, Neuilly, and Sevres carved new state boundaries out of their fallen territory. The guiding principle, in theory, was Woodrow Wilson's idea of national self-determination — that peoples should rule themselves — but the small print of each treaty was shaped by the Allied powers' strategic interests, by the demands of newly resurrected states for defensible frontiers, and by the simple fact that ethnic populations across central and eastern Europe had long lived mixed together, village by village. The settlement set the shape of interwar Europe, and the political tensions it created would be exactly what Adolf Hitler would exploit a generation later. The Ottoman settlement was handled separately in the 1920 Treaty of Sevres, which was essentially torn up by the new Turkish nationalist government under Mustafa Kemal and replaced in 1923 by the Treaty of Lausanne — the only peace treaty of the postwar settlement that one of the losing powers successfully renegotiated by force of arms. For the next twenty years ethnic Germans, Hungarians, Poles, Jews, Ukrainians, and others would quarrel bitterly over who really owned the new borderlands.

religious-liberty-at-the-founding-virgin.context_blurb: One of the great practical innovations of the American founding was the way it handled the historically explosive problem of religion in politics. In colonial America, religious establishment — a specific denomination officially supported by the government and funded by taxes — had been the normal arrangement in most colonies, though actual religious pluralism was growing on the ground. During the Revolutionary period, several states, led by Virginia under the influence of Thomas Jefferson and James Madison, began to disestablish their state churches and move toward full religious liberty. The Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, drafted by Jefferson and pushed through the Virginia legislature by Madison in 1786, is one of the clearest statements in Western history of the principle that no citizen should be forced to support any religious belief by law or taxes, that no one's civic rights should depend on religious views, and that religious belief is a matter between a human being and God in which the state has no competence. The First Amendment to the United States Constitution, ratified in 1791, applied the same two principles to the federal government: Congress may neither establish a religion nor interfere with the free exercise of one. This settlement is one of the deepest American contributions to modern politics.

rembrandt-dutch-golden-age.context_blurb: Rembrandt van Rijn (1606 to 1669) was the greatest Dutch painter of the 17th-century Dutch Golden Age, when the newly independent Dutch Republic was running a global trading empire out of Amsterdam, Rotterdam, and other merchant cities. The Dutch bourgeois market for art was unlike anything previously known in Europe — small merchant households wanted paintings on their walls, and the market demanded portraits, landscapes, still lifes, scenes of daily life, and small religious works rather than huge altarpieces for cardinals. A whole generation of specialist painters supplied the demand, and Rembrandt stood at the top. He produced hundreds of paintings, drawings, and etchings, including large group portraits of civic guards and surgical dissections, intimate biblical and mythological scenes, and an extraordinary series of self-portraits painted at every age from his twenties until just before his death. His use of light and dark, his willingness to leave much of his canvas in deep shadow, and his sense of the ordinary human face as a subject worthy of the most serious painting have influenced artists ever since. His personal life was marked by financial failures and the deaths of a wife and children, and he died in poverty. His paintings are now some of the most valuable in the world, and his etchings are quietly among the greatest ever made.

renaissance-humanism-petrarch.context_blurb: Francesco Petrarca — known in English as Petrarch — was a 14th-century Italian scholar, poet, and letter-writer who is traditionally called the father of Renaissance humanism. He was born in 1304 in Arezzo, lived in Avignon in southern France as a young man, and spent most of his adult life hunting for forgotten Latin manuscripts in European monastery libraries, visiting scholars, and writing an enormous volume of correspondence in beautiful classical Latin to friends across the Continent. He wrote love poetry in Italian too, 366 polished sonnets and songs addressed to a mysterious woman he called Laura, which gave later Italian poets the forms they would still be using three centuries later. But his lasting influence was in another direction. Petrarch and the scholars who followed him argued for a particular program of adult study, taking its models from a very specific period of the past and setting itself against the heavy learned Latin of the medieval universities. This program became known as 'the studies of humanity,' and the people who did it called themselves humanists. By the time Petrarch died in 1374 the movement he had helped launch was already running in cities across Italy, and it would reshape European education for the next four centuries.

renaissance-reformation-music-as-western.context_blurb: Church and court music during the Renaissance and Reformation was one of the quiet masterpieces of Western civilization. Across the 15th and 16th centuries, composers in Rome, Flanders, Venice, Paris, and London worked out the techniques of polyphony — intricate many-voiced choral music — to a level that would set the standard for serious Western composition for the next five hundred years. In Catholic Italy, a Roman composer named Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina wrote hundreds of masses and motets so pure in their counterpoint that his music was treated as a touchstone by generations of later composers. In Protestant England, royal chapel composers like Thomas Tallis and his younger pupil William Byrd kept writing extraordinary sacred music even as the English Reformation changed what the words were allowed to be. Lutheran Germany sang hymns in the pews for the first time, including Luther's own 'A Mighty Fortress Is Our God,' and that tradition would eventually flower into Johann Sebastian Bach, two centuries later. All of this music was tied to the Christian liturgy; it was written to glorify God and to be sung by a trained choir in a stone-walled chapel. Modern listeners who stumble across it in a cathedral or on a recording often say it is the most beautiful music they have ever heard.

renaissance-science-as-the-work-of-belie.context_blurb: The Renaissance and Reformation also produced the first stirrings of modern science, and the men who built it were, almost without exception, serious religious believers who understood themselves to be reading the second book that God had given the world — the book of Nature. Nicolaus Copernicus, a quietly Catholic Polish cathedral canon, proposed that the Earth moved around the Sun. The eccentric Danish Lutheran astronomer Tycho Brahe built the greatest observatory of the age, catalogued the stars by naked-eye measurement with unmatched precision, discovered a new star in 1572 that astonished every astronomer in Europe, and lived at his island observatory with a small court of eccentrics around him. Tycho's German Protestant assistant Johannes Kepler, a man of deep piety and relentless mathematical imagination, worked out that the orbits of the planets are not perfect circles, worked out mathematical laws linking a planet's distance from the Sun to how long its year is, and wrote a strange imaginative book that his own mother was briefly accused of witchcraft over. Galileo pointed the first good telescopes at the sky. Isaac Newton — raised in strict Protestant England — would eventually tie all of this together into a single physics. Modern readers sometimes miss that none of these men saw their work as a rebuke of their Christian faith; they thought they were doing the work for it.

righteous-rescuers-schindler-wallenberg.context_blurb: During the Holocaust, a small number of non-Jewish rescuers across occupied Europe risked their own lives to shelter and save Jewish neighbors, friends, and strangers from Nazi deportation. The State of Israel formally recognizes these rescuers through a program called the Righteous Among the Nations, which has honored over twenty-seven thousand individuals from more than fifty countries. The most famous include Oskar Schindler, a German industrialist and Nazi Party member who used his munitions factories in Poland and the Czech lands to shelter and protect roughly 1,200 Polish Jews from the extermination camps, bribing SS officers and bankrupting himself in the process; his story was told in Thomas Keneally's novel Schindler's Ark and Steven Spielberg's 1993 film Schindler's List. Raoul Wallenberg was a Swedish diplomat posted to Budapest in 1944 who issued Swedish protective passports to tens of thousands of Hungarian Jews, saving most of them from deportation; he was arrested by the advancing Soviet army in January 1945 and disappeared into Soviet custody, never to be heard from again. Chiune Sugihara, a Japanese consul in Lithuania, issued thousands of transit visas to Jewish refugees against his own government's orders. The quiet moral courage of these rescuers stands as a counterweight to the mass complicity of the age.

rise-of-islam-expansion-to-europe-s-edge.context_blurb: In the early 7th century, a merchant in a dusty Arabian trading town began receiving what he said were revelations from the one true God. In the space of a single lifetime he and his companions founded a new religion, built a new state around it, and launched a wave of conquests that in the century after his death would stretch from the Atlantic coast of Africa to the borders of India.
