The armies of this new faith took Spain within a few years of crossing from Africa, pushed north into Gaul, and crossed into southern Italy. In the east they besieged the great Christian city on the Bosphorus more than once but could not take it, and that failure helped set the eastern border of Christian Europe for centuries. The religion that came out of all this is still, today, one of the two largest in the world. The story covers its origin and its earliest sacred cities, the first word a tradition says the angel spoke to the Prophet, and the two famous places where the furthest reach of this early wave of expansion was finally and definitively held. It also covers the long aftermath of the first century of expansion, as a frontier settled across the Pyrenees, across the Mediterranean, and in time across the mountains between Anatolia and the Balkans, where Christian and Muslim rulers would meet, fight, trade, and translate each other for the rest of the Middle Ages.

rise-of-medieval-towns-guilds-commerce.context_blurb: After about the year 1000, Europe's long contraction reversed, and towns began to grow again along rivers, coasts, and crossroads. Towns bought charters from local lords and kings that let them run their own courts, markets, and militias, and over time a famous saying grew up in Germany about the special status a man gained after living inside a town's walls for a year and a day without being reclaimed by his old lord. Inside each town, craftsmen organized themselves into sworn guilds that controlled training, prices, and quality, and that often ran the town itself. A young apprentice who had served his years would produce a special test-piece to prove he had the skills of a full master in his craft, and only on that piece being accepted could he become a master in his own right. Merchants banded together into trading leagues that stretched from the Baltic to the Atlantic. The story covers the sworn oaths that founded towns, the long path a young craftsman took through apprenticeship to mastery, the long-distance trading leagues, and the saints, statues, and festivals the townsfolk made their own. The story covers the sworn urban communities, the apprentice-to-master path through a craft, the long-distance merchant networks that linked those towns, and the central role the king or emperor played above all of them as the ultimate guarantor of their new charters and new freedoms.

rise-of-militarist-japan.context_blurb: Through the 1920s and 1930s Japan drifted from a cautious parliamentary system into aggressive militarism, driven by a rising officer corps that believed Japan had been shortchanged at the Versailles conference and needed an empire of its own in East Asia. In September 1931 officers of Japan's Kwantung Army, stationed to protect the South Manchuria Railway, blew up a section of their own track outside Mukden and blamed the sabotage on Chinese soldiers; the fake incident gave them the pretext to seize all of Manchuria. The League of Nations condemned the invasion and the Japanese delegation walked out of the Assembly in response. The militarists kept pushing: in Tokyo in February 1936 a group of radical young army officers tried to assassinate the senior civilian cabinet and nearly succeeded, and in July 1937 a confused incident at the Marco Polo Bridge outside Beijing turned into a full-scale invasion of China that would last eight years. The invasion's lowest moment came that December when the Japanese army, after capturing the then-capital Nanking, massacred and raped the city's civilians over about six weeks in a horror that the world would later call the Rape of Nanking. Despite the mountain of evidence, high-ranking Japanese officers would mostly escape the postwar war-crimes tribunals for what had been done in China.

rise-of-mussolini-and-italian-fascism.context_blurb: Benito Mussolini started his political life as a left-wing socialist newspaper editor; his father, himself a socialist, had named him after a nineteenth-century political hero he admired. World War I turned Mussolini into a nationalist — he broke with his old party over Italy joining the war, and after the war he formed a new political movement in Milan in 1919 that took its name and emblem from the ancient Roman symbol of magisterial power and threw its early street fights against both communists and strikers. Mussolini's Blackshirts fought their way into power in October 1922 when columns of them converged on Rome demanding the government, and the Italian king, Victor Emmanuel III, invited Mussolini to form a cabinet rather than confront the march with the army. Once in office Mussolini pushed through a new election law that gave the leading party a huge legislative majority, and when the socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti rose in parliament to denounce Fascist violence, Mussolini's thugs made him disappear — a political murder that nearly brought the regime down but did not. Mussolini declared his dictatorship openly in 1925, and he himself coined the term 'totalitarianism' for the kind of all-encompassing state he was building. His foreign adventures — Ethiopia, Spain, Albania, and finally alliance with Nazi Germany — would end in his death at the hands of Italian partisans in 1945.

rise-of-stalin-and-the-ussr.context_blurb: After Lenin's death in 1924 Joseph Stalin outmaneuvered his rivals — most importantly Leon Trotsky, who was exiled and later murdered — and by about 1929 held unchallenged power over the Soviet state. His first great project was to force the Soviet Union through industrialization and the collectivization of agriculture at breakneck speed: he set wildly ambitious Five-Year Plans, built whole new industrial complexes from scratch, and sent the peasantry's grain abroad to pay for imported machinery while millions starved. He also launched a drive to celebrate heroic workers who overfulfilled their quotas, giving propaganda cover to men like the Donbas coal miner Alexei Stakhanov. In the 1930s Stalin turned on his own party in a wave of show trials and purges, dragging old Bolsheviks before the courts to confess invented crimes before being shot in NKVD cellars; a cruel secret policeman widely feared in those years ran the worst of the killings on Stalin's orders. By the time the Great Terror of 1937 and 1938 had run its course, hundreds of thousands of ordinary Soviet citizens — soldiers, engineers, teachers, Communist Party members, kulaks, ethnic Poles, ethnic Koreans — had been shot. The Austrian economists Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek had argued in print during the 1920s that any economy under central planning would run into a fundamental problem of knowledge; the famines, labor camps, and executions that filled the Soviet 1930s were, in their reading, the predicted outcome.

robert-boyle-and-the-birth-of-chemistry.context_blurb: Robert Boyle was a 17th-century Anglo-Irish nobleman, natural philosopher, and devout Christian who is often called the father of modern chemistry. He was born in 1627 as the youngest son of one of the richest men in Ireland, which gave him the rare freedom to spend his life doing experiments. He built an air pump with his assistant Robert Hooke that let him suck the air out of a glass chamber, and he used it to perform some of the most important experiments of his age, including the one that established the inverse relationship between the pressure of a gas and its volume. Boyle was also one of the first people to insist loudly that alchemy's secret mystical talk should give way to clear, repeatable experiments reported in plain language. He was a founding member of the Royal Society of London and funded Bible translations into Irish, Welsh, Turkish, and Malay with his own money, because he believed science and Christian mission were two faces of the same reverence for creation. He died in 1691 and left funds for an annual lecture series on natural theology that still runs under his name.

robin-hood-the-outlaw-legend.context_blurb: Somewhere in late medieval England, in ballads sung in markets and taverns rather than in the official chronicles, a legend grew up around a cheerful outlaw who lived in a great forest with a band of merry men, robbed the rich, gave to the poor, and defied a crooked local law officer and the grasping regent of an absent crusading king. The historical seed of the legend, if there is one, is lost in the woods. But the story ran: a yeoman archer and his companions, a fat and pious friar, a towering sidekick, and a loyal love, kept the common folk's idea of fairness alive against a bad government. In England, where law and the state really did sometimes seem to be on the side of the strong against the weak, this fantasy of a greenwood outside the king's writ was so popular that it eventually gave English the generic noun for a particular kind of thief, the kind who steals from the rich to give to the poor. The story covers both the legend and the famous legend of how its hero shot his last arrow from his sickbed and used the landing of that arrow to decide where he would be buried.

rodin-and-modern-sculpture-the-thinker.context_blurb: Auguste Rodin (1840 to 1917) was a French sculptor whose work, straddling the end of the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th, is often described as the start of modern sculpture. He trained in Paris but struggled to establish a reputation, failed admission to the main French sculpture school three times, and spent much of his early career as an assistant and ornamental sculptor. His breakthrough came in the 1870s with a near-life-sized male nude so realistic that critics accused him of having cast it from a live model. He went on to produce some of the most famous sculptures of the modern era: a seated nude male figure of a man thinking, originally designed as part of a huge unfinished bronze doors commission based on Dante's Inferno; a group of six civic hostages from a besieged French town during the Hundred Years' War; a famous eroded figure of a passionate kiss. Rodin broke with the smooth polished finish of academic Neoclassical sculpture, letting rough tool marks and partial surfaces show, which was shocking in his age and became standard practice afterward. His influence on sculpture at least into the mid-20th century — on Bourdelle, Maillol, Brancusi, and others — was enormous.

roentgen-and-the-x-ray.context_blurb: Wilhelm Conrad Roentgen was a German professor of physics at the University of Wurzburg in Bavaria. In the autumn of 1895 he was experimenting in a darkened laboratory with a sealed glass tube that fired electrons across a vacuum, a kind of apparatus physicists everywhere had been playing with for years. He had wrapped the tube in black cardboard to shut out its visible glow when he noticed something odd: a chemically coated screen several feet away was glowing faintly on its own, even though no light should have been able to reach it. Roentgen locked himself in the lab for most of the next seven weeks, barely emerging even for meals, and worked out the main properties of a strange new kind of ray that could pass straight through paper, wood, and even flesh, but was stopped by metal and bone. He asked his wife, Bertha, to hold her hand in a beam while a photographic plate below recorded its image; the picture of her bones, with her wedding ring floating in the middle, became one of the most famous images in the history of science. The medical world grasped the point almost instantly: within months doctors across Europe and America were using the new rays to find bullets, locate broken bones, and look for stones. Roentgen refused to patent the discovery, insisting it belonged to humanity. In 1901 he received the very first Nobel Prize in Physics.

roman-concrete-the-lost-dome-and-medieva.context_blurb: The ancient Romans built domes, aqueducts, and harbors out of a cement so good that pieces of it still stand after two thousand years, sometimes in direct contact with seawater. For most of the Middle Ages, the recipe for that cement was lost, and medieval masons who looked up at the dome of the Pantheon in Rome had no idea how the Romans had done it. In the 15th century, a trained goldsmith with no formal background as an architect finally figured out how to crown a famous European cathedral with a dome bigger than any built since antiquity, using an ingenious herringbone pattern of brick and a self-supporting double shell. Only in the 21st century did modern science finally understand why Roman concrete had been so stubbornly durable, and that answer turned out to involve a surprising mechanism baked into the cement itself. The story covers both the ancient feat and its medieval and modern echoes. It is also a quiet reminder that lost technology is a real thing, and that the people who come after a civilization sometimes have to work for centuries to recover what their ancestors already knew. It is also a reminder of how long the Pantheon in Rome has stood with the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, and of how many centuries went by before any later builder dared to try to beat it.

roman-engineering-aqueducts-roads-concre.context_blurb: The Romans were not the greatest theoretical scientists of the ancient world — that honour mostly went to the Greeks — but as practical engineers they have never really been surpassed. From the fourth century BC to the fifth century AD they stitched their vast empire together with a web of hard-surfaced long-distance roads that let soldiers, officials, and messengers move at reliable speeds across thousands of miles of varied country. They channelled fresh water into cities with elegant long gravity-fed conduits whose remains still stand in parts of Europe and North Africa. They invented a mortar of lime, water, and a special volcanic sand called pozzolana that set hard underwater and allowed them to pour vast walls, vaults, and spherical domes that no earlier civilisation had been able to attempt. Their harbour works at Caesarea in Palestine were cast directly in sea water. A number of their most ambitious concrete monuments in the city of Rome itself still stand nearly two thousand years after they were built, several of them with technical features that modern engineers are still studying today. Chemists examining old Roman walls have in recent years discovered that some ingredients once dismissed as sloppy workmanship actually give Roman concrete a surprising ability to behave very differently from its modern replacement when it meets water. Roman structures were built to last and often have.

roman-law-and-its-lasting-legacy.context_blurb: Roman law is the single greatest legal inheritance of Western civilization. It began as a small body of custom administered by priests in a tiny Italian city-state, became written law in the Republic's first century, grew enormous through centuries of imperial decrees and juristic commentary, and was finally gathered up into one systematic collection by order of the emperor Justinian in the sixth century AD. That collection, usually called the Corpus Juris Civilis, became the ancestor of all the civil-law systems of continental Europe and Latin America. The Roman jurists bequeathed principles that most modern people now assume are obvious: that the burden of proof falls on the accuser, that no one may be tried twice for the same offense, that the law should treat equals equally, that contracts should be honored, that private property is protected against arbitrary seizure, and much more. The medieval universities rediscovered the Corpus and taught it for centuries, which is why a modern lawyer in Rome, Paris, Berlin, or Buenos Aires still argues in categories a Roman jurist would recognize. Common-law countries like England and the United States borrow less directly, but even they trace key principles back through Roman influence.

roman-pantheon-and-the-concrete-dome.context_blurb: The Pantheon in the center of Rome is a huge round temple built in its present form around AD 125 by the emperor Hadrian on the site of an earlier temple built by Augustus's deputy Agrippa, whose name is still carved on the Hadrianic facade. It is one of the best-preserved buildings of antiquity because the Christian Church took it over in the 7th century and has used it continuously as a place of worship ever since. Its most impressive feature is its enormous dome, cast of a particular Roman concrete whose aggregate got lighter and lighter as the dome rose higher, so the whole structure stays up without any internal columns or buttresses. At the dome's crown is a single round opening open to the sky, letting a shaft of sunlight walk slowly across the colored marble interior throughout the day. The dome was the largest built in human history for well over a thousand years, until the Renaissance architect Brunelleschi finally matched it in 15th-century Florence. The Pantheon has influenced Western public architecture ever since, and anyone who has ever stepped inside a 19th-century rotunda or a domed state capitol has walked into a distant child of this one Roman building. It is still an active church, and tourists wander in and out of it most of every day of the week.

romantic-era-composers-chopin-tchaikovsk.context_blurb: The Romantic era in Western music ran from roughly the first decades of the 19th century into the first decades of the 20th, following the Classical era of Haydn, Mozart, and Beethoven. Romantic composers emphasized personal emotion, dramatic contrasts, programmatic descriptive music, enlarged orchestras, chromatic harmony, and connections between music and the national traditions of specific European peoples. The Polish-French pianist and composer Frederic Chopin (1810 to 1849) spent his short life as the great poet of the solo piano, writing nocturnes, waltzes, mazurkas, polonaises, ballades, and concertos. The Russian composer Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky (1840 to 1893) produced six symphonies, several enormously popular ballets, operas, concertos, and the famous 1812 Overture complete with its climactic bells and cannons. The German composer Richard Wagner (1813 to 1883) devoted himself to a new kind of music drama in which full operas were constructed as single enormous musical arcs, and his four-opera Ring cycle, based on Germanic mythology, took him more than two decades to write. These three among dozens of other great Romantic composers between them turned the European classical concert hall into one of the most emotionally charged places in Western culture, and the repertoire they left behind still forms a large part of the standard concert programming today.

romanticism-delacroix-and-turner.context_blurb: Romanticism was a broad cultural movement across Western Europe from the late 18th century into the mid-19th, reacting against the cool rationality of the Enlightenment and the strict severity of Neoclassicism in favor of emotion, imagination, nature in its wild aspect, exotic settings, medieval and folk subjects, and the dramatic lives of ordinary and extraordinary individuals. In painting, two of its greatest figures were Eugene Delacroix in France (1798 to 1863) and J. M. W. Turner in Britain (1775 to 1851). Delacroix painted huge dramatic scenes of battle, revolution, shipwreck, Arab tribesmen on horses, and classical mythology, with slashing brushwork and brilliantly saturated colors — one of his best-known paintings is a bare-breasted female figure of Liberty leading French revolutionaries across a barricade over the fallen bodies of their comrades. Turner painted the sea, the sky, and the industrial dawn of 19th-century England with an increasingly radical freedom of brushwork; his late paintings of storms, sunsets, snowstorms, and sinking slave ships dissolve into near-pure fields of color that half the critics of his age could not understand and that modern viewers see as the direct ancestor of Monet and the Impressionists. The two of them together bookend the dramatic emotional expansion of what Western painting could do before Impressionism arrived.

romulus-and-remus-the-founding-legend.context_blurb: The Romans told a founding story about themselves that explained why their city was special and why it was called Rome. According to the legend, the city was founded by twin brothers whose names begin with the same letter, descendants on their mother's side of the Trojan hero Aeneas and the war-god Mars. As infants they were set adrift on the Tiber River and left to die by an uncle who had seized the family's throne, but they survived in the wild under the care of a wolf and later a shepherd, grew up strong, took revenge on their uncle, and set out to found a new city. The brothers quarreled over the exact spot and over the signs from the gods, and the fight ended tragically with one brother killing the other and giving the city his own name. The legend placed the founding in the mid-700s BC and became a story every Roman child knew. The scene of the wolf nursing the twins became one of the enduring symbols of the city, cast in bronze and painted and stamped on coins for over two thousand years. Modern historians treat the whole tale as mostly myth, but it mattered enormously to how the Romans understood themselves.

rorke-s-drift-and-the-anglo-zulu-war.context_blurb: In 1879 a British colonial army crossed from Natal into the independent Zulu kingdom in southern Africa, under a British high commissioner who had engineered a war against the Zulu king Cetshwayo on fabricated grounds. Early on the morning after the invasion, the main British column was almost wiped out at Isandlwana by a Zulu army of over twenty thousand warriors — one of the worst disasters a British army ever suffered against a non-European opponent. Later that same day, a victorious wing of the Zulu force poured on toward a little mission station at a river crossing called Rorke's Drift. About 150 British soldiers, including many in the hospital, barricaded themselves inside the station's outbuildings and held off thousands of Zulu attackers through the afternoon, through the night, and into the next morning before the Zulu force finally withdrew. The questions ahead cover the household objects the defenders stacked up for walls, a famous number given to the little garrison afterward, and the shape of a classic Zulu battle formation that destroyed the main column earlier that day. It matters because Rorke's Drift became one of the most mythologized small battles in British military history, while the war as a whole closed in the Zulus' defeat, the capture of their king, and the end of their independent kingdom — part of the European scramble that would soon swallow most of Africa.

rousseau-and-the-social-contract.context_blurb: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was an 18th-century Genevan-born writer, composer, and philosopher who became one of the most influential and most troubling thinkers of the French Enlightenment. He wrote novels, operas, political theory, and a confessional autobiography, and in every form he argued that something had gone deeply wrong with modern civilization. In his most famous political book, The Social Contract, he argued that legitimate government must rest on the collective will of the people rather than on the authority of kings, nobles, or churches. His writing on education was almost as influential and reshaped how Europeans thought about raising children. Rousseau's personal life was a mess of quarrels, flights across borders, and broken friendships, and he abandoned his own children. He died in 1778, a year before the storm he had helped prepare. A decade later the leaders of the French Revolution quoted him constantly, and the Jacobins drew directly on his language about the general will when they justified their most ferocious policies. Rousseau has been loved and hated ever since, and often by the same reader on different days.

russian-revolution-of-1917.context_blurb: The Russian Revolution of 1917 happened in two acts. The first came in February, when strikes and bread riots in the capital Petrograd — strikes that began on a day of annual public demonstrations — brought thousands into the streets, and when the Tsar ordered the garrison to fire on the crowds the soldiers would not do it. Within days Nicholas II had abdicated the throne, and a Provisional Government took power under liberal and moderate socialist ministers. The second act came in October. The leader of the hardline Bolshevik party, Vladimir Lenin, had slipped back into Russia from Swiss exile that spring under a special arrangement with the German government, which was hoping he would knock Russia out of the war; and under slogans that spoke to a country tired of war and hungry for bread, the Bolsheviks took over the city soviets through the summer and autumn. In October the Bolsheviks stormed the Winter Palace in Petrograd and dispersed the Provisional Government. A few months later they dissolved by force the democratically elected Constituent Assembly, which they had failed to control at the ballot box — a short-lived parliament the next generation of Russians would barely remember. What began as a popular uprising for bread and peace ended, within months, under the one-party dictatorship that would run Russia for the next seventy-four years.

sakharov-havel-the-dissidents-of-conscie.context_blurb: Across the communist countries of Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union during the Cold War, small groups of intellectuals, writers, scientists, religious believers, and ordinary workers risked their careers, their freedom, and sometimes their lives to speak publicly against the regimes under which they lived. The Russian physicist Andrei Sakharov, one of the fathers of the Soviet hydrogen bomb, later became the most famous Soviet dissident, writing openly for human rights, nuclear disarmament, and the end of one-party rule, and was eventually banished to internal exile in the closed city of Gorky. The Czech playwright Vaclav Havel spent years in prison for his writings about living in truth under a corrupting regime and later became the first post-communist president of Czechoslovakia. The Russian novelist Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn documented the Soviet gulag camps and was expelled from the Soviet Union after his books were smuggled out and published abroad. The Polish electrician Lech Walesa founded the Solidarity union. The Russian poet Anna Akhmatova, the Hungarian economist Janos Kis, the East German pastor Rainer Eppelmann, and hundreds of less famous names did similar quiet work in their own countries. Their collective moral example helped delegitimize the communist regimes long before political change actually arrived.

saladin-and-the-recapture-of-jerusalem.context_blurb: Salah ad-Din — his name means 'Righteousness of the Faith' and the Latin West turned it into Saladin — was a Kurdish Muslim general who unified Egypt and Syria and drove the Crusader kingdoms back to the sea. His greatest victory came in July 1187 at the Horns of Hattin in Galilee, where he caught a thirsty Crusader army in dry country and smashed it so completely that nearly every knight in the Kingdom of Jerusalem was killed or captured in a single day. Three months later Jerusalem itself opened its gates, and Saladin treated the Christian inhabitants with a dignity that cost him almost nothing and shocked the Western chroniclers, because the First Crusade had taken the same city eighty-eight years earlier under very different and far bloodier terms. During the Third Crusade that followed, Saladin and the English king Richard the Lionheart never actually met in person, though they exchanged courtesies that became famous — Saladin became in Europe a kind of legend, the Christian knight's model of what a worthy enemy ought to be. At Hattin he also showed another side: he kept the Crusader lords alive to be ransomed, but he personally executed Reynald of Chatillon, a notorious oath-breaker who had attacked a Muslim pilgrim caravan, and he ordered the deaths of the captured members of the two great military orders of the kingdom.

saladin-richard-the-lionheart-third-crus.context_blurb: In the late 12th century, a Kurdish-born Muslim sultan who had just reunified Egypt and Syria won back the city of Jerusalem from the Christian kingdom that had held it for almost a century, triggering a huge counter-expedition from Europe. The two leaders who ended up at the center of the story, the sultan on one side and the English king who crossed half of Europe to fight him on the other, became famous enemies and, in a strange way, mutual admirers. Each of them did things to the other on and off the battlefield that neither Christians nor Muslims have ever quite forgotten, some of them generous, some of them bloody, and some of them small kindnesses extended between kings in the middle of a terrible war. In the end, the English king failed to take back the holy city itself, but he and the sultan negotiated a truce that allowed Christian pilgrims safe passage to it. The chivalry and the cruelty of this one war between two kings became a legend in both Christendom and the Islamic world, and the stories told in both traditions about the two men say almost as much about Christians and Muslims as they do about the kings themselves.

samuel-morse-and-the-telegraph.context_blurb: Samuel F. B. Morse was an American painter — a successful portraitist, a founder of the National Academy of Design — who turned, in middle age, into an inventor. On a ship home from Europe in 1832 he fell into a dinner conversation about recent experiments with electromagnetism and became convinced that one could flash a message instantly down a wire from city to city by making and breaking a circuit. He was not a trained engineer; he worked out his first clumsy prototype on an old picture frame in his New York studio. The problem of pushing a signal over long wires was finally cracked with the help of Leonard Gale and Alfred Vail, and in 1844 Morse opened the first long-distance line in the United States, between Washington and Baltimore, with a short message tapped out in the dot-and-dash alphabet he and Vail had devised. That alphabet, cleverly built so that the most common letters were given the shortest combinations and the rare ones got the longest, became the global language of wire and radio telegraphy for the next hundred years. By the 1860s telegraph wires crossed continents and oceans. News that would once have taken months to cross the Atlantic now took minutes. Morse himself grew rich and famous, fought years of patent lawsuits defending his claim to the invention, and lived long enough to see his dot-and-dash code tapping messages around the planet.

samurai-shoguns-bushido-feudal-japan.context_blurb: From the late 12th century until the 1860s, Japan was effectively ruled by a succession of military governments headed by a military dictator called the shogun, with the Japanese emperor kept as a ceremonial figure in the old capital of Kyoto. The warrior class that supported this system is remembered as the samurai, a hereditary caste of armed retainers who served particular feudal lords called daimyo. The samurai code — later romanticized under the name bushido, which means the way of the warrior — emphasized loyalty to one's lord, honor in battle, austere self-discipline, mastery of the sword and other weapons, and, when necessary, a willingness to commit ritual suicide (seppuku) rather than suffer disgrace or capture. During the Warring States period of the 15th and 16th centuries, Japan fragmented into dozens of warring domains. Three successive great unifiers in the late 1500s and early 1600s — Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, and Tokugawa Ieyasu — finally restored central authority under the Tokugawa shogunate, which ruled a largely closed, peaceful Japan from Edo (modern Tokyo) for over two hundred and fifty years. The samurai era ended with the Meiji Restoration of 1868 and the opening of Japan to the modern world.

saratoga-1777-the-turning-point.context_blurb: The Battle of Saratoga, actually two battles fought in September and October of 1777 in upstate New York, was the pivotal American military victory of the Revolutionary War. The British had planned a three-column strategy to cut New England off from the rest of the colonies by seizing the Hudson River valley from Canada south to New York City. The main column, under General John Burgoyne, moved south from Canada through the Lake Champlain corridor with an elaborate army including British regulars, German mercenaries, Canadian militia, and Native American allies. The supporting columns failed to arrive, and Burgoyne pressed on alone, overextending his supply lines through hostile country. American forces under General Horatio Gates, with the aggressive battlefield leadership of Benedict Arnold (whose treason came three years later), fought Burgoyne to a standstill and then surrounded his army. Burgoyne surrendered on October 17, 1777, with over five thousand men. The news of the American victory reached Paris that winter and was the decisive argument that convinced the French government to formally ally with the United States. The French alliance would eventually bring French soldiers, French ships, and French money into the war on the American side, and would make the ultimate victory possible.

sargon-of-akkad-s-empire.context_blurb: Sargon of Akkad was a twenty-fourth-century BC king who unified the city-states of ancient Mesopotamia under his personal rule and built what historians generally regard as the first empire in human history. His origins, as recorded in a famous Akkadian poetic legend, were obscure — he claimed to have been born in secret to a priestess, placed in a reed basket, and set adrift on the Euphrates River before being rescued by a date-grower and eventually working his way up to the service of the king of the Sumerian city of Kish. He later overthrew that king, conquered a series of Sumerian city-states, and extended his control from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean coast of what is now Syria. He is traditionally credited with founding the city of Akkad as his new capital (its exact location has not been definitively identified by modern archaeology) and with using Akkadian — a Semitic language — as the language of his administration, in place of the older Sumerian. His empire lasted a little over a century after him under his sons and grandson Naram-Sin, before being pulled apart by rebellions and (according to later tradition) by invasions of a highland people called the Gutians. The Akkadian imperial model shaped every later Mesopotamian empire.

scipio-zama-and-the-destruction-of-carth.context_blurb: Rome fought three long wars against the Phoenician trading city of Carthage, on the North African coast across from Sicily, between 264 and 146 BC. The second of these wars was the most dramatic, because the Carthaginian general Hannibal crossed the Alps with war elephants and marched his army up and down Italy for over a decade, winning crushing victories but failing to take Rome itself. The war finally ended when a brilliant young Roman general took the fight across to Africa and drew Hannibal home to defend his own city, where the two commanders met in open battle in 202 BC on North African ground, and Rome won. The Roman general was granted the honorific name that attached to his family afterward and became one of the Republic's most celebrated men. Fifty years later, Rome fought and won the third and final war, this time destroying Carthage utterly. Roman writers claimed the ground was sown with salt so that nothing would grow there again; no ancient source actually says that, and the story seems to be a much later invention. What is certain is that Carthage was burned, its people enslaved, and Rome had no serious rival in the western Mediterranean for the next six centuries.

seneca-falls-and-the-women-s-rights-move.context_blurb: On July 19 and 20, 1848, roughly three hundred people met at the Wesleyan Chapel in the small town of Seneca Falls in upstate New York for what is remembered as the first women's rights convention in the United States. The organizers included Elizabeth Cady Stanton, a sharp young mother tired of being shut out of the public life her abolitionist husband enjoyed, and Lucretia Mott, a famous Quaker preacher and abolitionist. They had conceived the idea years earlier at an international antislavery convention in London, where women delegates had been forced to sit behind a curtain and not speak. For the Seneca Falls meeting Stanton drafted a Declaration of Sentiments that deliberately echoed the Declaration of Independence, listed a long train of injustices against women, and demanded a set of remedies. The questions ahead cover a careful change Stanton made to the famous opening sentence of the Declaration, a problem the organizers had on arrival at the chapel, who ended up chairing the meeting on the first day and why, a famous abolitionist whose support helped pass the most controversial resolution, that most controversial resolution and why Stanton insisted on it, and a notable moment seventy-two years later when the suffrage amendment was finally ratified. It matters because Seneca Falls launched the long campaign for women's legal, educational, and political equality in the United States.

september-11-2001.context_blurb: On the morning of September 11, 2001, nineteen hijackers belonging to the Islamist terrorist network al-Qaeda commandeered four American civilian airliners after takeoff and used three of them as weapons against targets in the United States. Two were deliberately crashed into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in Lower Manhattan, which caught fire and collapsed within hours. The third was crashed into the Pentagon outside Washington, D.C. The fourth, apparently intended for either the United States Capitol or the White House, was taken back by its passengers in flight and crashed in a field in Pennsylvania, killing everyone aboard. Almost three thousand civilians died in the four coordinated attacks, which were the deadliest terrorist attacks in modern history and the deadliest foreign attack on American soil since Pearl Harbor in 1941. The United States responded with a sustained global military and intelligence campaign against al-Qaeda, including the invasion of Afghanistan (where the Taliban government had been sheltering al-Qaeda's leaders) later that same autumn. Al-Qaeda's founder Osama bin Laden was finally killed by American special operations forces in Pakistan in May 2011. The attacks reshaped American foreign policy, airline security, and the political mood of the entire developed world.

shaka-zulu-the-zulu-kingdom.context_blurb: Shaka was a king of the Zulu people in what is now the KwaZulu-Natal province of South Africa, who ruled from 1816 until his assassination in 1828 and in that short period transformed the Zulu from a small Nguni-speaking clan into one of the most powerful African military powers of the 19th century. Shaka's military reforms were sweeping: he abandoned the traditional light throwing spear in favor of a short stabbing spear, equipped his warriors with large cowhide shields designed to be used aggressively in close combat, organized them into disciplined age-regiments, and worked out a battlefield tactic sometimes called the horns of the buffalo in which a central mass of warriors pinned the enemy while two outflanking columns closed around them. He conquered neighboring peoples ferociously, and the resulting upheaval across southeastern Africa, called the Mfecane, caused massive migrations and the collapse of older political arrangements across the region. Shaka was eventually killed by his half-brothers in a palace coup. The Zulu kingdom continued under his successors for another fifty years and famously fought the British Empire at the Battle of Isandlwana in 1879, defeating a British column before eventually succumbing to the second expedition at Ulundi. His legend remains central to Zulu identity today.

shakespeare.context_blurb: William Shakespeare was an English poet, playwright, and part-owner of a London theater company who wrote the greatest body of plays in the English language. He was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564, the son of a glovemaker, married Anne Hathaway when he was eighteen and she was twenty-six, and left behind at least three children — one of whom died at eleven. Sometime in his twenties he moved to London and joined a theater company called the Lord Chamberlain's Men, which performed in open-air playhouses on the south bank of the Thames for crowds that ranged from the paying poor to the queen of England herself. In twenty years of writing he produced about three dozen plays, including the great tragedies (Hamlet, King Lear, Othello, Macbeth), the romantic comedies (As You Like It, Twelfth Night, Much Ado About Nothing), the English history plays, and the Roman plays, plus 154 sonnets so finely made that English teachers have never stopped assigning them. He retired home to Stratford a wealthy man and died there in 1616. His old friends and fellow actors gathered up his play scripts seven years later and published them together in a single large volume, and without that book Shakespeare's place in the world today would be very different.

shakespeare-the-plays-and-the-language.context_blurb: William Shakespeare (1564 to 1616) was an English poet, playwright, and actor from the small Warwickshire market town of Stratford-upon-Avon who moved to London as a young man and became part owner of the Globe Theatre and the leading dramatist of the Elizabethan and Jacobean stage. Over roughly two and a half decades of work, he wrote around thirty-seven plays — the exact number is still debated — and 154 sonnets, in an English of extraordinary range, invention, and texture. His tragedies include Hamlet, Macbeth, Othello, and King Lear; his comedies include A Midsummer Night's Dream, Twelfth Night, Much Ado About Nothing, and As You Like It; his history plays trace the English kings from Richard II through Henry V to Richard III. He is responsible for an astonishing number of phrases now embedded in everyday English: the dogs of war, star-crossed lovers, the primrose path, to thine own self be true, the course of true love never did run smooth, and hundreds more. The question of whether a glover's son from a provincial town really wrote these plays has been raised by cranks for the last two centuries, but mainstream scholarship has repeatedly concluded that he did. He remains the most-performed and most-studied playwright in human history.

shays-rebellion-1786-87.context_blurb: Shays' Rebellion was an uprising of indebted western Massachusetts farmers in the winter of 1786 to 1787, led by a Revolutionary War veteran named Daniel Shays. The farmers were in trouble because the Massachusetts state government, trying to pay off its share of the Revolutionary war debt in hard currency, had been imposing heavy taxes that fell especially hard on cash-poor rural landowners, who were increasingly being hauled into court for debt, having their property seized, and sometimes being sent to debtors' prison. Petitions and protests had gotten nowhere. In the fall of 1786, Shays and other veterans began organizing armed companies to close down the local courts that were trying debt cases, and in January 1787 they marched on the federal armory at Springfield to seize weapons. Massachusetts raised a private militia funded by Boston merchants and crushed the rebellion with a few sharp skirmishes. A dozen or so people were killed on both sides. The rebellion was shocking because it suggested that the national government, under the weak Articles of Confederation, was essentially unable to help a state suppress an armed uprising on its own soil. The scare in Boston and elsewhere helped build the political momentum for the Constitutional Convention that met in Philadelphia the following summer.

shostakovich-s-fifth-music-coded-under-s.context_blurb: Dmitri Shostakovich (1906 to 1975) was a Soviet composer whose career was defined by the constant need to compose music that would satisfy the ferocious cultural demands of the Stalinist state without betraying his own artistic conscience. He emerged in the 1920s as a modernist prodigy and premiered an opera called Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District that was initially a huge success and then in 1936 was publicly denounced in the official Communist Party newspaper Pravda, almost certainly on Stalin's own initiative, as decadent and incomprehensible. Shostakovich lived for months afterward with a bag packed beside the door of his apartment, expecting to be arrested in the night. The following year he premiered a Fifth Symphony that satisfied the regime's demand for a more accessible, triumphant, heroic music, and the symphony became an immediate hit. Later generations of listeners, however, have heard in its loud triumphant finale an undercurrent of forced hollow emptiness — a public mask over private grief — that may have been Shostakovich's quiet protest against the regime he could not openly defy. The composer himself hinted at something like this in private conversations and later writings. His case has become the standard example of what great art under totalitarian regimes actually looks like.

siege-of-leningrad.context_blurb: The Siege of Leningrad was a 872-day blockade and bombardment of the second-largest Soviet city by German and Finnish forces, running from September 1941 to January 1944 during the Second World War. The city, now called St. Petersburg, had been nearly surrounded by the end of September 1941 as German Army Group North advanced into northwestern Russia under Operation Barbarossa. A narrow corridor over frozen Lake Ladoga became the only Soviet supply route into the city during the first terrible winter, and even that was intermittent. Over the following two and a half years, the besieged population of over two and a half million people endured artillery bombardment, air raids, bitter cold, and systematic starvation. Civilians received ration cards for a few hundred grams of bread a day during the worst periods; people boiled wallpaper paste for calories, caught rats, and died by the thousand in the streets. By the time Soviet forces finally relieved the siege in January 1944, somewhere around a million Leningrad civilians had died of starvation, cold, and disease, with hundreds of thousands more killed by bombardment. The siege remains one of the deadliest episodes of urban warfare in human history and is a central element of modern Russian national memory of the Great Patriotic War.

sinking-of-the-lusitania.context_blurb: The RMS Lusitania was a Cunard luxury ocean liner — a bigger, faster sister to a certain other British liner lost three years earlier — that steamed from New York toward Liverpool in May 1915. On the afternoon of May 7, as she rounded the south coast of Ireland in bright sunlight, a German U-boat torpedoed her amidships; she sank, taking 1,198 of her 1,962 passengers and crew to the bottom. Among the dead were 128 Americans — a wave of outrage that the German imperial government deflected by pointing out that it had warned American passengers in Manhattan newspapers before the ship had even sailed, and that the Lusitania was carrying war materiel in her holds (a defense that modern diving on the wreck has substantially confirmed). The sinking did not quite bring the United States into the war; Woodrow Wilson used it instead to force Germany, for a time, to call off its unrestricted submarine warfare. But Americans would never forget 'Remember the Lusitania,' and when Germany restarted the submarine war in 1917, that forgotten anger returned. The Lusitania's name sits in American political memory the way the sinking of the Maine does for the Spanish-American War — the single image that fixes the quarrel in public consciousness.

smallpox-and-the-demographic-collapse.context_blurb: The deadliest weapons Europeans brought to the New World were not steel or gunpowder but the microbes they carried in their lungs and on their skin. The Americas had been cut off from Eurasian herd animals and the illnesses that cycle through them for at least ten thousand years, and the Native peoples who met Columbus's successors therefore faced a very different biological situation than Spanish, French, or English colonists did. The result, over the century after 1492, was the worst population catastrophe in recorded human history. Between half and nine-tenths of the entire population of the Americas is thought to have died, perhaps on the order of fifty million people. One disfiguring viral killer in particular ravaged the Mexica during the Spanish siege of their capital, and later struck the Inca world so hard that the royal succession there was thrown into chaos years before any Spanish party arrived. English Pilgrims landing a few years later still found whole stretches of New England cleared out, and often moved straight into cornfields and dwellings whose previous owners had been dead for only a season or two. Historians are still trying to work out exactly how much of what the colonists did next, and said about why they were able to do it, was shaped by the invisible wave of death that had rolled through the land ahead of them.

social-darwinism-and-the-civilizing-miss.context_blurb: In the second half of the nineteenth century, after Charles Darwin's theory of natural selection became famous, a set of writers tried to borrow its language and apply it to human societies. The result was a cluster of ideas usually grouped under the name Social Darwinism — not Darwin's own view, but a popular reworking in which 'the fit' societies, races, or classes were understood to be destined to triumph over 'the unfit,' and in which government or charitable efforts to help the losing side were sometimes attacked as interference with a natural process of progress. These ideas were taken up by politicians, essayists, business apologists, and the propagandists of empire, who turned them into a moral story about why European and American domination over the rest of the world was both inevitable and good. The questions ahead cover a famous late-century poem that gave the imperial project its most memorable English name, the Victorian philosopher who popularized many of these ideas, how Rudyard Kipling's poem framed the imperialist's self-image, how an African critic of King Leopold's Congo later described European 'civilizing' claims, and what Darwin himself actually meant by evolutionary success. It matters because these arguments were used in real time to justify colonial rule, racist immigration laws, and, later, the eugenics movement; understanding them is part of understanding how the next century's horrors became imaginable.

social-upheaval-after-the-plague.context_blurb: After the Black Death carried off a huge share of Europe, the people who were left discovered something uncomfortable for their lords: labor was now scarce, and workers were no longer easy to replace. Kings and lords tried to hold wages down by law. Peasants and craftsmen responded with foot-dragging, flight, and finally armed revolt, most dramatically in late-14th-century England, where a huge crowd marched on the capital, broke open prisons, burned royal officials' palaces, and nearly made the young king himself a hostage. In the chaos the boy king met the rebels in person and outmaneuvered them by a dramatic personal gesture at the moment their leader was killed in front of him. Within a short time afterward, the royal promises made under pressure were quietly undone, the main rebel leaders were killed, and in the short run very little changed. But the lords could never quite put the old world back together, and the price of ordinary work would never fall as low as it had been before the plague. The story also covers the strange whipping processions and anti-Jewish massacres that moved across Europe at the plague's peak, and the fate of the controversial priest who had helped put the English revolt's ideas into popular form.

socrates-trial-and-death-by-hemlock-399-.context_blurb: Socrates was a 5th-century BC Athenian stonemason who became the most famous teacher in Western philosophy by writing nothing down and by cross-examining his fellow citizens in the streets and market of Athens about what they thought they knew. He pretended to know nothing himself, which infuriated the proud. He had a strange personal habit of listening to an inner voice he said steered him away from certain actions. He fought bravely in the city's long war with Sparta, and when Athens lost that war and the city went through a brief ugly tyranny followed by a shaky restoration of democracy, Socrates was put on trial. He was accused of corrupting the young and of not honoring the city's gods. The jury convicted him by a small margin, and he was executed by poisoning, as Athenian law required. His pupil Plato wrote several dialogues reconstructing the trial and the final hours — the Apology, the Crito, the Phaedo — and these became the founding scenes of Western philosophy. The death of Socrates in 399 BC became one of the great images of the thinker who refuses to recant and dies for the integrity of his questions.

solferino-and-the-founding-of-the-red-cr.context_blurb: On June 24, 1859, three large armies collided in rolling countryside near a village called Solferino in northern Italy, during the war for Italian unification. On one side were French and Piedmontese troops under Emperor Napoleon III and King Victor Emmanuel II; on the other, the Austrian army under its young Emperor Franz Joseph. The battle lasted most of a long day, left tens of thousands of soldiers dead or wounded on the field, and overwhelmed the primitive medical services of both armies — many of the wounded simply lay where they had fallen through the following nights. A Swiss businessman named Henry Dunant, who had come to the area hoping to meet Napoleon III about a business matter, instead stumbled into the aftermath. For days he worked with local villagers in a nearby church, bringing water, bandaging wounds, writing letters home, and burying the dead, insisting without regard to uniform or language that every suffering man be helped. Years later he wrote a short book about what he had seen and proposed two things: that every country train volunteer societies to care for wounded soldiers, and that governments sign a treaty protecting medics and the wounded from attack. The questions ahead cover the simple phrase Dunant used in that church, and the emblem later chosen for the new international movement he inspired. It matters because out of his campaign came the Red Cross, the Geneva Conventions, and the modern laws of war that still, imperfectly, try to put limits on what armies may do to the helpless.

solidarity-the-polish-workers-movement.context_blurb: Solidarity was an independent trade union founded in August 1980 at the Lenin Shipyard in the Polish Baltic port of Gdansk by workers led by an electrician named Lech Walesa, during a wave of strikes against the Polish Communist government. It was the first legal independent trade union anywhere in the Soviet bloc, and within months it had grown to roughly ten million members across Poland — about a third of the entire adult population. The movement combined trade-union concerns about wages and working conditions with broader political demands for free press, religious freedom, and limits on Communist Party power. In December 1981 the Polish Communist government under General Wojciech Jaruzelski imposed martial law, arrested the Solidarity leadership including Walesa, and drove the union underground. Solidarity survived in the underground throughout the 1980s, sustained by the Polish Catholic Church, by Polish-Americans in the United States, by the Reagan administration, and by Pope John Paul II. In 1989 the collapsing Polish Communist government finally agreed to partially free elections, Solidarity candidates swept them, and within months Poland had the first non-Communist government in the Soviet bloc. Walesa was elected the first post-communist president of Poland in 1990 and later received the Nobel Peace Prize for his role.

song-dynasty-the-civil-service-exam-scho.context_blurb: The Song dynasty ruled China from 960 to 1279 and is often described by historians as the most sophisticated civilization in the world of its age. The Song did not match the territorial extent of the Han or the Tang — the dynasty lost control of the north in 1127 and ran the second half of its reign from a southern capital — but in terms of economic development, urbanization, printed-book literacy, technology, art, and philosophy, Song China may have been running ahead of every other civilization on Earth. During the Song, the use of movable-type printing began, gunpowder weapons were systematically developed, the magnetic compass was first used for navigation, iron production reached levels Europe would not match until the Industrial Revolution, paper money was issued, and dense merchant cities grew up on the lower Yangtze. The dynasty also matured the civil service examination system to the point where entry into government was dominantly through examinations on classical Confucian texts rather than through family connections or military service, which produced the long-lasting Chinese scholar-gentry class. The Song eventually fell to Mongol invasion from the north, with the final remnant of the imperial family drowning off the Chinese coast in 1279 rather than surrender.

songhai-empire-askia-the-great.context_blurb: After the slow decline of the Empire of Mali in the 15th century, political and commercial power in West Africa shifted northeast to the Songhai people along the great bend of the Niger River, who had broken free of Mali and built their own larger successor empire with its capital at the city of Gao. The decisive figure in Songhai's rise was Askia Muhammad (also called Askia the Great), who seized the throne in 1493 and reigned until 1528. Askia was a devout Muslim who undertook his own grand pilgrimage to Mecca modeled on Mansa Musa's a century and a half earlier, reorganized the empire's administration into effective provinces, and sponsored the Islamic scholarly tradition at the famous universities of Timbuktu and Djenne, which became the leading centers of African learning in the Sunni world. Under Askia and his successors, Timbuktu produced thousands of manuscripts on law, medicine, mathematics, grammar, poetry, and theology, many of which still survive in family libraries and only in recent decades have been systematically catalogued. The Songhai Empire eventually fell in 1591 to a long-range invasion by Moroccan musketeers who crossed the Sahara, which permanently broke the political power of the Niger bend trade cities and shifted the center of West African politics elsewhere.

soviet-mass-deportations-and-the-brutal-.context_blurb: During and after the Second World War, the Soviet Union carried out a series of mass deportations of entire ethnic nationalities within its own territory, uprooting hundreds of thousands of people from their homelands and shipping them in cattle cars to Soviet Central Asia and Siberia. Entire peoples were deported in the 1940s on Stalin's orders: the Chechens and Ingush in 1944, the Crimean Tatars also in 1944, the Volga Germans in 1941, the Kalmyks, the Karachay, the Balkars, the Meskhetian Turks, and others. Each deportation was carried out at short notice, usually within hours, with brutal selection criteria, long transport conditions that killed many of the deportees in transit, and primitive settlement conditions on arrival. Tens of thousands died in each operation. Beyond these ethnic-cleansing operations within the Soviet Union, the Red Army occupation of Eastern Europe at the end of the Second World War was marked by widespread atrocities including mass rape, looting, and summary executions of civilians and prisoners. These crimes were systematically covered up by Soviet authorities for the next four and a half decades, and only during and after the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 did honest documentation become possible. The crimes remain partially contested by the modern Russian Federation.

soviet-war-in-afghanistan.context_blurb: In December 1979, the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan in order to prop up a shaky Marxist government in Kabul that was losing control of the countryside to Afghan Muslim resistance fighters called the mujahideen. The Soviet intervention was expected to be brief. Instead it lasted nearly ten years, bogged the Soviet army down in a vicious counterinsurgency across the mountains and valleys of Afghanistan, killed over a million Afghan civilians, drove roughly five million Afghans into exile as refugees, and killed around fifteen thousand Soviet soldiers while wounding tens of thousands more. The mujahideen were armed, trained, and funded by a coalition that included the United States, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and Britain, with Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence agency as the main conduit. Shoulder-fired Stinger missiles provided by the Americans in the mid-1980s broke Soviet helicopter dominance over the countryside. The war badly damaged Soviet morale, strained Soviet finances, and contributed to the political reforms under Mikhail Gorbachev that would eventually bring the Soviet Union down. Soviet troops finally withdrew in February 1989. The Afghan civil war continued among competing factions, eventually producing the Taliban regime of the mid-1990s and (indirectly) the training grounds that al-Qaeda used before 9/11.

spanish-civil-war.context_blurb: In July 1936 a group of Spanish army generals led by Francisco Franco rose in revolt against the democratically elected Republican government of Spain, and the resulting three-year civil war divided the country into left-wing Republicans and right-wing Nationalists. The war quickly became an international proxy conflict: Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy sent planes, tanks, and troops to help Franco, while the Soviet Union sent aid to the Republican side and recruited the International Brigades, which drew volunteer idealists from Britain, France, Ireland, Canada, and the United States, including the writer George Orwell. The war's defining horror came in April 1937 when German bombers of the Condor Legion flattened the Basque market town of Guernica on a crowded market day, inspiring Pablo Picasso's great black-and-white painting of the massacre. Intense factional violence broke out on the Republican side as the war went on, which Orwell wrote the whole miserable story of in his memoir 'Homage to Catalonia.' Franco won in 1939 and ruled Spain as a dictator until his death in 1975 — and five months after Spain's fighting ended, Nazi Germany would set off a far larger war of its own on another European front. For many on both sides who lived through it, the Spanish Civil War was remembered as the first act of World War II, with the German and Italian militaries treating Spain as a live rehearsal.

spanish-galleons-the-manila-trade.context_blurb: After Spain seized the Philippines in the 1560s, a yearly convoy of enormous armed cargo ships began running back and forth between Manila and the Pacific port of Acapulco in Mexico. Westbound they carried silver coins minted from Potosi ore. Eastbound they carried Asian luxuries — porcelain, lacquerware, spices, and above all the one particular fabric that the Chinese could make better than anyone and that the imperial court in Beijing was happy to trade for Spanish-American silver. For 250 years, until Mexico broke from Spain, these galleons were the first steady maritime link between the Americas and Asia, and the Spanish-American silver dollar became the trusted currency of coastal China. The eastbound crossing was a nightmare, because the dominant trade winds along the obvious direct route blow stubbornly the wrong way for a return trip; Spanish captains had to take a famously long and difficult detour across the ocean to catch a reliable westerly, and voyages regularly stretched six months, with scurvy and starvation killing a third of a crew before the coast of California finally came up on the horizon. For much of its working life, this run was the single busiest and most profitable sea route anywhere in the world, and much of Southeast Asia's modern Spanish and Chinese cultural borrowings date back to its boom years.

sparta-s-helots-and-the-krypteia-the-pri.context_blurb: The city-state of Sparta kept itself a full-time warrior society by extracting its food from a conquered Greek population called the helots, who worked the fields in a form of state-owned bondage very different from ordinary slavery elsewhere in Greece. The helots outnumbered the Spartans themselves many times over and lived under permanent harsh control. Every year the Spartan rulers formally declared war on their own helots, which gave Spartan citizens legal cover to kill any helot they wished. The young men of Sparta's elite went through a terrifying rite of passage known as the krypteia, in which they were sent into the countryside at night with daggers, told to kill any strong or dangerous-looking helot they came across, and to live on what they could steal. The whole brutal system was the dark side of Sparta's famous military excellence, and the ancient Greeks themselves — including the great non-Spartan Greek writers — were uncomfortable with it. It is one reason modern admiration for Sparta tends to be shallow: the famous phalanx was fed by one of the ugliest arrangements in classical civilization.

sparta-the-agoge-and-warrior-society.context_blurb: Sparta, a city-state in the southern Peloponnese, organized its entire citizen life around producing the finest heavy infantry in the Greek world. From age seven, Spartan boys were taken from their families and raised in state-run groups where they lived under hard discipline, ate meager rationed food they were encouraged to steal to supplement, slept outdoors in all seasons, learned to fight, trained in choral singing and public speech, and were deliberately exposed to pain and hunger in order to toughen them. This system was called the agoge. Spartan girls received a parallel physical education — much more athletic than women in other Greek cities — because the Spartans wanted strong mothers for their next generation of warriors. Adult Spartan men lived in common military messes rather than at home with their wives for much of their early married life. The whole system produced soldiers who were astonishingly reliable in formation but a society of citizens that was culturally stunted compared to Athens, Corinth, or Thebes. The Spartan system both inspired and repelled other Greeks and has been read as a cautionary example by every later society that has flirted with militarizing its young.

spartacus-and-the-slave-revolt.context_blurb: Spartacus was a Thracian-born gladiator who in 73 BC led the largest slave uprising in Roman history. He and a small group of fellow gladiators escaped from a training school in the southern Italian city of Capua, took refuge on the slopes of a nearby mountain, and became the nucleus of an army of runaway slaves and desperate rural poor that eventually numbered in the tens of thousands. For nearly two years they roamed up and down Italy, defeating several Roman armies sent against them. Rome finally crushed the revolt in 71 BC under the command of the wealthy general Crassus, with Pompey arriving in time to claim credit for mopping up. Spartacus himself almost certainly died in the final battle, though his body was never identified. The surviving captives were executed in a brutal mass display along the main road leading north from Capua, as a warning to any other slaves who might think of revolt. The historical Spartacus has become a symbol for every age that wants to tell a story about courage, dignity, and the dream of freedom under impossible odds, from novels and films to Cold War political slogans.

spread-of-buddhism-into-china-xuanzang.context_blurb: Buddhism arrived in China by the trickle of the Han dynasty's Silk Road contacts in the early centuries AD, carried by missionary monks from Central Asia and India, and over the following several hundred years it became one of the three great religious and philosophical traditions of Chinese civilization alongside Confucianism and Daoism. One of the great episodes in this transmission was the long pilgrimage of a Chinese Buddhist monk named Xuanzang, who in the 7th century AD, in defiance of a Tang-dynasty travel ban, left China through the western deserts, crossed Central Asia, and spent nearly two decades traveling in India visiting Buddhist monasteries, studying with Indian masters, and collecting sacred texts. He returned to China around 645 with a huge library of Sanskrit manuscripts, which he spent the rest of his life translating into Chinese with the support of the Tang emperor. His own travel memoir, the Record of the Western Regions, is one of our best sources for the state of 7th-century India and Central Asia. His legend was later retold in enormously embellished and comic form as the beloved Chinese fantasy novel Journey to the West, in which the monk's quest is helped along by a magical monkey, a pig, and a river demon.

st-francis-of-assisi-the-friars.context_blurb: In the early 13th century, a wealthy young Italian cloth merchant's son stripped off his fine clothes in the town square, handed them back to his father in front of the bishop and the town, and walked out of his family's life to live as a beggar for Christ. He gathered a small band of followers who, like him, owned nothing, worked with their hands, and preached in the street in plain language that ordinary villagers could understand, and his order of friars grew so fast that within a generation it had houses from Ireland to the Holy Land. He is remembered for preaching to birds, for talking a wolf out of eating a town's livestock, and for pioneering new ways of making the Christmas story feel real and present to ordinary villagers in the countryside, not just as a painting in a church but as something they could stand next to and smell. His gentleness and his poverty rebuked a Church that had become rich and powerful, without ever leaving the Church, and his quiet example remains one of the most loved patterns of Christian life in the world today, imitated by religious men and women in every century since.

st-peter-s-basilica-and-the-renaissance-.context_blurb: The current St. Peter's Basilica in Rome, standing on the site traditionally believed to be the burial place of the apostle Peter, was built over the course of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries to replace an older fourth-century church begun by Constantine. The replacement project ran through a succession of architects including Bramante, Raphael, Antonio da Sangallo, Michelangelo (who designed the famous dome in his old age), and Carlo Maderno (who extended the nave eastward), with Gian Lorenzo Bernini finally designing both the great twisted bronze canopy over the high altar inside and the enormous curving colonnaded piazza outside. The project was funded partly by the sale of indulgences in Germany, which helped provoke Martin Luther's protest in 1517 and the Protestant Reformation. The finished basilica is the largest church building in the world by interior area, with a nave over 185 meters long and a dome 42 meters across — larger than the Pantheon's. Michelangelo was reportedly determined to build it larger than the ancient Roman dome and succeeded by a few feet. The basilica remains the ceremonial heart of the Roman Catholic Church, where popes are elected, enthroned, and buried, and where enormous public liturgies draw hundreds of thousands of pilgrims to Rome every year.

stamp-act-no-taxation-without-representa.context_blurb: In 1765 the British Parliament passed the Stamp Act, which required that virtually every piece of printed paper in the American colonies — newspapers, legal documents, licenses, playing cards, almanacs, pamphlets — carry a government-produced revenue stamp. The purpose was to raise money to help pay for the recent French and Indian War and the ongoing cost of garrisoning British troops in North America. The reaction in the colonies was explosive. The Stamp Act was the first British law that imposed a direct internal tax on American colonists rather than regulating trade, and the colonists had no representatives in the British Parliament that had passed it. Colonial politicians, pamphleteers, lawyers, and street mobs in nearly every port town denounced it loudly. The slogan No Taxation Without Representation, coined earlier in a slightly different form, became the rallying cry. Mobs in Boston attacked the house of the stamp collector; stamp agents in other cities resigned under threats; nine colonies sent delegates to a Stamp Act Congress in New York in October 1765. Parliament repealed the act the following year but passed the Declaratory Act asserting its right to legislate for the colonies in all cases whatsoever. The underlying argument had not been resolved, and the Revolution ten years later would resolve it violently.

star-spangled-banner-fort-mchenry.context_blurb: During the War of 1812 between the United States and Great Britain, a British fleet attempted in September 1814 to force its way into Baltimore Harbor by first destroying the city's main harbor defense, Fort McHenry. The fleet shelled the fort for twenty-five continuous hours through the night of September 13 to 14, 1814, firing rockets and mortar bombs that lit up the sky. A thirty-five-year-old American lawyer named Francis Scott Key was aboard a British ship as a prisoner-exchange negotiator and watched the bombardment from the deck. When the smoke cleared at dawn and he could see that the enormous American garrison flag was still flying over the fort, he was moved to write a four-stanza poem on a letter in his pocket, originally titled Defence of Fort M'Henry. The poem was quickly set to the tune of an existing popular British drinking-club song and renamed The Star-Spangled Banner. It was widely sung as a patriotic song throughout the 19th century and was finally made the official national anthem of the United States by Congress in 1931. The original flag that flew over Fort McHenry that night still exists, carefully preserved and on public display at the Smithsonian in Washington, D.C.

stoicism-and-epicureanism-hellenistic-ph.context_blurb: After Alexander the Great died in 323 BC and the small Greek city-states lost their political independence to the great Hellenistic kingdoms, Greek philosophy shifted its focus. The urgent question was no longer how to design the best possible polis but how an individual could live well in a world they could no longer control. Two new schools of philosophy answered the question. One, founded by Zeno of Citium in a painted portico in Athens, taught that the good life is lived in agreement with nature and reason, that external things like wealth, fame, pain, and even death are not truly good or bad, and that human freedom lies in training yourself to desire only what is within your power. The other, founded by Epicurus in a garden on the outskirts of Athens, taught that the good life is a quiet pleasure of mind, achieved by freeing yourself from unnecessary fears — especially the fear of the gods and the fear of death — and from unnecessary wants. The two schools agreed on more than they liked to admit, and both are enjoying a modern revival as practical philosophies for ordinary life in a world people often cannot change.

strategic-bombing-and-tokyo-firebombing.context_blurb: The Second World War was the first war in which heavy aerial bombardment of enemy cities was conducted on an industrial scale. All of the major combatants bombed each other's cities. The German Luftwaffe bombed Warsaw, Rotterdam, Belgrade, Coventry, London, and dozens of other British, Polish, Dutch, and Soviet cities during the first half of the war. The British Royal Air Force and the United States Army Air Forces conducted a sustained campaign of strategic bombing against German cities from 1942 to 1945, culminating in the destruction of Hamburg, Dresden, Berlin, Cologne, and dozens of other German cities, with civilian casualties running into the hundreds of thousands. In the Pacific, American B-29 bombers under General Curtis LeMay switched in early 1945 from high-altitude precision bombing to low-altitude incendiary attacks on Japanese cities. The most devastating single attack, on the night of March 9 to 10, 1945, burned out large sections of Tokyo and killed around a hundred thousand Japanese civilians in a single night — more immediate deaths than either of the atomic bombings that followed in August. Dozens of other Japanese cities were similarly firebombed over the following months. The moral record of Allied strategic bombing has been argued over by historians, moralists, and veterans for the eight decades since.

stravinsky-rite-of-spring-riot-1913.context_blurb: Igor Stravinsky (1882 to 1971) was a Russian-born composer who left Russia for Western Europe in his twenties and became one of the central figures of 20th-century music. He wrote three ballet scores for the great impresario Serge Diaghilev's Ballets Russes company in Paris in the years before the First World War, and the third of them, premiered on the evening of May 29, 1913, in a newly opened Paris theater, caused one of the most famous theatrical scandals in history. Stravinsky's score, with its violent pounding rhythms, its dissonant harmonies, and its pre-Christian pagan subject matter about ritual sacrifice in prehistoric Russia, together with Vaslav Nijinsky's unfamiliar modernist choreography, caused a riot in the audience within minutes, with yelling, booing, cheering, and reportedly some physical fighting. The scandal immediately made Stravinsky famous. His later career ran through many stylistic phases — Russian primitivist, Neoclassical, serial twelve-tone — and he kept composing almost until his death at eighty-eight in New York, where he had emigrated during the Second World War. He is now treated as one of the half-dozen most influential composers of the 20th century, and the ballet that caused the 1913 riot is now a standard concert and recording staple.

suez-crisis-1956.context_blurb: In the summer of 1956, the Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser abruptly nationalized the Suez Canal, the critical shipping lane between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea that had been built by French engineers in the 1860s and operated since then by an Anglo-French consortium. Britain, France, and Israel together planned a secret military operation to retake the canal and overthrow Nasser. Israel attacked across the Sinai Peninsula in late October; Britain and France pretended to intervene as neutral peacekeepers and bombed Egyptian military targets. The military operation succeeded on the ground. Politically it was a disaster.
