American President Dwight Eisenhower was furious at having not been informed, pressured the pound sterling in international financial markets, and publicly demanded the withdrawal of British, French, and Israeli forces. The Soviet Union made loud threats of nuclear intervention. Britain and France withdrew humiliatingly. The crisis marked the end of Britain and France as independent great powers in global affairs and the arrival of the United States and the Soviet Union as the two actors who really mattered in the Middle East. Nasser emerged from the crisis as a hero of the Arab world. The British prime minister Anthony Eden resigned in disgrace. The two European powers never again attempted a major independent military operation in the region.

sugar-plantations-the-encomienda-system.context_blurb: Sugar cane had been grown and processed on Mediterranean islands long before 1492, but the Spanish and Portuguese pushed the model across the Atlantic to Caribbean and Brazilian islands where the climate let planters harvest it almost year-round. Cutting cane and boiling it down to crystal sugar was brutal, dangerous work; an exhausted worker whose sleeve caught in the rollers of the crushing mill had only seconds before being dragged in alive, and overseers kept drastic emergency measures ready at every mill. To staff the fields the Spanish first used the encomienda, a legal fiction under which the Crown placed a group of Indian villagers in the care of a Spanish colonist, who was supposed to protect them and teach them Christianity in exchange for their labor and tribute, as if the villagers were a sort of ward of the household. In practice it was slavery in all but name, Indian populations collapsed from disease and overwork, and planters turned to importing enslaved Africans — the moral catastrophe that Bartolome de las Casas spent his life trying to undo and that priests of the Salamanca School began attacking from first principles. The sugar-and-labor model that took shape in these Caribbean islands would be exported across the Americas and became the economic backbone of the Atlantic world for the next three centuries.

sumer-and-the-first-city-states.context_blurb: Sumer was the civilization that developed in the southern floodplain of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers in what is now southern Iraq, starting around 4000 BC. The Sumerians built the earliest cities we can firmly document — Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Nippur, Eridu, Kish, Umma, and others — walled centers of between ten and fifty thousand people, each ruled by its own king and its own patron god, with the city's temple complex (centered on a stepped platform called a ziggurat) at its heart. Sumerian civilization gave the ancient world an astonishing number of its foundations: the first known system of writing (cuneiform), the first known schools, the first known codes of law, the first known literary texts including the Epic of Gilgamesh, the first known base-60 mathematics (which we still use for our hours and our circles), the use of the wheel for both pottery and transport, large-scale irrigation agriculture, and the earliest known organized religious hierarchy. The Sumerian city-states fought each other constantly and were eventually absorbed into successor Mesopotamian empires — the Akkadians, the Babylonians, the Assyrians — but Sumerian civilization left a cultural inheritance that every later ancient Near Eastern civilization built on. Sumerian itself became a dead liturgical language several centuries into the second millennium BC.

sumerian-inventions-wheel-plow-sail.context_blurb: The Sumerian civilization that flourished in southern Mesopotamia from the fourth through the second millennia BC produced an extraordinary number of early technological inventions. Sumerian potters developed the fast potter's wheel, which became the ancestor of all later wheels, including transport wheels fitted to carts in the fourth millennium BC. Sumerian farmers developed the ox-drawn plow, which multiplied the amount of land a single farm family could cultivate. Sumerian engineers worked out large-scale irrigation canal systems that let a few farmers feed a whole city for the first time in human history. Sumerian shipbuilders developed the sail, allowing cargo to move efficiently up and down the Tigris and Euphrates and along the Persian Gulf. Sumerian metalworkers developed bronze. Sumerian mathematicians developed a base-60 number system, with place-value notation and fractional arithmetic, that we still use today for angles, hours, and minutes. Sumerian astronomers kept careful observations of the planets and the Moon that fed into the later Babylonian astronomical tradition. The combined effect of these inventions was to make dense urban life possible for the first time, which is why Sumer is usually described as the cradle of civilization — a dense and slightly inaccurate phrase, but one that captures something real about what happened here first.

sundiata-keita-the-lion-king-of-mali.context_blurb: Sundiata Keita, called the Lion King, was the 13th-century founder of the Empire of Mali in West Africa. According to the famous Mande epic that has been passed down by griots for over seven hundred years, Sundiata was born crippled as the son of a king and a hunchbacked second wife, was mocked and underestimated as a child, taught himself to walk by sheer will in a scene that is still central to the oral epic, and eventually went into exile with his mother as rival factions seized the throne of his father's small kingdom. When a neighboring king named Soumaoro Kante conquered Sundiata's homeland and oppressed his people, Sundiata returned with an alliance of neighboring states, defeated Soumaoro at the Battle of Kirina around 1235, and founded the Mali Empire out of the wreckage. The empire he set up, with a council of elders representing the member states, is sometimes claimed by modern Mande scholars as the Kurukan Fuga charter — an early constitution that laid out rights and obligations for citizens of the new empire. Whether in exactly that form or not, Sundiata is one of the great founder-figures of medieval African history, and his epic is still performed in both oral and musical form across the Mande-speaking world today.

sunni-shia-split.context_blurb: The Sunni-Shia split is the oldest and deepest division within Islam, and it began almost immediately after the death of the Prophet Muhammad in 632 over a single question — who had the authority to lead the Muslim community after him. One party, which became the Sunni majority, held that the community should choose its own leader from among the most senior and respected companions, and so they followed Abu Bakr, Muhammad's close friend and father-in-law. The other party, the Shiat Ali or 'Party of Ali,' held that leadership belonged to Muhammad's own family and should have gone to his cousin and son-in-law Ali ibn Abi Talib, who was eventually chosen as the fourth caliph but was later assassinated at prayer. The deepest Shia wound of all came in the year 680 at Karbala in Iraq, when Ali's son Husayn — Muhammad's grandson — was surrounded with a small group of family and followers by an Umayyad army and killed, and Shia Muslims still commemorate that martyrdom every year with grief and ritual mourning. The two communities share the same Qur'an, the same prophet, and the same five pillars of worship, but they differ on the chain of religious authority after Muhammad and on which stories and sayings count as reliable traditions.

surrealism-dali-s-melting-clocks.context_blurb: Surrealism was a 20th-century artistic and literary movement, officially founded in Paris in 1924 by the French writer Andre Breton, which drew on Freudian psychoanalysis and sought to tap directly into the imagery of the unconscious mind as a source of art. Surrealist painters produced works that look like photographed dreams — recognizable objects placed in impossible scenes, melting watches draped across barren landscapes, trains emerging from fireplaces, apples floating in front of men's faces, elephants on long spider-thin legs, giraffes on fire. The movement included painters like Rene Magritte in Belgium (whose paintings deliberately played philosophical tricks on the viewer), Max Ernst, Joan Miro, Yves Tanguy, Giorgio de Chirico, and the Spanish painter Salvador Dali (1904 to 1989), who became the most publicly famous Surrealist of all, partly through his genuine technical gifts and partly through his talent for self-promoting theatrical persona (the waxed moustache, the pet ocelot, the appearances on American television). Dali's painting of soft watches draped across a barren landscape is one of the most-reproduced images of 20th-century art. The movement had its biggest practical reach not in painting but in its influence on advertising, cinema, and the visual conventions of commercial dreamscapes, which have been doing watered-down Surrealism ever since.

suttee-thuggee-and-foot-binding-ended-by.context_blurb: In the nineteenth century, a cluster of long-standing customs that caused appalling suffering to women and travelers in India and China came under sustained attack by named reformers — some of them colonial officials, some missionaries, some educated local figures working inside their own traditions. In India, two separate campaigns ran side by side. One targeted the Hindu custom in which a widow was burned alive on her husband's funeral pyre, a practice banned by a British governor-general working alongside Indian reformers. The other targeted a secretive hereditary network of highway stranglers who preyed on travelers along the Indian trunk roads, broken up by a sustained police campaign run under another British official. In China, a different movement — eventually joined by Chinese reformers and the republican leader Sun Yat-sen — attacked a thousand-year custom of binding wealthy girls' feet to keep them small, a practice that crippled generations of women. The questions ahead cover the weapon used by the Indian stranglers, the Chinese poetic name given to the bound foot, the British official who led the campaign against widow-burning, how a famous Baptist missionary responded to the moment he had to translate the ban into Bengali, the key technique used to roll up the strangler gangs, and the surprising modern tools Chinese anti-foot-binding reformers used alongside quotations from Chinese tradition. It matters because these campaigns are part of a long argument about moral universals — about whether human beings can look across cultures and say that a given custom should end.

taiping-rebellion.context_blurb: The Taiping Rebellion raged in southern and central China from 1850 to 1864 and was by far the largest internal war of nineteenth-century China. Its leader was Hong Xiuquan, a failed scholar from a Hakka village in Guangdong province who, after reading a Christian tract and suffering a serious illness, came to believe he had received visions revealing his true place in Heaven. He gathered a growing movement of peasants, miners, and discontented southerners, declared the founding of a Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace, swept north with an army of hundreds of thousands, captured the great southern city of Nanjing, and held it as his capital for over a decade. The Qing dynasty, already weakened by the Opium Wars, had to raise new regional armies under scholar-generals like Zeng Guofan, borrow modern weapons and officers from the Western powers in Shanghai, and fight the Taiping back city by city. The questions ahead cover Hong's central religious self-description — his claim about who he was in the cosmic order — and the overall death toll of the war when it finally ended. It matters because the Taiping war shattered central China, exposed how fragile Qing authority had become, and set up the long collapse of imperial China that would end with the republic in 1911.

taj-mahal.context_blurb: The Taj Mahal is a white marble mausoleum on the south bank of the Yamuna River in Agra, India, built between the 1630s and the 1650s by order of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as a memorial for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who had died in childbirth. The building is a classic example of Mughal architecture — a fusion of Persian, Islamic, and Indian architectural traditions — set on a raised platform with a long reflecting pool stretching in front of it through a formal four-part Persian garden representing paradise, with slender minarets at each corner. The central mausoleum is capped by a huge onion-shaped dome and clad in a particular white marble quarried in Rajasthan, inlaid in semiprecious stones in flowing floral patterns called pietra dura. The marble is treated so that the whole building shifts in color through the day with the changing light, from the rosy pink of dawn through dazzling white at noon to the gold and silver of sunset and moonlight. Tens of thousands of workers labored on it for over two decades. Shah Jahan was eventually deposed by his own son Aurangzeb and spent the last years of his life under house arrest, able to see the Taj from his window across the river, before being buried beside his wife inside it. It is one of the most-visited and most-photographed buildings in the world.

tang-dynasty-golden-age-of-poetry-arts.context_blurb: The Tang dynasty, which ruled China from 618 to 907 AD, is generally regarded as the golden age of Chinese civilization. During the Tang, China was the richest, largest, and probably most culturally vital society on Earth. The Tang capital of Chang'an, laid out on a careful grid under imperial planners, grew to over a million people and became a magnet for traders, students, and ambassadors from across Eurasia. Foreign quarters housed Persian, Jewish, Nestorian Christian, Arab, and Central Asian communities, and foreign fashions and foreign music were enormously popular at court. Tang scholars wrote some of the greatest poetry in the Chinese language — the names Li Bai (sometimes written Li Po) and Du Fu are still synonymous with lyric poetry in Chinese culture, and schoolchildren still memorize their poems well over a thousand years later. Tang craftsmen produced glazed polychrome tomb figurines, exquisite silver-work, and the earliest surviving block-printed books. Buddhism reached its highest influence on Chinese culture during the Tang before a 9th-century imperial persecution began its long decline. The dynasty collapsed into warlord fragmentation after a devastating mid-8th-century rebellion, but its cultural legacy has never been eclipsed in Chinese memory.

tenochtitlan-the-floating-aztec-capital.context_blurb: Tenochtitlan was the capital of the Aztec Empire, built in the middle of a shallow lake on the high plateau of central Mexico. According to Mexica tradition the city was founded on the exact spot where their long migration ended because they saw a sacred sign promised by their god Huitzilopochtli. Over two centuries the city grew outward from a small natural island as farmers patiently extended its footprint using soft lake-bottom materials to build the floating gardens the Aztecs called chinampas. Three long causeways tied the island to the mainland, broken by removable wooden bridges that could be managed to make or break access to the city at a moment's notice, and a double aqueduct brought fresh drinking water in from a hill called Chapultepec, with the second channel carefully designed so that one line could always be in service while the other was down for maintenance. Hernan Cortes's hard-bitten soldiers, cresting the mountains and seeing the shining white city for the first time, wrote home that they could hardly believe their own eyes. Two years later the Spanish starved it into submission in a long siege whose final blow struck at the very engineering that had kept the island capital alive.

teotihuacan-city-of-the-gods.context_blurb: Teotihuacan was a huge pre-Columbian city in the Valley of Mexico, about thirty miles northeast of modern Mexico City, that flourished from around the 1st century BC to the 7th century AD. At its height it covered over eight square miles and held perhaps a hundred thousand people, which made it one of the largest cities in the world at that time. Its layout was grand and deliberate: a long central avenue of monuments called the Avenue of the Dead, flanked by the enormous Pyramid of the Sun and the slightly smaller Pyramid of the Moon, with a precinct of the feathered serpent god near the center, and residential compounds laid out on a strict grid. The builders of Teotihuacan apparently did not speak Nahuatl; who exactly they were, in linguistic terms, is still being debated. By the time the Aztecs rose to power in the 14th century, the city had been in ruins for seven hundred years, and the Aztecs — awed by what they found — gave the site its name, which in Nahuatl means roughly the place where the gods were made. They treated it as a sacred pilgrimage destination and borrowed its iconography. Modern archaeology is still slowly uncovering the city's secrets, including the recent discovery of liquid mercury pooled in sealed chambers under the serpent temple.

terracotta-army.context_blurb: The Terracotta Army is a buried life-sized clay army of thousands of individually sculpted soldiers, horses, chariots, archers, and officers, placed in formation around the tomb of China's First Emperor Qin Shi Huang in the late 3rd century BC near the modern city of Xi'an. The figures were discovered in 1974 by local farmers digging a well, which hit a buried head. The subsequent excavations have uncovered pit after pit of soldiers arranged in battle order, each face individually shaped so that no two are quite alike, carrying real bronze weapons that were still sharp when they were unearthed. The scale of the project — thousands of figures, in multiple massive pits, representing just the outer defense of a much larger buried complex that has not yet been fully excavated — speaks to the resources Qin Shi Huang commanded and to his conviction that he could rule from beyond death the way he had ruled from his throne. The central tomb mound itself remains unexcavated; according to the Han historian Sima Qian, writing a century after the burial, the mound contains an elaborate underground palace with ceilings showing the heavens and floors containing flowing rivers of mercury. Modern soil samples around the mound confirm abnormally high mercury concentrations, so there may be something to the old story.

teutoburg-forest-varus-loses-three-legio.context_blurb: In AD 9, in the dense forests east of the Rhine River in what is now Germany, a Roman governor marching with three full legions and their support troops walked into the greatest military disaster in the history of the early empire. He was leading his force through unfamiliar woodland on word that there was unrest to the north, trusting the guidance of a local nobleman who had grown up as a Roman hostage and served loyally in the Roman army. The nobleman was in fact leading him into a carefully prepared ambush. The attack was spread over three days of running fights along narrow, boggy paths and ended with the almost total destruction of the Roman force. The commander killed himself to avoid capture. When the news reached Augustus in Rome, the elderly emperor is said to have beaten his head against a wall and cried out the name of his lost general over and over. Rome never seriously tried to annex Germania east of the Rhine after this, and the river stayed the frontier of the empire for the next four centuries. The battle has been remembered in German history as the moment when the deepest tribes of Germania pushed back the Roman tide.

the-abbasid-caliphate-and-baghdad.context_blurb: The Abbasid Caliphate replaced the Umayyads in 750 and ruled much of the Muslim world from a brand-new capital — Baghdad, built on the Tigris in a perfectly circular plan ordered by the caliph al-Mansur in 762. Under the Abbasids' first century, Baghdad grew into the single largest city in the world outside China, home to the Translation Movement and the House of Wisdom, where scholars from many communities rendered Greek, Persian, Indian, and Syriac texts into Arabic. From Baghdad's workshops came the Arab contributions to mathematics and astronomy, the first systematic treatments of medicine from al-Razi and Ibn Sina, and the folk-tale cycle that the world eventually knew by a different name through Antoine Galland's French edition. The caliphate's political power began to fracture in the ninth century as its outer provinces broke away and its generals' Turkic palace guard made and unmade caliphs almost at will. The end came in 1258, when the Mongol general Hulagu Khan sacked the city and executed the last Abbasid caliph, closing one of the great chapters of human civilization — though a surviving branch of the family would later be installed as nominal caliphs under the Egyptian Mamluks, the real power of the office never recovered, and the title was eventually claimed by the Ottomans after their conquest of Cairo in 1517.

the-american-home-front-rosie-the-rivete.context_blurb: During the Second World War, with millions of American men away in military service, American women entered the industrial workforce in enormous numbers to fill the labor demand of a wartime economy. Women took jobs welding, riveting, assembling aircraft, driving trucks, running cranes, repairing engines, keeping the shipyards and aircraft plants and munitions factories running on multiple shifts. Over six million American women took war-production jobs between 1941 and 1945, including over two million working directly in defense industries. The United States government ran a huge propaganda campaign encouraging women to take industrial jobs, and the iconic poster image of a strong-armed woman in a bandana and work clothes, flexing her bicep over the caption 'We Can Do It!,' has become one of the most-reproduced images of twentieth-century American patriotic art. The image is often called Rosie the Riveter, though the original 1943 poster did not use that name. After the war, many of these women were pushed back out of the workforce to make room for returning male veterans, but the experience of professional industrial work left a lasting cultural mark and contributed to the long-term reshaping of American gender expectations across the following decades.

the-ancient-hebrews-and-monotheism.context_blurb: The ancient Hebrews — the people who became the Jews — introduced into the ancient Near Eastern world a slowly developing conviction that there was one God, the creator and judge of all things, who had entered into a covenant relationship with their people. This idea, called monotheism, was almost unique in the ancient world, where every other people worshipped a pantheon of gods tied to specific places, elements of nature, or human activities. The Hebrew scriptures record the slow and often contested development of this conviction from the time of Abraham in the second millennium BC through Moses and the Exodus, the settlement of the land of Israel, the kingdom of David and Solomon, the writing of the prophets, and the Babylonian exile. The uncompromising ethical demand that followed from Hebrew monotheism — that human beings owe their obedience to a single moral law revealed by a single righteous God who demands justice and mercy — reshaped the entire moral vocabulary of the Western world. Judaism became the parent of Christianity and the great cousin of Islam, and the ancient Hebrew conviction about one God is now the religious inheritance of over half of humanity, directly or indirectly. The Hebrew Bible also contains some of the greatest poetry, legal writing, and historical narrative of the ancient world.

the-ancient-olympic-games-at-olympia.context_blurb: The ancient Olympic Games were a Greek athletic festival held every four years in honor of the king of the gods at his great sanctuary at Olympia in the western Peloponnese. The games had religious origins — their traditional founding date is 776 BC — and they continued almost without interruption for over a thousand years before a Christian Roman emperor finally shut them down in the late 4th century AD. During the games a sacred truce was proclaimed across the Greek world, so that athletes and spectators could travel safely to Olympia even in time of war. The events included footraces, boxing, wrestling, a brutal mixed-combat sport, chariot and horse racing, and later a famous long-distance footrace. Only free Greek men competed, in the nude, and only married women were barred from attending as spectators, which has puzzled historians. The winner of each event received a wreath of olive leaves — no gold medals, no cash prize at the games themselves — but victory brought enormous prestige in the athlete's home city, usually followed by free meals for life. The modern Olympic Games were founded in 1896 to revive the tradition, which is why they still carry the ancient name.

the-assyrian-war-machine.context_blurb: The Neo-Assyrian Empire, which ran from roughly 900 to 600 BC and dominated the ancient Near East at its peak, built one of the most formidable military organizations of the ancient world. The Assyrians were pioneers of large standing armies, systematic siege warfare, iron weapons on a mass scale, cavalry as a distinct arm, military engineering, and the deliberate use of terror as a political strategy. Assyrian royal inscriptions on palace walls boast with graphic imagery of flaying rebels alive, impaling defeated enemies on stakes, deporting entire populations to distant parts of the empire, and piling up skulls as monuments to Assyrian victory. The imagery was partly propaganda and partly real policy. The Assyrians conquered Babylonia, destroyed the northern Hebrew kingdom of Israel (and deported its population in what later Jewish tradition called the Ten Lost Tribes), briefly seized Egypt, and ran a huge imperial bureaucracy out of their capital cities of Nineveh and Nimrud. The empire collapsed suddenly in the late seventh century BC when the Medes and Babylonians allied against it. Nineveh fell in 612 BC with such complete destruction that its site was quietly lost for over two thousand years before European archaeologists rediscovered it in the nineteenth century, buried under its own mounds.

the-atlantic-triangular-slave-trade.context_blurb: For roughly four hundred years, European merchants ran a three-cornered trade across the Atlantic. Ships left ports like Liverpool, Bristol, and Nantes carrying guns, iron, cheap cloth, and a particular distilled drink the colonies had learned to make from sugar byproducts, and traded all of it on the West African coast to coastal African polities who had already captured interior peoples in warfare and raiding and now sold a share of them on. The captives were marched to the coast, held in stone fortresses, and packed into the lower decks of ships for the terrible middle leg to plantations in the Caribbean and the Americas. There the survivors were sold, and the ships took on sugar, tobacco, cotton, and the raw materials to make more of that same spirit for the voyage home. Over the whole run of the trade, millions of African men, women, and children were forced into that passage, and the largest single national destination — the one most often forgotten by American readers — lay far to the south. Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807 and spent the next sixty years using its navy to hunt down the ships of other nations still running it, a moral breakthrough won against stiff opposition and paid for in money, blood, and British lives.

the-atomic-bomb-and-the-manhattan-projec.context_blurb: The Manhattan Project was the enormous secret American effort during the Second World War to build an atomic bomb before Nazi Germany could. The project grew out of a 1939 letter signed by Albert Einstein and drafted by the Hungarian emigre physicist Leo Szilard, warning President Franklin Roosevelt that recent German discoveries about splitting the uranium atom could make a weapon of unprecedented destructive power. By 1942 General Leslie Groves was running the construction side and the physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer was running the scientific side out of a classified laboratory in the New Mexico desert at Los Alamos. More than 100,000 people worked on the project across huge industrial sites at Oak Ridge, Tennessee and Hanford, Washington, enriching the key isotopes and producing a brand-new element, plutonium, in specially built reactors. The first full prototype weapon was tested in the predawn darkness of July 16, 1945 at a site called Trinity in southern New Mexico. Three weeks later, on August 6 and August 9, 1945, atomic bombs were dropped on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki; Japan surrendered less than a week after the second bomb. The scientists who had built them spent the rest of their lives arguing about what they had done. Oppenheimer, who had read a great deal of Hindu scripture in the original Sanskrit as a young man, afterwards tried to put the weight of what he had seen into words of ancient religious literature.

the-automobile-and-the-internal-combusti.context_blurb: In the second half of the nineteenth century, European engineers finally cracked the problem of taming the explosion of a fuel-and-air mixture inside a sealed cylinder to drive a piston. Nikolaus Otto patented the four-stroke cycle in 1876, and Gottlieb Daimler and his quieter partner Wilhelm Maybach shrank Otto's engine down into something small, fast, and light enough to carry a vehicle under its own power. Karl Benz, working separately in Mannheim, assembled the first fully self-propelled, purpose-built horseless carriage with its own gasoline engine, which he filed for patent in 1886 under a short name of his own choosing. It was Benz's wife, Bertha, who really sold the thing to the world: in 1888 she set out before dawn, without telling her husband, and drove one of the early models with her two teenage sons more than a hundred kilometres from Mannheim to her mother's house in Pforzheim, improvising repairs on the road with the simple everyday objects she had in her pockets. She stopped at pharmacies for fuel because gasoline was then sold as a cleaning solvent. By the time she arrived she had become the world's first long-distance driver, proved that the machine really worked for ordinary people, and generated the kind of newspaper publicity her husband could never have bought. Within a generation, American engineers like Henry Ford had turned the finicky toy into a mass-produced consumer good that reshaped cities, courtship, work, and warfare across the twentieth century.

the-aztec-empire-and-the-triple-alliance.context_blurb: The Aztec Empire, as we usually call it, was in its own time a Triple Alliance of three city-states on and around the lake in the Valley of Mexico — Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, and Tlacopan — that had joined forces in 1428 after overthrowing the previous dominant power in the valley. The dominant partner was Tenochtitlan, with the Nahuatl-speaking Mexica people, and the alliance built a tributary empire across most of central Mexico over the next century. The Aztec state did not rule its subject cities directly; it demanded regular tribute in goods, labor, and sacrificial captives, and left local rulers in place as long as the tribute came in. The system worked by terror as much as by law — rebellious cities were put down with great cruelty — and it accumulated enormous resentment among the subject peoples. When Cortes arrived in 1519, that resentment is one of the main reasons his small Spanish force could gather tens of thousands of Indigenous allies to help him march on Tenochtitlan. The Aztec Empire was not an ancient civilization; it was less than a century old at its peak. The brilliance of its capital city and the brutality of its religious system both grew with astonishing speed in a very short historical window.

the-aztec-empire-tenochtitlan.context_blurb: The Aztec Empire, a Triple Alliance of three city-states led by Tenochtitlan on the lake in the Valley of Mexico, dominated central Mexico for about a century from the 1420s until its destruction by Spanish and Indigenous allied forces in 1521. Tenochtitlan itself was one of the most spectacular cities in the pre-contact world, built on an artificial-island complex in a shallow lake, connected to the surrounding shoreline by long causeways with removable bridges, laced with navigable canals, and fed by chinampas gardens that produced an abundance of corn, beans, chilies, and tomatoes. The city at its peak held several hundred thousand people, larger than any European city of its time. At its center stood the Templo Mayor, a huge twin-shrined stepped pyramid dedicated to the war-god and the rain-god, with its ceremonial precinct, its ball courts, its calmecac schools for noble youth, and its enormous market. The Aztecs ran their empire as a brutal tribute system, with routine mass human sacrifice at the great temples, and the resentment of subject peoples helped Hernan Cortes recruit the Indigenous allies who marched with him when the empire fell. Modern Mexico City sits directly on top of the drained lake and the ruined ceremonial precinct.

the-aztec-sun-stone-calendar-stone.context_blurb: The Aztec Sun Stone is a huge circular basalt monolith, nearly twelve feet across, carved in the late 15th century by Aztec sculptors in the capital Tenochtitlan. It was buried in the ruins of the great central temple precinct after the Spanish conquest and lost for over two hundred years. It was rediscovered in the main square of Mexico City in 1790 during paving work and set up for public display. The stone is sometimes called the Aztec calendar, which is partly misleading; it is really a cosmological disk showing the Aztec vision of the universe, with the face of a central sun god staring out at the viewer, surrounded by concentric rings carved with symbols for the day signs of the Aztec ritual calendar, past world-ages that the gods were believed to have created and destroyed, and other mythological imagery. It is now one of the most famous objects in the vast collection of the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City and is used throughout modern Mexico as a visual symbol of pre-conquest heritage. Its exact ceremonial purpose is still debated, but it is one of the great masterpieces of Aztec stone carving.

the-bantu-migrations.context_blurb: Over roughly three thousand years, beginning around 1000 BC in what is now Cameroon and southeastern Nigeria, Bantu-speaking farmer-herders migrated out across most of sub-equatorial Africa in one of the great human population movements in prehistory. They did not move in a single wave; the migration was a slow, uneven, generations-long diffusion of related peoples carrying with them farming techniques, pottery styles, iron-working, and a family of related languages that would eventually fragment into the hundreds of Bantu languages spoken today, from Swahili in East Africa to Zulu and Xhosa in South Africa to Kikuyu in Kenya and Lingala in Central Africa. Along the way the Bantu speakers absorbed, intermarried with, or displaced older populations of hunter-gatherers (the ancestors of today's San and other Khoisan peoples), and they transformed much of sub-equatorial Africa into a landscape of farming villages. The Bantu expansion is one of the biggest and best-documented long-distance migrations in human prehistory, and it explains why most of the languages spoken south of the equator across the continent are related to each other, often closely enough that speakers of one Bantu language can still hear echoes of their own in another.

the-barbarian-invasions-and-the-sack-of-.context_blurb: During the 4th and 5th centuries AD, waves of Germanic peoples — Goths, Vandals, Franks, Lombards, and others — moved into Roman territory, sometimes as allies and settlers, sometimes as raiders, and sometimes as full-scale armies. One group of them, the Visigoths, became the first foreign army in nearly eight hundred years to sack the city of Rome itself, in AD 410, under their king Alaric. A different Germanic people, the Vandals, sacked Rome again a few decades later with such thoroughness that their name eventually became a common word in English for wanton destruction. In the middle of this period a Hunnic warlord known for his terrifying energy swept across Europe at the head of a steppe army and became such a figure of dread that Christian writers nicknamed him the Scourge of God. The Christian theologian Augustine, watching all of this from Roman North Africa, wrote his great book The City of God in response, arguing that no earthly city is eternal and that the Christian hope lies elsewhere. The city of Rome itself survived, but the central authority of the western emperor dissolved over this period, and medieval Europe was slowly built out of the wreckage.

the-believing-scientists-of-the-revoluti.context_blurb: The Scientific Revolution of the 1500s, 1600s, and 1700s is sometimes told as the story of reason breaking free from religion. The actual record is more interesting: the great early scientists were, almost without exception, convinced Christians who believed the orderly universe they were uncovering was the handiwork of a rational God. Copernicus was a Catholic church official, Kepler was a devout Lutheran, Newton wrote more about theology than about physics, Boyle funded Bible translations, Pascal defended Christianity in writing of soaring beauty, and the Jesuits ran some of the best astronomical observatories in Europe. These scientists did not see themselves as fighting religion; they saw themselves as doing a kind of worship by reading what one of them called the second book God had written, the book of nature. The modern caricature of science versus religion was mostly invented in the 19th century. The real picture of the Scientific Revolution is a thousand believing Christians, with a few deists and freethinkers among them, hunting for the fingerprints of their Creator in the stars and the blood and the chemistry of fire.

the-bering-land-bridge-and-peopling-of-t.context_blurb: During the last Ice Age, when enormous quantities of water were locked up in continental ice sheets and sea levels were much lower than they are today, a wide stretch of land, now called Beringia, was exposed between what is now northeastern Siberia and Alaska. Beringia was a tundra-steppe environment with grasses, large grazing mammals, and enough resources to support human bands, and the people who inhabited it were the ancestors of nearly all the Indigenous peoples of the Americas. Over thousands of years before and during the end of the Ice Age, their descendants moved south down the Pacific coast and inland corridors into the main body of North and South America. The traditional archaeological picture had this migration happening relatively recently and all at once, but newer genetic and archaeological evidence suggests multiple waves of movement, considerable time spent in Beringia itself, and possibly coastal migrations by boat as well as overland walking. Rising sea levels at the end of the Ice Age drowned the land bridge, leaving today's Bering Strait. The genetic and linguistic diversity of Native American peoples today reflects thousands of years of adaptation across the whole hemisphere after that long entry.

the-berlin-wall-goes-up-1961.context_blurb: Between the end of the Second World War and the summer of 1961, nearly three million East Germans fled from East Germany into West Berlin, which, as an island of Western occupation inside the Soviet occupation zone, had become the main escape valve from the Soviet-controlled East to the free West. The exodus was catastrophic for East Germany — most of the refugees were skilled workers, young people, and professionals, exactly the population the regime could least afford to lose. In the early hours of August 13, 1961, East German soldiers under Soviet direction began laying barbed wire across every street, alleyway, canal, and rail line between East and West Berlin. Within days the wire had been turned into a concrete wall, with watchtowers, cleared death strips, trained guard dogs, armed sentries, and standing orders to shoot anyone attempting to cross from east to west. Berliners woke up to find themselves cut off from family members, workplaces, and whole neighborhoods on the other side. The United States and its Western allies protested loudly but did nothing to tear down the wall, which stood for twenty-eight years as the most visible symbol of the Cold War division of Europe before being torn open by the East Germans themselves in November 1989.

the-bhagavad-gita-s-battlefield-dilemma.context_blurb: The Bhagavad Gita, literally the Song of the Lord, is a short dialogue of about seven hundred Sanskrit verses embedded in the Mahabharata, usually read as a standalone religious text and treated as one of the central scriptures of Hinduism. It records a conversation that takes place on the eve of a huge battle between two sides of the same royal family. The warrior prince Arjuna, surveying the ranks drawn up against him and recognizing uncles, cousins, teachers, and friends about to be killed, is overcome by grief and despair and sits down in his chariot refusing to fight. His charioteer, who turns out to be the god Krishna in human form, spends the next eighteen chapters answering him in a conversation that ranges across duty (dharma), the immortality of the soul, the proper way to act in the world without attachment to the results, several kinds of spiritual discipline, and the ultimate nature of reality. The Gita's teaching that action done without selfish attachment to its fruits can be a path to liberation has influenced Hindu religion, Western philosophy, and modern figures from Mahatma Gandhi to J. Robert Oppenheimer, who quoted it when watching the first atomic test and seeing what he thought he had helped unleash.

the-big-three-yalta-and-potsdam.context_blurb: During the Second World War, the leaders of the three main Allied powers — the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union — were often called in Allied propaganda the Big Three. They met in person three times at summit conferences to coordinate strategy and plan the postwar order. At Tehran in late 1943, Franklin Roosevelt, Winston Churchill, and Joseph Stalin met for the first time, agreed on the broad strategy for ending the war, and confirmed the Western Allied commitment to open a Western Front in France. At Yalta on the Crimean peninsula in February 1945, the same three men met again as the war in Europe was clearly ending and agreed on the division of Germany into occupation zones, Soviet entry into the war against Japan, and vague terms about free elections in liberated Eastern Europe that Stalin would quickly ignore. At Potsdam near Berlin in July and August 1945, after Germany had surrendered, Harry Truman (now president after Roosevelt's death), Churchill (replaced mid-conference by Clement Attlee after a British election), and Stalin met one last time. During Potsdam, Truman received word of the successful atomic test at Trinity. The three conferences are often studied as the moment the Cold War was quietly being set up.

the-black-death-1347-1351.context_blurb: In the late 1340s, a terrible disease carried by fleas on rats, and spread between people by cough and droplet in its more aggressive forms, rolled across Europe along the trade routes from the East. It killed an enormous share of everyone it touched. Whole villages were abandoned, mass graves had to be dug, priests ran out as fast as patients, and desperate people tried everything they could think of, from fixed-length waiting periods on arriving ships to self-whipping processions through the streets to the hunting and burning of scapegoats. One of the ugliest responses was a wave of mass killings of Jewish communities, falsely blamed for poisoning the wells; many towns had their Jewish quarters wiped out before the plague itself had even arrived there. The disease kept coming back in waves for centuries, and the social, religious, and economic shocks it caused reshaped Europe. The story covers how it moved, how people understood it at the time, how they tried to fight it with the medical knowledge they had, and some of the stories, true, exaggerated, and plain invented, that grew up around it both in its own century and in the centuries since. The story also covers the strange mix of real medical knowledge, real public-health response (the first serious quarantines in Europe), and the darker reflexes of panic, from scapegoat violence to the whipping processions, that the disease pulled out of a frightened and faithful society.

the-blitz.context_blurb: The Blitz was the sustained German bombing campaign against British cities during the Second World War, running from September 1940 to May 1941 after the Royal Air Force had defeated the German Luftwaffe in the Battle of Britain and the Germans had switched tactics from daylight attacks on British airfields to night bombing of British urban areas. London was the main target, bombed on fifty-seven consecutive nights at the campaign's peak, but Birmingham, Coventry, Liverpool, Manchester, Belfast, and dozens of other British cities were also attacked. Coventry suffered one particularly devastating raid in November 1940 that destroyed much of the city center and gave the English language the dark verb to coventrate — meaning to flatten a city by bombing. The Blitz killed roughly forty thousand British civilians across its nine months and left over a million people homeless. The British population held together under the pounding, with mass public sheltering in the London Underground stations and in Anderson shelters in back gardens, and the Blitz Spirit became a central element of British wartime identity. The campaign ended in May 1941 when the Luftwaffe shifted its forces east for the invasion of the Soviet Union. German attacks on British cities would continue sporadically, including the V-1 and V-2 attacks of 1944 and 1945.

the-british-raj-in-india.context_blurb: After the great Indian uprising of 1857 — which the British called the Sepoy Mutiny and which Indians often call the First War of Independence — the British government took direct control of India away from the old East India Company and placed it under the Crown. The period from 1858 until Indian independence in 1947 is called the British Raj, from the Hindi word for 'rule.' In 1876 Parliament passed an act making Queen Victoria Empress of India. During the Raj the British built an enormous railway network, laid down a legal code that is in large part still in force today, trained a famous elite civil service, and governed a diverse subcontinent of hundreds of millions of people through a small layer of British officials and a large layer of Indian soldiers, clerks, and princes. It was also an era of famines, of economic drain to the imperial center, of brutal responses to resistance, and of growing Indian nationalism. The questions ahead cover the dazzling Indian diamond that ended up in the British Crown Jewels, the famous Indian who became the first non-European Nobel laureate, English words Victorian children learned from the Raj, a notorious grievance about greased rifle cartridges that helped set off the 1857 uprising, how Indian princes signaled their rank, the end of an Indian queen who led resistance against the British, the metaphor used for the Indian Civil Service, a custom the British famously tried to abolish, and the shocking caloric level recorded during a late-Raj famine. It matters because the Raj's long shadow — in law, language, migration, trade, and bitter memory — still shapes India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Britain today.

the-buddha-siddhartha-gautama.context_blurb: The historical founder of what later became Buddhism was a man named Siddhartha Gautama, born in the 6th or 5th century BC in a small kingdom in what is now the border region between India and Nepal, into a ruling warrior family. According to the traditional biography, he grew up in princely comfort inside walled palaces, married, and fathered a son, before his first encounters as a young adult with sickness, old age, and death outside the palace walls shocked him into leaving his family and his inheritance to search for a solution to the problem of human suffering. He spent years as a wandering ascetic trying every spiritual discipline he could find, finally abandoned extreme asceticism as not working either, and reached what he called full awakening while sitting under a particular fig tree. For the next forty-plus years he traveled across northern India teaching his method to anyone who would listen, gathered a monastic community of followers, and died in old age. His disciples preserved his teachings orally for centuries before they were written down. The religion that grew from his teachings eventually spread across most of Asia and now reaches around the world, with hundreds of millions of followers across many quite different schools.

the-carolingian-renaissance.context_blurb: In the late 8th and 9th centuries, the great Frankish emperor and his advisors mounted a deliberate campaign to pull western Europe out of a long slump in literacy and learning. They imported scholars from Britain and elsewhere, standardized a cleaner form of handwriting that made books far easier to read, and set monks across the empire to copy out ancient works in huge numbers. The vast majority of what has survived of classical Latin literature from the ancient world has reached us only because it was recopied during this one burst of medieval industry. Educated people today still read Cicero, Virgil, and Caesar in editions descended from these manuscripts, and even the Latin alphabet in its modern form has quietly carried habits from this period forward. The movement did not last long as a formal court program, and the empire itself soon broke up. But its surviving books, its schools, and its handwriting became the taproot of every later European renaissance, including the great one of the 15th century that often gets all the credit for recovering the ancient world. The story covers the scholars, the schools, the books, and the simple fact that without this one burst of medieval copying, almost everything we now call the classical heritage of Rome would simply have been lost to the mice and the mold of a thousand quiet medieval attics.

the-caste-system-varnas.context_blurb: The traditional Indian social system that developed over roughly three thousand years divided society into layered hereditary groups whose members performed particular kinds of work, married within their group, and ate with their group. The oldest classical division, named in the ancient Vedic texts, was fourfold: priests at the top, warriors and rulers beneath them, merchants and farmers under them, and laborers and servants below those. Over the centuries, especially during the later classical and medieval periods, this fourfold scheme hardened and splintered into thousands of narrower occupational and regional subgroups called jati, each with its own strict rules. Outside the fourfold scheme entirely were groups historically treated as untouchables and assigned the most polluting work, who suffered under centuries of systematic social exclusion. Independent India outlawed caste-based discrimination in 1950 and has run large affirmative-action programs for historically disadvantaged groups ever since, with real and significant effects on urban and professional life. Caste identity nonetheless remains a central feature of Indian social and political life for over a billion people. The modern Indian social system is one of the most argued-over topics in the social sciences, and its history runs much deeper and messier than any simple textbook description.

the-christianization-of-scandinavia-the-.context_blurb: Over roughly the 10th and 11th centuries, the Scandinavian peoples whose longships had terrorized Christian Europe became Christian themselves, sometimes gently, sometimes by royal force. In Iceland in the year 1000, a famously tense national assembly nearly broke the island in two, Christian versus pagan, before a wise speaker was given authority by both sides to settle the question in a single declaration. In mainland Norway, a Christian king toured the countryside with sword and staff, dismantling famous pagan temples and shutting down old blood-sacrifice sites, and his encounter with one of the greatest wooden statues in the pagan north was retold in sagas for centuries afterward. The old gods did not disappear overnight; sagas, poems, place names, and runestones kept their stories alive, and many Christianized Vikings quietly wore the hammer of Thor and the cross as a sort of double insurance. But the public culture of regular human and animal sacrifice died within a few generations, and Christian kingdoms and bishoprics replaced the pagan temples of the North. The story covers that transition, from the great sacrificial groves of Uppsala to the first great churches of the Nordic kingdoms. It is one of the great quiet turning points of medieval Europe, and the Scandinavia that eventually produced its own saints, cathedrals, and universities was built on top of the pagan world that had come before.

the-christmas-truce-of-1914.context_blurb: On Christmas Eve in 1914 — four months into World War I, before the war had fully revealed its cold industrial face — British and German soldiers in the trenches of Flanders put down their rifles and climbed out into no-man's-land to meet each other. The informal truce started that evening when German troops set small Christmas trees along their parapets, lit candles, and sang Christmas carols; the British began singing back in their own language, and later carols that both sides knew were sung antiphonally across the mud. The next morning men stepped into no-man's-land to exchange cigarettes, chocolate, buttons, cap-badges, and little bits of equipment as souvenirs, and some units played impromptu football matches. Officers on both sides tried to crack down on the whole business and threatened the men with court-martial. Nothing like the Christmas Truce happened again on the Western Front, in part because the war soon settled into the gas, machine-gun, and mass-casualty rhythms that made any kind of fraternization unthinkable. Officers in subsequent Christmases issued strict orders against repeat performances, and gunners on each side were told to fire on the enemy lines at midnight on Christmas Eve just to make the point. The 1914 truce remains the great Christmas story of the twentieth century — a strange, brief moment when ordinary men on two sides of a line in the mud chose to behave, for an afternoon, like neighbors.

the-civil-rights-movement-as-moral-victo.context_blurb: The American Civil Rights Movement of the 1950s and 1960s was one of the great moral victories of the modern American tradition. In the states of the former Confederacy, black Americans had been systematically denied the right to vote, confined to segregated schools and public accommodations, barred from most professional occupations, and routinely victimized by both state law and private violence for nearly a century after the end of slavery. A long multi-generational black-led freedom struggle, operating through black churches, historic black colleges, labor unions, and civic organizations, produced in the postwar period an extraordinary generation of leaders. The Baptist minister Martin Luther King Jr. became the movement's most famous spokesman, articulating the moral case for integration and nonviolent resistance in a Christian idiom that gave the movement national moral authority. Rosa Parks, Fannie Lou Hamer, Thurgood Marshall, John Lewis, Medgar Evers, and hundreds of other leaders worked alongside him. A series of federal legal and legislative victories — Brown v. Board of Education, the Civil Rights Act, the Voting Rights Act — formally ended the legal structure of segregation. Dr. King was assassinated in 1968, and his widow and children continued his work. The movement is now rightly regarded as one of the defining achievements of the postwar American tradition.

the-closing-of-the-islamic-golden-age-al.context_blurb: The Islamic Golden Age ended not in a single moment but through a combination of events, the two most famous being an intellectual turn and a catastrophe. The intellectual turn came through al-Ghazali, an eleventh-century theologian so towering that later Muslims called him 'the proof of Islam,' who taught at the great Nizamiyya school in Baghdad before leaving abruptly after a personal spiritual crisis to spend a decade in wandering and prayer. His 'Incoherence of the Philosophers' attacked the Greek-influenced philosophers of his own tradition — especially the followers of Ibn Sina — arguing that their reasoning on certain theological points had drifted into positions impossible for a Muslim to hold, and his masterpiece 'Revival of the Religious Sciences' put religious experience and devotion back at the center of Islamic learning. The catastrophe came in 1258, when the Mongols under Hulagu Khan sacked Baghdad, ended the Abbasid caliphate, and destroyed so many of its libraries and schools that the city's role as a world center of science could not be revived. Historians argue over how much of the long closing of the Islamic scientific tradition was al-Ghazali's doing and how much was simply what happens after a civilization's cultural heart is leveled — but together with a slow turning toward settled precedent over fresh inquiry, these forces narrowed what later generations of Muslim scholars dared to explore.

the-colosseum-and-gladiator-games.context_blurb: The great amphitheater in the center of Rome, built in the AD 70s and 80s by three emperors of the Flavian dynasty on ground that had once been a lake in Nero's private palace, is the single most famous Roman building that survives. It could seat tens of thousands of spectators under a huge retractable cloth awning operated by sailors from the Roman fleet, and under its sand floor was a wooden network of trapdoors, elevators, cages, and corridors that fed animals and performers into the arena from below. The games held there combined professional gladiatorial combat, mock sea battles that briefly filled the lower levels with water, animal hunts, and public executions of condemned criminals, often staged with sadistic imagination. The Roman poor sat for free in the top tiers; senators got the best seats near the sand. The sport was dangerous but not quite the automatic death-fight of popular legend — gladiators were expensive investments and most bouts did not end in killing. The Colosseum remained in regular use for several centuries, and its enduring ruin in the center of modern Rome is the most instantly recognizable Roman building on Earth.

the-columbian-exchange.context_blurb: Historians use one short, now-famous phrase for the sudden two-way flood of plants, animals, people, and microbes between the Old World and the New after 1492, when the two hemispheres were abruptly reunited after roughly ten thousand years of near-total isolation. The Americas sent eastward a basket of staple crops and new flavors that would feed the world and reshape every cuisine on the planet. Eurasia and Africa sent back cereal grains, cane sugar, coffee, bananas, and a parade of domesticated livestock, as well as devastating illnesses that killed much of the Native American population — and, running the other direction, a particularly nasty disease that burned through Europe in the 1490s and whose exact origins are still debated by medical historians. One particular European-reintroduced large animal in particular remade whole native peoples when it returned to the plains, and the plains hunting cultures that rose on its back are impossible to picture without it. The exchange tied the hemispheres together for good, for better and for worse, and the global diet and global ecology we live in today are largely its product. It was one of the most profound biological events in the history of the species, and it unfolded almost entirely in the space of a few decades.

the-columbian-exchange-and-indigenous-di.context_blurb: After Columbus's first voyage in 1492, Europeans and Americans began exchanging plants, animals, and microbes across the Atlantic in a huge biological transfer historians now call the Columbian Exchange. Potatoes, maize, tomatoes, chili peppers, cacao, tobacco, and turkeys went east into the Old World; wheat, horses, cattle, pigs, sheep, chickens, bananas, sugar, coffee, and citrus went west into the Americas. The food trade reshaped diets on both sides of the ocean. But the microbes mattered even more. The native peoples of the Americas had no previous exposure to and almost no immunity against smallpox, measles, mumps, influenza, and many other European and African diseases, and the resulting epidemic waves killed catastrophic percentages of Indigenous populations across the hemisphere, sometimes before any European had ever set foot in a given area. The best modern estimates place the demographic collapse somewhere between fifty and ninety percent of the pre-contact Indigenous population over the first century and a half after Columbus. The depopulation of the Americas by disease is probably the single greatest human catastrophe in recorded history, and it is one of the dominant facts of the modern age.

the-computer-pioneers-babbage-lovelace-t.context_blurb: The idea of a machine that could carry out any mental calculation on its own has a surprisingly long pedigree. In the 1830s and 1840s the eccentric English mathematician Charles Babbage designed, on paper and in part in brass, an enormous steam-powered calculating engine that borrowed its paper-tape control system from an industrial machine already running in textile factories of the day. He could never find the money to finish it. His young friend Ada King, Countess of Lovelace — the mathematically gifted only legitimate child of a famous and infamous father whose name made her a celebrity before she had done anything on her own — translated an Italian description of Babbage's design and in her own long explanatory notes wrote what later readers have called the first published computer program and the first clear statement that such a machine could handle not just numbers but any symbol you could code into it. A century later the English mathematician Alan Turing worked out, in a famous 1936 paper, a precise definition of what it means for a problem to be computable at all, by imagining an idealised reading-head machine of a very particular type. In the Second World War he led the team at Bletchley Park that cracked a notorious German military cipher and helped shorten the war in Europe. He also pioneered the modern question of machine intelligence. Prosecuted by the British state for his homosexuality in 1952, Turing died by suicide at forty-one. The United Kingdom gave him an official posthumous pardon in 2013; he is now on the fifty-pound note.

the-constitution-separation-of-powers-ch.context_blurb: The United States Constitution, drafted at Philadelphia in 1787 and ratified by state conventions in 1787 and 1788, created a federal government divided into three branches: a legislative branch (Congress, itself divided into two houses), an executive branch (the president), and a judicial branch (the Supreme Court and such inferior courts as Congress might create). The division was deliberate. The framers, drawing on Montesquieu and on their own experience with corrupt colonial governments, were convinced that any government that concentrated the power to make, enforce, and judge the law in a single pair of hands would eventually tyrannize the people. By splitting those three functions and giving each branch some ability to check the others — presidential vetoes of laws, Senate confirmation of appointments, judicial review of statutes, impeachment of officials — they tried to build a government that would be strong enough to run a continental republic but internally braced against its own worst impulses. The design was not perfect. It depended, as James Madison famously admitted, on the ambitions of the officeholders in each branch pushing back against the ambitions of the others. It has nevertheless held together for over two and a third centuries, which makes it one of the most successful political designs in human history.

the-counter-reformation-council-of-trent.context_blurb: The Counter-Reformation was the Catholic Church's answer to the Protestant Reformation across the second half of the 16th century. Faced with a Christendom suddenly torn in two by Luther and Calvin, the pope convened a general council of the Catholic Church that met on and off in a northern Italian town in the Alps between 1545 and 1563 — a long council, repeatedly interrupted by war, plague, and the quarrels of secular rulers. The Council of Trent, as it is known, did two things at once: it dealt firmly with some of the real abuses the Protestants had pointed at, and it introduced wholesale reforms in Catholic church life. But it also hardened Catholic teaching on every single point the Protestants had wanted to change, drawing a sharp line between Rome and the Protestant churches that would last four centuries. At the same time, new or reformed religious orders — the Jesuits above all — poured out of Italy into every part of the world, Catholic Europe exploded into the dazzling style now called baroque in painting, sculpture, music, and architecture, and the Catholic Church reclaimed much of what it had briefly lost. By the time the smoke cleared in the 17th century, the Catholic Church was still the largest Christian body in the world and had thoroughly re-energized itself, even as the shape of Western Christendom was permanently split.

the-crusades.context_blurb: The Crusades were a series of Christian military expeditions to the eastern Mediterranean between 1096 and 1291, called by successive popes to recover Jerusalem and the Holy Land from Muslim rule and to answer a desperate plea from the Byzantine emperor whose territories were being overrun by the Seljuk Turks. The First Crusade, launched after Pope Urban II's sermon at Clermont, actually succeeded against long odds: a shoestring Christian army crossed Anatolia on foot, took Antioch, and in July 1099 stormed Jerusalem in a battle whose aftermath — a brutal massacre of the city's Muslim and Jewish inhabitants — stained the Crusader kingdoms' reputation and still rings down in Muslim memory. Later Crusades had decidedly mixed records: the Third Crusade of Richard the Lionheart failed to retake Jerusalem but preserved a Christian coastal strip; the infamous Fourth Crusade in 1204 never reached the Holy Land at all, but was diverted onto the storming and sack of Christian Constantinople, which the Greek Orthodox East never forgave. Military religious orders of knight-monks were founded during the Crusades, and the pope offered Crusaders a special spiritual reward for taking up the campaign. By 1291 the last Crusader fortress at Acre had fallen, the Holy Land was fully back in Muslim hands, and the lasting damage of the whole enterprise was arguably not in the East but in the deepening of the schism between Rome and Constantinople after the sack of 1204.

the-cyrus-cylinder-and-early-imperial-to.context_blurb: The Cyrus Cylinder is a baked clay cylinder about nine inches long covered in Akkadian cuneiform inscription, produced after the Persian king Cyrus the Great conquered Babylon in 539 BC. The cylinder was discovered by a British Museum expedition in the ruins of Babylon in the 1870s and is now in the British Museum collection in London. The inscription records Cyrus's capture of Babylon and his subsequent policies, including his claim to have restored the local gods to their proper temples, to have allowed displaced peoples to return to their homes, and to have ruled with regard for the welfare of his subjects. These policies are consistent with the account preserved in the Hebrew Bible of Cyrus allowing the exiled Jewish community in Babylon to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple that Nebuchadnezzar had destroyed about fifty years earlier. Modern enthusiasts have sometimes called the Cyrus Cylinder the oldest declaration of human rights, which is an exaggeration — the cylinder is standard ancient royal propaganda praising the king for his wisdom — but there is a genuine kernel of truth to the claim that Cyrus's imperial policy was unusually tolerant for its age, and the cylinder is now treated with great respect by modern Iran, where Cyrus is one of the great national heroes.

the-diet-of-worms.context_blurb: The Diet of Worms was the formal imperial assembly of the Holy Roman Empire that met in the German city of Worms (pronounced closer to 'Vorms') in the spring of 1521, under the young emperor Charles V. It is remembered today because Charles summoned Martin Luther to appear before it. Luther was now famous across Germany for his open attack on the pope and the sale of indulgences, and the imperial authorities wanted him to recant everything he had written. Luther went to Worms under an imperial safe-conduct — a legal guarantee of safe passage out of the city, however the hearing went — and over two days of questioning, when he was finally pressed to withdraw his books, he refused. The Diet declared him an outlaw, which under imperial law meant any subject could kill him without penalty. On the road home a friendly German prince staged a mock kidnapping to pull Luther out of harm's way, and Luther spent the next ten months at a mountain fortress called the Wartburg under an assumed identity, working on a German translation of the New Testament. The imperial outlaw declaration was never enforced in his lifetime, in part because Charles V was quickly distracted by wars with France and the Turks, and the Protestant Reformation gained twenty critical years in which to take root.

the-domesday-book-1086.context_blurb: Twenty years after a Norman duke conquered England, he ordered his new kingdom surveyed in detail that no one in Europe had attempted since the Romans. His commissioners rode out across the kingdom in teams, asking a fixed list of questions about who owned what land, how many plowteams it supported, how many free men and slaves lived on it, and what it was worth before the Conquest and after. Their questions were put to local jurors in each hundred under oath, and no one was allowed to appeal against the final answers. The resulting great book settled, in principle, every property question in England as of a single day, and its decisions were final, as final, chroniclers said, as the Last Judgment, and the familiar English nickname that stuck to the book is just the medieval English way of saying so. More than nine hundred years later, courts in England have still occasionally cited this book to resolve very old land claims, which is a longer working life than anyone involved in its making could have imagined, and a demonstration of how seriously the new Norman rulers of England took the business of knowing exactly what they now owned.

the-dust-bowl.context_blurb: Through the 1920s American farmers broke millions of acres of the dry Great Plains to the plow, using powerful new machinery to tear out the deep-rooted native grasses that had held the soil down since the end of the last Ice Age. When the drought years of the early 1930s arrived, there was nothing left to hold the topsoil in place. Enormous dust storms rolled across Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, and Colorado and darkened the sky as far east as Washington, D.C.; on 'Black Sunday,' April 14, 1935, the biggest of them turned the afternoon in Boise City, Oklahoma, as dark as midnight. Hundreds of thousands of ruined farm families loaded their belongings into Model A Fords and headed west toward California, where John Steinbeck would later tell their story in his novel 'The Grapes of Wrath.' Franklin Roosevelt's government took the problem on with new programs for the land, and in time the plains partly recovered — though the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles still lose topsoil to the wind in dry years today. The folk singer Woody Guthrie, who had lived through the storms in Pampa, Texas, wrote some of his best-known songs about what he and his neighbors had seen; the photographer Dorothea Lange made the images of the dust refugees that fixed the whole decade in the American memory.

the-early-muslim-conquests.context_blurb: The early Muslim conquests exploded out of Arabia within a decade of Muhammad's death in 632. In less than a hundred years, Arab-Muslim armies had taken all of Persia, Egypt, North Africa, Syria, and the Levant from the two superpowers of the ancient world — the Sasanian Persian Empire and the East Roman (Byzantine) Empire — both of which had been catastrophically weakened at a terrible moment for their defense. The conquest of Spain in 711 was launched across the strait from Africa by a general named Tariq ibn Ziyad, whose landing-rock on the European side still carries his name in a slightly worn-down form. Muslim armies reached as far east as the Indian subcontinent and as far west as the Pyrenees within a hundred years of Muhammad's death, and only at the battle of Tours in 732 in central France were they decisively turned back by the Frankish army of Charles Martel, whose grandson Charlemagne would eventually be crowned the first Western emperor since the fall of Rome. The conquered peoples kept their own religions under the dhimma system but paid a special tax; many eventually converted to Islam and adopted Arabic, which is why today Egypt, Morocco, Iraq, and Syria speak Arabic rather than their older languages.

the-economic-verdict-how-the-west-bankru.context_blurb: The Cold War ended not in a hot war but in an economic verdict, as the planned-economy model of the Soviet bloc proved itself unable, over the long run, to feed, clothe, and house its own population at anything like the level of the market economies of the West. By the 1970s and 1980s, the gap between consumer life in Western and Eastern Europe had become too obvious to hide, and the obviousness was itself delegitimizing the Soviet system in the eyes of the people living under it. The Austrian school economists — Ludwig von Mises, Friedrich Hayek, and later Milton Friedman — had been arguing since the 1920s that socialist central planning was theoretically impossible because without market prices generated by voluntary exchange, planners could not know what was scarce and what was plentiful and so could not direct resources rationally. By the late 1980s this long-dismissed critique had been thoroughly vindicated by the empirical record. The Soviet Union poured a huge fraction of its national product into its military while losing ground every year to the West on consumer goods, agricultural productivity, and technology. The Reagan-era arms buildup put further strain on the system. When Mikhail Gorbachev tried to reform the economy from within, the whole structure collapsed within six years.

the-eiffel-tower-and-the-1889-world-s-fa.context_blurb: The Eiffel Tower was built in Paris between 1887 and 1889 as the dramatic centerpiece of the Exposition Universelle of 1889 — the world's fair held to mark the hundredth anniversary of the French Revolution. It was the work of the French civil engineer Gustave Eiffel and his firm, which had already made its reputation building iron railway bridges. The tower was an unprecedented structure of wrought-iron latticework: much taller than any building then standing, held up by only four flaring feet, and open to the sky through all its levels. Not everyone loved it. A famous public protest was signed by three hundred Parisian artists and writers denouncing the half-built tower as a 'useless and monstrous' iron smokestack, and one of them, the novelist Guy de Maupassant, became attached to a famous story about his dining habits on it. Eiffel himself knew the tower was only supposed to stand for twenty years, and worked hard during its first two decades to make it indispensable to the French state. The questions ahead cover that famous story about Maupassant's dining habits and the key scientific repurposing Eiffel found for his tower that kept it from being torn down after the fair. It matters because the Eiffel Tower was not just an attraction but a demonstration — of what iron could do, of a confident late-nineteenth-century Europe at its industrial and scientific peak, and of what we now call engineering as a cultural achievement.

the-electricity-pioneers-faraday-tesla-f.context_blurb: Three men stand at three different hinges of the long story of taming electricity. The eighteenth-century American polymath Benjamin Franklin — printer, diplomat, Founding Father — showed through famous outdoor experiments that lightning itself is an electrical phenomenon, and his writings put into general use the pair of plain-spoken labels for electric charge that scientists use to this day. He also invented the lightning rod. Half a century later the Englishman Michael Faraday, raised in poverty and self-educated by a kind of apprenticeship that gave him unusual access to printed books, worked his way into the Royal Institution in London as the lab assistant of the chemist Humphry Davy and then outshone his master. Faraday worked out how electricity and magnetism are deeply connected, and his experiments laid the practical foundation for both the electric motor and the generator — the pair of ideas that make the modern electrified world physically possible. He had almost no formal mathematical training and did it all by patient physical intuition. The Serbian-American Nikola Tesla, working mostly in the United States at the end of the nineteenth century, pushed Faraday's discoveries into the age of practical power distribution. He championed alternating current against Thomas Edison's rival direct-current system, won the long and bitter 'war of the currents' with the backing of the industrialist George Westinghouse, and designed the first great hydroelectric generating station at Niagara Falls. Tesla died in a New York hotel room in 1943, mostly broke, after a lifetime of business decisions that would, had he made them differently, have made him one of the richest men who ever lived.

the-emancipation-proclamation.context_blurb: The Emancipation Proclamation was a presidential order issued by Abraham Lincoln on January 1, 1863, during the American Civil War. It declared that all enslaved people in those parts of the Confederacy still in rebellion against the United States were, from that day on, free. By itself the proclamation did not instantly free everyone — it did not reach into Union-controlled states like Kentucky or Maryland, and in rebel territory it could only be enforced where Union armies advanced — but it changed the nature of the war.
