Lincoln had drafted the document in secret during the summer of 1862 and waited for a Union battlefield success before announcing a preliminary version in September; the final proclamation went out on New Year's Day. The questions ahead cover the ringing phrase at the heart of the document, the all-night prayer services Black congregations held waiting for the moment it took effect, a hymn sung the next morning, the later holiday that celebrates the day the news reached Texas, Lincoln's own quiet words as he signed, which battlefield success triggered the preliminary announcement, a key provision about freed men serving the Union, the condition Lincoln had set for issuing the preliminary version, a prediction of its effect, the fate of the signed original manuscript, the words Lincoln chose to describe it, and the constitutional change that followed later and locked in its results nationwide. It matters because the Proclamation turned a war to save the Union into also a war to end slavery, opened the way to roughly 180,000 Black men serving in Union uniforms, and set up the Thirteenth Amendment that abolished slavery nationwide.

the-english-longbow-crecy-agincourt.context_blurb: For about two centuries in the later Middle Ages, English kings fielded armies with a secret weapon few other kingdoms could match: whole battalions of commoner archers trained from boyhood with a huge yew-and-sinew bow whose draw weight was so punishing that modern re-enactors trying to use authentic reproductions find them extremely difficult to pull. The archers could shoot clouds of arrows faster than almost any other missile weapon on the medieval battlefield, and their special armor-piercing points could, under the right conditions, punch straight through plate. Twice in the long Anglo-French war, at two famous French battles decades apart, these archers massacred the finest cavalry of France, who were slowed by rain and mud and funneled onto a prepared killing ground by simple physical barriers planted into the earth in front of the archers' line. English kings for a time banned certain popular commoner sports to make sure that boys would spend their free time practicing with the bow instead, and the skeletons dug up from a famous Tudor warship, with its drowned medieval archers still aboard, show bodies permanently reshaped by a lifetime at the string. The story covers the weapon itself, the tactics that framed it, the famous victories it won, the quieter cost it exacted on the men who spent their lives drawing it, and the royal laws that worked to make sure England would never run out of trained hands at the string.

the-epic-of-gilgamesh.context_blurb: The Epic of Gilgamesh is the oldest major work of literature in human history. It was composed in Sumerian and later Akkadian over roughly a thousand years, from around 2100 BC to around 1200 BC, with its best-known version preserved on twelve cuneiform tablets from the royal library of King Ashurbanipal of Assyria in the seventh century BC. The epic tells the story of Gilgamesh, a legendary king of the Sumerian city of Uruk — a historical figure who may have ruled in the twenty-seventh century BC and gradually accumulated legend around him. In the poem, Gilgamesh is two-thirds god and one-third human, tyrannizes his subjects, meets a wild man named Enkidu who becomes his friend, undertakes with Enkidu a quest to the Cedar Forest to kill its monstrous guardian, loses Enkidu to divine punishment, and then wanders the earth in grief trying to find the secret of immortality from a flood survivor named Utnapishtim. The flood narrative inside the epic is strikingly close to the biblical story of Noah and probably shares an older common source. The epic was lost for two thousand years before the Victorian decipherment of cuneiform brought it back to life. It is one of the great treasures of ancient literature.

the-exodus-and-the-birth-of-a-covenant-p.context_blurb: The biblical book of Exodus describes the central foundational event of ancient Israel: the escape of the Hebrews from slavery in Egypt under the leadership of the prophet Moses, their forty years of wandering in the Sinai desert, and their reception of the covenant and the law at Mount Sinai. The historical reality of the Exodus is debated by modern scholars. The archaeological record has not produced direct evidence of the specific events, and precise dating is uncertain; most scholars who treat the Exodus as rooted in a historical event place it somewhere in the Late Bronze Age, with proposals ranging from the fifteenth to the thirteenth century BC. What is clearer is that the story of the Exodus became the central self-defining narrative of the Jewish people. Every year at Passover, Jewish families around the world retell the story — the Hebrew enslavement, the ten plagues on Egypt, the parting of the Red Sea, the giving of the law — and apply its moral demand that a free people should treat the oppressed as it would wish to have been treated when it was in bondage. Through its influence on Christianity and later Western political thought, the Exodus story has become one of the single most influential political narratives in human history, invoked by abolitionists, civil-rights leaders, and many others.

the-factory-system-and-textile-mills.context_blurb: The factory system was the central social invention of the Industrial Revolution. Before it, most textile work was done in cottages — spinners and weavers worked at home, at their own pace, often as whole families, and merchants carried the yarn and cloth around on horseback. Beginning in Britain in the late eighteenth century, a cascade of inventions in cotton spinning and weaving pushed the work out of the cottage and into large purpose-built mills powered first by water and then by steam, where hundreds of workers tended machines that ran on the owner's clock, in the owner's building, under the owner's foreman. The questions ahead walk you through the inventors and inventions and villages of that transformation — a frame that spun several threads at once, a lucky accident in a cottage that gave an inventor his idea, a law that quietly protected poor cottage spinners, a famously ambitious businessman who had started life in a very different trade, the brutal shift schedule of the new mills, the fines docked from latecomers' wages, the first purpose-built factory village in the world and the enormous wealth it brought its builder, another spinning machine built by yet another inventor, another English inventor behind a key weaving machine, a daring act of industrial espionage by a young English mechanic who later rebuilt the system in Rhode Island and how he smuggled the design across the Atlantic, the dangerous jobs little children were used for in the mill, a Dickens novel of childhood labor, how overseers kept exhausted children awake, and the moment the famous Lowell mill girls fought back against a wage cut. It matters because this is the moment the modern world of wage labor, discipline by the clock, and mass-produced goods comes into existence.

the-fall-of-the-western-roman-empire-476.context_blurb: The traditional date for the fall of the Western Roman Empire is AD 476, when a Germanic general named Odoacer deposed the last boy to carry the title of Roman emperor in the West, a teenaged puppet whose two personal names ironically combined the names of Rome's legendary founder and its first emperor. There was no replacement; the imperial insignia were sent east to Constantinople, and no one wore them in the West again. The real fall was not a single event but a long unraveling across the fifth century, as Roman field armies decayed, taxes collapsed, barbarian federates were settled on Roman soil, provinces slipped out of imperial control, and the people of the western Mediterranean quietly began to live in a world no longer run from Rome. The eastern half of the empire, ruled from Constantinople, continued without interruption for another thousand years. The question of why Rome fell has been asked ever since, most famously in the 18th-century masterpiece written by an English historian who blamed Christianity among other things. Modern historians now talk less about catastrophic fall and more about transformation, but something fundamental ended in the West in the late 5th century.

the-fertile-crescent-mesopotamia-s-river.context_blurb: The Fertile Crescent is a modern term, coined by the American archaeologist James Henry Breasted in the early twentieth century, for the arc of agriculturally productive land that runs from the Nile valley in Egypt up the eastern Mediterranean coast and curves down through the Tigris and Euphrates valley of ancient Mesopotamia (modern Iraq). This region holds the earliest known sites of plant domestication, animal domestication, settled farming villages, and eventually the first cities. The two great river valleys of the eastern crescent — the Tigris and the Euphrates — flooded unpredictably but could be managed with large-scale canal irrigation, which was gradually developed by the Sumerians in the fourth millennium BC. The surplus food this produced allowed Mesopotamian city-states to support priests, kings, soldiers, scribes, and specialized craftsmen who did not grow their own food. Early Mesopotamian civilization developed writing, mathematics, large-scale architecture, systematic law, and complex religious hierarchy here, and almost everything characteristic of civilization in the Western Old World grew outward from this region or from parallel developments along the Nile. The whole crescent sits in a precarious climate zone, and climate shifts, drought, salinization of soil from irrigation, and the collapse of empires regularly rearranged who lived where across its long history.

the-final-solution-and-wannsee-conferenc.context_blurb: The Final Solution to the Jewish Question — the formal Nazi name for the systematic physical extermination of European Jewry — was decided upon by the Nazi leadership during 1941, in parallel with Operation Barbarossa and the escalation of mass killing of Jews by special killing squads (Einsatzgruppen) following the German army into the Soviet Union. In January 1942 the SS officer Reinhard Heydrich convened a conference of senior German civil-service and party officials at a lakeside villa at Wannsee outside Berlin to coordinate the administrative mechanics of the extermination program across the agencies of the Nazi state. The minutes of the Wannsee Conference survived the war and are now one of the most chillingly bureaucratic documents of the Holocaust: senior officials sitting around a conference table discussing the logistics of killing eleven million Jews across all of Europe. The conference itself did not initiate the killing program, which was already under way; what it did was ensure smooth administrative cooperation among the various agencies of the Nazi state. Over the following three and a half years, roughly six million European Jews were murdered under the Final Solution. Heydrich was assassinated by Czech partisans in Prague in May 1942. Most of the other Wannsee participants survived the war and faced varying degrees of postwar justice.

the-first-crusade-capture-of-jerusalem-1.context_blurb: At the end of the 11th century, a pope at a council in France called on Western knights to march east to help their fellow Christians against the Turks and to recover the city of Jerusalem itself, and the response stunned everyone, including him. Tens of thousands of knights, peasants, priests, and poor pilgrims set off across Europe marked out with the sign of the cross, mostly on foot. A chaotic early movement of commoners rushed ahead of the main armies and met disaster. The main army, after it finally assembled, took three bloody years to fight its way through Anatolia and Syria to the holy city, and when it got there the siege was brutal, and the sack of the city after the walls fell was so savage that even Christian chroniclers recorded it in horrified language. From the wreckage, four small Christian states carved out a precarious life in the Holy Land, and new military orders of warrior-monks were founded to defend them. The movement they started would last two centuries, send Europeans deep into the eastern Mediterranean, and leave both Christianity and Islam permanently marked by the memory of what their fighters did to each other there.

the-forgotten-allies-of-the-east-polish-.context_blurb: The Polish contribution to the Allied war effort during the Second World War was substantial and is often underrepresented in Western wartime memory. Before the war, Polish mathematicians at the Polish Cipher Bureau had made the first critical breakthroughs in reading the German Enigma cipher, and they shared their work with British and French intelligence just weeks before the war began. Polish pilots who had escaped to Britain in 1940 flew with the Royal Air Force in the Battle of Britain, where several Polish squadrons produced the highest kill rates in Fighter Command. Polish ground forces fought under British and American command across North Africa, Italy (including a critical role at the capture of Monte Cassino in 1944), and Northwest Europe. The Polish Home Army inside occupied Poland was one of the largest resistance movements of the war. In August 1944, as the Red Army approached Warsaw from the east, the Polish Home Army launched the Warsaw Uprising against the German occupation forces in the city, hoping to liberate the city before the Soviets arrived. The Red Army waited on the far side of the Vistula River for sixty-three days while the Germans systematically destroyed Warsaw and killed roughly two hundred thousand Poles. The Polish wartime record was then overshadowed by the postwar Soviet imposition of a communist government on Poland.

the-french-revolution-s-terror-as-the-en.context_blurb: The French Revolution began in 1789 with a storming of a Paris prison and the promise of Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity. Within five years it had executed its king, its queen, its most famous scientist, many of its best writers, and eventually its own leaders, in a period called the Terror. The men running the Terror justified their mass killings with the language of pure reason and virtue; they believed they were purifying the nation to build a rational republic, and they trusted their own theories more than they trusted the people they ruled. Thousands of ordinary Frenchmen — not just aristocrats, but shopkeepers, priests, servants, and peasants — went to the guillotine. The Terror ended when its chief architect, Maximilien Robespierre, was himself swept up and killed by the same machinery. The Revolution's long chaos finally ended when a popular young general seized power and crowned himself emperor. The Terror became the great cautionary tale for everyone who came after about what happens when revolutionary ideas, loosed from inherited tradition, religion, and common humanity, go to work on actual human beings. Edmund Burke had predicted most of it in 1790. He was called an alarmist until the blood started.

the-gettysburg-address.context_blurb: On November 19, 1863, four and a half months after the Battle of Gettysburg, a crowd gathered on the battlefield to dedicate a new cemetery for the Union dead. The featured speaker of the day was Edward Everett, a former senator, Harvard president, and Secretary of State, widely considered the greatest classical orator of his generation; he spoke for two hours in the grand style of the time. President Abraham Lincoln had been invited almost as an afterthought to add a few remarks after Everett's oration. Lincoln's remarks lasted a bit over two minutes and ran to about 272 words. He wrote them himself, worked on them up to the morning of the ceremony, and delivered them in a plain Midwestern voice; many in the crowd did not realize he had finished before he was already sitting back down. The questions ahead cover the most famous phrase in that short speech, and the gracious private letter Everett sent to Lincoln the next day about how the two speeches compared. It matters because the Gettysburg Address became the compact statement of what Lincoln believed the Civil War was really about — a new birth of freedom and the survival of self-government — and because it is now routinely treated as the greatest short speech in English.

the-gilded-age-industrialists.context_blurb: The Gilded Age is the name later given — by the writer Mark Twain, with real sarcasm — to roughly the last three decades of the nineteenth century in the United States, when a small group of businessmen built astonishing fortunes on steel, oil, railroads, meatpacking, and finance. Andrew Carnegie, a Scottish immigrant who started as a bobbin boy in a cotton mill, built a steel empire and later became one of the great American philanthropists of his age. John D. Rockefeller cornered the oil-refining industry through Standard Oil and became the richest man in the country. Cornelius Vanderbilt built a steamboat and railroad empire from early beginnings in New York harbor. J. P. Morgan assembled the firms that financed much of it. These men were called 'captains of industry' by their admirers and 'robber barons' by their enemies, and both nicknames fit — they built the industrial infrastructure of modern America and crushed competitors, strikebreakers, and small producers along the way. The questions ahead cover Carnegie's long-term use of his fortune, Vanderbilt's nickname, the small coins Rockefeller liked to hand out as he grew older, a famous strike at a Carnegie steel mill handled by his lieutenant Henry Clay Frick, and Carnegie's own famous line in his essay 'The Gospel of Wealth' about rich men who hoard their money to the grave. It matters because this is the generation that forged American industrial capitalism — and that forced the country to begin asking the modern questions about monopoly, labor rights, and the duties of the very rich.

the-gordian-knot.context_blurb: The Gordian Knot was, according to the Greek legend, a famously intricate rope knot tied in the ancient city of Gordium in central Anatolia and bound to a wagon that had once belonged to a legendary king. An oracle had announced that whoever untied the knot would become ruler of all Asia. When Alexander the Great passed through Gordium in 333 BC on his way east to confront the Persian king, he visited the knot. One version of the story has him patiently working at it; the better-known version has him growing impatient and simply cutting through the whole thing with his sword, satisfying the letter of the prophecy by force rather than cleverness. He went on to conquer most of what the Greeks of his day called Asia, which the Alexander-friendly storytellers afterwards treated as proof that the oracle had been right. The phrase "cutting the Gordian knot" has survived more than two thousand years in Western languages to mean solving a stubborn, complicated problem by a bold stroke that bypasses the complication rather than working through it. It is a kind of thinking Alexander himself was good at and that is still called by his legend.

the-gracchi-brothers-and-the-republic-s-.context_blurb: Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus were two brothers from a distinguished Roman family who held the office of tribune of the people in the late 2nd century BC. The office gave them the right to call the people's assembly, propose laws, and veto any action of the Senate. They used it to push a radical program of land reform, aimed at breaking up vast estates run by slave labor and distributing the land to small farmers, who had been drifting into the Roman mob after years of military service. The Senate hated them. In 133 BC, Tiberius was beaten to death with sticks and broken benches in a political riot during an election dispute. A decade later, his younger brother Gaius was hunted down and killed in another riot, and three thousand of their supporters were executed in the aftermath without trial. The killings established a new Roman habit: political disputes were now settled by armed violence inside the city rather than by law and vote. From the Gracchi onward, the Republic slowly bled toward the dictatorship it would get a century later, and the Romans themselves looked back on their deaths as the moment the old system had stopped working.

the-great-depression.context_blurb: The Great Depression that began with the October 1929 Wall Street crash was the worst economic catastrophe in modern American history. By 1933 unemployment had climbed higher than anyone had thought possible, with millions of Americans out of work, banks failing in waves, and the national economy badly contracted from its 1929 level. Homeless families built shantytowns on the edges of American cities and gave them a bitter political nickname that stuck. The slump reached around the world and was especially vicious in Germany, where mass joblessness fed support for extremist parties on both the left and the right. The two schools of economists who dominated the debate about what to do fought bitterly over its causes: John Maynard Keynes in Cambridge argued that governments had to intervene actively to pull economies out of slumps, while the Austrian economists Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek argued the opposite — that the boom of the 1920s had been fueled by cheap central-bank credit, that the bust was the painful but necessary correction, and that government interference with the adjustment would only prolong the suffering. The American economist Milton Friedman would later publish a detailed technical case about Federal Reserve policy failures in those critical years. Franklin Roosevelt won the 1932 election promising a 'New Deal' for the American people.

the-great-mosque-of-cordoba-and-the-alha.context_blurb: The Great Mosque of Cordoba — the Mezquita — was begun in 785 by the Umayyad emir Abd al-Rahman I on the site of a Visigothic Christian church, and over the next two centuries each new ruler extended it until it became one of the largest mosques in the world. Its most famous feature is a forest of nearly a thousand slender columns of recycled Roman and Visigothic stonework, holding up a striking roof structure of alternating red brick and white stone that the architects designed to raise the ceiling despite the shortness of the old columns. When Cordoba fell to the Christians in 1236, King Ferdinand III reconsecrated the Mezquita as a cathedral and later Spanish kings carved a Renaissance choir and transept straight into the middle of it, which is why the building today is still mostly a Muslim mosque with a Catholic church bursting out of its center. The Alhambra, the last great Moorish palace, was built on a hill above Granada in the fourteenth century by the Nasrid dynasty, the final Muslim rulers of Spain, who held out there until 1492. Its stucco walls are carved so finely that the honeycomb vaulting looks like white lace, and its courtyards and fountains were designed as a working model of Qur'anic descriptions of paradise.

the-great-pyramids-of-giza.context_blurb: The Great Pyramids of Giza, on the west bank of the Nile just outside modern Cairo, are a group of three massive stone pyramid tombs plus the Great Sphinx and a cluster of smaller satellite tombs and causeway complexes. They were built in the Fourth Dynasty of the Egyptian Old Kingdom, around 2600 to 2500 BC, as tombs for the pharaohs Khufu (Cheops), Khafre (Chephren), and Menkaure (Mycerinus). The pyramid of Khufu is the largest, originally rising about 481 feet high (now 455 feet after the loss of its outer casing stones), containing an estimated 2.3 million limestone blocks of varying sizes, and remaining the tallest man-made structure in the world for over 3,800 years until surpassed by medieval European cathedral spires. Modern Egyptologists have progressively dismantled many of the romantic nineteenth-century theories about how the pyramids were built; it is now clear that they were constructed by paid skilled workmen living in planned worker villages adjacent to the construction sites, not by hordes of enslaved laborers as popular tradition long had it. The three Giza pyramids are the last surviving ancient wonder of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and they are the oldest and most famous structures of their kind on Earth.

the-great-schism-of-1054.context_blurb: The Great Schism of 1054 was the formal break between the Catholic (Latin-speaking) Church of the West and the Orthodox (Greek-speaking) Church of the East, two halves of what had once been a single Christian communion. The split had been coming for a long time — the Greeks and Latins had drifted apart on language, on how to make bread for communion, on how to date Easter, on whether priests could marry, and most of all on whether the pope held authority over the whole Church or was simply the honored first among equals. The flashpoint came when Pope Leo IX sent a stern Lombard cardinal named Humbert of Silva Candida to Constantinople to deal with the patriarch, Michael Cerularius; the two men came to despise each other, and Humbert eventually marched into the Hagia Sophia during the liturgy and laid a parchment of excommunication on the main altar. Michael responded with his own excommunication, but by then relations were so poisoned that nobody wanted to repair them, and the two Churches have been formally out of communion ever since. Pope Paul VI and the Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras lifted the ancient curses in 1965 as a shared gesture of goodwill — though full reunion remains, almost a thousand years later, as far away as ever.

the-great-sphinx.context_blurb: The Great Sphinx of Giza is a huge limestone statue, carved directly out of the bedrock of the Giza plateau, with the body of a reclining lion and the head of a man. It sits in front of the Pyramid of Khafre and is one of the largest and oldest monolithic statues in the world — about 240 feet long and 66 feet tall. Modern Egyptologists generally believe it was carved during the reign of the Fourth Dynasty pharaoh Khafre (Chephren) in the twenty-sixth century BC, as part of the mortuary complex associated with his pyramid, and that the human face is a portrait of Khafre himself (though both the attribution and the specific identification are debated). The Sphinx was partly buried in sand for most of its history; several ancient pharaohs undertook excavation projects to uncover it, and a long inscription on a stela between its paws records a dream in which the pharaoh Thutmose IV, then still a prince, was promised the Egyptian throne if he would clear the sand. The statue's nose is famously missing. Several legends have blamed Napoleon's soldiers for shooting it off; the real culprit was almost certainly a Sufi Muslim named Muhammad Sa'im al-Dahr, who defaced the Sphinx in the fourteenth century as an idolatrous image.

the-great-wall-of-china.context_blurb: The Great Wall of China is not a single wall and was not built all at once. The various walls now grouped together under that name were built, rebuilt, extended, and connected in different sections by successive Chinese dynasties over more than two thousand years, beginning with early defensive walls thrown up by individual Warring States in the 7th and 6th centuries BC. The Qin dynasty's First Emperor connected many of these in the late 3rd century BC, and the Han, Jin, Northern Qi, Sui, Liao, Jin, and especially the Ming all expanded the system. The imposing stone-and-brick walls that most modern tourists visit outside Beijing are mainly Ming-dynasty work from the 15th and 16th centuries, when the Ming empire was defending itself against the Mongol confederations to the north. The total length of all the various walls combined is thousands of miles, running up and down ridges across north China from the eastern coast nearly to the deserts of Central Asia. The folk belief that the wall is visible from space is simply false — astronauts have confirmed many times that it isn't, mostly because it is long but very narrow. The wall is nonetheless one of the most extraordinary pieces of defensive engineering ever built, representing the labor of millions of people over many generations.

the-gulag-solzhenitsyn-s-witness.context_blurb: The Soviet Union ran, from the 1920s through the 1980s, a huge network of forced-labor camps, prisons, and settlements officially called the Main Camp Administration, or Gulag in its Russian acronym. Tens of millions of Soviet citizens passed through this system over its sixty years, including common criminals, political prisoners, religious believers, suspected foreign agents, deported ethnic minorities, soldiers who had surrendered in combat, and anyone the regime wished to remove from society. Estimates of total deaths in the Gulag range from somewhere over a million to several million, with the worst years occurring during Stalin's terror of the 1930s and the Second World War. The Gulag was documented in a devastating three-volume work of literary journalism by the Russian writer and former prisoner Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, who had been arrested as a Red Army officer during the Second World War for a single critical remark about Stalin in a private letter, served years in the camps, and was later diagnosed with cancer and told he would die. He wrote his book in secret pages hidden across the Soviet Union, had it smuggled abroad, and had it published in Paris. The Soviet state expelled him from the country in 1974. The book did enormous moral damage to the Soviet system and is one of the great works of twentieth-century witness.

the-hellenistic-age-spread-of-greek-cult.context_blurb: After Alexander the Great's death in 323 BC, his vast empire was partitioned among his generals, who turned themselves into kings over huge new kingdoms stretching from Greece and Egypt through Mesopotamia and Persia into Central Asia. The three centuries that follow, until the gradual Roman absorption of the Hellenistic kingdoms ended with the fall of Egypt in 30 BC, are called the Hellenistic Age. During this period, Greek language, Greek urban design, Greek education, Greek drama, Greek sculpture, and Greek habits of thought spread across an enormous belt of the Old World. New Greek-speaking cities were founded on the sites of older towns from the Mediterranean coast to the edge of India, with gymnasia, theaters, agoras, and temples. The city of Alexandria in Egypt became the great intellectual capital of the era, with its famous library and its lighthouse. Greek-speaking Jews in Alexandria translated the Hebrew scriptures into Greek, which is how the Christian scriptures a few centuries later could circulate throughout the Mediterranean world. The Hellenistic Age set the cultural stage on which the Roman Empire and early Christianity would grow.

the-hittites-and-ironworking.context_blurb: The Hittites were an Indo-European-speaking people who built a large empire in central Anatolia (modern Turkey) and northern Syria from roughly 1600 BC to 1200 BC. At their peak, the Hittites were one of the handful of great powers of the Late Bronze Age, maintaining diplomatic correspondence with Egypt, Assyria, and Mycenaean Greece and controlling important trade routes between Mesopotamia and the Aegean. The Hittites famously fought a major chariot battle with the Egyptians under Ramesses II at Kadesh in Syria around 1274 BC, and the surviving Egyptian-Hittite peace treaty signed afterward is one of the oldest formal international treaties whose text has survived. The Hittites are sometimes credited with being among the earliest systematic iron-workers; they almost certainly had iron weapons at a time when most of the surrounding Bronze Age world was still working with bronze, though recent archaeology suggests they did not have a monopoly on iron as earlier historians sometimes claimed. The Hittite capital at Hattusa in central Turkey has been extensively excavated and has yielded tens of thousands of cuneiform tablets in Hittite, Akkadian, and several other ancient languages. The Hittite Empire collapsed suddenly around 1200 BC in the general wave of Late Bronze Age Collapse that affected the whole eastern Mediterranean.

the-holodomor-stalin-s-terror-famine-in-.context_blurb: In 1932 and 1933, Josef Stalin's forced collectivization of Soviet agriculture turned into a deliberate terror-famine aimed at Ukraine, the republic the Soviet state treated as both its grain bowl and its chief nationalist threat. Moscow set impossible grain quotas and sent out armed brigades to seize whatever grain, livestock, and seed-corn Ukrainian peasants had left, and systematically cut the villages off from any outside help. Millions of Ukrainian peasants died. The young Welsh reporter Gareth Jones traveled through famine-struck Ukrainian villages on foot in March 1933 and came out determined to tell the world; he was promptly denounced in the Western press by Walter Duranty, the Moscow correspondent of the New York Times, who insisted — against his own private knowledge — that no famine was happening. Duranty would later be revealed to have been protecting both his access and the Soviet line, and Jones himself would be murdered in Inner Mongolia in 1935 under suspicious circumstances. The Soviet state denied for decades that the famine had happened; Ukraine today remembers the catastrophe under the name 'Holodomor' — 'death by hunger.' It is one of the great crimes of the twentieth century, and modern Ukrainian and Western scholarship treats it as a genocide.

the-holodomor-walter-duranty-s-cover-up.context_blurb: In 1932 and 1933 the Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin's regime deliberately engineered a famine across the Soviet republic of Ukraine, as a weapon against Ukrainian peasant resistance to the Communist Party's forced collectivization of agriculture. Grain was systematically seized from Ukrainian villages by state agents, even seed grain and household food reserves. Peasants were forbidden to leave their villages in search of food. Internal passports were used to seal off starving regions from Russian cities. Estimates of the resulting dead range from roughly 3.5 million to over 7 million Ukrainians, in a famine Ukrainians today call the Holodomor, meaning death by hunger. The famine was systematically denied by the Soviet government at the time, and most of the Western press passed through Moscow at the time repeated the denials. The New York Times Moscow correspondent Walter Duranty, who had privileged access to the Kremlin, personally dismissed reports of famine as absurd and received a Pulitzer Prize for his reporting from Russia in the same period. Modern Ukraine, modern historians, and modern archive scholarship have since fully documented the Holodomor. The United States, Canada, several European parliaments, and an increasing number of countries now officially recognize it as an act of genocide against the Ukrainian people.

the-horse-returns-to-the-americas.context_blurb: The horse is often thought of as a European animal that was brought to the New World, but the deeper story is weirder and more interesting. The ancestor of modern horses actually evolved in the Western Hemisphere, roamed its grasslands in large herds for millions of years, and then disappeared from the Americas around the end of the last Ice Age, in the same mass die-off that took the mammoths and the giant ground sloths. By the time Columbus arrived, the species had been absent from its homeland for roughly ten thousand years. When Spanish ships began landing them in the Caribbean in the 1490s, and when a few runaways and raided herds spread north out of Mexico onto the Great Plains, the horse found exactly the kind of grassland its distant ancestors had thrived in and multiplied explosively. Plains peoples who had hunted bison on foot adopted the new animal within a generation and rebuilt their whole way of life around it. The reunion was so complete and so natural-feeling that Plains languages often used familiar older vocabulary already in use for a smaller, already-domesticated animal to name the surprising new one. It is one of the oddest and most beautiful footnotes of the whole Columbian Exchange.

the-house-of-wisdom.context_blurb: The House of Wisdom was the great translation and research academy of Abbasid Baghdad, growing out of a royal library founded by Harun al-Rashid and expanded dramatically under his son al-Ma'mun in the early ninth century. Its scholars translated into Arabic almost everything the Greek, Persian, Indian, and Syriac traditions had produced in medicine, mathematics, astronomy, and philosophy — the caliphs reportedly paid their translators extravagantly, and much of what we have of ancient Greek thought today survives only because of these Arabic versions. Original work followed the translations closely: al-Khwarizmi founded one of the great branches of modern mathematics at the House, al-Kindi laid the foundations of modern cryptanalysis, al-Razi and others overhauled Greek medicine, and the astronomers under al-Ma'mun made measurements of remarkable precision in a time when European astronomy had largely gone quiet. The library's books were counted in the hundreds of thousands by the time of the Mongol invasion in 1258, and when the invaders came, almost all of them were destroyed. Something like the House's spirit continued in Spain and Sicily, where Latin translators later turned those Arabic versions back into the Western languages, feeding the medieval universities and eventually the Renaissance — the medieval world's single greatest chain of transmission, running Greek learning through Syriac and Arabic hands and finally back into Christian Europe through Toledo and Palermo.

the-human-cost-and-shell-shock.context_blurb: The scale of casualties on the Western Front shattered a generation of young men — nearly 10 million soldiers killed worldwide and more than 20 million wounded, with a great many more coming home carrying wounds no doctor could see. Military doctors in 1914 and 1915 kept noticing men who had been near heavy shellfire but had no physical wound coming into the field hospitals unable to speak, trembling uncontrollably, blinded, deaf, or paralyzed in limbs that worked perfectly in anatomical terms. The British army initially blamed the mysterious new condition on physical concussion of the brain by nearby explosions, but as cases mounted the medical establishment slowly came to understand that what they were seeing was psychological injury. Treatment was often harsh — some army doctors used painful methods meant to make malingering more unpleasant than returning to the front — and some British, French, and other soldiers whose minds broke were shot by their own side for 'cowardice,' sentences the British government eventually, in 2006, formally pardoned. The great English war poets — Wilfred Owen, Siegfried Sassoon, Isaac Rosenberg — all served in the trenches and wrote the bitterness of the war into some of the most unforgiving verse in the English language.

the-hundred-years-war.context_blurb: From the mid-14th century into the mid-15th, English and French kings fought a long, interrupted series of wars over who should rule France. English kings, descended through a princess from a French royal line that had failed, claimed the French crown; French kings fought to keep it. The war actually went on for so much longer than a hundred years that modern historians disagree on the exact count. It is remembered for the first great victories of the English longbow against French armored cavalry, for strange and chivalrous moments between captured kings and their captors, for a teenage girl from a village in eastern France who turned the whole thing around for her side at a desperate low point, for new infantry tactics, early cannon, and the slow birth of national feeling on both sides of the Channel. By the end, the English had been pushed almost entirely out of France, keeping only a tiny foothold on the French coast, and most of the French-speaking continental lands England had claimed as its own for centuries were gone. The story covers the famous battles, the famous captures, and the long slow national hardening on both sides that the war helped create.

the-iconoclasm-controversy.context_blurb: The Iconoclasm controversy was a Byzantine civil war inside Christianity, running on and off between 726 and 843, over whether making and venerating images of Christ, Mary, and the saints was a form of idol-worship forbidden by the Ten Commandments. The emperor Leo III started it in 726 by ordering a famous icon of Christ pulled down from the gate of his palace, and generations of imperial decrees followed — icons smashed, monasteries emptied, defenders beaten and sometimes blinded. The theological defense of icons was finally articulated by the Syrian monk John of Damascus and later by the empresses Irene and Theodora, who argued that the Incarnation of Christ had itself permitted images because God had taken on a visible human form. In their argument, the honor given to a holy picture is not a worship of wood and paint but passes through the image to the person depicted, exactly as a kiss given to a photograph of a loved one is really meant for the person in the picture. The Second Council of Nicaea in 787 and the final 'Triumph of Orthodoxy' in 843 settled the matter in favor of the icons — which is why the Byzantine churches of that era, and the Eastern Orthodox churches that are their heirs, remain full of them.

the-ides-of-march-caesar-s-assassination.context_blurb: The Ides of March were the middle of the month in the Roman calendar, and the Ides of March 44 BC are the single most famous day on that calendar because that is the day Julius Caesar was assassinated in Rome. Caesar had made himself dictator for life, had been offered a crown in public and theatrically refused it, had put his own face on coins, and was openly treating the Senate as a rubber stamp. A conspiracy of senators, including some of his closest allies, decided that killing him was the only way to save the old Republic. They attacked him in a hall near the Theater of Pompey while he arrived for a meeting of the Senate, stabbing him many times. Legend has it he said one last phrase of surprise and grief when he saw his friend Brutus among the attackers. The conspirators thought they were restoring the Republic; instead they had removed the last man strong enough to hold it together. The civil wars that followed would end only with Caesar's adopted son installed as the first Roman emperor, Augustus. The phrase "Beware the Ides of March" has echoed through Western literature ever since.

the-inca-empire-and-cusco.context_blurb: The Inca built the largest empire in the pre-Columbian Americas, running most of the length of the Andean coast and highlands from modern-day Ecuador down into Chile and Argentina. Their capital was Cusco, high in the central Peruvian Andes, where the first Inca ruler had legendarily struck a golden rod into the earth to mark the city's founding. The empire expanded explosively under the ruler Pachacuti in the mid-15th century and reached its greatest extent under his grandson Huayna Capac just before 1500. The Inca spoke Quechua, worshipped the Sun as their imperial god, managed a vast system of state storehouses and road-and-bridge networks, and ran a central redistributive economy without money or markets, using the quipu for records. Everything about the empire — its roads, its masonry, its agriculture on terraced mountain slopes, its administration — bore the mark of extraordinary engineering talent. When Pizarro arrived in 1532 the empire had just been through a devastating civil war between rival imperial brothers, which is one of the reasons it fell as quickly as it did. Cusco survived the conquest and became a colonial Spanish city built on top of Inca foundations, which is why it still carries its old Inca masonry today.

the-inca-empire-machu-picchu.context_blurb: The Inca ran the largest empire in the pre-Columbian Americas, stretching along the Andean spine from southern Colombia to central Chile. Starting from the city of Cusco in highland Peru, the Inca state expanded explosively in the mid-15th century under the ruler Pachacuti and his son and grandson, until it ran its central redistributive economy over a population of perhaps ten million people. The Inca spoke Quechua, worshipped the Sun as their imperial deity, kept their records on knotted-cord quipus, built an enormous system of state roads and granaries, and expanded their territory through a mix of brilliant diplomacy and brutal military force. They have been admired by modern writers for the sophistication of their stonework, for the social-welfare orientation of their state economy, and for the astonishing high-mountain estates they built in places like Machu Picchu, a 15th-century royal retreat perched on a ridge above the Urubamba River that was never discovered by the Spanish and so survived largely intact. The empire fell in just a few years in the 1530s to a very small Spanish force under Francisco Pizarro, taking advantage of a recent Inca civil war and the devastation of smallpox. Quechua is still spoken by millions of Andean people today.

the-inca-road-system-and-rope-bridges.context_blurb: The Inca Empire was held together physically by one of the greatest road networks of the ancient world: tens of thousands of miles of paved, drained, and surveyed roads running the length of the Andes and the Pacific coast. The roads connected the imperial capital of Cusco to the farthest provinces, carried relay runners called chasquis who could pass messages from one end of the empire to the other in just a few days, and supplied government warehouses stocked for the army and for emergency food distribution during drought years. Where the roads had to cross deep mountain gorges, Inca engineers wove suspension bridges out of twisted plant-fiber ropes, maintained by local villages whose annual duty it was to rebuild them. One such bridge, near the small Peruvian village of Huinchiri, is still rebuilt every year by the surrounding communities using the traditional braided-ichu-grass method, in a public festival that is one of the last unbroken living fragments of Inca state engineering. Spanish chroniclers, who were accustomed to Roman roads, repeatedly expressed astonishment at the quality and reach of the Inca roadway system across country they considered impossibly rugged.

the-industrial-revolution-as-the-great-e.context_blurb: For almost all of human history, nearly all people in nearly all places lived at some version of the same material standard — a daily ration measured in a modest number of pounds of grain, a handful of garments made at home, a small, drafty dwelling heated by a wood or dung fire, and a short, hard life threatened constantly by famine, infection, and childbirth. Economic historians sometimes describe this long baseline as the 'Malthusian trap,' because any gain in productivity tended to be eaten up by population growth, pulling living standards back down. Then, beginning in Britain in the late eighteenth century and spreading outward through the nineteenth and twentieth, something extraordinary happened: output per person, measured against inflation, began to climb steeply and did not stop. The economic historian Deirdre McCloskey has called this transformation the Great Enrichment and argued that by now ordinary people in rich countries live, by any honest material measure, several dozen times better than their ancestors did in 1800. The questions ahead cover roughly where average incomes in the poorest parts of the world still sit today, which marks the near-end of that pre-industrial ceiling, and one of the great indicators of human flourishing that began changing during the nineteenth century — a change we think of as normal now, but which no earlier century had ever seen. It matters because this upward break is arguably the single most important event in the entire economic history of our species.

the-internal-african-slave-trade-and-the.context_blurb: The transatlantic slave trade is only one half of the slave-trading story. Even as Britain outlawed its own slave trade in 1807, enslaved African captives were still being taken from the African interior by raiding and warfare, marched hundreds of miles overland to coastal ports, and shipped out — now often by Portuguese, Spanish, Brazilian, Cuban, or Arab-run slave traders. Across much of eastern and central Africa, powerful slave-raiding warlords, some of them African, some of them Zanzibari Arab, built kingdoms on the trade. In response, the Royal Navy maintained the West Africa Squadron off the Atlantic coast and later the East Africa Squadron off the Indian Ocean coast, intercepting slave ships, freeing the captives aboard, and burning or buying the barracoons where they were held before loading. The questions ahead cover a striking fact about the former life of one of the Royal Navy's most successful anti-slavery warships, a feared east-African slaver and the surprising origin of his nickname, the ritual conducted at coastal departure points before the final loading, the brutal overland journeys of the ivory trade, the exceptional capture record of one Royal Navy vessel, the shrine coastal communities built over a slave-market site after the trade ended, and the price the European powers at Berlin promised Africans in return for abolishing the trade — a promise paired with their own conquest. It matters because this is the part of the story where abolition stopped being a British parliamentary debate and became a long, bloody enforcement campaign across two oceans and a continent.

the-internal-african-slave-trade-its-wes.context_blurb: Slavery in Africa long predated European contact. Various African kingdoms and polities, from the medieval West African empires to the Swahili coastal city-states to the East African inland kingdoms, had practiced forms of slavery and had traded enslaved people northward across the Sahara into the Mediterranean Islamic world and eastward across the Red Sea for over a thousand years before any European ship arrived. Those internal and trans-Saharan slave networks continued, in various forms, well into the 19th and in some corners of Africa the 20th century. The Atlantic slave trade, which lasted from the 1500s to the 1800s, was partly superimposed on this older system. The crucial moral turning point came not in Africa and not in the Islamic world, but in Christian Europe and its colonial offshoots. Beginning in the late 1700s, a mostly British evangelical Christian movement led by William Wilberforce, Thomas Clarkson, and a long roster of other campaigners pushed first Britain and then one European power after another to abolish the trade, the institution, and eventually, through the Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron, to actively suppress slave-trading operations on the African coast and the high seas. This Western abolition of a worldwide practice is one of the few genuine moral breakthroughs in world history, and the Christian conscience that drove it deserves honest credit.

the-internal-african-slave-trade-that-fe.context_blurb: The Atlantic slave trade did not happen in a vacuum; it plugged into older slave-trading systems that had operated inside Africa and across the Sahara and Indian Ocean for many centuries before any European ship arrived. Powerful West African kingdoms — the Oyo, the Ashanti, Dahomey, the kingdom of Kongo, the Aro confederacy and others — made captives of enemies, criminals, and debtors through warfare and raiding, and then sold a share of them on. Along large swaths of the West African coast, Europeans never ventured inland themselves; they anchored off the shore and bought from African merchants who delivered the captives in chains to the slave fortresses. European buyers paid in goods African elites wanted, including textiles, metal bars, cowrie shells, and liquor, as well as one specific category of imported European technology that quickly became the most sought-after of all because of what it let its new owners do to their neighbors on the next raid. The visible marks of status in many of these courts had their own grim shape, closely tied to the whole business. None of that lessens the moral weight of what Europe did; it does mean the trade only grew to its horrifying scale because partners on both ends profited from it.

the-internet-and-the-world-wide-web.context_blurb: The Internet grew out of an American military research project of the 1960s called ARPANET, a Pentagon-funded network designed to let scientific computers at different universities swap data over telephone lines. Its first message was sent in October 1969 between a computer at UCLA and one at Stanford Research Institute; famously, the system promptly crashed before even one complete word reached the other end, so what did arrive is often listed as the real 'first message' of the Internet. Over the following two decades a loose group of engineers, mostly working for universities and governments, extended ARPANET into a global web of interconnected networks that spoke a common set of rules called TCP/IP. By the late 1980s academics and curious hobbyists around the world were already emailing one another over this growing network, but it was still clunky and text-only. In 1989 an English physicist named Tim Berners-Lee, working at CERN — the big European particle-physics laboratory outside Geneva — wrote a proposal for a system that would layer hyperlinked documents on top of the existing Internet. He wrote the first browser and the first web server himself over the next year or two. In 1993 CERN made what may be the single most consequential decision in the history of the medium: it chose to handle the fledgling Web in a very particular legal way that would in retrospect shape the whole business of the modern Internet. Within five years the Web was changing the world. Berners-Lee was knighted in 2004 and has spent much of his later career campaigning against the capture of what he built by a handful of big companies.

the-iron-curtain-descends-origins-of-the.context_blurb: Within months of the end of the Second World War in 1945, the alliance of convenience that had united the Western democracies with the Soviet Union against Nazi Germany began to come apart. Across the Soviet-occupied zone of Eastern Europe, the Red Army and local Communist Party operatives systematically consolidated single-party control through rigged elections, intimidation, show trials, and in Czechoslovakia a straight-up coup in February 1948. By 1948 Poland, East Germany, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, Yugoslavia (initially), and Albania had all been brought under communist governments aligned with Moscow. In March 1946 the former British prime minister Winston Churchill gave a famous speech at Westminster College in Fulton, Missouri, describing a long political barrier dropping across the continent from the Baltic Sea to the Adriatic Sea, cutting off the capitals of a line of European states that had passed into the Soviet sphere. The phrase that passed into English from that speech — iron curtain — became one of the defining images of the entire Cold War that followed. Over the next four decades the division of Europe into a Western free world and a Soviet-controlled East would shape most of the great power politics of the planet, until the collapse of communism in 1989 to 1991 brought it to an end.

the-iroquois-confederacy-haudenosaunee.context_blurb: The Iroquois Confederacy, whose own name for themselves is Haudenosaunee, was a league of originally five related nations — the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca — living across what is now upstate New York, with a sixth nation, the Tuscarora, joining in the 1700s. According to Iroquois tradition, the confederacy was founded centuries before European contact by two legendary figures, the Peacemaker and his companion Hiawatha, who persuaded the warring nations to bury their weapons under a great white pine tree and come together in a shared political structure. The confederacy was governed by a council of chiefs selected by the clan mothers of each nation, met in longhouse meetings, and reached decisions by consensus rather than by majority vote. Several of the American founders, including Benjamin Franklin, had direct dealings with Haudenosaunee leaders and admired aspects of the system, and historians continue to debate how much the Iroquois example influenced the design of the United States Constitution. The Haudenosaunee are still a functioning polity today, with their own passports, lacrosse team, and relations with both Canada and the United States, and their ceremonies continue in longhouses across the old homeland.

the-italian-renaissance-florence.context_blurb: The Italian Renaissance was the sweeping cultural movement that transformed the city-states of northern and central Italy from roughly the 14th through the 16th centuries. Its unofficial capital was Florence, a small inland city on the Arno River whose banking families had grown fabulously wealthy and could afford to turn themselves into patrons of the arts on a scale no Italian city had seen since Roman times. The Florentine 15th century, in particular, produced an astonishing concentration of artistic and intellectual talent in a few decades: new ways of thinking about the human body, new ways of drawing architectural space on a flat panel, a huge dome crowning the city's unfinished cathedral, bronze doors on the baptistery that a visiting Michelangelo was supposed to have said belonged on the gates of Paradise, and a running conversation between humanist scholars combing through recovered Latin texts and painters and sculptors looking at the surviving statuary of ancient Rome. The Medici family dominated the political life of the city for most of the 15th century and bankrolled much of the art, though they held no official title. Florentine civic pride was fierce. Florence considered itself the heir of republican Rome, and its citizens tended to speak of the Greek and Roman past as a living inheritance that was being handed back to them, not as something merely studied in school.

the-july-crisis-and-alliance-system.context_blurb: The six weeks between the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand on June 28, 1914, and the outbreak of general European war on August 4 are called the July Crisis. Austria-Hungary wanted to crush Serbia for the murder, and the German government promised Vienna its full backing whatever Russia did. Russia had promised to protect its small Slavic cousin Serbia; France had promised to back Russia; and Britain had promised nothing explicit but had been edging closer to France for a decade. When Austria issued an ultimatum to Serbia designed to be rejected, and then declared war, the mobilization timetables of the great European armies — tens of thousands of trains carrying millions of reservists on precisely scheduled routes — rolled into motion, and even monarchs who were first cousins (Kaiser Wilhelm II of Germany and Tsar Nicholas II of Russia were related through Queen Victoria) could not stop them. Germany invaded neutral Belgium to swing around the French armies, a decision that pulled Britain, which had guaranteed Belgian neutrality in an 1839 treaty, straight into the war. By August 4 all the great powers of Europe were at war. Historians have argued about blame ever since: whether Germany's blank check to Austria started it, whether the Russian mobilization forced the German hand, whether French revanchism and British alliance guarantees made containment impossible — but almost nobody now believes the war was somehow unavoidable.

the-kamikaze-failed-mongol-invasions-of-.context_blurb: In the 1270s and 1280s, after his conquest of Song China, Kublai Khan of the Mongol Yuan dynasty attempted twice to extend Mongol rule across the sea to the Japanese islands. Both invasions ended in disaster for the Mongols. In 1274, a Mongol-Korean fleet landed on the coast of Kyushu but was driven back by Japanese resistance and then shattered by a storm on the voyage home. A much larger second invasion in 1281, assembled from both Korea and conquered south China, landed near the same stretch of coast and was again fought to a standstill by Japanese samurai defenders — including, famously, at hastily built coastal walls — before an enormous summer typhoon struck the invading fleet at anchor and destroyed the greater part of it, drowning tens of thousands of invaders. The Japanese attributed the storm to divine protection of their islands and later called it the kamikaze or divine wind. Modern archaeology has recovered a great deal of the sunken Mongol fleet off the coast, confirming the scale of the disaster. The idea of the kamikaze became a potent national myth in Japan and was deliberately revived in a dark way during the Second World War, when it was given to the suicide-pilot squadrons sent against American warships.

the-katyn-forest-massacre.context_blurb: In August 1939, Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union signed a secret non-aggression pact dividing Eastern Europe between them. In September 1939, after Germany invaded western Poland from the west, the Soviet Union invaded eastern Poland from the east. The two totalitarian powers divided the country between them along a prearranged line. Over the following year, the Soviet secret police rounded up an estimated 22,000 Polish officers, policemen, intellectuals, priests, and civic leaders captured during the invasion, and in the spring of 1940 systematically executed them with pistol shots to the back of the head and buried them in mass graves at several sites, the most famous being the Katyn Forest near Smolensk in western Russia. When German troops discovered the mass graves after invading the Soviet Union in 1941, the Soviet Union initially blamed Nazi Germany for the massacre. The Soviet government maintained that cover story for the next forty-nine years. Only in 1990, under Mikhail Gorbachev, did the Soviet Union formally admit that the Katyn massacre had been carried out by its own secret police. The massacre remains one of the clearest, documented atrocities of the Soviet regime, and its denial poisoned Polish-Soviet relations for the whole postwar period.

the-khmer-rouge-the-killing-fields.context_blurb: In April 1975, after years of civil war destabilized by the overspill of the Vietnam War into neighboring Cambodia, the Communist guerrilla movement known as the Khmer Rouge, under the leadership of its chief Pol Pot, marched into the Cambodian capital of Phnom Penh and seized the country. Over the next three years and eight months, the Khmer Rouge regime attempted the most radical social experiment ever carried out: a sudden, violent, total return to an imagined agrarian year zero. They immediately emptied the cities at gunpoint, forced the entire urban population into the countryside, abolished money, markets, schools, religion, and private property, and killed anyone they considered a class enemy — professionals, teachers, officials, Buddhist monks, speakers of foreign languages, people with glasses. Somewhere between 1.5 million and 2 million Cambodians died from execution, starvation, forced labor, and disease during the regime, out of a total population of just over seven million. Mass graves across the country became known as the Killing Fields. The regime was finally overthrown by a Vietnamese invasion in January 1979. Pol Pot himself escaped and died a natural death in the jungle in 1998 before he could be fully tried. The Khmer Rouge are now one of the clearest cases in modern history of ideology-driven mass killing.

the-league-of-nations.context_blurb: The League of Nations was the brainchild of American president Woodrow Wilson — part of his Fourteen Points — and was created at the Paris Peace Conference of 1919 as an international body meant to prevent another world war through collective security and open diplomacy. The League opened in Geneva and quickly began mediating minor disputes; it never attracted the full participation of all the great powers who had made it. It did useful work on refugees, labor conditions, and public health, but its central idea — that the great powers would stand together against aggression — collapsed under its first serious tests. When Japan seized Manchuria from China in 1931, the League's investigation condemned the move but Japan rejected the findings and simply ignored them. When Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935, Britain and France made halfhearted gestures of economic pressure while quietly cutting a side deal that would have handed Mussolini most of what he wanted; the deal leaked, the public was outraged, and the whole episode destroyed what remained of the League's authority. Haile Selassie, the emperor of Ethiopia, came to Geneva in person and warned the League's member states of what they would lose by abandoning collective defense.

the-library-and-lighthouse-of-alexandria.context_blurb: The Egyptian city of Alexandria, founded by Alexander the Great in 331 BC and ruled afterward by the Greek-speaking Ptolemaic dynasty, became the greatest city of the Hellenistic world and the center of its intellectual life. The Ptolemies poured royal patronage into a research institution attached to a famous library that gathered scrolls from across the Mediterranean and beyond, with teams of translators and copyists at work in its reading rooms. Scholars came to Alexandria from everywhere; it is where Euclid wrote the Elements, where Eratosthenes measured the Earth, where early anatomists dissected the human body for the first time in centuries, and where Jewish scholars translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek. In the harbor stood another wonder: an enormous lighthouse that guided ships into the port for centuries and became one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. The library eventually declined over several centuries through a mixture of political neglect and the occasional fire during Roman civil wars, and the lighthouse finally fell in an earthquake in the Middle Ages. Modern Alexandria still carries the ghost of what was once the brightest city of the ancient Mediterranean.

the-maya-and-their-stepped-pyramids.context_blurb: The ancient Maya built hundreds of ceremonial centers across the lowland rainforests and highland basins of what is now southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, and western Honduras, with the great cities of the Classic era rising from the first century AD through the ninth. Each major Maya city centered on a plaza framed by stepped pyramid-temples of carved limestone rising in sharp terraces, royal palaces, ballcourts for the ritual Mesoamerican ballgame, and stone stelae carved with the hieroglyphic histories of their divine kings. The Maya were not one unified empire; they were a shifting world of competing city-states each ruled by its own royal line, with alliances and brutal wars between them. Their art, their mathematics (including a working concept of zero), their astronomy, and their writing system together make them one of the great original civilizations of the ancient world. Later Maya civilization in the northern Yucatan built the famous site of Chichen Itza, with its square stepped pyramid of the feathered serpent god, before being gradually absorbed into the Toltec and finally the Spanish spheres of influence. Millions of people today still speak Maya languages and live in the old homeland.

the-maya-civilization.context_blurb: The Maya civilization of southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, and western Honduras is one of the great original civilizations of the ancient world. Rising from a long preclassic period around 2000 BC, the Classic Maya cities flourished from AD 250 to 900, during which the Maya built most of their famous stone pyramid-temples, royal palaces, and ritual ball courts, and carved thousands of hieroglyphic monuments recording the deeds of their divine kings. Each Maya city was its own independent polity, and the whole lowland world was a shifting pattern of alliances and wars between city-states. The Maya made real intellectual achievements, including a sophisticated calendar system, a working concept of zero as a mathematical placeholder, a complete phonetic writing system that no other pre-Columbian people developed, and precise astronomical observations. The great southern cities collapsed over the 9th century in a long drought-driven implosion. The Maya people themselves did not disappear; northern Yucatan cities like Chichen Itza continued to flourish into the post-classic era, highland Maya kingdoms persisted until the Spanish conquest in the 1500s, and today millions of Maya people still live across the old region and speak dozens of surviving Maya languages. The civilization is one of the few outside the Old World to have arrived independently at a fully developed phonetic script.

the-medici-of-florence.context_blurb: The Medici were a Florentine banking family that produced four popes, two queens of France, and the dominant political dynasty of the city of Florence from the early 15th into the 18th century. They started as moneylenders, parlayed a long-standing financial relationship with the papacy into one of the richest banks in Europe, and under the shrewd leadership of Cosimo the Elder, in the 15th century, began using their wealth to run Florentine politics from behind the scenes while piously financing public works and commissioning the greatest artists of the age. Cosimo's grandson Lorenzo, nicknamed 'the Magnificent,' presided over Florence during what many consider the peak of its Renaissance, surviving an assassination attempt by a rival banking family during Mass at the city's cathedral in 1478. The failed assassins were hanged from the windows of Florence's main government building the same day, in scenes that drew some of the city's artists into the crowd to sketch. Later Medici heirs became Dukes and then Grand Dukes of Tuscany, and the family's younger sons and daughters married into most of the royal houses of Europe. Two members of the family became popes during the Reformation century, both of whom made consequential decisions about the religious upheaval they lived through. The last Medici died in 1743, by which time the family had been shaping European life for a solid three hundred years.

the-medieval-catholic-church-the-pope.context_blurb: In medieval Europe, the Church was the one institution that touched almost every life. It baptized infants, married couples, buried the dead, and ran schools, hospitals, orphanages, and vast charitable networks. Parish tithes supported its priests, and in a world where ordinary peasants rarely saw cash the law expected those tithes to be paid in whatever form a family's harvest and household could produce. At its head stood the pope, who crowned emperors, excommunicated kings, called crusades, and insisted that in the deepest sense his spiritual authority outranked any ruler's worldly one. The Church also had corruptions, from the fundraising scandal of indulgence-selling to vicious political rivalries inside Rome itself, and reformers inside and outside the Church spent centuries trying to clean these up. The story covers the Church's reach into daily life, from the ringing of bells for the hours to the sacraments at the heart of a village's spiritual year, from the great hospital in Paris that still exists to the sharp political theories that popes developed about where their own authority stopped and where kings' began. The story covers the parish, the sacraments, the bells, the shrines, the orders of friars and monks, the medieval popes who tried to be shepherds and the medieval popes who tried to be kings, and the quieter saints who did more than any of them to shape the Christian faith that medieval Europeans actually lived.

the-meiji-restoration-and-japan-s-modern.context_blurb: Only fifteen years after Commodore Perry's black ships forced Japan open, a group of young reform-minded samurai from southern Japan overthrew the Tokugawa shogunate, 'restored' the young emperor Mutsuhito to direct rule, and in his name launched one of the fastest and most ambitious state-led modernizations in history. The era, 1868 to 1912, is named for the emperor's reign-name. Within a single generation Japan abolished its old feudal class divisions, built a modern conscript army on the German model and a modern navy on the British model, laid railways and telegraph lines, built the first large-scale industrial sector in Asia, adopted a Prussian-style constitution, and sent its brightest students to Europe and America to bring back whatever they could learn. The questions ahead cover the meaning of the reign-name itself, a wild popular rumor about what Western-style conscription would really do to peasant conscripts, how many great domains and clans had to merge into the new centralized state, what the government did with huge quantities of a specific traditional metal artifact to pay for modernization, and the fate of Saigo Takamori, the great samurai hero of the Restoration who ended up leading one last rebellion against the modern state he had helped build. It matters because Japan became the first non-Western country to go through a full industrial revolution and win a modern war against a European great power, which permanently changed the global story about who could modernize and under what terms.

the-mesoamerican-ballgame.context_blurb: A ritual team ballgame was played across Mesoamerica for at least three thousand years, from the Olmecs through the Maya and the Aztecs. The game was played on a long stone-walled court shaped like a capital letter I, with a solid rubber ball about the size of a large grapefruit that players had to keep in the air without using their hands or feet, bouncing it off their hips, buttocks, forearms, and specialized padded gear. The ball was heavy and could break bones. In the later versions of the game, stone rings mounted high on the side walls of the court served as goals, and getting the ball through a ring at least once was so rare that it typically ended the game. The game was more than a sport; it had deep religious meaning as a reenactment of cosmic struggle between the daytime and nighttime powers, and some matches at major ceremonial centers ended in the ritual sacrifice of either the losing team or the winning team, depending on the local tradition. The Spanish conquerors were astonished at the behavior of the solid rubber ball — Europe had nothing like it — and the ballcourts can still be found in dozens of ancient Mesoamerican sites open to visitors today.

the-microscope-and-microorganisms.context_blurb: The compound microscope was developed in the late 1500s, probably by a father-and-son team of Dutch spectacle-makers, and over the next hundred years it opened up a whole new world. In England, the natural philosopher Robert Hooke used an early microscope to publish Micrographia in 1665, a book full of beautifully drawn fleas, mites, and the surfaces of leaves and feathers, which became an immediate bestseller. In the Netherlands, a self-taught cloth merchant named Antonie van Leeuwenhoek built his own tiny but startlingly powerful lenses and used them to look at pond water, scrapings from his teeth, and drops of rain. What he saw there — crawling, swimming, living creatures invisible to the naked eye — was so unexpected that he had to send extra witnesses to confirm it before the Royal Society would believe him. His discoveries founded microbiology, though no one grasped what any of it meant for disease for nearly two more centuries. The microscope is one of the great quiet instruments of the Scientific Revolution; it lets a human being see the universe at a scale no human eye was built for, and it changed what counts as evidence in science.

the-middle-passage.context_blurb: The Middle Passage was the sea leg of the Atlantic slave trade — the crossing from West Africa to the plantations of the Americas, during which enslaved people were packed into slave decks less than five feet tall, chained in pairs, and lay in their own filth for six to twelve weeks. On average between ten and twenty percent of the human cargo of a given ship died at sea, from dysentery, scurvy, smallpox, suicide, or the shock of what sailors called 'fixed melancholy,' and the dead were simply thrown overboard. Many captives, who had never seen a European or an ocean, were convinced the pale sailors meant them some unspeakable final fate. Olaudah Equiano, a Nigerian-born abolitionist who survived the passage as a child and later bought his own freedom and wrote one of the first widely read slave memoirs in English, described the heat, the stench, and the sounds of what he had seen as a hell no mind could have imagined. His book, printed again and again, helped turn British public opinion against the trade and became one of the key texts of the long campaign that ultimately ended it. The abolitionist Christians who finally pushed the trade out of English law could point to his testimony and the accumulating evidence of other eye-witnesses as a kind of moral mountain the slave trade's defenders could not finally overcome.

the-moche-civilization.context_blurb: The Moche were a pre-Columbian people who flourished along the dry northern coast of what is now Peru from around AD 100 to 800, long before the Inca. They built two enormous mud-brick ceremonial platforms, one called the Huaca del Sol and the other the Huaca de la Luna, outside the modern city of Trujillo, and they produced some of the finest and most lifelike portrait ceramics of the ancient world, with individualized human faces that still speak off the shelves of museum displays. The Moche are also famous — or infamous — for the richness and the dark imagery of their art, which includes scenes of human sacrifice, prisoner torture, and ritualized bloodletting that modern archaeologists have since confirmed in the skeletal evidence from their temple complexes. One especially spectacular Moche royal burial, the Lord of Sipan, excavated in the 1980s, matched the richest finds of ancient Egypt in gold and semiprecious ornament. The Moche civilization appears to have collapsed in the 7th or 8th century AD, probably under the strain of repeated El Nino climate disruptions, and the coast was later taken over by other peoples. Their art, their irrigation canals, and their desert temples continue to be studied and admired.

the-mound-builders-adena-and-hopewell.context_blurb: Long before the great city of Cahokia, hunter-gardener peoples across the eastern woodlands of what is now the United States built an elaborate culture of earthen mounds, geometric earthworks, and long-distance trade. The Adena culture, which flourished roughly from 1000 BC to AD 200 in the Ohio Valley, built conical burial mounds whose chambers held skeletons dressed in copper beads and carved stone pipes. The successor Hopewell culture, from around 200 BC to AD 500, took the whole system further: enormous geometric earthworks of linked circles, squares, and octagons laid out with precise astronomical alignments across huge tracts of land in modern Ohio, Indiana, and beyond.
