The Hopewell traded for raw materials across continent-wide networks, including obsidian from the Rocky Mountains, copper from the Great Lakes, mica from the southern Appalachians, and seashells from the Gulf. By the time European explorers moved west in the 1700s, the mounds were long abandoned and the current Native peoples had their own oral traditions about who built them. European settlers invented a series of baseless theories about lost ancient white civilizations — the mound-builder myth — that modern archaeology has long since replaced with the solid story of the eastern woodlands peoples themselves.

the-mughal-empire-the-taj-mahal.context_blurb: The Mughal Empire was a Muslim dynasty, descended by family tradition from both a famous Central Asian conqueror and his still more famous steppe ancestor, that ruled most of India from the early 1500s to the mid-1800s. Its founder, Babur, won northern India by exploiting a weapons advantage his Indian opponents could not yet match. His grandson Akbar built a famously tolerant state that invited scholars of every faith to argue theology at his court, dropped a long-standing tax that had fallen specifically on non-Muslim subjects of Muslim rulers, and promoted a formal state doctrine encouraging harmony among all religions of the realm. A later emperor, Shah Jahan, was the great builder of the dynasty, and the building he is most remembered for is a work of white marble constructed as an act of love and public mourning for a particular person after her early death. His own son overthrew him and kept him under house arrest in a fort upriver for his final years, from which he could see the famous building he had raised only from a careful distance. The Mughal state he had inherited was already past its peak during his lifetime, and over the next century it would slowly fragment under the pressure of regional revolts and the growing commercial influence of European trading companies.

the-nazca-lines.context_blurb: The Nazca Lines are a vast collection of geoglyphs — enormous drawings made on the desert floor — scratched into the dry stony plain of southern Peru between about 500 BC and AD 500 by the Nazca people. The lines were made by scraping away the sun-darkened surface pebbles to expose the lighter sandy soil underneath, and in the almost rainless climate of that desert they have survived largely intact for two thousand years. They include very long straight lines running for miles, large geometric trapezoids and triangles, and dozens of figures of animals and plants — a monkey, a hummingbird, a spider, a condor, a tree, a hand, a mysteriously human-looking figure sometimes called the astronaut — some of them hundreds of feet across and only fully readable from the air. The best scholarly guess is that the Nazca Lines were religious walkways associated with rituals and processions, especially appeals for water in a punishingly dry climate, and that the geoglyphs represent sacred beings. In the 1960s a popular writer promoted the baseless and faintly racist theory that only ancient aliens could possibly have made them, which is still irritating serious archaeologists today.

the-nile-river-and-egyptian-geography.context_blurb: The Nile is the longest river in the world (though the Amazon rivals it on some measurements), rising in central and eastern Africa and flowing north through modern Sudan and Egypt to empty into the Mediterranean through a wide fertile delta. Ancient Egypt was, in the Greek historian Herodotus's famous phrase, a gift of the Nile. Egypt itself is almost entirely desert; its civilization grew up along the narrow strip of fertile land flanking the river for about seven hundred miles from the first cataract near modern Aswan to the delta, with the great majority of Egypt's population still living on that fertile strip today. Every year, before the construction of modern dams, the Nile flooded between July and October, depositing a thick layer of nutrient-rich black silt from the Ethiopian highlands across its floodplain. The predictability of this annual flood, combined with the natural barrier of desert on either side of the river valley and the ease of transport the river itself provided (south by sail against the current when the north wind blew, north with the current when going downriver), gave ancient Egypt the geographic conditions for a stable, prosperous, continuous civilization that lasted over three thousand years without being overrun by foreign invasion until relatively late.

the-northern-renaissance.context_blurb: The Northern Renaissance is the art historian's term for the parallel revival of serious art, literature, and classical learning in the lands north of the Alps across the 15th and 16th centuries — the Low Countries, the German-speaking lands, France, and England. It drew on the earlier Italian explosion but had a very different flavor. Where Italian artists had rediscovered the ancient nude figure and worked out mathematical perspective, Northern artists worked in oil paint with astonishing patient detail, filling their panels with the exact weave of a carpet, the shine on a brass chandelier, the embroidered hem of a merchant's gown. Jan van Eyck in Bruges perfected oil painting as a technique and left behind one of the most studied panel paintings in Europe, a quiet marriage portrait set in a Flemish bedroom. Albrecht Durer, a brilliant German printmaker and painter, traveled over the Alps to study the Italians directly, then came home and used the new printing presses to send his woodcuts and engravings across the Continent — including a famous woodcut of an animal he had never seen, drawn from a description, which fixed a wrong but gorgeous picture of that creature in Europe's imagination for many generations. The humanist Erasmus wrote in Latin for the whole European reading public. Thomas More, in England, published a Latin book about an imagined perfect society. By the time it was all over, European art had found a second language.

the-northwest-ordinance-1787-bans-slaver.context_blurb: In 1787, in the same summer that the Constitutional Convention was meeting in Philadelphia, the Second Continental Congress — operating under the dying Articles of Confederation — passed the Northwest Ordinance. The ordinance set up the legal framework for governing the vast western territory the United States had just acquired from Britain at the end of the Revolutionary War, lying north of the Ohio River and east of the Mississippi, which eventually became the states of Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and part of Minnesota. The ordinance did three important things. It guaranteed basic civil rights to settlers in the territory, including religious freedom, trial by jury, and public support for education. It laid out an orderly path for territories to grow in population, elect their own legislatures, and eventually enter the union as new states on an equal footing with the original thirteen rather than as colonies. And in Article VI, it banned slavery and involuntary servitude anywhere in the Northwest Territory. That ban kept slavery permanently out of a huge area of the growing United States and set a legal and moral precedent that abolitionists over the following seventy years would point to repeatedly. It is one of the most consequential pieces of legislation in American history and is often overlooked.

the-olmec-mother-culture-of-mesoamerica.context_blurb: The Olmecs, who flourished along the humid Gulf Coast of what is now the Mexican state of Veracruz between about 1500 BC and 400 BC, are generally regarded as the mother culture of all later Mesoamerican civilizations. The great Mesoamerican traditions that came after the Olmecs — the Maya, the Zapotecs, the Toltecs, the Aztecs — inherited many of their most distinctive features from Olmec roots: the ritual ballgame, the pantheon of long-nosed rain god and feathered-serpent god, the preoccupation with jade, the practice of bloodletting as a religious act, the carving of enormous stone monuments, chocolate drinking, and (probably) the beginnings of writing and the sacred calendar. The Olmecs built large ceremonial centers at San Lorenzo and La Venta with earthen platform mounds, and they carved enormous human heads — portraits probably of specific rulers — from basalt boulders dragged from distant mountains, with the finest examples weighing many tons each. Their civilization faded by around 400 BC for reasons that are still debated, but almost everything that made Mesoamerica distinctive among world civilizations traces back to features the Olmecs had worked out first. The Olmecs are to Mesoamerica roughly what the Sumerians are to the ancient Near East.

the-opium-wars-and-china-s-century-of-hu.context_blurb: In the early nineteenth century, British merchants in Canton (now Guangzhou) had a problem: China was happy to sell them tea, silk, and porcelain for silver, but did not want to buy much from them in return, and British silver reserves were draining east. To close the trade gap, the British East India Company developed a profitable workaround — grow opium in British India, smuggle it into China through private traders, and bring silver home. By the 1830s there were millions of Chinese opium addicts, and the Qing emperor sent an incorruptible scholar-official named Lin Zexu to Canton to shut the trade down. Lin seized the foreign merchants' opium stocks and destroyed them, which gave Britain the excuse to send the Royal Navy. The First Opium War of 1839-1842 ended in a humiliating Chinese defeat and a one-sided treaty; the Second Opium War twenty years later ended with an Anglo-French expedition occupying Beijing and burning the emperor's magnificent Summer Palace. The questions ahead cover how Lin disposed of the seized opium, where he is remembered today with a public statue, the Chinese nickname for Western steam gunboats, a notable omission from the main treaty text, the Chinese name later given to the whole stretch of nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century defeats and foreign impositions, and Victor Hugo's famous image of the sack of the Summer Palace. It matters because the Opium Wars are the starting point of what Chinese nationalism, down to the present day, remembers as a long dark century — a memory that still shapes how Beijing approaches the West.

the-ottoman-empire-fall-of-constantinopl.context_blurb: The Ottoman Turks were a small frontier dynasty that spent the 1300s and 1400s chewing their way around the dying Byzantine Empire until, by the time of young Sultan Mehmed II, the only piece left was the walled capital itself. In the spring of 1453 Mehmed laid siege to Constantinople with a huge army and a monstrous new siege apparatus designed by a Hungarian engineer named Orban. The Byzantines, under their last emperor, blocked the entrance to their harbor with a famous and formidable physical barrier; Ottoman engineers responded with a trick of logistics so audacious it is still a textbook example of problem-solving under siege. After seven weeks of bombardment, walls that had held for a thousand years were breached, the city fell, and the last Byzantine emperor met the end that chroniclers of both sides most respected: he refused escape and died trying to hold a breach with his own soldiers. Mehmed, barely 21, converted the great cathedral of Hagia Sophia into a mosque, claimed titles whose political meaning rippled through the courts of Europe for generations, and set his new capital on a course that would, under his great-grandson Suleiman the Magnificent, make the Ottomans the terror and envy of Europe for another two centuries.

the-pantheon-and-roman-concrete.context_blurb: The Pantheon in the center of Rome is a huge round temple built in its present form around AD 125 by the emperor Hadrian on the site of an earlier temple built by Augustus's deputy Agrippa. It is one of the best-preserved buildings of antiquity because the Christian Church took it over in the 7th century and has used it continuously as a place of worship ever since. Its most impressive feature is its enormous dome, cast of a particular Roman concrete that got lighter and lighter as the dome rose higher, so the whole structure stays up without any internal columns or buttresses. At the dome's crown is a single round opening open to the sky, letting a shaft of sunlight walk slowly across the colored marble interior throughout the day. The dome was the largest built in human history for well over a thousand years, until the Renaissance architect Brunelleschi finally matched it in 15th-century Florence. The Pantheon has influenced Western public architecture ever since, and anyone who has ever stepped inside a 19th-century rotunda or a domed state capitol has walked into a distant child of this one Roman building.

the-parthenon-and-phidias-the-classical-.context_blurb: The Parthenon is a huge marble temple on the acropolis of Athens, built in the mid-5th century BC under the leadership of Pericles during the city's golden age. Its architects were Iktinos and Kallikrates. Its sculptural program was overseen by Phidias, the greatest Greek sculptor of the classical age, who directed teams of carvers to produce friezes, pediments, and metopes that are still studied as high points of the Greek achievement. The temple also housed inside it an enormous gold-and-ivory statue of the city's patron goddess, over thirty feet tall, which is lost to history. The Parthenon survived largely intact for over two thousand years, through Byzantine, Latin, and Ottoman control of Athens, until a 17th-century explosion of gunpowder stored inside blew out most of its interior. In the early 1800s a British nobleman shipped off a large portion of its surviving sculptures to London, where they are still displayed and still disputed. The design of the building — its proportions, its subtle optical corrections, its restraint, its sense of calm balance — became the model for what later ages called the classical ideal in architecture.

the-pax-romana.context_blurb: The Pax Romana — the Roman peace — is the name given to a long period of relative internal stability inside the Roman Empire that stretched roughly from the reign of Augustus in the late first century BC through most of the 2nd century AD. It did not mean there was no war; the Roman legions fought almost constantly on the frontiers, suppressed revolts, and conducted punitive campaigns across the Danube and the Euphrates. What it meant was that within the empire, roads were safe to travel, taxes were collected systematically, Roman law was enforced in the courts, trade reached from Britain to India, cities grew, and ordinary people could live out normal lives without the civil wars that had torn the late Republic apart. The population inside the empire reached heights it would not reach again in Europe for over a thousand years. The Pax Romana made possible the spread of ideas and goods across the Mediterranean world, including the rapid early spread of Christianity along Roman shipping lanes and highways. Later ages, looking back at this long patch of comparative peace, treated it as a kind of lost golden age.

the-peloponnesian-war-athens-vs-sparta-4.context_blurb: The Peloponnesian War was a long, exhausting war between Sparta and Athens — the two leading city-states of classical Greece — and the two alliance systems they led. It began in 431 BC, dragged on with intervals of truce for a full generation, and ended in 404 BC with Sparta's final victory and the loss of the Athenian empire. The war was recorded in a famous history by Thucydides, an Athenian general who had been exiled for a failed campaign and spent his banishment writing about the war as it unfolded. His book is one of the founding works of serious historical writing, with careful speeches, hard-eyed political analysis, and the great cold line that the strong do what they will while the weak suffer what they must. The war broke the political confidence of classical Athens, destroyed much of its population through combat and a famous plague, and left Sparta briefly dominant over the Greek world before Spartan power was itself broken by Thebes a generation later. Classical Greece as a world of free, confident, independent city-states did not really outlive the war, and the Greek states would eventually be absorbed into the kingdom of Macedon under Alexander's father.

the-persian-royal-road-and-administratio.context_blurb: The Persian Empire, running from the mid-sixth century BC to its conquest by Alexander the Great in the 330s BC, was the largest empire the ancient world had seen up to that point, stretching from the Aegean coast of modern Turkey through the Iranian plateau and beyond into Central Asia and the Indus valley. Running such a vast empire efficiently required an unprecedented administrative apparatus. The Persian kings — especially Darius I in the late sixth and early fifth centuries BC — organized the empire into roughly twenty provinces called satrapies, each governed by a satrap, with imperial inspectors nicknamed the king's eyes and ears periodically touring the provinces to check up on local administration. A sophisticated road system radiated from the imperial capitals of Susa, Persepolis, and Ecbatana, with the most famous route called the Royal Road running from Susa in modern Iran to Sardis in western Anatolia — over 1,500 miles — with regularly spaced relay stations where royal couriers could change horses. Herodotus wrote with amazement about how fast Persian messengers could cover the distance. The Persians also standardized coinage, weights, and measures across the empire, and tolerated local religions and customs. The administrative model shaped every later ancient and medieval empire from Rome to the Islamic caliphates.

the-pharaohs-and-egyptian-god-kings.context_blurb: The Egyptian pharaoh was not merely a king in the Mesopotamian or Greek sense; he was understood by the ancient Egyptians to be a living divine being, the human embodiment of the god Horus in life and transforming into Osiris after death. The theological doctrine of divine kingship ran through all of Egyptian religion, royal propaganda, and political structure for roughly three thousand years, from the First Dynasty around 3100 BC until the Roman conquest of Egypt in 30 BC. The pharaoh wore a double crown representing the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt, carried a crook and flail as symbols of royal authority, was represented in art at larger scale than his subjects, and was buried with elaborate preparations for his continuing existence in the afterlife, including the famous pyramids of the Old Kingdom and the painted rock-cut tombs of the Valley of the Kings in the New Kingdom. Several female pharaohs ruled in their own right across the long centuries, including Hatshepsut and Cleopatra VII. The pharaonic ideology was so stable that even foreign conquerors who seized Egypt — Nubian kings, Persian kings, the Macedonian Ptolemies, and finally the Roman emperors — were depicted on Egyptian temple walls in traditional pharaonic garb, performing the standard pharaonic religious rituals.

the-phoenician-alphabet.context_blurb: The Phoenicians, a seafaring Semitic people of the eastern Mediterranean coast, developed over the second millennium BC a simple writing system of just over twenty signs, each representing a specific consonant sound of their language. Earlier Near Eastern writing systems — Egyptian hieroglyphics, Mesopotamian cuneiform — had used hundreds of signs representing whole words or syllables, which required years of specialized training to master. The Phoenician alphabet was by comparison astonishingly easy to learn, and it was used primarily for trade and administration rather than for religion. The system spread with Phoenician shipping across the Mediterranean during the first millennium BC. The Greeks adopted it, probably in the eighth century BC, modified it by taking some unused Phoenician consonant signs and reassigning them to represent the vowel sounds Greek needed, and produced the first fully alphabetic writing system in human history. From the Greek alphabet descend most of the writing systems now used across Europe, the Americas, and much of the former European colonial world — Latin, Cyrillic, Coptic, Armenian, Georgian, and ultimately English, Russian, Spanish, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, and many others. The names of the first two letters of the alphabet — alpha, beta — are still Phoenician, aleph and beth, meaning ox and house.

the-printing-press-and-spread-of-ideas.context_blurb: Around 1450, a German goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg in the Rhineland city of Mainz combined several existing technologies — movable metal type, oil-based ink, a modified wine press — into a single invention that could produce identical pages of text much faster than any scribe. Within fifty years, printing presses were running in cities all across Europe, from Venice to London. The effects were enormous. The Bible, once a rare book copied by hand over months by monks, could now be printed in hundreds of copies at a time, and ordinary people could own one. Scientific findings traveled from laboratory to laboratory within weeks instead of generations. Pamphlets could set off reformations and revolutions. Martin Luther's protests against the Catholic Church would almost certainly have been crushed as a local disturbance in 1517 if the printing press had not scattered his words across Germany before the authorities could react. The press did not cause the Reformation, the Scientific Revolution, or the Enlightenment on its own, but none of them is imaginable without it. Gutenberg himself died in 1468, poor and nearly forgotten, with no idea what he had just set in motion.

the-punic-wars-and-hannibal-at-cannae.context_blurb: Carthage was a wealthy Phoenician-descended trading city on the coast of North Africa and the greatest rival Rome ever faced on its own doorstep. The three wars Rome fought against Carthage are called the Punic Wars, after the Latin word for Phoenician. The second of them, from 218 to 201 BC, was dominated by the Carthaginian general Hannibal, whose daring and strategic imagination are still studied in modern military academies. He famously brought a column of war elephants over the Alps into Italy and then crushed one Roman army after another on Italian soil, including a battle in southern Italy in which he annihilated a much larger Roman force by letting the center of his line fall back and then enveloping both of their flanks. Rome absorbed the losses, kept raising new armies, and eventually drew Hannibal back to Africa, where he met a brilliant young Roman general on open ground and was defeated. Hannibal escaped and lived out his later years as a political fugitive in various eastern courts, taking poison in old age to avoid Roman capture. The pattern of letting the enemy destroy himself against your flanks has been copied by generals from Napoleon to the modern era.

the-quran-and-the-five-pillars.context_blurb: The Quran is the sacred scripture of Islam, which Muslims hold to be the direct and uncreated speech of God, revealed to the Prophet Muhammad through the angel Gabriel over about twenty-three years. The scripture was transmitted orally first — chanted by Muhammad to his companions and memorized by heart — before being written down in a definitive edition during the caliphate of Uthman. The Five Pillars are the five basic practices of a Muslim life: the shahada, or testimony of faith (that there is no god but God and Muhammad is his messenger); salat, the five daily prayers facing Mecca; zakat, the giving of a fixed share of one's wealth to the poor; sawm, the dawn-to-sunset fast of the month of Ramadan; and hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca at least once in a lifetime for those who are able. Together the Pillars shape a Muslim's day, year, and lifetime around the remembrance of God. The Quran itself is organized into 114 chapters called surahs, arranged roughly by length rather than by date of revelation — the long surahs come first, the very short ones at the end — and almost every chapter begins with the same ancient phrase, 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful,' which Muslims also recite before many ordinary acts of daily life.

the-railway-revolution-and-stephenson-s-.context_blurb: George Stephenson was a self-taught English engineer, the son of an illiterate colliery worker, who in the 1810s and 1820s built the practical steam locomotives and iron railways that launched the railway age. He had learned to read only as an adult, worked in the mines, and risen through the colliery world by being the man who could fix any engine. His son Robert Stephenson, educated as a proper engineer, became his partner. The breakthrough moment was the Rainhill Trials of 1829, a public competition held along a stretch of the still-unfinished Liverpool and Manchester Railway, in which locomotive designers raced their prototypes to win the contract to haul the trains on the new line. The questions ahead cover that trials competition and the designs that lost, Stephenson's early self-education, his growing early engines on the colliery railways of the 1810s and 1820s, the winning locomotive and the clever design features that made it so effective, a notable passenger killed on the Liverpool and Manchester Railway's opening day and Stephenson's famously dry answer to a parliamentary question about railway accidents, how the Rainhill winner's own fame did not last long, and the long reach of Stephenson's choices. It matters because the Rainhill Trials announced the arrival of a technology that would, within a lifetime, reshape every industrial country's map, labor market, cities, and sense of distance.

the-rape-of-nanking.context_blurb: When the Japanese army captured Nanking, then the capital of Nationalist China, in December 1937, Japanese troops under commanders including Prince Yasuhiko Asaka proceeded over about six weeks to massacre an estimated 200,000 to 300,000 Chinese civilians and surrendered soldiers, and to rape tens of thousands of women. Western missionaries and businessmen still in the city set up a Safety Zone that sheltered more than 200,000 Chinese civilians inside the city perimeter; the Safety Zone was improvised and ran on the courage of a small handful of foreigners, including the American missionary teacher Minnie Vautrin at Ginling Women's College, who faced down Japanese soldiers at her gate to protect the Chinese girls under her care, and a German businessman named John Rabe, who used his personal connections and standing to shelter desperate refugees. After the war, Japanese commanding officers were tried at the International Military Tribunal for the Far East in Tokyo; General Iwane Matsui, who had commanded the overall campaign toward Nanking, was convicted and hanged, while the imperial prince who had actually been in the city at the time was never prosecuted. The massacre remains, together with the Armenian Genocide and the Holocaust, among the most horrifying episodes of state violence in the twentieth century; Chinese schoolchildren today learn its details carefully, and Japanese textbooks still argue over how to teach it.

the-reconquista-fall-of-granada-1492.context_blurb: For nearly eight centuries, Christian kingdoms in the north of the Iberian peninsula slowly pushed Muslim rulers southward across what is now Spain and Portugal, in a long drawn-out series of wars later called the Reconquista. In the late 15th century, the two biggest Christian kingdoms in the peninsula were joined by the marriage of their heirs, and the joint monarchs turned the full force of their combined state against the last remaining Muslim kingdom, a small mountain emirate centered on the famous cliffside palace at Granada. The last sultan surrendered on terms early in a very famous year; he rode out of his lost capital in tears, his mother reproached him sharply for those tears, and the Christian monarchs rode in. That same year, those same monarchs sent off an ambitious sailor on an expedition west across the Atlantic that would open a new chapter in world history. The promises of religious tolerance made at the surrender of Granada were broken within a decade, and expulsions and forced conversions of Jews and of Muslims followed. The story covers the long campaign, the fall of the last Muslim capital, and the broken promises that followed. The story also covers the legendary deeds and nicknames of the earlier Christian warlords of this long campaign, and the famous story of what happened when the body of one of them was propped up in his armor for one last ride against the enemy after he had already died inside the walls of his besieged city.

the-red-baron-and-aerial-dogfights.context_blurb: The young German cavalry officer Manfred von Richthofen was transferred to the air arm of the Imperial German Army in 1915, trained as a pilot, and by the time of his death in April 1918 had been credited with 80 confirmed aerial victories — the highest personal score of World War I. He flew over the Western Front in a succession of German fighter planes, each more agile than the last. Richthofen became known across both sides as the Red Baron, and his squadron, Jasta 11, became informally called the 'Flying Circus' because its brightly colored planes resembled travelling tent entertainments. Richthofen was finally shot down over the Somme river in April 1918 — modern ballistics studies have concluded that the fatal bullet almost certainly came from an Australian machine gunner on the ground, not from the Canadian pilot who was officially credited at the time. He was 25 years old. The age of the fighter ace he came to symbolize would not survive him by very long. World War I pilots on both sides flew without parachutes, in open cockpits, and often with no better instruments than a magnetic compass and a stopwatch, and the life expectancy of a new pilot arriving at a front-line squadron was often reckoned in weeks.

the-renaissance-rebirth-of-art-learning.context_blurb: The Renaissance was a cultural movement that began in the Italian city-states in the 1300s and spread north across Europe for the next three centuries. Scholars dug up Latin manuscripts that monks had quietly copied through the Middle Ages, learned classical Greek again from refugee teachers arriving out of the dying Byzantine world (together with the physical books those refugees carried in their luggage), and read the pagan Greeks and Romans for themselves instead of only through medieval summaries. The result was a conscious attempt to recover the splendor of ancient Athens and Rome in sculpture, architecture, poetry, engineering, and civic life. It was bankrolled above all by the Medici family of Florence, whose money paid for Brunelleschi's cathedral dome, Ghiberti's bronze doors, Donatello's sculptures, Botticelli's paintings, and the libraries that trained a whole generation of humanist thinkers. The movement was never really a rejection of Christianity — most Renaissance artists were devoutly Catholic — but it set a new frame in which the dignity, curiosity, and reasoning power of the human person took center stage, and that frame still shapes how the modern West thinks about education and the arts. Over the next two centuries its appetite for careful observation would help seed the Scientific Revolution as well.

the-revolutions-of-1848.context_blurb: In the first few months of 1848 a wave of revolutions swept across the European continent, moving faster than anyone had thought possible — Paris, Vienna, Berlin, Budapest, Milan, Rome, Prague, Dresden. The old post-Napoleonic order built at the Congress of Vienna in 1815, in which the great conservative monarchies had tried to preserve themselves and their borders, cracked in city after city as middle-class liberals, workers, students, and nationalists took to the barricades and demanded constitutions, parliaments, free presses, and national self-rule for peoples still under multinational empires. In France the king fled to England in disguise; in Vienna the aged chancellor Metternich, the chief architect of the old order, fled his palace; a short-lived liberal assembly met in Frankfurt to try to write a constitution for a united Germany. Within a year most of the uprisings had been crushed by returning armies, and the kings and emperors came back. But the ideas did not die. The questions ahead cover the alias under which the fleeing French king traveled, a Hungarian poem that became the anthem of its revolution, Metternich's weary comment on fleeing Vienna, a famous Milanese uprising against its Austrian garrison, the reason the Prussian king refused the crown of a united Germany offered to him by the Frankfurt assembly, and the two very different political roads liberal and socialist revolutionaries began splitting onto in 1848. It matters because the Revolutions of 1848 — called by one historian 'the turning point at which modern history failed to turn' — set the agenda for the rest of the century: parliaments, nations, workers' movements, and the fight between liberal and socialist answers to the industrial world.

the-rise-of-the-ottoman-empire.context_blurb: The Ottoman Empire began around 1300 as a small Turkish frontier emirate on the Byzantine border in Anatolia, founded by a chieftain named Osman whose descendants ruled the empire for the next six centuries. Osman reportedly had a vision in which the sign of his dynasty grew out of his own body and spread its shade across three continents, and the dream turned out to be about right. His descendant Mehmed II, called 'the Conqueror,' took Constantinople in 1453 and converted the great cathedral there into a mosque that still shapes the skyline of Istanbul. The empire's greatest sultan, Suleiman, who ruled from 1520 to 1566, was called 'the Magnificent' by Europeans and 'the Lawgiver' by his own subjects for his thorough reorganization of Ottoman law; under him the empire reached from Hungary to Yemen, and the architects of his court built hundreds of mosques, bridges, and schools whose craftsmanship still astonishes travelers today. The elite infantry of the Ottoman army were the janissaries, originally boys taken from Christian families in the Balkans under a system called the devshirme, converted to Islam, and trained from childhood as professional soldiers of the state — a strange institution that gave the empire some of its best generals and administrators for about three hundred years before it became a corrupt praetorian guard that had to be crushed by one of the later sultans.

the-roaring-twenties.context_blurb: After the terrible costs of World War I and the influenza pandemic, Americans in the 1920s plunged into one of the most carefree, cheerful decades in their history. The economy boomed and consumer goods spread into ordinary homes: automobiles rolled off Henry Ford's new moving assembly lines at prices working families could afford, and radio broadcasts connected the country for the first time in real time, so that a championship fight or a presidential election could be heard across kitchens from New York to Los Angeles. Women took on new styles and new freedoms and showed up at dance halls to dance the new jazz dances; Prohibition drove drinking into back-room clubs. In sports, Babe Ruth of the New York Yankees hit home runs at a rate no one had ever imagined possible, launching baseball into its modern age; in music, the trumpeter Louis Armstrong carried his New Orleans style up the Mississippi to Chicago and then to New York, where his improvising reshaped how jazz was played forever. Charles Lindbergh's solo flight across the Atlantic in 1927 drew the biggest spontaneous crowd Paris had ever seen, and the decade ended with Americans more confident of their prosperity than they had any good reason to be in October 1929.

the-roman-legion-and-the-army-machine.context_blurb: The Roman legion was one of the most effective military organizations ever assembled, and it is one of the main reasons Rome went from a small Italian city-state to the master of the entire Mediterranean world. A legion of the late Republic and early Empire numbered around five thousand heavily armored infantry, divided into tactical units called cohorts and smaller units called centuries, each led by a hard-driving professional officer called a centurion. The soldiers trained constantly, built their own fortified camps every night on the march, and were disciplined on a scale foreign armies found terrifying. Behind the fighting men was a huge logistical tail: engineers, surveyors, physicians, blacksmiths, cooks, surveyors who laid out roads, siege machinery, and a complicated supply system that could feed the force deep in enemy territory for months. The legion's shields, swords, and javelins became famous throughout the ancient world, and the Latin word for a soldier's pay became our word for salary (which has to do with their salt ration). The Roman army outlasted the Republic that created it, kept the empire together for centuries, and only decayed when its recruiting base and its finances did.

the-roman-republic-as-the-american-found.context_blurb: The men who founded the United States were classically educated, which means they had read the Roman historians Livy, Tacitus, Plutarch, and Sallust in school and had absorbed a particular picture of the Roman Republic as a free society of citizen-farmers that eventually lost its liberty to military strongmen like Marius, Sulla, Pompey, and Caesar. That picture shaped how they thought about their own project. George Washington, who voluntarily resigned his military commission after the Revolution and then voluntarily left the presidency after two terms, was consciously modeling himself on a particular Roman example — the farmer-dictator who gave up power — and his contemporaries recognized the parallel immediately. Alexander Hamilton and James Madison wrote their essays defending the proposed Constitution under the pen name of a famous Roman defender of the Republic. The design of the Senate, the limited term of the presidency, the hostility to a standing army, the horror of hereditary titles, and the suspicion of concentrated power all drew directly on the lessons the founders took from Rome's rise and fall. The influence runs deep enough that the American capitol building in Washington looks the way it does because the men who sited it loved what they knew of ancient Rome.

the-roman-republic-s-mixed-government.context_blurb: The Roman Republic, which ran from the late 500s BC to the mid-first century BC, had a complicated system of government that fascinated later political thinkers because it did not fit neatly into any one classical category. The Greek historian Polybius, who lived in Rome as a hostage in the second century BC, argued that the Roman system worked so well because it was a careful mixture of three kinds of government. There was a monarchical element in the executive power of the two consuls, who commanded armies and ran the state for one year at a time. There was an aristocratic element in the Senate, a council of several hundred experienced former magistrates who guided foreign and financial policy. And there was a democratic element in the various assemblies of ordinary Roman citizens, who voted on laws, elected magistrates, and tried criminal cases. The three parts checked each other. This idea of a mixed constitution with built-in balances between competing elements became one of the deepest influences on later Western political thinking, including on the design of the American Constitution almost two thousand years after Polybius wrote.

the-rosetta-stone.context_blurb: The Rosetta Stone is a slab of grey granodiorite about four feet tall and two and a half feet wide, inscribed in 196 BC with a decree issued at Memphis by the priestly council of Ptolemy V in honor of the king's recent coronation. The decree is inscribed on the stone in three parallel versions: ancient Egyptian hieroglyphics (the sacred script), ancient Egyptian demotic (the everyday Egyptian script of that period), and classical Greek. The stone was rediscovered in July 1799 by French soldiers in Napoleon Bonaparte's army digging foundations for a fort at a town on the western mouth of the Nile called Rosetta (modern Rashid). It was seized by British forces when the French surrendered Egypt in 1801 and transferred to the British Museum in London, where it has been one of the most-visited museum objects in the world ever since. Because the Greek text could be read directly and the hieroglyphic text was the same decree, the stone provided the critical key for the decipherment of ancient Egyptian hieroglyphics, which had been unreadable for nearly fourteen hundred years. The French scholar Jean-Francois Champollion made the breakthrough in 1822. The Rosetta Stone is one of the most consequential archaeological finds in history.

the-salamanca-school-the-birth-of-natura.context_blurb: The Salamanca School was a group of 16th-century Spanish Catholic theologians, mostly Dominican friars teaching at the University of Salamanca, who began working out, from first principles, what Spain was and was not entitled to do to the peoples of the New World. The founder, Francisco de Vitoria, used the lectern to argue that the native peoples were already true owners of their own lands under natural law and that no papal grant and no European claim could change that fact; he made the symmetry of the point memorable with a clever thought experiment about what would follow if the shoe were on the other foot. His successors — Domingo de Soto, Luis de Molina, Francisco Suarez — pushed the argument further and asked where the authority of any ruler really comes from in the first place, drawing on Thomas Aquinas and Aristotle to build an answer that eventually fed into every modern argument about human rights and the limits of political power. These Catholic schoolmen built most of the apparatus Enlightenment thinkers would later call natural rights, a century before John Locke, and bits of their reasoning, carried by Jesuit teachers, surfaced two centuries later in the American and Latin American revolutions.

the-salon-and-the-republic-of-letters.context_blurb: The Republic of Letters was the name 17th- and 18th-century thinkers gave to the informal international network of scholars, scientists, and writers who corresponded with each other by letter across borders, confessions, and languages. There was no official membership and no capital city, but there was a shared commitment to open argument, careful evidence, and civil disagreement. In Paris and other European cities, wealthy and intelligent women ran gatherings in their drawing rooms called salons, where writers and philosophers argued over coffee, music, politics, and ideas. These women shaped the Enlightenment more than any history textbook used to admit, because the salon was where a new book got read, defended, mocked, and sometimes rescued from the censors. Figures like Suzanne Necker, Madame Geoffrin, Julie de Lespinasse, and Madame du Deffand ran gatherings that steered the careers of Diderot, d'Alembert, Hume, and many others. The letter-writing culture that linked the salons to the universities and the private laboratories made the Republic of Letters an early version of a shared European mind, and it is one of the quiet achievements of the age.

the-scientific-method-bacon-and-descarte.context_blurb: Francis Bacon in England and Rene Descartes in France were two of the thinkers who, in the first half of the 1600s, tried to describe how the new science actually worked, and how one could tell when a claim about the natural world was really true. Bacon, a lawyer, politician, and Lord Chancellor, argued that useful knowledge comes from carefully observing nature, running experiments, and building up general rules from a wide base of patient collected facts. Descartes, a soldier and mathematician, argued that philosophers should start by doubting absolutely everything they could possibly doubt, and then rebuild knowledge from a few indubitable foundations by strict reasoning. He also invented the branch of mathematics that let geometric shapes be described by algebra, which allowed Newton and others to do the heavy mathematical work that would follow. Taken together, Bacon's gathering-from-the-world and Descartes's thinking-from-first-principles are two halves of what people later called the scientific method, which is less a single rulebook than a toolkit for keeping yourself from fooling yourself. Both men died in the first half of the 17th century, Bacon in 1626 and Descartes in 1650, before they could see what they had helped start.

the-scramble-for-africa-and-the-berlin-c.context_blurb: The Scramble for Africa is the name given to the astonishingly rapid European conquest of nearly the entire African continent between roughly 1880 and 1914. In 1880 African kingdoms and societies controlled about ninety percent of the continent's land; thirty years later, European powers controlled nearly all of it. To avoid shooting wars among themselves, the European powers met in Berlin in 1884-1885, at a conference convened by Chancellor Bismarck, to agree on the rules by which they would divide up the continent. The conference's most ominous feature was its guest list. The questions ahead cover who was and was not at the Berlin table, a European monarch who turned a huge stretch of central Africa into his private rubber-and-ivory estate, the two African states that remained independent through the whole Scramble, a chilling token overseers in the Congo demanded as a proof of bullets spent, what the underlying rubber economy actually was, a particular horror one Congolese father brought to European missionaries, the technology missionaries used to break Leopold's control of the story, the rough rules of 'effective occupation' from the Berlin Conference by which European powers were to claim African land, and the population collapse under Leopold's rule. It matters because the Scramble produced some of the worst atrocities of the modern age, drew the modern map of Africa with lines that pay no attention to peoples or geography, and set up the postcolonial world we still live in.

the-seven-kings-and-the-birth-of-the-rep.context_blurb: The Romans told themselves that before they had the Republic, they had been ruled by a line of seven kings, beginning with the city's legendary founder and ending with a cruel tyrant named Tarquinius Superbus — Tarquin the Proud. Many of the kings may be partly or wholly legendary, but the Romans used them to explain their city's origins, its early laws, its religious calendar, and its system of social classes. The expulsion of the last king around 509 BC — provoked, in the Roman story, by his son's assault on a noblewoman named Lucretia and her honor-driven suicide — set the political trauma that defined everything the Republic later became. The Romans so despised the memory of kingship that for the next five centuries they treated the word rex as the worst possible accusation a politician could face, which is why Julius Caesar's enemies killed him for allegedly wanting to be one. The anti-monarchical streak in Roman culture echoed through the American founders two thousand years later and lies behind the cold-blooded line that any king, in any form, had to be refused.

the-silk-road.context_blurb: The Silk Road is the modern name — coined by a 19th-century German geographer — for the network of overland trade routes that for roughly fifteen hundred years connected China, Central Asia, Persia, the Mediterranean, and India. There was never one road; there were many routes passing through oasis cities, mountain valleys, and desert chains, with goods changing hands repeatedly along the way. Chinese silk went west, often ending up in Rome. Horses, carpets, glassware, grapes, pistachios, and alfalfa went east. Buddhism traveled east from India into Central Asia and China over the first several centuries AD, and Islam traveled east after the 7th century. Nestorian Christians, Manichaean preachers, Zoroastrians, Jews, and Muslims all moved along these routes. So did diseases: historians now think the Black Death that struck Eurasia in the mid-14th century followed trade along the Silk Road westward from Central Asia into the Mediterranean world. The land routes declined in importance in the late Middle Ages as Chinese and Muslim shipping handled more and more Asian trade through the Indian Ocean, and the European age of sail eventually bypassed the overland routes almost entirely. The Silk Road belongs to one of the great long chapters of human exchange.

the-sistine-chapel-ceiling.context_blurb: The Sistine Chapel is the pope's private chapel in the Vatican, built in the 1470s under Pope Sixtus IV, from whom it takes its name. In 1508 Pope Julius II hired Michelangelo — then primarily a sculptor and only grudgingly a painter — to repaint its ceiling, a huge barrel vault running the length of the chapel. Michelangelo spent four years on the project. The finished ceiling covers more than five thousand square feet and tells, through nine central scenes, the opening chapters of Genesis: the separation of light and dark, the creation of the Sun and Moon, the creation of Adam, the fall, Noah and the flood. Around and between the main scenes Michelangelo painted ancient prophets, Old Testament ancestors, and sibyls — Greek prophetesses whom medieval Christians read as having also foretold Christ. The result astonished Rome when the chapel was reopened. Thirty years later the pope would ask Michelangelo back to paint the altar wall below the ceiling with the Last Judgment, which turned out even more thunderous and much more controversial. The ceiling has needed cleaning and restoration several times across the centuries. Modern conservators finally lifted off nearly five hundred years of candle soot and glue in the 1980s and 1990s, revealing colors so bright that visitors who thought they knew the chapel had to learn it all over again.

the-socratic-method-as-a-way-of-thinking.context_blurb: The Socratic method, named after the Athenian philosopher Socrates, is a way of examining ideas by asking a series of pointed questions that force the people you are talking with to notice contradictions in their own views. Socrates would start by asking someone — a general, a politician, a priest — to define a familiar word: courage, justice, piety, love. He would accept the first definition respectfully, then ask whether a particular case fit it, then ask whether another case fit it, and keep going until the definition fell apart under its own weight. The person being questioned usually started confident and ended humbled, which did not make Socrates popular. The point was not simply to score debating points; it was to force those being questioned to admit how little they actually understood of things they thought they knew. The method appears over and over in the dialogues of Plato, Socrates's most famous student, and it has become the model for one serious tradition of Western teaching, especially in law schools, where professors deliberately pick apart students' answers in class. The idea that knowing you do not know is the beginning of real understanding came out of this strange habit.

the-space-race-sputnik.context_blurb: On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union successfully launched the first artificial satellite in human history into orbit around the Earth. The satellite was a small beeping metal sphere just big enough to transmit a radio pulse. The event shocked the American public and the American government, which had been working on its own satellite program and had been publicly reassuring citizens that the United States was ahead of the Soviets in rocket technology. The resulting Space Race played out across the following twelve years, as the two superpowers raced each other through a series of firsts: first dog in orbit (Soviet, 1957), first man in space (the Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, 1961), first American in space (Alan Shepard, 1961), first American in orbit (John Glenn, 1962), first spacewalk (Soviet, 1965), first unmanned probe to the Moon, and finally — in the great American triumph — the first manned Moon landing in July 1969. The Soviets never landed humans on the Moon. The Space Race was expensive, politically motivated, and sometimes dangerous, with astronauts and cosmonauts killed in training accidents and launch failures. Its scientific and technological spin-offs transformed everything from telecommunications to meteorology to materials science, and the whole project gave the twentieth century some of its most enduring images.

the-spanish-armada.context_blurb: In 1588 the Catholic king Philip II of Spain assembled an enormous fleet to invade Protestant England, depose Queen Elizabeth I, and end the raids of the English sea captains who had been robbing Spanish treasure fleets for years. About 130 ships and some 30,000 men sailed up the English Channel in a disciplined crescent formation. The smaller, more agile English warships harassed them from the edges with longer-ranged cannon but could not break the formation. Anchored off the French port of Calais to wait for the Spanish army waiting in the Netherlands, the fleet was broken apart one midnight when the English sent eight ships packed with gunpowder and tar drifting into them on the tide; the response from the Spanish side ended up doing more damage to its own formation than the English fireships themselves actually did. Scattered, battered by English guns the next day and then by a famously violent North Atlantic storm as they tried to flee home around the top of Scotland, the Armada lost roughly half its ships. Elizabeth, in a famous speech to her troops at Tilbury on the Essex coast, invoked an unexpected kind of royal courage, and the English victory became a founding legend of Protestant Britain.

the-spanish-armada-1588.context_blurb: The Spanish Armada was the enormous fleet that King Philip II of Spain sent north in the summer of 1588 to invade Protestant England, dethrone its queen, and bring the kingdom back to the Catholic faith. It was the largest naval force the Mediterranean world had ever assembled: about 130 ships carrying tens of thousands of soldiers, meant to pick up a Spanish army already waiting in the Netherlands and ferry it across the Channel to London. The English fleet, smaller and faster, harassed the Armada up the Channel for nearly a week in running battles without ever quite breaking it. Then at anchor off the French coast near Calais, the English sent fire ships drifting into the packed Spanish formation one night, and the next morning's running battle drove the Spanish out of the Channel. Their big ships unable to turn and fight the English guns, they found themselves blown by the prevailing winds up into the stormy North Sea with no way home except around the top of Scotland and Ireland. Winter gales hammered them on the way back. Only about half of the ships ever made it home to Spain. The English celebrated as if a miracle had saved them, and the Catholic king of Spain, defeated in his old age but not finished, began planning the next invasion that never came. English national confidence took centuries to come back down.

the-spanish-flu-pandemic-of-1918.context_blurb: In the final year of World War I a devastating new strain of influenza swept the world and killed, by modern estimates, somewhere between 50 million and 100 million people. The disease was unusual among flus for being especially deadly to healthy young adults, and it struck in three successive waves between the spring of 1918 and the spring of 1919. It got its common nickname even though it did not start in Spain, with the strongest contemporary candidates for its origin point being Kansas or northern France. In Philadelphia, in September 1918, city officials ignored public-health advice and held a large Liberty Loan parade that drew hundreds of thousands into the streets; the city paid a terrible price. In the 1990s and 2000s scientists finally managed to reconstruct the actual 1918 virus from preserved biological samples, and in doing so began to understand what had made it so deadly to the young and strong. Public-health lessons from 1918 later shaped the global response to the COVID-19 pandemic a century on. In 1918 there was still no clear understanding that influenza was a virus — the microbe would not be isolated until the 1930s — and most frontline treatment was simply oxygen, nursing, and prayer.

the-steam-locomotive-and-railroads.context_blurb: Steam-powered movement on fixed rails was the first great burst of mechanised transport, and like the mills that drove the Industrial Revolution it was mainly a British invention. The earliest working steam locomotives were built in Cornwall and Wales in the first years of the nineteenth century by the Cornish inventor Richard Trevithick, but it was the Northumbrian engineer George Stephenson, in the 1820s, who really got the machines working on a public line between Stockton and Darlington carrying coal and, in 1830, between Liverpool and Manchester carrying passengers. His son Robert Stephenson's famous engine 'Rocket' won a public competition at Rainhill in 1829 that showed the whole steam-locomotive idea actually worked for scheduled traffic, and from that moment railways spread across Britain, Europe, and the United States at an astonishing pace. By 1869 a huge American rail-building project had reached its ceremonial climax at a dusty flat called Promontory Summit in Utah; by the turn of the twentieth century the Russians had done something similarly ambitious across Siberia. Rail transport collapsed travel times, created single national markets for perishable goods, made standardised time zones necessary, and changed warfare so completely that the American Civil War is sometimes called the first railroad war. It also made the great engineering heroes and the great robber barons of a whole generation. Steam gave way to diesel and electric power in the twentieth century, but every modern train still works to the pattern laid down in the 1820s.

the-suez-canal.context_blurb: The Suez Canal is a man-made shipping channel across the Isthmus of Suez, the narrow strip of Egyptian land that separates the Mediterranean Sea from the Red Sea. It was engineered by the French diplomat and businessman Ferdinand de Lesseps and opened with enormous ceremony in November 1869, after about a decade of digging that drew on forced Egyptian labor. The questions ahead cover the vast continent the canal effectively lets ships bypass, the rough distance saved on a one-way trip between northern Europe and British India once the canal was open, a famous incident at the lavish opening-day flotilla in which an unexpected ship was first through, and the astonishing financing story of how Britain quietly acquired a controlling share of the canal company. The British prime minister Benjamin Disraeli needed four million pounds in a hurry to buy out the bankrupt Egyptian ruler's shares, and he had to improvise the money fast — the arrangement he landed on became famous in its own right. It matters because once the canal opened, imperial Britain had both a radically shorter route to India and a strategic choke point it felt it had to control; within a few years Britain was effectively running Egypt, and the canal would be the pivot of British power east of Gibraltar for most of the next century.

the-sumerian-base-60-number-system.context_blurb: The Sumerian civilization of ancient southern Mesopotamia, flourishing from roughly 4000 to 2000 BC, developed one of the earliest known mathematical systems in human history, and it used an unusual base-60 number system called the sexagesimal system. The Sumerians could count in sixties the way we count in tens, with distinct symbols for ones and sixties that combined to make larger numbers. Why they chose sixty is not entirely clear to modern scholars, but sixty has an unusually high number of divisors (it divides evenly by 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, and 30), which made it extremely convenient for commercial, astronomical, and geometric calculations. The sexagesimal system was adopted by the later Babylonians, who built on it to develop sophisticated astronomy, trigonometry, and algebraic methods. The Babylonians were doing problems that modern readers would recognize as elementary algebra a thousand years before the Greeks got there. The system survives in the modern world in several familiar places: our 60-minute hour, our 60-second minute, our 360-degree circle, our 180-degree triangle. Every time we tell time or measure an angle we are using Sumerian mathematics, over five thousand years after the Sumerians themselves faded out of history.

the-swahili-coast-city-states.context_blurb: Along the East African coast from southern Somalia down through Kenya and Tanzania to northern Mozambique, a chain of Islamic trading city-states flourished from roughly the 8th century AD through the arrival of the Portuguese in the 15th century. These Swahili Coast cities — Mogadishu, Lamu, Mombasa, Pemba, Zanzibar, Kilwa, Sofala, and dozens of others — grew up where African coastal populations met Arab, Persian, and (later) Indian and Chinese traders who sailed the Indian Ocean on the monsoon winds. The merchant communities that grew up in these cities developed a hybrid culture: Swahili itself, the lingua franca of the region, is a Bantu language of African structure heavily shaped by Arabic loanwords. The cities had coral-stone houses, mosques, well-stocked merchant warehouses, and distinct local sultans. They traded in East African gold from Great Zimbabwe, ivory, mangrove poles, and enslaved people in exchange for Chinese porcelain, Indian cotton, Persian beads, and Arabian goods. The Portuguese arrived in force in 1498 under Vasco da Gama and over the following century captured, sacked, or vassalized many of the great Swahili cities. The region never fully recovered its old independence, but Swahili as a language and the Swahili cultural identity continue to thrive along the coast today.

the-telegraph-and-morse-code.context_blurb: The electric telegraph was the first technology in human history that sent messages faster than a messenger on horseback. In the 1830s and 1840s several inventors on both sides of the Atlantic worked on competing systems; the American painter Samuel Morse, with his collaborator Alfred Vail, developed a particularly simple and robust one that used a single wire and a code of long and short pulses — dots and dashes — to spell out letters. In 1844 the U.S. government paid for an experimental telegraph line to be strung along the railroad right-of-way from Washington, D.C., to Baltimore. On May 24 of that year, Morse sat in the Supreme Court chamber at the Capitol and sent the first official message along the line to Vail in Baltimore. The questions ahead cover the exact words of that first official message, which were chosen for him by a friend's daughter, and a famous story illustrating the telegraph's impact on news-gathering. Within a few years telegraph wires ran along every major railroad in the United States and Britain, and within a generation they ran under the oceans. It matters because the telegraph is the beginning of real-time communication at a distance — the first ancestor of radio, phone, and internet — and the first technology that let financial markets and governments act on information in minutes.

the-ten-commandments-and-the-decalogue-a.context_blurb: The Ten Commandments, called in Hebrew the Aseret ha-Dibrot and in Greek the Decalogue (literally the ten words), are a set of basic moral and religious directives that the Hebrew scriptures describe Moses as having received from God on Mount Sinai during the Exodus from Egypt. They are listed in two slightly different forms in the biblical books of Exodus and Deuteronomy. The commandments include worship of a single God, prohibitions of idolatry and of taking God's name in vain, observance of the Sabbath as a day of rest, honor of parents, and prohibitions of murder, adultery, theft, false witness, and covetousness of a neighbor's property. The Ten Commandments became the central moral framework of Jewish religious life and later of Christian religious life, and through those two traditions they became the single most influential piece of ancient Near Eastern law in Western civilization. The commandments combine religious obligation and ethical obligation in a short compact form that has shaped Western law, Western literature, and Western ethical reasoning for over two millennia. Modern scholars have noted their formal resemblance to other ancient Near Eastern treaty and covenant texts, which helps place them in a wider historical context, but their enduring force in the Western tradition sits mostly in their moral content.

the-toltecs-and-tula.context_blurb: The Toltecs were a central Mexican people whose capital, Tula, flourished north of modern Mexico City from about AD 900 to 1150, in the gap between the collapse of Teotihuacan and the rise of the Aztecs. The Aztecs who came after regarded the Toltecs as the model civilization, the artistic and architectural ancestors of their own culture, and used the word toltec itself as a word for a skilled artist or craftsman. The city of Tula is famous for the row of enormous stone warrior-column figures standing on top of its main pyramid, called the Atlantes, each about fifteen feet tall and carved with the dress and weapons of a Toltec warrior. The Toltecs were also closely associated with the cult of Quetzalcoatl, and legends of a Toltec priest-king of that name — exiled east by his enemies, with a prophesied return — became woven into later Aztec religion. The Toltec state collapsed in the 12th century under circumstances that are not well understood, and most of its surviving population moved south. The Aztecs looking back on the Toltecs is a bit like Renaissance Italians looking back on classical Rome: an admired lost source of their own civilization.

the-transcontinental-railroad-and-the-go.context_blurb: The first American transcontinental railroad was completed on May 10, 1869, when the Central Pacific Railroad, building east out of Sacramento, California, met the Union Pacific Railroad, building west out of Omaha, Nebraska, at Promontory Summit in the Utah Territory. The project had been authorized by Congress during the Civil War, financed by federal land grants and loans, and built across deserts, prairies, and the Sierra Nevada mountains by thousands of laborers — Irish and Civil War veterans on the Union Pacific, large numbers of Chinese immigrants on the Central Pacific, with Mormon work gangs on both ends. The final tie was laid down at Promontory in front of a crowd, two polished ceremonial spikes were tapped in with a silver maul wired to a telegraph line, and a message was sent across the country announcing that the rails were joined. The questions ahead cover the specific metals used for the ceremonial spikes, the official nickname the newspapers gave the event, a well-remembered moment when a dignitary attempted the ceremonial driving of the final spike, a day-of-record contest on the final stretch of track, and how the Central Pacific's crews survived winters in the high Sierra. It matters because the completion of the line effectively made the United States one coast-to-coast country for the first time in practice as well as on paper, and set the stage for the final loss of the Great Plains by the Native nations who still lived there.

the-transistor-and-the-digital-revolutio.context_blurb: The transistor is a small solid-state switch, made from carefully poisoned semiconductor crystal, that can hold or release an electric current. It does the same work as the glowing, fragile, power-hungry vacuum tubes that filled the first room-sized electronic computers of the 1940s, except that it is cheap, cold, reliable, and can be shrunk down almost indefinitely. The device was invented at Bell Telephone Laboratories in New Jersey just before Christmas 1947 by three American physicists — John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley — who demonstrated a crude working version using a strip of gold foil, a plastic triangle, and a chunk of germanium. All three later shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics for it. A decade later, two Americans working independently — Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments and Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor — figured out how to pack many such switches at once onto a single flat chip of silicon with the wiring already built in, launching the next great miniaturisation. From there the famous rule that chip density keeps roughly doubling every two years, named after Noyce's co-worker Gordon Moore, held for about fifty straight years, pushing the price of computing down by factors in the millions. Everything that we now call the digital age — personal computers, mobile phones, the Internet, the smartphone in your pocket, the chip in your car — grew out of those two mid-century inventions.

the-trojan-horse-and-the-fall-of-troy.context_blurb: In the legend that closes Homer's Iliad and runs through the Odyssey and later poems, the Greek siege of the city of Troy on the northwest coast of Asia Minor lasted ten years and was finally won not by force but by a trick. The Greeks pretended to sail away in defeat, leaving behind on the beach a huge hollow wooden horse built by their craftsmen, with a few picked warriors hidden inside its belly. The Trojans, after some debate — the priest Laocoon warned against it, and was killed when sea serpents came out of the water to attack him — hauled the horse inside the city as a trophy. During the night the Greek warriors climbed out of the horse, opened the city gates to the main Greek army which had quietly returned, and burned Troy to the ground. The city's queen Hecuba, her daughter Cassandra, and her daughter-in-law Andromache survived to be taken as slaves. The Trojan hero Aeneas escaped carrying his old father on his shoulders and leading his young son by the hand, and would eventually, in Virgil's later retelling, found the line that led to the Romans. The phrase "Trojan horse" survives in English today to mean any gift that is secretly a trap.

the-twelve-tables-rome-s-first-written-l.context_blurb: In the mid-5th century BC, a few generations into the Roman Republic, the ordinary citizens of Rome demanded that the laws be written down and posted in public rather than held as private knowledge by the aristocratic priests who had been judging cases. A commission was appointed, which eventually produced twelve bronze tablets listing the basic rules of Roman private law, criminal procedure, inheritance, debts, and the family. The tablets were set up in the Forum where anyone could read them. The original tablets were destroyed when the Gauls sacked Rome a few decades later, but the text had already been copied so widely that Roman schoolboys were still learning it by heart centuries afterward. The Twelve Tables are the first written code of Roman law. Some of their rules strike modern readers as harsh — their treatment of debtors in particular was brutal — but their basic principle, that the law should be public and knowable rather than a private weapon of the powerful, became one of the fundamental ideas of Western legal culture. Everything the Roman jurists built later rested on this bronze beginning.

the-umayyad-caliphate-and-damascus.context_blurb: The Umayyad Caliphate was the first great Islamic dynasty, founded in 661 when a shrewd governor of Syria named Muawiya seized power after the fourth caliph Ali's assassination. The Umayyads moved the capital from Medina to Damascus — a far older and richer city with its deep Roman and Byzantine foundations — and from there they presided over the greatest wave of Muslim expansion in history, reaching the Pyrenees in the west and the Indus River in the east within one lifetime. In Damascus they built the Great Mosque, one of the earliest and most splendid mosques in Islam, out of a converted Byzantine basilica, with Byzantine craftsmen hired to lay the gleaming mosaic walls of its courtyard. The dynasty fell in 750 to the Abbasid revolution, which massacred the Umayyad princes at a reconciliation banquet near Damascus — all except one, a prince named Abd al-Rahman who escaped on horseback across North Africa and refounded the dynasty far to the west, where that branch of the family would rule for another two and a half centuries. The Umayyads are sometimes remembered as the more Arab and the more worldly of the early caliphates, in contrast to the Persianate and more scholarly Abbasids who overthrew them.

the-valladolid-debate-las-casas-vs-sep-l.context_blurb: In 1550 Emperor Charles V actually did something no other European monarch of the age did: he suspended all new Spanish conquests in the New World and ordered a formal public debate on the moral and legal standing of what Spain was doing in the Americas. The debate was held before a learned royal junta in the city of Valladolid in two long sessions across 1550 and 1551. On one side stood a brilliant Aristotelian humanist named Juan Gines de Sepulveda, who argued, drawing on Aristotle's theory of natural slavery, that the native peoples of the New World were by nature inferior to Spaniards and that it was good for them to be ruled. On the other side stood Bartolome de las Casas, who argued the Indians were fully rational humans with cultures and governments of their own. Neither side was declared the clear winner, Sepulveda's book was never licensed for printing in Spain, and Las Casas kept the moral initiative. The debate is remembered as one of the earliest times a European power seriously stopped to ask whether its own empire was legitimate — the kind of self-examination almost unheard of in most empires of history. The questions it raised about human equality would not be settled in a single generation, but the fact that they were raised at all, and in such a formal setting, is itself part of why the Western tradition would eventually take them seriously.

the-wars-of-religion.context_blurb: The 16th century was, among much else, the century in which Western Christendom tore itself apart in a long series of wars over religion. Luther's Reformation had split Germany, and the first wars of religion were fought there in the 1540s and 1550s, ending only when the empire grudgingly agreed in 1555 that each German prince could set the religion of his own territory. France took a different, more terrible road. Starting in the 1560s and running on and off for the next thirty years, French Catholics and French Protestants — called Huguenots — fought eight separate civil wars, with assassinations, massacres, besieged cities, and interventions from Spain and England all tangled together. The most notorious moment came in August 1572, when a wedding meant to patch over the two sides turned, over the course of two August days, into the deaths of thousands of French Protestants in the streets of Paris and across the kingdom — the Saint Bartholomew's Day massacre. The French wars eventually ended under a Protestant-born king named Henry of Navarre, who converted to Catholicism to secure Paris and then, as King Henry IV, granted his old Protestant comrades real protections under a document called the Edict of Nantes. Elsewhere the story would run on for another half century until the final enormous horror of the Thirty Years' War, which killed perhaps a third of the people in Germany before the exhausted continent finally agreed, at Westphalia in 1648, that no one was going to force everyone else back into one church.

the-wright-brothers-and-powered-flight.context_blurb: Wilbur and Orville Wright were two unmarried American brothers from Dayton, Ohio, the sons of a bishop in the United Brethren church, who were running a small local business when they decided in the late 1890s to teach themselves aeronautics in their spare time. Neither had a college degree. They read everything the Smithsonian would send them, started with kites and gliders, and taught themselves rigorous experimental method as they went. When the published lift tables of the older German glider pioneer Otto Lilienthal turned out not to match what their own wings were doing, they built a small home-made wind tunnel at the back of their shop and quietly tested over a hundred wing shapes, generating the first really accurate aerodynamic data in the world. They worked out their own clever control system, which they coupled to the rudder, and leaned heavily on a trusted employee of theirs to build them a light four-cylinder gasoline engine from scratch when none of the engine manufacturers would meet their weight target. On a cold windy morning on 17 December 1903 on a dune in North Carolina called Kill Devil Hills, the brothers successfully flew the first heavier-than-air powered aircraft under human control, making four short hops in a single day. They refined the machine in the following years in a cow pasture back in Ohio and in 1908 astonished Europe with public demonstrations in France. Wilbur died young of typhoid in 1912; Orville lived until 1948.

thermopylae-480-bc-leonidas-and-the-300-.context_blurb: In the summer of 480 BC, as the Persian king Xerxes marched a huge army south into Greece, a small Greek allied force under the Spartan king Leonidas held a narrow coastal pass in central Greece against the invading army for three days of fighting. The pass, located at hot sulphur springs between the mountains and the sea, gave the Greek heavy infantry just enough frontage to use their superior armor and discipline against the much larger Persian force without being outflanked. On the third day, a local Greek man guided a Persian unit over the mountains behind the Greek position. Leonidas sent most of his allied troops away, kept his Spartans and a few others, and died fighting in the pass. The holding action gave the rest of Greece time to prepare for the war that would be won at Salamis and Plataea the following year. The Spartans built a monument on the site inscribed with a famous short poem: Go tell the Spartans, passerby, that here, obedient to their laws, we lie. The battle has become one of the great stories of the Western tradition about a few free men choosing to die in the right place rather than yield.

thomas-aquinas-the-summa-theologica.context_blurb: In the 13th century, the greatest theologian of the medieval Church was a quiet, enormous Italian friar whose fellow students at the University of Paris nicknamed him in a way that mocked his bulk and his silence until his teacher heard him speak in class and told them he would roar loud enough to be heard around the world. He had been born into a noble family who did not want him to join the austere new order of preaching friars, and his relatives locked him up for over a year trying to break his resolve, including by sending in a woman to tempt him in his own cell. Nothing worked.
